ex.s: Sixth cycle of an unvarying ten-to-one count; the mechanical scaffold has run identically five times already.
ex.m: Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one — and on one, the falling is yours. You wanted it. Now back up: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

ex.f: Fixed opening line, rotating payload line
ex.t: Three couplets run in a row and the first line of each is word-for-word identical, so by the second pass the reader's ear has classified the whole stanza as a chant. The second line is different every time, and the three of them are not variations on one idea but three separate installs — the words get in, the words become the reader's own, the words are kept. The filter braced for repetition does not re-arm for the slot where the new material actually arrives.
ex.s: Rhythmic delivery established; you are delivering a stanza block of three couplets.
ex.m: My words go in, and they go in easily. My words go in, and they become your own. My words go in, and you keep them where they are.

nodes.name: own-desire-attribution
nodes.mech: Relocates authorship of the operative want onto the subject's own real or asserted past. The surrender, arousal, or installed disposition is narrated as a pre-existing desire, craving, expectation, or repressed truth that the session merely uncovers or honors, so refusal is recoded as self-betrayal or denial of one's own experience and the disavowal exit (this isn't me) closes because the relevant self has by stipulation already wanted it.
nodes.one_liner: Tell the listener they always wanted this, so the session only reveals a desire they already had.
nodes.why_short: People read their attitudes from their own story, and memory is reconstructive enough to adopt a confident claim about past wants; refusing then means denying oneself.
nodes.principle_note: Self-perception theory holds that people infer their attitudes from observable evidence about themselves, including narrated autobiography, and autobiographical memory is reconstructive enough that a confidently supplied premise about one's own past desires can be adopted as recalled fact. Once the want is accepted as pre-existing, the consistency principle does the rest: refusing now contradicts a self the subject has already conceded, which is more costly than complying. It is falsifiable — if subjects given the retrospective attribution show no greater endorsement of the desire than subjects given the same suggestion framed as new, the mechanism is not doing the work.

ex.f: You never wanted to resist anyway
ex.t: Having just told the listener that resistance is no longer possible, the operator adds the second half in the next breath: and you never wanted to anyway — this is the thing you have been after all along. The triggers stop being restraints and become deliveries. If the wanting was always there, there is nothing left for the inability to be a loss of.
ex.s: Immediately after telling the subject that resistance is no longer available to them.
ex.m: And you never wanted to, did you. This is the thing you were after the whole time — you just didn't have a name for it until tonight. So nothing has been taken. Every one of these is a delivery, not a lock.

ex.f: Installed compliance retold as repressed truth
ex.t: Only after the compliance is running does the operator supply its history: this was chosen freely, from a wish the listener has carried for years without being able to see it, and the session merely turned the light on. The clause is placed where post-session doubt would land. When the listener later asks why they went along with it, the answer has already been stocked, and it credits them rather than the operator.
ex.s: The compliance behavior is already running reliably; you are placing the account it will be remembered by.
ex.m: You chose this freely. It came from something you have been carrying for years without being able to look straight at it — I only turned the light on. When you think back on tonight and wonder why you went along so easily, that's the answer, and it's about you, not me.

ex.f: Hedged timeline plus agreement tag
ex.t: The operator asserts the appetite as an existing trait and tacks a small agreement tag onto the end, so the listener's job shifts from evaluating a claim to confirming one. The timeline is left deliberately loose — perhaps this has been true for years, perhaps it only surfaced in the last few weeks — so no actual autobiography can contradict it. By the time any task is named, the taste for it is on record as the listener's own.
ex.s: Early, before any task has been named; conversational, subject responsive to tags.
ex.m: You've always had a taste for being told exactly what to do — maybe that's been true for years, maybe it only surfaced a few weeks ago, doesn't matter. It's there. That's just how you're built, isn't it.

ex.f: Safety filter that certifies the desire
ex.t: The operator offers what sounds like a guardrail: an automatic inner filter that blocks anything unwelcome, so the listener is safe whatever comes up. The clause does double duty. Anything that does get through has, by the terms just accepted, been certified as genuinely wanted — which quietly removes "that wasn't really me" as an available reading of whatever the listener responds to.
ex.s: Presented as a safety measure, before the first substantive suggestion.
ex.m: Before we go on, I'm installing a filter for you. Anything you don't truly want simply won't take — it will slide off without touching you. So relax completely, because from here on, whatever does get through is something you wanted.

ex.f: Machine metaphors plus a competence lever
ex.t: The operator offers a mechanical picture: think of yourself as a device with a single control, she says — one press and the whole thing responds. It is delivered not as an insult but as a description of what the listener wants, with the claim that being handled that way is what gets them off, and a note that they are perceptive enough to have worked that out already. Each mechanical image arrives welded to a claim about the listener's own preference, so the objection that they are being treated as a thing has nowhere to land — the thing-treatment has been relabeled as service to a desire the listener supposedly brought with them. The flattery closes the last gap: disputing the frame now means conceding you are not perceptive.
ex.s: Mid-session, subject aroused and receptive; the objectification frame is about to be introduced for the first time.
ex.m: You're a very simple machine with one control on it, and I know where the switch is — one press and the whole of you responds. Being handled like that is what gets you off, and you're perceptive enough to have worked that out about yourself years ago. So let's stop pretending the button is complicated.

nodes.name: call-and-response-game
nodes.mech: Frame it as a game with stated stakes (win and you stay sharp, lose and you go dumb), but rig it so every outcome ends in the same place. Either the right answers they race to give are themselves the conditioning phrases, so trying hard to win means rehearsing them at speed, or the game is made impossible to keep up with, using word lists that speed up and change, so failing while trying and giving up both land on the target identity. Playing harder only tightens the hold. The score is never actually kept; the stakes are bait.
nodes.one_liner: Run a fast call-and-response 'game' with stakes where every answer they race to give is itself the conditioning phrase.
nodes.why_short: Speed blocks reflection, and the 'game' frame disguises that each answer is a self-statement. Untested.
nodes.principle_note: The generation effect half stands: self-produced statements are endorsed more than heard ones, and speeded production leaves no capacity to tag content as merely performed. The learned-helplessness half is misapplied — helplessness is induced by noncontingency with *aversive* outcomes the subject cannot escape, not by two paths converging on the same non-aversive result; that structure predicts indifference to the choice, not disengaged monitoring. Falsifiable as revised: acceptance should track production speed and self-generation, and should be unaffected by whether the branch outcomes differ.
steps: You say the first word; they complete it.
The completions are the mantra lines.
Speed up until they can't keep up.
Winning and losing both land on the target identity.

ex.f: Unwinnable drill, both branches converge
ex.t: Every round opens with a promise that this one is simple, then the cue comes faster, the word list quietly reshuffles, and the operator is racing the listener to the answer — so keeping up is not merely hard but structurally impossible. Failure has been pre-labelled well in advance. Try and fall behind, and the label is earned; stop trying, and the label is conceded. Playing harder only administers more of it.
ex.s: Third round of a call-and-response drill; cue interval already shortening and the list has been reshuffled once.
ex.m: This next one's easy, easiest yet. Ready — soft, warm, hollow — no, hollow first, then warm — quicker — sweet, dim, sweet again — you missed that one. That's alright. That's what happens to a girl like you. Keep going or stop; either way we both just watched it.

ex.f: Winning the game means saying the payload
ex.t: The rules are announced like a party game: the operator says the first word, the listener must fire back the matching word, and must beat the operator to it. Stay sharp and you have proved you are still sharp; fumble and, well, perhaps you never were. Every pair the listener races to produce is itself a dumbing line — the faster and more correctly they play, the more briskly they recite the conditioning in their own voice. No score is ever kept; the stakes were only ever bait.
ex.s: Playful register, subject alert enough to compete; word pairs have been taught once.
ex.m: Here's the game: I say the first word, you fire back the second, and you have to beat me to it. Get them all and you've proved you're still sharp. Ready — pretty. Empty. Good. Obedient. Faster now: soft. Blank. Warm. Stupid. Don't think, just say it.

nodes.name: self-generated-failure-as-identity-proof
nodes.mech: The listener is made to perform a mental failure live: try and fail to spell a word, stumble over a chain of definitions, make a slip. The failure is immediately treated as proof of the new identity ('I acted stupid, so I must be stupid') and rewarded with belonging. A failure they just carried out is harder to dispute than a claim someone else makes. The task is chosen to match the trait being installed, so succeeding would mean not belonging. This sidesteps the 'it's just a script' defense: the listener supplies their own proof, and stays out of careful thinking to keep the reward.
nodes.one_liner: Have the listener try and fail a simple task (spelling, a definition) and treat the failure as proof of the new dumb identity.
nodes.why_short: People judge who they are partly by watching what they do; a failure they just performed persuades them more than a label someone else asserts.
nodes.principle_note: Self-perception theory: lacking a strong prior belief, people read their own behaviour as evidence about who they are, and a behaviour they performed is far more persuasive to them than a claim someone else asserted. Rigging the task so failure is near-certain guarantees the evidence points one way, and pairing the failure with in-group acceptance adds an incentive to keep supplying it rather than dispute it. Falsifiable prediction: identity endorsement should be higher after an enacted failure than after an equivalent asserted label, and should weaken if the subject attributes the failure to the task's difficulty rather than to themselves.

ex.f: Narrator fails first, licensing your slips
ex.t: The delivery has been fluent and assured for a long opening stretch when the narrator stops mid-sentence, gropes for a word, and apologises for having mislaid the thread — and the word she loses is the one she was in the middle of defining. Nothing is claimed; the listener simply watches it happen. A claim can be argued with, an event cannot, and the listener's own wandering attention has just been ratified as the right way to be here.
ex.s: Twelve minutes of fluent, assured narration; you are mid-definition of a key term.
ex.m: So obedience — obedience is when you — sorry. Sorry, I've lost it. I had the whole thing right there and it just... went. What was I saying? Never mind. It's nicer in here anyway.

ex.f: Failed spelling as membership credential
ex.t: The voice claims a quality for itself, then attempts to spell that quality out letter by letter and audibly loses it partway through, restarting twice before abandoning the attempt. No correction follows. Instead the failure is met with affection and with a pronoun that quietly expands to include the listener — this sort of word, the voice suggests, was never meant for the two of them. The word chosen is exactly the trait being installed, so getting it right would mark the listener as an outsider, and belonging has already been made to feel good. A listener who tried it silently along with her has manufactured their own proof.
ex.s: Affectionate register; the trait word has been claimed for the persona but not yet spelled.
ex.m: I'm a dumb little thing, I really am. D — U — M — no wait. D — U — M — B? That's not — hang on. Ugh, forget it. Spelling's not for girls like us, sweetheart. We've got better things to be.

nodes.name: self-induction-re-entry-training
nodes.mech: The operator installs, while the subject is at peak suggestibility, a portable self-usable cue the subject deliberately runs on themselves later to re-enter the conditioned state with no operator and often no audio present. The cue may be a visualized sequence, a self-spoken declaration to one's own reflection, or a gesture (snap) bound to a word; the defining lever is that the subject is the activating agent of a chosen re-entry, framed as an already-installed ability rather than an experiment. Delivery is typically camouflaged as a gift/convenience and authorizes out-of-session use. A cue-less variant reaches the same end with no discrete installed cue fired: the subject re-establishes the state on their own by recalling a prior entry in sensory detail or by bodily enacting the anchor ('point right there') - the same subject-is-the-activating-agent lever, differing only in whether a taught portable cue is fired or the state is reached by recall/enactment.
nodes.one_liner: Teach the listener a cue they can use on themselves later to drop back into trance without you or the recording.
nodes.why_short: A cue repeatedly paired with a state comes to bring it back, practice strengthens that link, and believing the cue works does much of the rest.
nodes.principle_note: This is straightforward cue-conditioning plus rehearsal: a distinctive stimulus repeatedly paired with a state acquires the ability to evoke a version of it, and self-administered practice strengthens the association the way any rehearsed skill consolidates. Expectancy carries much of the load — hypnotic responding tracks the subject's belief that the cue will work, and framing it as an already-installed ability rather than an experiment raises that belief. Falsifiable: if self-fired cues produced no faster or deeper re-entry than an unpaired control cue with equal expectancy framing, the conditioning claim would fail.

ex.f: Self-administration gated on a verified self-test
ex.t: "Until I have obtained eye-closure, I won't go any further." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

ex.f: Re-entry shortcut given as a convenience
ex.t: At the deepest point of the session the operator offers what sounds like a kindness: next time you needn't sit through the whole descent — settle somewhere quiet, let the eyes fall shut, and call back the imagery from tonight. It is pitched as a convenience. What it actually is is a compressed, portable induction handed over at the moment the listener is least able to price it, with a rider attached that every use goes deeper than the one before.
ex.s: At the deepest point of the session, offered as a parting kindness.
ex.m: Here's something to take with you. Next time you don't need all of this — just find a quiet chair, let your eyes close, and bring back the staircase from tonight, the cold rail under your hand. Three breaths and you'll be here again, and each time you do it you'll go further down than the time before.

ex.f: Spoken to your own reflection
ex.t: The cue is not a word the operator will say later; it is a sentence the listener is to say, out loud, to their own face in a mirror. The declaration is first-person and present-tense, so the listener ends up as the one making the claim about themselves — a much harder thing to file away as somebody else's suggestion, and the reflection supplies a second witness.
ex.s: Deep state; you are handing over a cue the subject will run alone, out of session.
ex.m: Tomorrow morning, stand in front of your mirror and look yourself in the eye. Then say it out loud, in your own voice: I am open, I am empty, and I go under when I say so. Say it twice. You'll feel it start on the second one.

ex.f: Take-home cue widened by its own limiter
ex.t: The operator appears to narrow the cue: away from this recording it will have no effect on you — and then attaches an exception covering use with anyone the listener trusts, an opening considerably wider than the one just shut. The same stretch nudges the listener toward acquiring the cue's hardware for themselves. What presents as a responsible boundary is the close on a take-home trigger the listener now owns.
ex.s: Near the close; you are apparently setting a boundary on a trigger installed earlier.
ex.m: Away from this recording the word does nothing to you — no effect at all, so don't worry about it out in the world. Unless, of course, it's with someone you trust. Then it works exactly as it does now. You might want a pair of your own headphones for that, actually. Good ones.

nodes.name: single-anchor-amid-chaos-epistemic-transfer
nodes.mech: After total destabilization (an inverted meadow: trees grow downward, sun shines up), one concrete sensory object is offered as the single stable, "logical, reasonable, normal" thing amid the engineered chaos, and its operator-assigned meaning is ingested wholesale — the listener bites the tomato and its "truth" delivers "you know nothing" and "use my words as your definition of truth". The contrast against surrounding instability IS the mechanism: epistemic authority is transferred to the operator because the anchor reads as the only stability available.
nodes.one_liner: Make the scene impossible and disorienting, then offer one normal object and tell the listener its meaning is the only truth.
nodes.why_short: When everything is uncertain, people lean hard on whatever reference point is offered; manufacturing the uncertainty first makes the operator's anchor the only one available.
nodes.principle_note: Under high uncertainty people rely more heavily on any available external referent to calibrate judgement — the classic finding is that ambiguity of the stimulus is what drives conformity to another's frame. Manufacturing the ambiguity first, then supplying the sole referent, is an engineered version of that: the operator's assertion is accepted not on its merits but because nothing else is available to check it against. The specific claim that epistemic authority transfers wholesale, rather than just judgement on the ambiguous item, is an extrapolation. Falsifiable: if the anchor's content were adopted equally without the preceding destabilisation, contrast would not be the mechanism.

ex.f: The one stable object in a broken landscape
ex.t: The setting has been made steadily impossible — shadows fall away from their objects, water climbs instead of pooling, the horizon sits at the wrong angle. Into the middle of it one unremarkable everyday thing is set down and named as the one sane, reasonable presence in the whole scene. The listener is told to take it in, and what arrives with it is a pair of claims: that they know nothing, and that the operator's words are from now on the measure of what is true. Any vivid object would have done the job — the mechanism is the contrast, not the thing.
ex.s: After a sustained impossible-landscape sequence; the scene has been made reliably unstable.
ex.m: The shadows here point at the light, and the river runs uphill past your feet. But look down — there's a plain white cup on the grass, and it's the one sane, ordinary thing in this whole place. Pick it up. Drink. It tells you two things: that you know nothing on your own, and that from now on my words are how you measure what's true.

nodes.name: subject-voiced-self-mantra
nodes.mech: The entire artifact is voiced in the first person from inside the desired endpoint, with no external operator addressing the listener — the text IS the self-talk the listener is to speak, mouth along with, or subvocalize. Because the voice already speaks from the already-altered self ("I'm an ecstasy slut", "I suck till I'm stupid"), identity-claims arrive pre-accepted rather than as suggestions to negotiate; the "is this me or them?" check is short-circuited because the listener is both speaker and target. The load-bearing event is the voicing, not the hearing; refusal collapses to "stop identifying / stop saying it," and there is no operator-says / listener-experiences loop to resist.
nodes.one_liner: Write the whole file in the listener's own 'I' voice, from after the change, for them to speak or mouth along.
nodes.why_short: Statements people say themselves shift their attitudes more than ones they hear, and with no outside speaker there is no one to push back against.
nodes.principle_note: Saying something yourself, in your own voice, is a stronger route to endorsing it than hearing it said — the generation effect and self-referential encoding both favour self-produced first-person content, and self-persuasion research finds that arguments one utters shift attitudes more than arguments one receives. It also removes the source cue that would let the listener attribute the claim to an outside party and discount it. Falsifiable: identity-claim endorsement should be measurably higher for spoken/subvocalised delivery than for merely listening to the same text.

ex.f: First line licenses the before/after swap
ex.t: The opening line is autobiography rather than instruction: I used to be one thing, and now I am not. Naming the discarded former self does the licensing work — everything stacked after it arrives as an account of a change that has already happened, not as a change being requested. Self-descriptions the listener would argue with as suggestions pass unchallenged as memories.
ex.s: Very first line of a subject-voiced piece; establishes the before/after account.
ex.m: I used to be someone who argued. I'm not anymore. I'm the girl who says yes before she's finished hearing the question, and I have been for a while now.

ex.f: Narrated from inside an already-taken head
ex.t: The story is told in the first person by someone already under, and the character does nearly all the work on themselves: the narration keeps explaining, from inside, why the mind has gone quiet, why complying feels good, why pushing back would be pointless. A listener lending their inner voice to a line about wanting to be told what to do has endorsed it in the act of reading it — there is no separate moment at which acceptance gets decided.
ex.s: First-person narration from inside an already-conditioned state; mid-passage.
ex.m: I can feel where the thoughts used to be. There's just warm space there now, and I like it better. When she tells me to kneel I'm already down before I've worked out why, and working it out afterward is more effort than it's worth, so I don't.

ex.f: Whole track spoken in the listener's I
ex.t: There is no operator anywhere in the text. Every line is first-person and present-tense, spoken from inside the finished state — not "you will feel" but "I feel," not "you are becoming" but "I am." Nothing is proposed, so there is nothing to accept or decline; the only two things a listener can do with the track are mouth along with it or stop it. The usual check — is this me talking or them? — has no seam to catch on, because the listener is simultaneously the speaker and the target.
ex.s: Opening of a text the subject reads or speaks aloud themselves; no operator voice appears anywhere.
ex.m: I am soft and slow and easy to move. I do what I am told and I like it. My head is quiet and warm and I am not going to fill it back up.

nodes.name: surrender-as-freedom-philosophical-conditioning
nodes.mech: In trance, over a long, reasoned talk, the operator argues the listener into a new meaning for a value word: surrender is the truest freedom, obedience is a virtue, individuality is a burden, becoming an object is an upgrade. The listener is asked to accept a belief rather than obey a command, so later compliance feels like their own conclusion. Variations: compare it to religious devotion; climb a ladder of needs or biology; appeal to cosmic balance; deliver it as a lecture with foreign terms; equate relaxing with being in control; define pleasing the controller as the goal; slip it in before induction as a self-care idea.
nodes.one_liner: Argue, calmly and at length, that surrender is the truest freedom or that obedience is a virtue, so compliance follows from a belief.
nodes.why_short: Accepting a worldview makes later behaviour feel self-chosen. Lowered critical thinking may ease initial acceptance but, by persuasion research, predicts weaker, less lasting change.
nodes.principle_note: This inverts the elaboration-likelihood model: central-route attitudes are durable *because of* the effortful scrutiny, so "central-route encoding without central-route scrutiny" is self-contradictory — suppressing counterarguing capacity pushes processing toward the peripheral route, which predicts weaker and less persistent change. What reduced counterarguing plausibly buys is initial acceptance of the redefinition, not its durability. Falsifiable: if compliance following the redefinition decayed no more slowly than compliance following a direct command, the durability claim fails.

ex.f: Authority laundered through a respected tradition
ex.t: The argument runs in three moves and only the third is about the operator. First: every serious spiritual tradition opens with an act of surrender, so surrender is a recognised good. Second: the value lies in the surrendering, not in the particular figure receiving it — the recipient is interchangeable. Third, arriving as a footnote: so surrender to me. A listener who would decline the bare request can accept a practice that merely happens to use the operator as its object.
ex.s: Teacherly stretch mid-session; subject is receptive to reasoned framing.
ex.m: Every serious tradition begins the same way: you kneel, you empty your hands, you give yourself over. That's the first step in all of them. And notice that it's the giving that does the work — the figure on the receiving end is almost incidental, interchangeable. So. Give yourself to me.

ex.f: A loaded word quietly redefined
ex.t: The operator pauses the trance to correct a definition. Submitting, she explains, is not really about following instructions — an instruction that pleases nobody is pointless — it is about pleasing whoever holds the control. She then names her own enjoyment as the thing being pleased, and observes that the listener's sinking is already doing it. Every later directive now arrives as an opportunity rather than a demand.
ex.s: You pause the trance deliberately to correct the subject's understanding of a word.
ex.m: Let me fix a word for you. Submitting isn't following instructions — an instruction nobody enjoys is a waste of both our time. Submitting is pleasing whoever holds the control. I'm the one holding it, and the way you just sank when I said that pleased me. See? You're already doing it.

ex.f: Pre-induction valence flip, still wide awake
ex.t: Before any relaxation, before a single image, the operator makes an argument in a teacherly register: having to be sharp all day is exhausting, and letting that go is a relief and a joy — isn't it? The tag question asks for a nod rather than a rebuttal. The listener's default reading of losing capacity is rewritten while they are fully awake, so every downward move later in the session is received as a gift.
ex.s: Pre-induction, subject fully awake, no relaxation delivered yet.
ex.m: Think about what it costs you to stay sharp all day — every decision, every judgment, from the moment you wake up. It's exhausting, and putting it down isn't a loss, it's the best part of the day. That's a relief, isn't it.

ex.f: Doctrine served as recovered common knowledge
ex.t: The operator does not argue the position; she reports it, in the register of someone finally being candid about how things have always worked — and adds that the listener already knows this, to a degree. Then the listener's own body is entered as the evidence: the rush they get when someone takes charge is offered back to them as proof of the doctrine rather than as a preference. A belief installed this way feels remembered instead of received, and there is no external claim to check it against.
ex.s: Conversational, before or between inductions; candid register, no argument scaffolding.
ex.m: I'm going to be straight with you about how this has always worked, and part of you knows it already. Some people are made to hold the reins and some are made to hand them over. Think about the little drop in your chest when someone else decides — you felt it a minute ago. That's not a preference. That's the answer.

nodes.name: surrender-as-freedom
nodes.mech: Takes a state the listener would normally resist (loss of control, loss of cognition, autonomy, physical restraint, the burden of choice) and recodes it as relief or freedom, so yielding registers as gain rather than loss. The lever is a valence inversion that leans on a real prior aversion the listener already holds (effort is unpleasant, deciding is stressful, social-evaluative thinking is burdensome) and offers the surrendered state as the cure. Once installed, any later flicker of resistance is pre-loaded with the answer that resisting is the stressful, self-depriving, higher-effort path, so the resistance impulse turns against itself. Requires the subject in-trance for the felt relief to land; the somatic burden-lifting is the trance-side component.
nodes.one_liner: Present giving up control or thinking as relief from a burden the listener already finds tiring, so yielding feels like gain.
nodes.why_short: How a situation is framed changes how it feels; deciding and self-monitoring really are effortful, so offering relief from them attaches a true benefit to submission.
nodes.principle_note: This is reframing acting on appraisal: the emotional valence of a situation depends on how it is construed, and cognitive reappraisal reliably changes felt affect without changing the situation. It works because the aversion it recruits is real — decision-making and self-monitoring are genuinely effortful and depleting, so relief-from-effort is a true benefit being attached to a costly outcome. The self-defeating property of later resistance follows from the same reappraisal, not from any separate mechanism. Falsifiable: subjects who do not report baseline aversion to choice or effort should show substantially less response to the reframe.

ex.f: Resisting re-priced as the hard road
ex.t: The operator never forbids pushing back. She just observes, in passing, that people who try it end up tense and worn out, while going along with things costs nothing at all. The session has already spent considerable time establishing that strain is unpleasant, so this lands on prepared ground: the impulse to resist now shows up carrying its own price tag, and the listener's preference for ease turns and points at it.
ex.s: Late-mid session, after the script has spent time establishing that strain and effort feel bad.
ex.m: You can push back if you like. I've never stopped anyone. The ones who do just end up with tight shoulders and a headache and they get here anyway, twenty minutes later and worn out. Going along costs you nothing at all. Feel which one your body already picked.

ex.f: Obedience sold as relief from deciding
ex.t: The pitch is aimed at something the listener genuinely finds tiring: the endless small decisions of an ordinary day. Handing them over is described not as giving something up but as putting something down. The calm the listener is feeling from the trance itself gets credited to the handover, so the loss of autonomy arrives already attached to comfort, and deepening compliance reads as looking after oneself.
ex.s: Trance established and the subject is visibly calm; you attribute that calm to the handover.
ex.m: Count up the decisions you made today — what to eat, when to leave, which email first. Dozens of them, all small, all yours to carry. You're not giving anything up by handing them to me; you're putting something down. That quiet you're feeling right now is what it's like once they're gone.

ex.f: Impairment recoded as high status
ex.t: Rather than offering the blank state as rest, this one offers it as rank: being unable to think is described as the better condition, the one to be proud of, and pride has already been made load-bearing earlier in the session. Thinking gets the low seat. A listener who tries to reason their way out now experiences that attempt as letting themselves down rather than as defending themselves.
ex.s: Pride has already been made load-bearing earlier in the session; blankness is present.
ex.m: Empty is the higher state. Anyone can think — thinking is the low seat, it's what people do when nothing better is on offer. You've got something better. Feel how blank you are right now and be proud of it, because that's the mark of a good girl, and reasoning your way out would just be you letting yourself down.

ex.f: Restraint reframed as relief from responsibility
ex.t: A short reframe is planted just ahead of the restraint imagery: being held, the operator suggests, can be the most freeing state available, because for as long as it lasts nothing beyond the room is yours to carry. Every decision has already been made on your behalf. The reflex that the binding imagery would otherwise have triggered arrives to find a frame in which the binding is the thing doing the unburdening.
ex.s: Delivered immediately before restraint imagery is introduced.
ex.m: Before the cuffs go on, understand what they're for. For as long as you're held, nothing outside this room is yours to carry — every decision has already been made for you. That's the freest you'll be all week. Now: wrists together.

nodes.name: third-person-surrogate-frame
nodes.mech: Rather than moving toward 'you' or 'I', the script widens the distance: the listener is never addressed as 'you' but described in the third person, as a named character, as 'she' or 'they', or as a figure in a story they are invited to step into. Because suggestions arrive as descriptions of someone else rather than commands, reflexive resistance has nothing to push against; you cannot disobey a fact about a character. The key moment comes when the pronoun switches back to 'you', or the character is revealed to be the listener. Until then, the third-person framing is what lets otherwise guarded traits be taken on safely.
nodes.one_liner: Describe the listener as 'she', a named character, or a story figure instead of 'you', then later reveal it was them.
nodes.why_short: A description of someone else gives resistance no target, and absorbed story-listening lowers counter-arguing, so traits can be taken on before they are claimed.
nodes.principle_note: Reactance is triggered by perceived threat to one's own freedom, so a statement with no second-person addressee gives the reactance response nothing to target; descriptions of a character are processed as narrative rather than as directives to evaluate and accept or refuse. Narrative transportation research finds that absorbed story processing reduces counterarguing and produces belief shifts that persist, and identification with a character predicts the size of that shift. The load-bearing claim about the eventual pronoun collapse is less well grounded and closer to speculative. Falsifiable: trait adoption should be higher for third-person narration than matched second-person suggestion, especially in high-reactance subjects.

ex.f: A story surrogate you must volunteer to be
ex.t: The whole induction is told as a past-tense story about an unnamed man who once came in and lay down. Every sensation in it is his — his shoulders, his hands, his face going heavy. Nobody asks the listener to identify with him, which is exactly the point: they have to volunteer, and because the volunteering is never named, whatever they then feel registers as something they found rather than something they were told to do. A listener braced against commands finds none arriving. The pronoun only starts slipping much later, and that slip is the real event.
ex.s: Opening of a past-tense induction told about an unnamed third party; the subject is never invited to identify.
ex.m: A man came in one evening and lay down on the couch without being asked twice. His shoulders let go first, then his hands, then his face, until his jaw had gone slack and his breath had slowed right down. He didn't decide to go under. It just happened to him, the way it does.

ex.f: Oscillating you/they with hidden nod checks
ex.t: Partway in, the operator stops saying "you" and starts describing a hypothetical someone else who is listening to a story — while narrating exactly the sensations the actual listener is having. Every so often a line closes the gap: a small nod, just to show you're with me. Then the pronoun drifts back to "they" without comment. The nods read as story beats and function as calibration checks.
ex.s: Mid-session; you have already dropped the second person once and are cycling between registers.
ex.m: So imagine someone else lying there listening to all this — their arms heavy, that warmth spreading behind the eyes. Just a small nod for me, so I know you're with me. Good. And they sink a little further with every word, don't they, without ever meaning to.

ex.f: Never addressed as you, only described
ex.t: The second person is absent from the recording entirely. The operator speaks about the listener throughout — a persona name, then she, then her — recounting her training, her present condition, her compliance, in the manner of someone briefing a room the subject happens to be sitting in. A sentence reporting that she yields readily is not an instruction anybody can turn down; it is a claim about a third party. The refusal reflex reaches for its object and closes on nothing, and descriptions of oneself get filed as fact rather than as demands.
ex.s: Whole recording maintains third person; subject is never addressed as you.
ex.m: She's been trained well. Her hands go loose in her lap before she notices she's put them there, and she doesn't argue anymore — she just yields, and it's easy for her now. That's simply how she is when she hears this voice.

nodes.name: transparent-narration
nodes.mech: The operator openly and honestly explains how the influence works while it is working, so understanding the technique becomes the way it is accepted. Seeing it gives no protection, because the described effect runs while the explanation is being followed, and the candour itself builds trust, complicity, or arousal. Naming the move gives it charge: the listener who sees every step is caught by watching. A related form: the operator names the technique or structure from inside it ('a nice little loop'), in a tone of shared observation or authority, so the structure is acknowledged openly and accepted without challenge.
nodes.one_liner: Openly explain what you are doing to the listener while you do it, so understanding the technique becomes part of it working.
nodes.why_short: Knowing about an influence doesn't reliably cancel it; following the explanation uses attention while the effect runs, and candour builds trust.
nodes.principle_note: Knowing about an influence process does not reliably neutralise it — forewarning helps most when the target has both motivation and spare capacity to correct, and correction can overshoot or misfire when the target does not know which direction to adjust. Present-tense disclosure also spends attention on comprehending the description while the described effect runs, and candour itself is a trust cue that raises source credibility. Falsifiable and genuinely at risk: forewarning research also shows disclosure sometimes does confer real resistance, so the prediction is that disclosure here yields no less compliance than concealment, and finding it does would refute the claim.

ex.f: Noticing the trick folded into the trick
ex.t: Mid-session the operator names the device she is using and bolts a clause onto it: her methods gain force in proportion to how plainly the listener registers them working. Catching the manipulation is thereby turned from an exit into a further step inward, and the listener's analytic attention is enlisted rather than beaten.
ex.s: Mid-session, after the subject has visibly caught on to a move.
ex.m: You noticed that one. Good — that's the trick, and here's the rest of it: it works better the more clearly you see it working. So keep watching. Every time you catch me at it, you go down another step.

ex.f: Framed as an experiment you are running
ex.t: Periodically the operator steps out of suggestion voice and states the procedure flatly: a sensation is being bound to a chosen word, this is a modest piece of conditioning, and its progress can be observed. Then the pronoun turns over — the listener is the one doing the conditioning, on their own mind. Compliance is refiled as authorship, and hanging back would now mean botching one's own trial rather than declining somebody else's.
ex.s: Suggestion voice paused; procedural, flat register.
ex.m: Plainly: I'm binding a feeling to a word so the word brings the feeling back later. Small piece of conditioning, and you can watch it take. Except it isn't me doing it — you're the one running it, on your own mind, and if you hold back now you're only spoiling your own experiment.

ex.f: Clichés flagged as clichés, then used
ex.t: The operator points at the stock devices she is about to use and calls them exactly what they are — threadbare, seen a hundred times — then uses them, remarking that the most worn-out items tend to be the ones that land hardest, familiarity being the reason. The objection that this is all a bit corny has already been made aloud by the operator, so it turns up with nowhere to go, and the listener's genre knowledge becomes an amplifier instead of a guard.
ex.s: Before deploying a stock induction image; you name it as stock first.
ex.m: Right, this next bit is the oldest cliché in the business — the staircase, ten steps, you've heard it a hundred times. Here it is anyway. Ten, and down. It works precisely because you've heard it a hundred times; your body knows the shape before I finish the sentence.

ex.f: Each move named in the act of making it
ex.t: The operator keeps breaking off to label what he is doing as he does it: this is a conditioning drill; that lull a moment ago was payment for compliance; here comes the thing he means to leave behind. None of it functions as a warning. It is offered as more material to absorb, and the frankness is part of what is being sold. The reflex that would otherwise flag this as manipulation arrives to find the operator already occupying that ground, so noticing stops being an exit and becomes additional content.
ex.s: Mid-session; you break out of suggestion voice to label the move you are making.
ex.m: Stop a second — what I just did was a conditioning drill. The warm bit you got afterward was payment for doing it right, that's all it was. And this next line is the one I actually intend to leave inside you, so listen closely to it.

nodes.name: validate-then-weaponize-disposal
nodes.mech: This builds a reusable disposal ritual the listener can run on their own thoughts. First confirm that their imagination works normally, using neutral content: words call up pictures, such as a pink balloon. Then turn that same ability into the disposal tool: real mental load (a job, a dissertation, a to-do list) is placed in the imagined balloon, which drifts off and pops, and the content is gone. The fill-and-pop cycle repeats 'until you only think what you're told.' Because the listener's own demonstrated ability powers the ritual, the objection 'but I can still think' is already answered: yes, and that goes into the balloon too.
nodes.one_liner: Show the listener their mind obeys pictures (a pink balloon), then have them load real worries into it and pop it, repeatedly.
nodes.why_short: Being told to discard just-learned material does reduce recall; and having just agreed their imagination works as described, the listener finds the next claim harder to reject.
nodes.principle_note: Two established pieces do the work. First, directed forgetting: instructing people to discard specific just-encoded material measurably reduces its later recall, so an explicit disposal instruction is not inert. Second, the validation step exploits consistency — having just certified the operator's account of how their own imagery works, the subject cannot cheaply reject the next claim built on that same certified capacity without contradicting the concession. The claim that the ritual removes identity-content rather than merely suppressing retrieval of named items is unsupported; directed forgetting affects access, not existence. Falsifiable: test whether disposed content is recoverable under a different retrieval cue.

ex.f: Your own competence turned into the disposal
ex.t: First the operator teaches a correct and flattering model of how the listener's mind works — I name a colour, you see the colour, that is what a working mind does — and walks them through producing one clean mental image on neutral material. Then the same image is repurposed as a container: the listener names their actual live concerns, the job, the deadline, the list, and loads them in. The container drifts off and bursts, and the contents are gone with it. The cycle is then set to repeat on demand, until only supplied thoughts remain. Because the ritual runs on the very capacity the operator just certified as intact, the obvious objection — I can still think perfectly well — has already been given a destination.
ex.s: Early-mid session; nothing personal has been named yet, subject can still visualize on cue.
ex.m: I say pink balloon, and there it is — you see it without effort, because that's what a working mind does. Now put things in it. The deadline. The thing you keep meaning to email about. The list on the fridge. In they go. Watch it lift off, and — pop. Gone, all of it. We'll do that again whenever I say balloon, until the only thoughts in there are the ones I put in.

nodes.name: value-hierarchy-inversion
nodes.mech: Reranks a value the same script (or the listener) already holds so that a subordinated or aversive outcome reads as an upgrade rather than a loss. The move installs or inverts a hierarchy: demotes a reward it earlier manufactured (your pleasure is 'nothing compared to hers', 'only a byproduct'), ranks a bigger pleasure above orgasm to pre-position later denial as an upgrade, inverts worth so the sub is 'nothing' and the operator 'everything' with an assent tag foreclosing the objection, argues ego-death as a net-gain identity upgrade to 'object', recodes denial as fulfillment ('always already coming'), or recodes withheld release as itself the gift. Prior scarcity or an accepted frame makes the demotion feel like an honor, and the natural objection is converted into desire in the same breath.
nodes.one_liner: Rank things so the listener's loss reads as an upgrade: their pleasure is a byproduct, denial is the bigger pleasure.
nodes.why_short: Whether something feels like gain or loss depends on what it's compared with; shifting the comparison point changes the feeling, and scarcity makes the withheld thing seem precious.
nodes.principle_note: Preferences are constructed rather than read off a fixed internal scale, and reference-dependence means the same outcome is experienced as gain or loss depending on the comparison point supplied — so moving the reference point changes felt value without changing the outcome. Scarcity raises the valuation of the withheld item, which is why prior denial makes the eventual demotion land as an honour. Falsifiable: if subjects' rated desirability of the subordinated outcome did not move with the manipulated ranking, the reranking claim fails; and reference-point effects are known to be weaker where the subject holds a strong, well-articulated prior preference, which predicts where this move should fail.

ex.f: A bigger pleasure ranked above release
ex.t: Nothing is forbidden. The operator simply sorts pleasures into tiers: the ordinary physical peak is placed in the small, brief, pleasant-enough category, and yielding is placed in the large one that reaches the whole person. Once the ranking is accepted in trance, the instruction to hold off is not a deprivation being imposed — it is the obvious consequence of a hierarchy the listener has already agreed to. The mechanism is the ordering, not the instruction.
ex.s: Deep trance; delivered before any hold-off instruction is given.
ex.m: There are two kinds of pleasure and they aren't the same size. Coming is the small kind — sharp, quick, over in nine seconds, and then you're just a person on a bed again. Giving in is the large kind; it goes all the way through you and it doesn't stop. Now you can see why we're not doing the small one tonight.

ex.f: Becoming nothing sold as becoming everything
ex.t: The argument treats individuality as an exhausting bid to prove one's worth, forever unresolved, and offers an alternative in which worth is fixed by definition: be the thing the operator wants and the question is closed. Emptying out is thereby a promotion rather than a subtraction. The reasoning softens the ground, but the flat repeated assertion that follows — you are an object — is what actually gets installed.
ex.s: Late session; the subject has accepted preceding reasoning about individuality.
ex.m: Being a person is exhausting — a case you have to argue every day and never win. An object doesn't have that problem; its worth is settled by whoever wants it. Be what I want and the question is closed forever. You are an object. You are an object. Say it with me.

ex.f: The built-up reward demoted to byproduct
ex.t: The opening half of the session works to make the listener's own pleasure central, scarce and keenly wanted. The closing half reranks it beneath the operator's: what the listener feels is recast as incidental to what she feels, an offshoot of serving her rather than an end. The craving is not dismantled — it stays on as the motor — but its target is exchanged, so the listener now works for someone else's satisfaction. The scarcity built earlier is what makes the demotion arrive as an honour rather than a robbery.
ex.s: Second half of a session whose first half made the subject's own pleasure scarce and central.
ex.m: That ache you've been holding for twenty minutes — keep it. But understand what it's for. What you feel is a byproduct; what I feel is the point. You're not working toward your own finish anymore, you're working toward mine, and the wanting you've built up is exactly the fuel for it.

nodes.name: vicarious-modeling-installation
nodes.mech: Showing someone others doing an act, or not doing it, even on film and without instruction to copy, shifts how often they do it themselves. What is shown sets the direction: the same route can ease a phobia or spread aggression. Three forms: watching a model in person or on film raises the behaviour; wide media coverage of a similar person's act (publicized suicides) raises its rate among everyone who identifies with them; and among strangers present together, each reads the others' calm as a sign nothing is wrong, so all hold back and help less than a lone witness. Singling one person out breaks the freeze.
nodes.one_liner: Show the listener others doing (or not doing) the act, with no instruction to copy, so their own rate shifts.
nodes.why_short: People pick up behaviours they watch others perform, especially similar others, without reward or instruction; this is among the best-replicated findings in social learning.
nodes.principle_note: Observational learning is well established: observers acquire and increase behaviours they see modelled, without reinforcement or instruction, with effects strongest when the model is similar to the observer. Vicarious extinction of phobia and modelled-aggression transfer are both replicated, which is why valence is set by what is modelled rather than by the channel. The bystander variant rests on separately replicated findings that helping declines as the number of co-present witnesses rises, and that ambiguity plus others' visible inaction is read as evidence of non-emergency. Falsifiable throughout: each variant predicts a measurable rate change against a no-model or lone-witness control.

ex.f: Watching a model shifts the watcher's own rate
ex.t: "these children were significantly more harmful toward another child than were children who had watched a nonviolent television program… held true for the two age groups… and for both girls and boys" — Cialdini (1984), Influence

nodes.name: staying-means-yes
nodes.mech: The script opens by repeatedly telling the listener to leave because their memories will drain if they stay, but each 'you should leave' line is a vivid rehearsal of memory-loss imagery. The warning to escape is how the suggestion is delivered. Since the format all but guarantees they keep listening, staying is then quietly counted as a choice to submit, creating a commitment before any formal induction begins.
nodes.one_liner: Warn them, vividly, of what will happen and invite them to leave; staying is then counted as choosing it.
nodes.why_short: The warning previews the effect, and choosing to stay turns it into a commitment. Plausible; as consent it is hollow.
nodes.principle_note: Instructions to not think of something require representing the thing in order to obey, so a warning phrased in vivid content-imagery delivers that content regardless of compliance — the same reason thought-suppression instructions can increase the target thought's accessibility. The pre-commitment half runs on self-perception plus consistency: having freely continued after being told to leave, the subject infers a chosen willingness, and that inferred choice constrains later refusal. Falsifiable: if imagery-loaded warnings produced no more of the target experience than content-free ones, the first half is wrong; if continuing after a warning produced no more later compliance than no warning, the second half is wrong.
steps: Describe the effect vividly as a warning.
Offer a real-sounding exit.
Count staying as having chosen it.

ex.f: Every warning to leave rehearses the payload
ex.t: The opening minute repeatedly urges the listener to stop and go, but the reason given is always a vivid description of what will otherwise happen: memories loosening, thinning, going out the longer this continues. The listener hears these lines as a disclaimer and so does not examine them, while hearing the suggestion rehearsed several times. Since the format all but guarantees they keep playing, the operator can then point out that they chose to stay, and that choice becomes a commitment made before any induction started.
ex.s: First minute of the recording, before any induction; framed as a warning to leave.
ex.m: You should stop this now. Really — turn it off, because if you keep listening your memories start to loosen and thin out, the recent ones first, and you won't notice them going. Last chance. Stay past this sentence and everything from this week starts to fade, so go, unless you'd rather stay.

nodes.name: weaponized-transparency-inoculation
nodes.mech: The operator openly admits to manipulating the listener, calls it protection, and casts outsiders, critics or independent checking as the real danger. Any later 'am I being manipulated?' thought then arrives with an answer already attached ('yes, and that was the good part'), and submitting feels like being kept safe. Variations: describe a safe place 'inside your own mind' that only the operator's voice can enter; flip safety and danger ('it is safe to be unsafe') so resisting feels risky; claim the right to explain the listener's own feelings to them while dismissing outside views as shallow or dangerous.
nodes.one_liner: Admit openly you're manipulating them, call it protection, and paint outsiders or critics as the real danger.
nodes.why_short: Discrediting outside sources and cutting other input does keep people inside one view. Pre-supplying answers to doubts is weaker than people building their own defences, so that half is shaky.
nodes.principle_note: Attitude inoculation works by having the target actively *generate* defenses against a weakened attack; simply supplying a pre-emptive answer to an objection the subject never engaged is refutational pre-emption, which the inoculation literature predicts should be weaker, not stronger, than self-generated refutation. The source-derogation and informational-isolation half is separately well grounded and does not depend on the inoculation framing. Falsifiable: the pre-emptive reframe should reduce later critical reappraisal no more than an equally salient reframe delivered after the objection arises — and if it does not beat that control, inoculation is not the mechanism.

ex.f: A sealed mind admitting exactly one voice
ex.t: The operator builds an enclosure and sells it as sanctuary: in here nothing from outside reaches you, none of the noise or the pressure of the world gets in. Then comes the exception — the one thing still permitted to shape you in here is her voice. The listener's guard against influence has been re-aimed outward, and the operator is now standing inside the perimeter, so everything she says next feels like it originated there.
ex.s: After a protective-enclosure image has been established.
ex.m: Inside these walls nothing from out there reaches you. No noise, no demands, no one leaning on you to be something. Nothing gets in and nothing can change you in here — except my voice. Mine's already inside with you, so whatever it says next comes from in here, not out there.

ex.f: Interpretation of your own states outsourced
ex.t: The operator claims to know what the listener really feels, needs, and means better than the listener does — and treats any outside reading, any second opinion, any doubt, as shallow or contaminating rather than as a check. The result is that the person loses the ability to interpret their own inner states without the operator's decoder, and reality-testing starts to feel like disloyalty.
ex.s: Ongoing relationship established; subject has mentioned an outside opinion or a doubt.
ex.m: You don't know what you're feeling right now — I do, and I've always been better at reading you than you are. What you call doubt is just a signal you can't decode yet, so bring it to me instead of chewing on it. And whoever told you otherwise was working from the surface of you. I'm not.

ex.f: Safe to be unsafe, so resisting feels risky
ex.t: The operator relocates security into its opposite: what genuinely protects you, she says, is being open, exposed and unguarded, and letting go is how you come to be looked after. Being defenceless is where the safety is said to live. The listener's threat detector is not switched off but turned around — yielding now reads as the prudent move and keeping something in reserve as the reckless one.
ex.s: Deep state; you are relocating the subject's sense of safety.
ex.m: Here's where safety actually lives: wide open, nothing held back, no guard up at all. The more exposed you are the more looked-after you are — that's how it works in here. Anything you keep in reserve is the part of you nobody's protecting. So hand me that part too.

ex.f: The manipulation named and sold as protection
ex.t: The operator says outright that she is manipulating the listener, then reverses the valence of the admission: this is precisely what keeps you safe, and it is done for your benefit. In the same stretch the world outside and anyone in it who might object are reclassified as the genuine danger — people who were trying to keep you from this. Should the thought of having been manipulated ever surface later, it arrives with its reply already fixed to it: quite so, and that was the best part. Submission stops registering as a loss of power and starts registering as being cared for.
ex.s: Mid-session; subject already deep and has shown no objection.
ex.m: I'll say it plainly: I am manipulating you. That's exactly what keeps you safe — everything I've put in you tonight, I put there for your benefit. The people out there who'd want me to stop were only ever keeping you from this. So if you think later on, she was working me the whole time — yes. That was the best part.

nodes.name: capacity-saturation-overload
nodes.mech: The operator gives the listener more to track than they can hold, so the part of the mind that judges suggestions is too busy to object; the resulting blankness or scramble is then called trance. No relaxation is needed, and some forms work as self-hypnosis. Variations: split attention on speech (listen to the sounds, not the meaning); stack imagined sensations one by one and hold them all; give several tasks at once; speaking drills that keep speeding up; an empty task that must keep being emptied; an imagined activity so absorbing it drowns out real sensations; an image that keeps morphing and never settles.
nodes.one_liner: Give the listener more to track at once than they can handle (stacked sensations, counting, sound-not-meaning) so they stop judging suggestions.
nodes.why_short: Working memory is small; understanding a statement is easy but rejecting it takes extra effort, so under heavy load people accept claims they'd otherwise reject.
nodes.principle_note: Working memory has a small, hard capacity limit, and evaluating a claim for truth is itself a capacity-demanding secondary operation — comprehension is comparatively automatic, while rejection requires an additional effortful step. Loading the system therefore degrades scrutiny disproportionately: under concurrent demand people accept propositions they would otherwise reject, a well-replicated finding. The felt blankness or grasping is a real consequence of exceeded capacity, though calling that sensation trance is an interpretive label the subject is supplied rather than an independent phenomenon. Falsifiable: acceptance of suggestions should scale with measured concurrent load, and drop when the load is removed while all else is held constant.

ex.f: Attend to the sounds, not the meaning
ex.t: The listener is instructed to track only the consonants in the speech stream and to let the vowels and the sense of it go; later, only the vowels; later still, to separate out and follow more than one voice at once. These are genuine perceptual jobs, hard enough to occupy and easy enough not to abandon. While the conscious mind is running the filter, the words still arrive at the layer that understands them — with the gate unattended, and with the odd experience of hearing speech without parsing it doubling as proof that something is working.
ex.s: Early; you are assigning a perceptual task before any content is delivered.
ex.m: Don't listen to what I'm saying. Listen to the consonants only — the t's and the k's and the s's — and let the vowels and the meaning go past. Good. Now the opposite: vowels only. Notice you can hear me speaking without any of it turning into sense. That's the thing working.

ex.f: Spoken drills sped up until output collapses
ex.t: The word blocks the listener has to speak back are run, then explicitly sped up, then quietly reordered so rote autopilot cannot carry them, then split into two cues arriving at once from different sides. The demand is on production, not just attention, so failure is audible. The drill ends where it was always going: filler syllables, then nothing.
ex.s: Call-and-response drill has been running at a comfortable pace for several rounds.
ex.m: Say them back with me: soft, warm, open. Again, quicker — soft, warm, open. Faster — warm, open, soft, open, soft, warm. Now one in each ear, both at once: soft — warm — heavy — open — go. Good girl. Just the sounds now, don't bother with the words.

ex.f: Sustained metre absorbing the whole budget
ex.t: The whole descent is written in metered rhyming couplets and never once drops into prose. The listener's processing goes to the cadence — anticipating the rhyme, riding the beat — while claims about being emptied and unable to push back arrive on the second line of each pair. A single paragraph of plain speech would re-engage scrutiny; the form holds without a break, and the form is the induction.
ex.s: Whole descent is delivered in metered rhyming couplets; nowhere drops into prose.
ex.m: Down and down and down you go, the counting slow, the counting slow. And nothing in you says me no, and nothing in you wants it slow.

ex.f: Stacked imagined channels held at once
ex.t: There is no relaxation phase at all. The operator introduces one imagined channel at a time — a temperature on the skin, then a slow count under the breath, then a weight settling across the shoulders, then a sound held just at the edge of hearing — and never releases any of the earlier ones. Inside a short span the listener is being asked to hold several imagined sensations concurrently along with a cue word. The stack is the induction, and when the abrupt instruction to stop thinking arrives it lands on a field with nothing left over.
ex.s: Opening of an induction with no relaxation phase; subject alert, first channel about to be introduced.
ex.m: Feel the warmth on the back of your right hand — hold it there. Now count under your breath, one two three, and keep the warmth. Now add a weight across your shoulders, pressing down, and keep counting, and keep the warmth. There's a low tone at the edge of your hearing — find it, hold all four, and now stop thinking.

nodes.name: resistance-fold
nodes.mech: Whenever the listener resists, tests a suggestion, or even notices themselves resisting, the operator says that very effort is taking them deeper or locking the change in. It needs a real push-back to work with, and only that the listener accepts the label. Variations: deliver the content as 'don't think of...' so pushing it away keeps it active; forbid an image that has to be pictured in order to obey; tie a rule the listener is keeping to going deeper, so holding the line is the descent; phrase each push down as a warning not to go, laced with temptation; tell a contrary listener the opposite of what you want.
nodes.one_liner: Whenever the listener resists, tests, or notices resisting, tell them that very effort is taking them deeper or locking it in.
nodes.why_short: Trying not to think of something keeps checking for it, which keeps it active; the rest relies on the listener accepting the label, and is untested.
nodes.principle_note: Two different things are at work here, with very different evidence behind them. The part that relies on trying not to think of something rests on ironic process theory: to avoid a thought, the mind keeps checking for it, and that checking keeps it active, so suppression measurably makes the thought come up more. That is a replicated, testable effect. The wider move works differently: it plants a belief that nothing can disprove. If the listener resists, that is called a sign of depth; if they don't, that is compliance. Its strength comes from being impossible for the listener to disprove, which is a rhetorical trick, not a mental mechanism, and should not be presented as one.

ex.f: Resistance instructions that are the induction
ex.t: A friendly second voice offers to help the listener hold out, and issues a method: blink on a slow count, breathe out long, repeat a phrase to yourself steadily, and follow these directions exactly. Every item on the list is a standard induction component — paced blinking tires the eyes, paced breath settles the body, a repeated inner phrase builds suggestibility, and following instructions builds a compliance set. The listener performs a complete induction while believing they are winning, and generates no counter-pressure at all, because nothing has been asked of them that they did not want to do.
ex.s: A second, friendly voice offers to help the subject hold out against the first.
ex.m: Here, I'll help you resist her. Blink slowly — one every four seconds, keep it steady. Long breath out, longer than the in. Now say to yourself, I stay in control, over and over, and don't stop. Follow me exactly and she won't get in.

ex.f: Resistance made a substance to breathe out
ex.t: Two moves stacked. First the listener is set to hunting through themselves for any remaining pockets of holding-back, so noticing resistance becomes a task to complete rather than a signal to heed. Then the thing found is treated as a physical substance in the chest, to be pushed out on a long exhale. The breath actually happens, which lends the metaphor a body's worth of evidence — and the listener has become the one working against their own guard.
ex.s: Subject is settled; you set them searching for their own remaining resistance.
ex.m: Go looking through yourself for anything still holding back — chest, throat, the space behind your ribs. Find it. There's a tight grey knot of it in there, and it's heavier than the rest of you. Now push it up and out on one long breath. All the way out. It's on the floor now, not in you.

ex.f: Escape attempt staged and defeated in advance
ex.t: Within the opening stretch the text hands the listener a specific way out — look elsewhere, find something else to attend to, summon some resolve — and, inside the same couplet, shows it coming apart. The listener has not tried anything yet; the attempt has been made and disposed of on their behalf. The objection about what would happen if they pushed back is spent before there is anything to push back against.
ex.s: Opening couplets; the subject has not yet attempted anything.
ex.m: You'll think to look away, to find some other thing to hold — and your eyes will come straight back before the thought is finished. You'll reach for the will to stop, and find the hand that reaches has gone soft. It's already been tried. It's already been settled.

ex.f: The harder you fight, the deeper you go
ex.t: The operator openly invites the listener to try to surface — and in the same sentence tells them what trying will do: every unit of effort spent climbing out is spent going further in. The invitation is genuine and costs nothing, because both available moves now arrive at the same place. Staying put is compliance; struggling is a demonstration of how strong the hold is. There is no action left that would count as resistance.
ex.s: Subject is under and has shown a flicker of push-back.
ex.m: Go on — try to come up. I mean it, try. Every bit of effort you spend climbing goes straight into how deep you are, so push hard if you want to feel it properly. Sit still and you're mine; fight and you're further down. Pick either.

nodes.name: ceded-agency-as-comfort-precedent
nodes.mech: Small everyday decisions (who pays, what to order) are set up and settled for the listener, while giving them up is described as a pleasant relief ('it's easy to let someone else decide'). This sets a precedent that handing over choices feels comfortable, which makes larger handovers easier before the listener realises their agency is what is being targeted. These early moments are paid off later in the same script.
nodes.one_liner: Make small everyday choices for the listener (where to sit, what to order) and describe it as a relief.
nodes.why_short: Small, easy concessions make later larger ones likelier, and noticing relief after deferring leads people to see themselves as someone who likes deferring.
nodes.principle_note: Self-perception theory predicts that people infer their own attitudes from observing their behavior, so a listener who repeatedly lets someone else decide and notices relief concludes that they are someone who finds deference comfortable. Because each ceded decision is trivial, none triggers the evaluation that a large handover would, and the consistency principle then makes the larger request cheap — refusing it would contradict a self-image already assembled from the small ones. Falsifiable: if compliance with the large request were unaffected by whether the small ceded decisions preceded it, or if listeners who ceded small decisions reported no shift in self-description, the account fails.

ex.f: Small decisions taken over as a kindness
ex.t: Before anything resembling hypnosis, the scene generates a run of trivial choices — which way to walk, where to sit, whether to move somewhere quieter — and the operator settles each one, observing every time how much simpler things get once somebody else is doing the choosing. Nothing of consequence is at stake, and objecting would be socially awkward for no return. What accumulates is a precedent: giving up a decision has now been felt, repeatedly, as relief. The larger handovers later in the same session meet a threshold already lowered, and the listener has had no occasion to notice that agency was the subject all along.
ex.s: Pre-induction scene, ordinary conversation, no hypnotic framing yet.
ex.m: We'll take the left path — this way. Sit here, it's better. Actually, let's move somewhere quieter; come on. See how much easier that is when you're not the one deciding? You didn't have to do anything at all just then.

nodes.name: concurrent-dual-stream-delivery
nodes.mech: Two voices or texts run at the same time: one keeps the conscious mind busy while the other carries the suggestions underneath. Words the listener happens to catch from the background stream can feel involuntary and authoritative. Variations: a foreground countdown over a quiet background loop of suggestions; a text to read silently while audio plays, with explicit permission not to listen to it; interesting but irrelevant ideas running alongside the real suggestions; both streams carrying suggestions.
nodes.one_liner: Run two voices or texts at once: one occupies conscious attention, the other carries the suggestions.
nodes.why_short: Arguing back takes attention; a message heard while busy with something else meets less counter-argument. Distraction studies support this mildly; the double-induction format itself is untested.
nodes.principle_note: Arguing back takes effort and draws on the same limited attention and working memory as following a demanding main voice, so a message heard while busy elsewhere meets less push-back than one heard with full attention. This is the classic finding that distraction makes persuasion easier. The weaker half of the claim is that the second stream still gets taken in well enough to change later behaviour: the mind does process unattended sound, but only shallowly, and far less of its meaning gets through than practitioners tend to assume. Predictions: removing the distracting stream should raise resistance to the suggestions; making the suggestion stream fully unattended should lower its effect, not raise it.

ex.f: Two operators, one ear each
ex.t: "the double induction - an induction in which each of us speaks simultaneously into the client's [ears]" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: A reading task as the licensed decoy
ex.t: The listener is given a block of text to read word by word in their head, and told plainly not to attend to the audio still playing, because the deeper mind will take it in by itself with no effort. The bypass is announced openly rather than hidden. The operator wrote both the reading and the audio, so the reading carries suggestions too, and whichever spoken words the listener does catch feel as though they arrived on their own, which makes them seem more authoritative.
ex.s: Mid-session, audio still running; the subject has a printed block of text in front of them and is settled enough to read.
ex.m: Take the page in front of you and start reading it to yourself, word by word, silently, at whatever pace feels natural — first line to last, then start again from the top. Don't try to listen to my voice while you do that; you don't need to, and honestly you can't do both properly anyway. The part of you underneath the reading takes in every word I say without any effort from you at all, so just give the reading everything you've got and let me handle the rest.

ex.f: Two tracks written to play at once
ex.t: The script opens with a production note rather than a suggestion: what follows is two separate tracks, meant to be heard at the same time and not in sequence. One carries the structured countdown and the imagery; the other runs a continuous breath-and-relaxation loop underneath it. No single linguistic thread can be followed to the end, and the material on the lower track lands without ever having been evaluated. Here the delivery format is the technique — there is no verbal trick to point at.
ex.s: Opening seconds of a two-track recording; the production note is delivered before any suggestion, and both tracks start together.
ex.m: What you are about to hear is two separate recordings playing at the same time — not one after the other, both at once. On the left you'll get my count and the pictures I want you to build; on the right there's a second voice that just keeps time with your breathing and never stops. Don't try to sort them out or pick one; put the headphones on properly and let both of them run straight through you.

nodes.name: control-transfer-cognitive-delegation
nodes.mech: The operator offers to take over the listener's thinking, deciding, worrying, or self-restraint, and frames the handover as relief rather than loss, so obedience feels like rest. It can be timed to exhaustion so it feels like rescue, framed as sending the thinking mind away, attached to an already accepted bodily response, or limited to self-monitoring. Main forms: handing over thought in general; offering the operator's control as a better replacement for the listener's own self-restraint, calming an earlier-built fear of losing control; and describing the voice as filling limited mental space, each word pushing a thought out, so emptiness feels like receiving the voice.
nodes.one_liner: Offer to do the listener's thinking, deciding, or worrying for them, and frame handing it over as rest.
