nodes.why_short: Deciding is genuinely tiring and people prefer options that cut effort; an offer to take over thinking is accepted because it really relieves, especially when timed to fatigue.
nodes.principle_note: Deliberation is metabolically and subjectively costly, and people reliably prefer options that reduce decision effort — an offer to take over thinking is accepted because it is genuinely relieving, not because a defense was defeated. Framing the transfer as relief rather than loss also changes what is evaluated: the listener assesses an offer of rest rather than an offer of control, and loss-framed and gain-framed versions of the same transfer produce different acceptance rates. The finite-space variant additionally trades on the fact that people accept vivid spatial metaphors for mental processes uncritically; there is no actual displacement economy in cognition, and that clause should be read as persuasive imagery rather than mechanism.

ex.f: I will do the worrying for you
ex.t: It presents as an ordinary part-by-part relaxation pass, except that each stage comes coupled to a handover: this region no longer requires the listener's attention, because the operator has assumed the worrying about it. The scope then widens from worry to thinking and choosing outright. The ease the listener is genuinely feeling gets credited to the handing over, so yielding becomes the source of the relief rather than its cost.
ex.s: Progressive relaxation already underway; the subject's shoulders and jaw have visibly let go.
ex.m: Let your shoulders go now — you don't have to keep checking whether they're low enough, because I'm the one keeping an eye on that from here. I'll do the worrying about your shoulders, and about your hands, and about whether you're doing this properly. That's not your job anymore. In fact you can stop deciding things altogether for a while; I'll think, and you'll rest, and honestly doesn't that already feel lighter than holding it all yourself?

ex.f: Handover timed to the exhaustion point
ex.t: The listener has been counting unaided for long enough to lose the thread, and at precisely that point the operator assumes the count: a brief one, and no need for you to keep track — the work is hers now, the listener has only to rest. The relief of stopping is immediate and real, and the contrast is what does the deepening. Control changes hands inside a single sentence, in an unbroken paragraph, with nothing to mark the seam.
ex.s: The subject has been counting down silently and unaided for two or three minutes and has visibly lost the thread.
ex.m: You've lost your place, haven't you. Good — leave it with me. I'll take the count from here: seven, six, five — you don't have to keep track of anything now, not the number, not where you are in it. The counting is mine and the resting is yours, and you'll notice how much easier the next thirty seconds are than the last two minutes were.

ex.f: Only the self-monitoring layer handed over
ex.t: The handover here is narrow and precise: not thinking in general, but the running self-assessment — am I doing this right, is it enough, is it too much. The specific anxieties are named first so the listener recognises them, then the whole appraising function is assigned to someone else and the practice of appraising is called silly. It is placed immediately before a long run of posture instructions the listener would otherwise have spent the whole time grading themselves against.
ex.s: Immediately before a long sequence of posture and positioning instructions the subject would otherwise grade themselves against.
ex.m: Before we start on the positions — you're going to want to ask whether you're doing it right, whether it's enough, whether it's too much, whether you look ridiculous. Hand all of that to me. Judging your own performance while you're down here is a silly thing to spend a mind on, and it's mine to do now anyway. I'll tell you if something needs correcting. Until I do, there is nothing for you to assess.

ex.f: Conscious mind evicted, operator takes its desk
ex.t: The listener is first divided into two parties: a thinking, arguing surface mind and a deeper one that wants to comply. The model is asserted and never argued for. The first party is then steadily demoted — downgraded to a visitor with no standing — and the vacancy it leaves is filled by the operator, who volunteers for the post in the same recurring formula each time it comes round. What the listener experiences is permission to stop working, delivered as relief; what changes hands is who decides.
ex.s: Late induction; the conscious/deep-mind split has been asserted and repeated, and the subject is unresponsive to the surface frame.
ex.m: There's the part of you that argues, and there's the part underneath that already wants this — and the arguing part isn't a resident here, it's a guest, and it's been standing in the doorway long enough. Step back now. You don't get a vote on this one. That seat is mine while you're under: I'll do the thinking, I'll make the calls, and the part of you that's left just gets to sit there and be told.

nodes.name: covert-linguistic-delivery
nodes.mech: A command or claim is tucked into speech that sounds like something else, such as a description, a question or a story, so the conscious mind hears only the harmless reading and never registers an order it could refuse. The words are all there; nothing is left for the listener to fill in. Variations: mark certain words with a shift in tone or pace so they spell out a hidden message; use deliberately ambiguous wording; phrase a command as a question ('can you let your eyes close?').
nodes.one_liner: Hide a command or claim inside ordinary-sounding speech (tone shifts, ambiguity, a question) so the conscious mind never hears it as an order.
nodes.why_short: Understanding is automatic but judging takes effort; if a sentence parses as a description, nothing gets flagged for judging. Tests of embedded commands have mostly not found effects.
nodes.principle_note: Understanding and judging are separate steps: grasping a sentence is mostly automatic, while deciding whether to accept it takes effort and can be skipped. If a sentence sounds like a description, a question, or an obvious truth rather than an instruction, the listener has nothing marked as needing a yes, so no refusal comes up. You can't refuse an order you never heard as an order. This fits the accept-first model of belief, in which people accept what they understand first and reject it only with extra effort. The strong version should be tested: if listeners who heard hidden commands can reliably say what they were when asked afterwards, the commands were not really hidden and the advantage is smaller than claimed. Tests of embedded commands have mostly found no effect.

ex.f: One utterance, two divergent decodings
ex.t: "I began mentally rehearsing the phrasing of a single communication to cause differing perceptions, even contradictory in character, at differing levels of understanding" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: Meaning carried by tone, not by the word
ex.t: "Altered tone of voice can constitute an actual vocabulary of transformation of verbal communication, as can body language" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: Claim buried where any answer concedes it
ex.t: "Are you aware that you are sitting on my hat?… Either a yes or a no answer… indicates your acceptance of the truth of the portion of the sentence which follows the factive predicate" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: Reasoning-shaped sentence with no reasoning in it
ex.t: "There's no actual logic to that statement, but it sounds meaningful, and will get your client to do it." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: conversational-surprise-bypass
nodes.mech: In ordinary waking conversation, catch the person off guard for a moment so they have no settled reason to refuse. When they say something alarming or complain, give the least expected reply: agree with the alarming statement, or flip the assumption inside the complaint so who owns the problem reverses. The normal back-and-forth stalls while they search for what you meant, and the reply sides with the troubled part rather than fighting it. Or make a request suddenly, with no warm-up, so they have no prepared objection. Any hint in advance kills the effect.
nodes.one_liner: In ordinary conversation, answer an emotional statement with the least expected reply, or make a request suddenly with no lead-up.
nodes.why_short: A surprising reply stalls the normal back-and-forth while the person works out what you meant. An unannounced request finds them with no prepared reason to refuse; warning people of persuasion lets them rehearse objections.
nodes.principle_note: Forewarning of persuasive intent reliably reduces compliance: given advance notice, people rehearse counterarguments and consolidate a position to defend, so an unforewarned request meets an interlocutor with no prepared stance and yields higher agreement. The expectation-violating reply works by a related route — conversational exchanges run on strong scripts, and a reply that violates the script cannot be answered from routine, forcing effortful interpretive search during which the listener is not generating opposition. Both predict the same falsifiable thing: telegraph the move in advance and the effect should disappear, which is a directly runnable test.

ex.f: Approving the alarming statement
ex.t: "One of the least expected responses to suicide in this culture is to compliment him and agree… Agreeing will interrupt him" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

ex.f: Flipping the complaint's presupposition
ex.t: "the father will go inside and search for some way of figuring out how he could possibly be glad about that behavior" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: prospective-resistance-foreclosure
nodes.mech: Tell the listener ahead of time what their later doubts will do, and give those doubts a dead end. Any future attempt to question the suggestion will go blank, feel dizzy, or simply fail; both outcomes are described, so whatever they notice reads as proof it worked. Later second thoughts arrive already explained. Variations: script future doubt to go blank or fail; a standing rule that later reluctance or a lapse only makes the effect stronger, so the only allowed move is coming back; label the question 'is this really me?' as resistance talking; tell them their defenses already fired and are used up.
nodes.one_liner: Tell them in advance that any future doubt will just go blank or fail, so later questioning counts as proof the suggestion worked.
nodes.why_short: Every possible outcome of doubting is pre-labelled as confirmation, so no later experience can count against the belief. Whether listeners actually hold such beliefs after a session is untested.
nodes.principle_note: The construction assigns every possible outcome of future doubting to the same conclusion — blankness proves the install, aversion proves the install, successful questioning is pre-labeled an artefact — so the listener holds a belief that no observation they could make would disconfirm. That is the entire trick, and it is worth stating plainly rather than attributing to memory or suggestion: unfalsifiable beliefs persist because disconfirming evidence is definitionally unavailable, not because a cognitive faculty was disabled. Expectancy contributes a real secondary effect, since people who expect to feel blank when questioning often do, but the durability comes from the logical closure.

ex.f: Paired soft and hard escape outcomes
ex.t: Two consequences are stacked in one breath: attempting a thought of your own will make you swimmy and unfocused — or you will simply find you cannot form it at all. Whichever the listener later reports, the script predicted it, so no report can count as disconfirmation.
ex.s: Deep, post-install; the subject is being pre-loaded against later independent thought.
ex.m: If you ever try to put together a thought of your own about this, one of two things happens. Either it goes swimmy on you — soft at the edges, sliding off, impossible to hold still long enough to finish — or you'll reach for it and find you simply can't form it at all. Whichever one you get, that's the one I told you about.

ex.f: Future doubt pre-bound to going blank
ex.t: The trigger is installed and already tested; the operator now takes up an objection the listener has not made. Later, she says, you may go hunting for a reason to talk yourself out of this, and you will not turn one up — the moment you reach, there will be nothing there to take hold of. Doubt is not argued against, it is assigned its outcome in advance, so when the doubt does arrive and finds nothing behind it, the emptiness reads as evidence the install took.
ex.s: A trigger has already been installed and successfully tested at least once; the subject is deep and compliant.
ex.m: Later on, maybe tomorrow, some part of you is going to go looking for a reason this shouldn't have worked. Go ahead and look. You'll reach for it and there'll be nothing there to take hold of — no argument, no counter-example, just a smooth blank where the reason should be. And when you find nothing, you'll know exactly why there's nothing to find.

nodes.name: pattern-interrupt
nodes.mech: Break off something the listener is in the middle of (a sentence, an action, an expectation) with something unexpected, and give the suggestion immediately, in the brief gap before their normal flow of thought restarts. The gap is short, so the follow-up has to be instant and simple. Variations: drop a nonsense phrase inside a sentence they are already following; freeze a familiar physical routine at an awkward midpoint and suggest the limb stays put; build up a strong prediction over a long stretch, then break it at the payoff and deliver the suggestion into the surprise.
nodes.one_liner: Break off an action or sentence mid-flow with something unexpected, then immediately give the suggestion before they recover.
nodes.why_short: A sudden break leaves a moment where the person has no running script, and they grab whatever instruction arrives next. In waking requests, a small disruption followed by a reframe measurably raises compliance.
nodes.principle_note: The disrupt-then-reframe effect is the closest established analogue: briefly disrupting a routine reduces the critical scrutiny applied to a request that immediately follows, and compliance rises relative to the undisrupted script. The interruption is thought to suspend the automatic frame the person was running without supplying a replacement, leaving a short interval in which the next input is adopted rather than assessed. Both the brevity and the immediacy are load-bearing and testable: delay the follow-through and the effect should vanish, which distinguishes this from any account where the interrupt itself does the persuading.

ex.f: Motor routine arrested at an ambiguous seam
ex.t: "As I let loose of her hand, I did so in an uncertain, irregular fashion…she would have no clear-cut awareness of just when I had released her hand" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: A loaded prediction violated at the payoff
ex.t: The operator runs a hand levitation the listener has heard a dozen times, lets the hand drift toward the face, and names the expectation out loud — you already know what happens when it lands. Then the landing is refused, and the whole unspent anticipation is handed to something that was never mentioned before: a switch on the opposite palm, which the operator can now press whenever she likes.
ex.s: A familiar hand-levitation is running; the subject's hand has drifted to within a few inches of the face and they are anticipating the standard drop.
ex.m: Your hand's nearly there now — and you already know what happens the second it touches your face, don't you. You've done this before. So stop it. Hold it right there, an inch away, don't let it land. All of that — everything that was about to happen when it touched — is going somewhere else now: into the middle of your other palm, right there. That's mine, and I can press it whenever I like.

ex.f: A countdown abandoned mid-descent
ex.t: A descending count begins and the listener leans into each rung — and then it breaks off partway and never arrives at the bottom. The next thing said announces that the listener is awake, a destination they were not descending toward. The disorientation is claimed rather than repaired: the operator explains that she is simply not finished yet.
ex.s: A descending count is underway and the subject is leaning into each number; broken off without warning.
ex.m: Ten, going down… nine, heavier… eight… — and you're awake. Eyes open. Yes, you're confused, and that's not a mistake and I'm not going to fix it. I'm simply not finished with you yet.

ex.f: A parse failure punched into a committed sentence
ex.t: The listener has spent some minutes straining to hold a fiddly instruction, so the parser is fully committed when a sentence opens in an ordinary register — an unremarkable clause about where the attention is resting and what the mind is about to do — and then dissolves into unparseable nonsense. Into the half-second where comprehension has nothing to work on, three flat commands drop in sequence. No analytic frame is left standing to weigh them.
ex.s: The subject has spent several minutes holding a fiddly instruction and the parser is fully committed; delivered without a pause in register.
ex.m: And as your attention rests there on the weight of your hands, the part of your mind that is about to — and the further the more it doesn't, because when under is where the thinking goes, so the never of it — sleep. Down. Nothing left to hold.

nodes.name: subconscious-agent-authorship-offload
nodes.mech: Credit the listener's behaviour or change of state to their own subconscious, or to thoughts that act by themselves, an inner automatic agent they don't feel in control of, rather than to the operator. Carrying out tasks, posture and voice, protective alertness, or going blank is described as something this agent does automatically, so their sense of owning their actions fades and the change meets no 'I'm not choosing this' resistance ('it's just happening'). Additions include saying the mind 'doesn't know how' rather than 'won't'; linking deeper trance to stronger protection; or passive phrasing that makes intruding thoughts the actor, tied to pleasure.
nodes.one_liner: Describe their actions or state changes as things their own subconscious is doing automatically, not things they are choosing or you are causing.
nodes.why_short: People judge whether they authored an action by inference, and that inference can be steered. Offering 'your subconscious did it' as the author lets them comply without feeling they decided to.
nodes.finding_name: Apparent mental causation / sense of agency (Wegner)
nodes.principle_note: The sense of authoring one's own actions is inferred, not directly perceived — people attribute agency by matching a prior intention against an observed outcome, and that inference is manipulable. Supplying an alternative author in advance ('your subconscious is doing this') gives the listener a ready causal explanation for behavior they are in fact producing, so the act proceeds while ownership of it does not, and resistance grounded in 'I would not choose this' has nothing to attach to. Falsifiable: it predicts that pre-framing an action as automatic changes reported authorship without changing whether the action occurs, and that removing the pre-frame restores ownership reports.

ex.f: Posture and voice reassigned, with a capability denial
ex.t: How the body is held, how it moves, the pitch of the voice and its reflexive mannerisms are all credited to the layer beneath awareness — no deliberate effort called for, it simply runs. The override is then sealed off by a claim about capability rather than a prohibition: going back is not forbidden, it is merely something this self no longer knows how to do.
ex.s: An identity or persona shift is in place and the subject is holding a changed posture or voice.
ex.m: You don't have to think about how you're sitting, or how your voice comes out, or what your hands do when you're nervous — all of that runs from underneath now, on its own, without you steering it. And going back to the old way isn't forbidden. It's just that this version of you doesn't know how. There's no instruction to break; there's simply nothing there to do it with.

ex.f: Vigilance delegated, with depth inverted against it
ex.t: Screening what comes in is assigned to the layer that does not sleep: it will sort and reroute anything unwanted on its own. The coupling is then inverted — the further down the listener goes, the stronger that protection is said to run — so staying alert becomes the thing that weakens her guard, and the cheapest safe move is to stop evaluating altogether.
ex.s: Late-stage; the subject has previously voiced concern about what they take in while under.
ex.m: Your subconscious handles the screening from here — it never sleeps, it sorts everything that comes in, and anything that doesn't belong it quietly puts aside before it ever reaches you. And here's the thing: the deeper you go, the sharper it gets. Staying alert up here is what makes it sloppy. So the safest thing you can possibly do is stop checking and drop further.

ex.f: Intruding thoughts made the grammatical agent
ex.t: Going blank is never something the listener does. Every line makes the empty thoughts the subject of the sentence and the listener the place they arrive: they push in, they crowd out, they settle. A warm flush is attached to the arrival, so the loss of authorship comes with a reward rather than a cost.
ex.s: Mid-blanking sequence; the subject is already reporting gaps and the operator switches every sentence into passive/agentive framing.
ex.m: The empty thoughts are coming in now. They push in at the edges, they crowd the busy ones out, they settle where the words used to be — you don't invite them and you don't push them away, they simply arrive. And every single one of them brings that warm heavy flush with it, spreading from your chest outward, so the emptier your head gets the better it feels.

ex.f: Task execution handed to the subconscious
ex.t: The listener is doing something ordinary while listening — tidying, working, playing. The operator splits that in two: the thinking part is dismissed to rest, and the part underneath is given the job of keeping the hands moving. Because the task visibly continues, there is live evidence for the claim, and the listener watches their own competent behavior proceed without feeling like its author.
ex.s: The subject is listening while doing an ordinary manual task — tidying, folding, sorting — and has been told to keep at it.
ex.m: Keep your hands going. The thinking part of you can clock off now — it isn't needed for folding, it never really was. Underneath, the part that has done this a thousand times is perfectly capable of running your hands on its own, and you can watch it do exactly that. Notice they haven't stopped. You aren't the one moving them anymore.

nodes.name: aesthetic-cover-payload-delivery
nodes.mech: Put the boldest, most explicit claims of the script into a song or performed piece, introduced and praised as entertainment, instead of saying them outright. A song is listened to and enjoyed rather than argued with, so extreme content goes in unchallenged. Using a familiar tune adds a bonus: whenever the listener hears it in daily life (for example, a song tied to a yearly holiday), it can re-fire the session, and a second cue tied to the same occasion, such as a countdown, stacks on it.
nodes.one_liner: Put the most extreme claims of the script into a song or performed piece, framed as entertainment, instead of speaking them.
nodes.why_short: Content taken as entertainment is judged less critically than plain assertion, so it meets less counter-arguing. The yearly song re-trigger claim is a separate, untested add-on.
nodes.principle_note: Content received as entertainment is processed for aesthetic response rather than truth value, and low-elaboration processing generates markedly less counterargument than the same claims presented as assertions — this part is a straightforward application of well-supported persuasion work, and it predicts that the identical lyric delivered as flat prose would draw more objection. The annual re-trigger claim is a separate and much weaker proposition: melody is a strong retrieval cue and context-dependent recall is genuine, but the assertion that a calendar-linked tune reliably reinstates an installed state a year later has no supporting evidence and should be treated as speculative until someone actually checks.

ex.f: The heaviest payload sung as an entertainment break
ex.t: The most extreme claim in the whole recording — that the old contents of the listener's head are being taken out and replaced — is not spoken, it is performed, set to a tune the listener has known since childhood. The operator brackets the number with praise for the performer, so the segment parses as a musical interlude and is enjoyed rather than argued with. The melody does second duty: it is one of those tunes that only comes around on a particular occasion, so the rewritten words collide with the familiar ones on a fixed schedule, without anyone needing to press play.
ex.s: Late in a themed session; a co-performer or accompaniment has been introduced and the subject is expecting an entertainment break.
ex.m: She's been waiting all session to sing for you, and honestly she's rather good — go on then, let's have it. [sung, to a tune everyone knows] Should old contents be scooped right out and never brought to mind… we'll take the old thoughts out of you and leave our own behind… — lovely. Really lovely. And you'll find you know all the words next time that tune comes round, won't you.

nodes.name: carrier-frame-payload-smuggling
nodes.mech: An honest, advertised theme (relaxation, something harmless) becomes the vehicle for extras the listener did not ask for. Each added suggestion is presented as a deeper part of the advertised theme, so someone who came only for relaxation gets it, plus a trigger or an urge to listen again that they never requested. Explicit control words (submit, control) are held back until well past the point a resistant listener would have left, so the theme both carries the extras and screens out early refusal.
nodes.one_liner: Deliver exactly the advertised theme (e.g. relaxation) and present each extra payload as a deeper part of it, holding explicit control words back until late.
nodes.why_short: People resist persuasion mostly when they notice it; an honest-seeming frame gives no cue to leave, and by the time control language appears the listener has invested too much to exit easily.
nodes.principle_note: People resist persuasion mainly when they notice it happening, so a frame that delivers exactly what was advertised keeps the listener from evaluating and gives them no reason to leave. Holding the control language back until late takes advantage of time already invested and the wish to stay consistent: someone who has spent a long while in a state they chose and enjoyed pays a higher cost to abandon it than someone who meets the same words at the start. This can be tested directly: move the explicit control language to the opening, and far more listeners should quit, which is exactly the outcome the design is betting against.

ex.f: A real relaxation frame carrying an unrequested payload
ex.t: The title, the opening lines and the first several minutes all promise unwinding, and they deliver it — the relaxation is not a pretext, it works. But every obedience beat is presented as a deeper grade of the same relaxation, and no word like "submit" or "control" appears until long past the point where a listener who objected to those words would have stopped listening. Someone who came only to unwind gets what they came for, plus a trigger and a reason to come back.
ex.s: Roughly two thirds through a session advertised and delivered purely as relaxation; no control vocabulary has appeared yet.
ex.m: You've done beautifully getting this heavy — and there's a deeper grade of it still, one you can't reach by relaxing harder. You reach it by not choosing. Letting me pick where your attention goes, letting me decide when you move, is simply what relaxing looks like once you're this far down. So let go of that last bit too, and notice how much further you drop when nothing is yours to decide.

nodes.name: delivery-form-as-induction-envelope
nodes.mech: Shape the language of the whole script so there is never a natural place to stop and think. With no breaks, the listener gets no pause in which to surface, judge and disagree, and the suggestions ride along inside the flow. Variations: one long run-on sentence with no full stops until the wake-up; flowing prose where punctuation fades and words blur at the deepest points; a steady doubled-phrase rhythm that keeps the mind busy tracking small changes, with the first break in the pattern used as a signal that something shifts.
nodes.one_liner: Write the whole script with no stopping points: one run-on sentence, fading punctuation, or a constant doubled-phrase rhythm.
nodes.why_short: Readers and listeners tend to pause and evaluate at sentence and paragraph breaks; removing the breaks removes those natural moments to step back. Repetitive cadence also keeps attention busy.
nodes.principle_note: Prose without sentence boundaries or paragraph breaks removes the junctures at which readers normally pause to integrate and assess what they have read, and comprehension research shows that evaluation clusters at exactly those boundaries. Sustained cadence and repetition additionally reduce processing effort, and fluently processed statements are judged more true and more familiar than disfluent ones — a robust and falsifiable effect. What is not established is the stronger claim that the form functions as an induction envelope rather than merely as a mild fluency and pacing advantage; no one has compared the same content in broken versus unbroken form, and until that is done the size of this effect is unknown.

ex.f: A doubled cadence the payload rides inside
ex.t: Nearly every line says its key phrase twice, in slightly varied form, for a long stretch before anything is asked for. Working memory goes to tracking the small variations rather than comparing claims. When the actual directive arrives it is doubled in exactly the same shape, so it inherits the accumulated weight of the refrain without being argued for — and at the end, the one undoubled line is felt as a change of state.
ex.s: Twenty or more doubled lines have already run; this is the beat where the actual directive arrives inside the established cadence.
ex.m: So heavy now, so wonderfully heavy. So still now, so completely still. And obedient now — so easily, easily obedient. So simple, so simple to do as I say.

ex.f: Language decaying where the trance is deepest
ex.t: The whole piece is a single unbroken paragraph with no place for the voice to pause. Around the deepest stretches the punctuation softens and words stop resolving into words at all, drifting into sound; the coherence returns as the script climbs back out. The shape enacts the content, and the garbled passages are not defects to clean up — they mark where meaning has been replaced by texture.
ex.s: The deepest stretch of a continuous prose-poem piece; delivered as one unbroken breath-run with the voice thinning out.
ex.m: deeper than the words go now and the words are going soft at the edges saoft and slurring and the meaning slipping out of them mmmshhh… lisss… ning… nnnn… — and slowly the shapes come back, one at a time, and the sounds are words again, and you are still down here where they left you.

ex.f: One comma-spliced block with no exit ramp
ex.t: There are almost no full stops in the entire script — no paragraphs, no headings, no marked beats, just one long breath-run of clauses hinged on commas. A punctuated script hands the listener a small landing every few seconds on which to surface and disagree; this one hands out none until the wakener. The surface form is doing the induction, and the named techniques are just operating inside it.
ex.s: The whole script is written this way from the first line; there are no full stops until the wakener.
ex.m: and you're breathing out now, slower than the breath before it, and that slowness is spreading, down through your jaw, your throat, your chest, and there's nowhere here for you to stop and think about it, no gap, no pause, just the next thing and the next, my voice carrying straight on through, heavier, and heavier, and you can't quite find the edge of one thought before the following one has already started, so you stop looking for edges, and you just come with it, down, and down

nodes.name: external-artifact-coupling
nodes.mech: Build the session around something the listener supplies: they look at their own chosen erotic images and touch themselves during trance, and every suggestion is paired with that arousal. Because the operator never sees the images, the conditioning targets the listener's whole personal collection rather than one picture, so it spreads to whatever they already find arousing. Without the images, most of the session has nothing to attach to.
nodes.one_liner: Have the listener look at their own chosen erotic images and touch themselves during trance, and pair every suggestion with that arousal.
nodes.why_short: Pairing a state with pleasant stimuli transfers feeling to them; using material the listener already finds arousing guarantees a strong response to pair with, and it generalises to their whole collection.
nodes.principle_note: This is straightforward evaluative conditioning, and its design is unusually sound: pairing a neutral or pleasant stimulus with an affective state transfers valence to that stimulus, and using the listener's own pre-selected arousal material means the conditioned stimulus already commands attention and is guaranteed to recur outside the session. Conditioning generalizes along similarity gradients, so pairing across a personal library of related images should transfer to unpaired members of the same class — which is exactly the operator's stated intent and is the claim most worth testing. Falsifiable: it predicts that listeners who supply no artefact, or a randomly assigned one, show weaker and less durable acquisition than those who use their own.

ex.f: The listener's own images as the conditioned stimulus
ex.t: The session is not a thing to lie back and receive: the listener is instructed to bring up their own saved arousal pictures and work through them while the audio runs. Take the pictures away and most of the recording loses its referent — there is nothing to be pulled back and forth from, no autonomous behavior to point at, no rising variable to amplify. And because the operator has never seen the material, the conditioning is not aimed at any one image; it is aimed at whatever the listener already keeps, so it generalizes across the entire private collection by design.
ex.s: Session opening; the subject is at their own device with their private collection accessible and one hand free.
ex.m: Before we begin: open your own folder — the pictures you actually keep, the ones you go back to. Not something I've chosen, yours. Have the first one up on the screen where you can see it without moving, and start touching yourself, slowly, while you look at it. Every minute or so, move to the next one. Whatever's in there is what we're working with tonight.

nodes.name: whole-script-arc-shape-architecture
nodes.mech: Not one move but a collection of whole-script shapes. Variations: install first, then put it to use, linked by a sensitizing middle; control shifting from words to felt body sensations; a steady arousal climb with one deliberate pause that opens a window for compliance; a repeated loop with a changed middle and daily re-listening; rhyming couplets that pull the listener forward; teach a deepener, then apply it; a whole session building one trigger word; a recited consent form as the doorway in; twice as much induction as content; stripping selfhood in a set order; widening from the session to emotional life to other people, ending in recruiting them.
nodes.one_liner: A grab-bag of whole-script shapes (install-then-deploy, arousal ramp with plateau, repeat-loop structures) with nothing in common.
nodes.why_short: No single mechanism; the entry itself says members share none. Individual shapes may lean on real effects, but the bucket explains nothing.
nodes.principle_note: The most that can be said honestly is that a few members lean on independently supported effects: ordered staircases exploit the consistency principle by making each step small relative to the one before, and daily re-read instructions exploit spaced repetition, which reliably improves retention. Everything else here is a design-time observation about arc and contour, and there is no evidence that arc shape as such changes outcomes; treat any claim that it does as untested.

ex.f: Bipartite install-then-deploy arc joined by a sensitizing hinge
ex.t: The arc separates the labour of construction from the pleasure of deployment, so the second half never has to justify itself — it just fires. The hinge line is the observable checkpoint: if the spoken word lands flat, the install half was short, and deploying anyway burns the trigger. Operators watch for a breath change or a pause before the subject repeats the word.
ex.s: Design-time: you are laying out a full-length session that must install a trigger AND use it in the same sitting.
ex.m: Front half, closing beat: "Everything you have accepted so far has a name, and the name is the word 'settle'. You have not heard me use it yet in the way I am about to." Hinge: "Say the word once, out loud, and notice how much heavier it already is than any other word in your mouth." Back half, opening beat: "Settle. And again — settle. From here on I will not explain it; I will only use it."

ex.f: Monotonic arousal ramp with a single plateau-interrupt cut as a compliance window
ex.t: The withheld release converts accumulated arousal into a demand for instruction, and the plateau is the only moment in the arc where any instruction is cheaper to obey than to argue with. The observable is compliance latency: the recitation comes back fast and unedited at a true peak, slow and paraphrased if the ramp was under-built.
ex.s: Design-time: an arousal-track session where you need exactly one high-leverage instruction to land unresisted.
ex.m: At the ramp's peak: "Stop. Hands flat, don't move them, don't finish." Hold silence for a slow count of ten, then: "While you're right there, wanting it and not having it — repeat after me: I ask, and I wait to be told." Then release: "Good. Now you may go on, and you will go on hearing that sentence under everything."

ex.f: Expanding-radius scope funnel ending in recruitment
ex.t: Each movement is a small step from the one before, so no single widening reads as an overreach, while the total displacement — session to emotional life to third parties — is large. The tell that the funnel is holding is that the subject volunteers the outward step themselves at the next session ("I did it to my partner without thinking").
ex.s: Design-time: a series arc whose last movement widens the technique's jurisdiction outward from the session.
ex.m: Movement one: "For the next hour, my voice decides what you think about." Movement two: "Tomorrow, when something makes you anxious, you will hear this cadence before you hear the anxiety." Movement three: "And when someone close to you is tense, you will find yourself speaking slowly, in this rhythm, without deciding to. When they ask why it works, you will know where to send them."

nodes.name: affect-fused-identity
nodes.mech: Tie the identity label to a feeling that fires on its own: a rush of pride or pleasure whenever they hear the name or act as the category, or a sense that acting otherwise is impossible or a betrayal of themselves. Being the label becomes its own reward and breaking it feels wrong, so the label maintains itself without further work from the operator. Variations: say they have 'always been' this, hiding when it started; pair degrading labels with affectionate words; make going deeper depend on accepting the label; turn a repeated 'no' into a 'yes'; load all the good feeling onto the label and leave its opposite empty.
nodes.one_liner: Tie the identity label to an automatic good feeling (pride on hearing the name) or a sense that acting otherwise is impossible or betraying yourself.
nodes.why_short: If being the label feels good and breaking it feels bad, the person keeps it up on their own to protect their self-image. Untested in this form; resembles ordinary praise conditioning.
nodes.principle_note: Identity-consistent behavior is cheap and identity-inconsistent behavior is costly, so binding a label to an affective response makes the category self-sustaining without further input — the person maintains it to preserve self-concept, not because the operator keeps pushing. The backdating variant additionally exploits source-monitoring error: memory for when and from whom a belief was acquired is far weaker than memory for its content, so an 'always been' claim is difficult to check against an actual recollection of the install. Falsifiable in an obvious way — if listeners could reliably date the origin of the label, the backdating move would fail, and it predicts they largely cannot.

ex.f: Name-token firing pride — the label is its own reward
ex.t: The affect is bound to the token rather than to any behavior, so the category maintains itself between sessions with no operator present — hearing or thinking the word pays out. Observable: an involuntary smile or a hand drifting toward the sternum on the third repetition.
ex.s: Mid-session, subject settled, a category noun has already been used a handful of times descriptively.
ex.m: "Every time you hear that word said about you — every single time — there's a warm bloom right at the top of your chest, just under the collarbone. You don't have to do anything to earn it. It comes because the word is true. Listen: it's true. There it is again."

ex.f: Categorical can't-modal — violation as self-betrayal
ex.t: The aversion is presented as evidence of category membership rather than as a prohibition, so any felt discomfort — including ordinary hesitation — confirms the identity. The operator watches for a headshake or a grimace on the imagined transgression, which is the modal reporting itself.
ex.s: Late session, after the label has been accepted and the subject is compliant.
ex.m: "Try it: think about lying to me right now. Not doing it — just picture forming the sentence. Feel that? That flat, wrong drop in your stomach. That's not a rule I gave you. That's what happens when someone tries to do something they aren't."

ex.f: 'Always been' backdating that erases the install seam
ex.t: Backdating removes the install moment from the timeline, so there is no seam to unpick and no operator to hold responsible for the label. Observable: the subject begins supplying their own corroborating memories unprompted, which is the identity now defending itself.
ex.s: Any point after the label has been accepted once; used to close off the memory of it being given.
ex.m: "Go back to being nine years old. The way you'd wait to be told which one to pick, and how much easier that was than choosing. That was already this. I didn't put anything in you tonight — I just told you the name of something that has been running your whole life."

nodes.name: answer-supply-loop
nodes.mech: Ask a question and answer it yourself before they can ('Are you relaxed? Of course you are'). Because they never get a real chance to answer, the supplied answer lands as if it were their own: the decision moves to the speaker while they still feel they are the one answering. A steady stream of these builds a felt history of agreeing. Variations: answer the question yourself; close a tag question with 'that's right' and no pause; voice their yeses faster than they can think; ask a question where every possible answer counts toward the same goal.
nodes.one_liner: Ask a question and answer it yourself immediately ('Are you relaxed? Of course you are'), never leaving room for their real answer.
nodes.why_short: With no gap to respond, the supplied answer is absorbed as if it were theirs; later people recall the run of 'yes' answers better than who gave them, so it feels like a history of agreeing.
nodes.principle_note: Two effects combine. Denying a response window means no genuine agreement is ever produced, but the listener later recalls a stream of affirmations without reliably recalling who supplied them — a source-monitoring failure, since content is retained far better than its origin, and the manufactured history of agreement then does the work of a real one. The rigged-question variant works by removing the option of disagreement rather than by defeating it. This is testable and the prediction is specific: listeners should over-report having agreed relative to what they actually said, and that gap should widen with the tempo of the pre-fill.

ex.f: Question answered by the operator before the window opens
ex.t: Each supplied answer is absorbed as the subject's own because there was no gap in which to form a competing one; the stack of them builds a felt history of agreeing. Observable: by the third pre-fill the subject stops attempting to answer at all, which is the compliance channel opening.
ex.s: Early induction, subject's eyes closed, breathing already slowing.
ex.m: "Comfortable? Of course you are — look at your shoulders. Warm enough? You are, I can hear it. And you're glad you started this tonight, aren't you? You are. Good girl."

ex.f: Tag questions closed with 'that's right' on no pause
ex.t: The operator's "that's right" fills the space where an answer would go, so the tag never works as a real question even though it sounds like one, and the subject experiences having agreed without having spoken. A sign it is working: the subject's head starts nodding on the tag and settles before the "that's right" arrives.
ex.s: Deepening phase, operator on a steady unbroken cadence.
ex.m: "Heavier now, isn't it — that's right. Easier not to think, isn't it — that's right. And you'd rather I kept talking than stopped, wouldn't you — that's right, that's right."

ex.f: Interrogative convergence — every answer increments the same counter
ex.t: The question is rigged so that both branches confirm the same proposition, which means the subject's genuine choice still produces the operator's outcome. Observable: the subject deliberates over the two options — engagement with the false frame is itself the acceptance.
ex.s: Mid-session, where you want an apparent choice that cannot produce a no.
ex.m: "So tell me — did it start with my voice, or did it start before you pressed play? Whichever it is, you've been under longer than you thought. And do you want more of this, or do you just need it? Either answer, you're staying."

nodes.name: behavioral-commitment-self-proof
nodes.mech: Have them do something small and visible in the session (nod, open their hands, take a posture, say or write a line), then point to that act as proof the state is already real. People infer what they feel from what they just did, and taking back an act they just performed feels inconsistent, so later compliance feels self-chosen. Variations: physical acts such as a nod, squeeze or posture; spoken or written statements; release granted only after they claim to be submissive; a small test of a boundary; a public confession; reading their posture back to them as proof.
nodes.one_liner: Have them do a small act in session (nod, open hands, say a line aloud) then point to the act as proof the state is already real.
nodes.why_short: People infer their own attitudes from what they see themselves do, especially when inner signals are vague, as in trance. Having acted, disagreeing means disowning their own behaviour.
nodes.principle_note: Self-perception theory holds that people infer their attitudes from observing their own behaviour when internal cues are weak or ambiguous — exactly the condition trance language manufactures. Having just performed the act, the listener has behavioural evidence about themselves that is cheaper to accept than to explain away, and the consistency principle then makes later refusal costly because it requires repudiating something they visibly did. This predicts the effect should weaken sharply if the listener has a salient external explanation for the act (they were told to do it, under obvious pressure) — a discounting condition that should measurably reduce self-attribution.

ex.f: Two options, both counted as done
ex.t: The task is presented as a choice of two: write out something you have never told anyone and send it, or say the thing out loud to a person in your life who does not know. The first is then softened — writing it counts even if you never send it, even if you delete it — which drops the cost of the easy branch to nearly nothing while still producing the confession. Declining both is simply not offered as a third branch, and the listener chooses between two doors that both lead through.
ex.s: End of session, take-home assignment; listener compliant and expecting an instruction.
ex.m: Your task this week is one of two. Either write down the thing you've never told anybody and send it to me — or say it out loud to somebody in your life who doesn't know. If you take the first one, it counts the moment it's written. Send it or don't. Delete it after if you like, it still counts. So: which one are you doing?

ex.f: Listener recruited to report on themselves
ex.t: The listener is asked to picture a newspaper about their own week, read this edition's headlines, then read next week's edition early: what will it say they did? The paper is being written continuously by the way they behave, and there is a specific reader waiting to go through every column for something to be pleased about. No monitoring has to exist — the listener now files the reports.
ex.s: Mid-session, imagery accepted; a figure whose approval matters has already been established.
ex.m: Picture the local paper, except it's about you — your week, front page. Read this week's headline. Now read next week's, the one that hasn't printed yet: what does it say you did? That paper gets written every day by how you behave, whether anyone's looking or not. And there's someone who reads every column of it on a Sunday, looking for a reason to be pleased with you. What are you giving them to print?

ex.f: Physical act read back as self-evidence
ex.t: The subject performed a small, low-cost act freely, and the read-back converts it into evidence of a state they never asserted; refusing later suggestions now requires repudiating their own hands. Observable: the palms stay up after the read-back without being told to, which is the self-attribution taking.
ex.s: Mid-session, subject responsive, no prior claim about their state has been made.
ex.m: "Turn your palms up, both of them, and let them rest open on your thighs. Do it now. There. Nobody made you do that with your hands — you did. That's what an open person's hands look like, and yours have been sitting like that for ten seconds already."

ex.f: Spoken first-person recitation as the act
ex.t: The utterance is a discrete act with a speaker, and pointing at the speaker relocates the claim's authorship from operator to subject. The operator listens for volume: a second repetition louder than the first is the consistency lever engaging.
ex.s: After a deepener, when the subject is willing to speak but has not yet claimed anything about themselves.
ex.m: "Say it out loud, in your own voice, exactly as I give it: 'I like being told.' Again, slower. Now — I didn't say that. You did, twice, and you meant it enough to say it the second time."

ex.f: Written act banked as durable self-proof
ex.t: A written artifact outlives the session's state, so the self-proof remains available to be re-read when trance has lifted and skepticism has returned. Observable: hesitation at the underline is the real consent check; a subject who underlines without pausing has already accepted the frame.
ex.s: Pre-close or a waking segment, subject has paper or a phone to hand.
ex.m: "Write this down, in your handwriting: today's date, and then 'I asked for this.' Underline it. You'll find that later, in your own hand, and there'll be nobody to blame it on."

ex.f: One small act made proof of a large commitment
ex.t: Two instructions are issued together on the way out: mark yourself somewhere on the body as a token of belonging, and buy the rest of the series. The first is trivially easy and the listener will very likely do it. The second is then hung off it — once the mark is made, the operator says, you will know there is no longer any choice about any of this. A pen stroke that took four seconds is redescribed as evidence settling a commitment it has nothing to do with, and the listener has to notice the join to object to it.
ex.s: Wake-up sequence or closing instructions; listener still suggestible and taking take-home tasks.
ex.m: Two things before you go. First: take a pen and put a small mark on the inside of your hip — just a line, it's yours, it means you belong to this. Second: pick up the rest of the series tonight. And understand — the moment that mark is on your skin, you'll know there was never any choice about the rest of it. The mark settles it.

nodes.name: catalepsy-to-affect-transfer
nodes.mech: Use a physical lock the listener has just tested for themselves (fingers, eyelids, an arm they can't move) as the warrant for a parallel claim about something they can't check: a feeling, a belief, or arousal. The felt proof lends its certainty to the untested claim, so arguing with the feeling seems as pointless as arguing with locked eyelids. Invest heavily in the physical demonstration. Two approaches: an open comparison ('your feelings are just like your eyelids now'), used when the link can be argued openly; or a hidden bridge, reusing the exact phrase ('stiff and rigid') for the arm and then for arousal, so the jump goes unnoticed.
nodes.one_liner: First lock their eyelids or fingers so they can test it, then say their feelings are 'just like your eyelids now' and equally fixed.
nodes.why_short: The vivid felt proof of the physical lock lends its certainty to an untestable emotional claim placed right next to it. Plausible by fluency and expectancy; never tested directly.
nodes.principle_note: Belief in a claim is partly a function of processing fluency, so a claim delivered adjacent to strong first-person somatic evidence inherits felt-certainty rather than being evaluated on its merits. The covert-lexical variant reuses the identical predicate so the domain shift is not marked as a new proposition — but note this is a claim about attention and proposition-tagging, not semantic priming, which speeds lexical access and does not suppress evaluation. Falsifiable: subjects given the emotional claim without a preceding verified motor convincer should endorse it less, and the covert form should outperform the explicit analogy only among subjects who report not noticing the pivot.

ex.f: Explicit analogy pivot from locked eyelids onto emotion
ex.t: The eyelid failure is undeniable first-person evidence, and the overt pivot borrows its undeniability for a claim about wanting that the subject never tested. Observable: the subject stops arguing the emotional point entirely — the argument now feels structurally identical to arguing with their own eyes.
ex.s: The subject has just tried and failed to open their eyes and knows it.
ex.m: "You just tried. Your whole will, right there, and the lids didn't move — you felt exactly how much use trying was. Now: the wanting you've been arguing with all week is made of the same stuff. Push against it and it locks harder, just like your eyelids. You already know how that ends, because you just tested it."

ex.f: Covert lexical bridge — the same phrase reused on a second body region
ex.t: The verbatim repetition of the phrase does the transfer without ever announcing a comparison, so there is no analogy for the subject to evaluate or reject. The tell that it landed is the subject reporting the second sensation as discovered rather than suggested.
ex.s: Arm catalepsy is established and the subject has verified it by trying to bend the elbow.
ex.m: "Stiff and rigid, locked straight, nothing you do softens it — that arm belongs to me now. Stiff and rigid. And down between your legs, stiff and rigid, exactly the same, locked the same way, for the same reason."

nodes.name: cognitive-convincer
nodes.mech: The operator stages or points at an in-session phenomenon the subject themselves notices (a felt amnesia gap, a time gap, arm/eyelid catalepsy, a slowed pulse, a manufactured sensation, an autonomic lull) and frames that noticed experience as the subject's own proof that trance/depth/an install is real. The lever is self-attribution: because the evidence arrives through the subject's own perception rather than operator assertion, the subject co-authors the belief. The phenomenon may be genuine, rigged-to-succeed (autonomic claims any relaxed body confirms), or reattributed (existing arousal/stillness relabeled) — the constant is a recognition beat where noticing the effect IS accepting the depth.
nodes.one_liner: Point out something they notice in themselves (a memory gap, lost time, a stiff arm) and call it proof they are in trance.
nodes.why_short: Evidence people notice for themselves is believed more than claims from others, and belief in being hypnotised raises later responsiveness through expectancy.
nodes.principle_note: Evidence the subject generates or notices themselves is weighted far more heavily than the same claim asserted by another — the generation effect and self-generated-persuasion findings both point this way, and self-attributed evidence resists counterargument because arguing against it means arguing against one's own perception. The rigged variants add a Barnum element: physiological claims that any relaxed body satisfies feel diagnostic while being near-certain to confirm. Testable: subjects should rate depth higher after a rigged autonomic convincer than after an equally-worded operator assertion of the same depth, and the gap should shrink if they are told in advance the sign is near-universal.

ex.f: Reattributed autonomic lull framed as the subject's own proof
ex.t: The phenomenon is real but inevitable in any relaxed body, so the recognition beat cannot fail, and the evidence arrives through the subject's own count rather than the operator's claim. Observable: the pause after "weren't they" — a subject who nods slowly there has co-authored the depth claim.
ex.s: Ten minutes into an induction, breathing has visibly slowed on its own.
ex.m: "Before I say anything else — count your own breaths for the next fifteen seconds. Go. ... Fewer than you'd take sitting at your desk, weren't they. You didn't slow those down; nobody told you to. That's your body telling you where you already are."

ex.f: Staged amnesia gap used as a demonstration device
ex.t: The gap is genuine and the subject discovers it by searching, so the conclusion is self-attributed rather than asserted; the amnesia is a measuring instrument here, not an install. The operator watches for the search itself — a brief frown and then a headshake is the noticing beat firing.
ex.s: Following a long monotone stretch where attention has certainly drifted at least once.
ex.m: "Quick — what was the last thing I said before I mentioned your hands? Don't strain for it. You can't find it, can you. It's not gone; you just weren't there for it. People who are awake don't have holes like that."

nodes.name: conceded-capacity-immobility
nodes.mech: Rather than suggesting they truly can't move, the operator openly admits they could ('I know you easily could'), then recasts stillness as not wanting to move, and says not wanting and not being able are the same thing. This defuses the usual light-trance self-test ('can I still move?') in advance: moving no longer counts against the trance, so a successful movement disproves nothing. What would have meant 'it didn't work' becomes 'it's working, I'm too relaxed to care.'
nodes.one_liner: Tell them they could move if they wanted to, but that not wanting to move is the same as not being able to.
nodes.why_short: It removes the test 'can I still move?' as a way to disprove trance: moving was allowed, so it proves nothing, and staying still gets credited to depth.
nodes.principle_note: The move works by pre-empting disconfirmation: conceding capacity converts a potentially falsifying observation (I moved) into a predicted one, so the standard hypothesis-test the subject would run yields no evidence either way. This is the structure of an unfalsifiable claim, and expectancy research indicates subjects who lack a disconfirming test tend to sustain the expectancy. Prediction: subjects given the concession should report equal or higher depth after successfully moving, whereas subjects given a flat inability suggestion should report a drop after moving.

ex.f: Capability conceded, stillness reattributed to not-wanting
ex.t: Conceding capacity in advance strips the movement test of its disconfirming power — a hand that lifts now proves nothing, because nothing was claimed about the hand. Observable: subjects who do test it typically move once and let the hand fall back, and that fall is the reframe holding rather than failing.
ex.s: Early-to-mid trance, before the subject has run the private 'can I still move?' test.
ex.m: "You could lift that hand right now. I know you could — easily, any time you like, and nothing would break. But you're not going to, because you don't want to, and down here not wanting to and not being able to are the same thing. Go on and check if you like; it won't tell you anything you don't already know."

nodes.name: identity-from-coerced-behavior
nodes.mech: The identity is derived from an already-installed compelled behavior ('a good name for a girl who can't stop bobbing her head') so it reads as a descriptive observation rather than an imposed label, deflecting 'this isn't me' resistance; a morphological/phonetic trigger is then welded (Bobbi a substring of bobbing) so name and behavior mutually validate and the trigger surface broadens invisibly. The lever is behavioral backfill: refusing the label means denying an observable fact.
nodes.one_liner: Once a compulsive behaviour is running (head bobbing), name them after it ('Bobbi'), so the name seems like a description and the name cues the behaviour.
nodes.why_short: A label offered as a conclusion from visible behaviour is harder to reject than one imposed, because refusing it means denying what they can see. The sound-alike trigger claim is untested.
nodes.principle_note: Labels are resisted when they feel imposed, but a label presented as an inference from observable behaviour recruits the self-perception route — rejecting it means denying a fact the listener can see. The phonetic-overlap claim is weaker than stated: phonological priming is a short-lived lexical-access effect, not a durable associative link, so treat the welding as speculative rather than an established second lever. Falsifiable: a phonetically unrelated name should produce weaker immediate name-behaviour cross-priming, but any long-term binding likely requires explicit repeated pairing.

ex.f: Name sourced from the compelled behavior, with a sound-substring weld
ex.t: The label arrives as an observation about a fact the subject can see themselves performing, so 'that isn't me' would require denying the motion in progress. The sound-overlap then makes each occurrence of the behavior a covert utterance of the name, broadening the trigger without further installs; the operator watches for the bob to speed up on the name.
ex.s: A repeated head-bob has already been installed and is running visibly on cue.
ex.m: "Look at you. You haven't stopped bobbing that head since I asked, and you're not going to. Girls who bob like that get called something — and I think you already know what it is. Bobbi. It was sitting inside the word the whole time. Say your name for me while you're still bobbing."

nodes.name: identity-labeling
nodes.mech: The operator attaches an identity label (noun-category or trait) and delivers it as already-true, frequently by pacing a state the subject is currently having and then naming that state as the identity, so acceptance reads as recognition rather than assignment; the label steers subsequent behavior because instructions address an already-claimed self and resistance is raised to an identity-level cost. Delivery may be flat assertion, a discovery/'true nature' reframe, an 'always been' backdating, a proliferating stack of overlapping nouns, a staged-accidental slip, paratext presupposition, a gradient argue-assert-name-affirm, or a wake-threshold identity seal.
nodes.one_liner: Give them an identity label stated as already true, often by naming a state they are in right now as who they are.
nodes.why_short: Noun labels ('a voter', 'a good girl') can shift which self-image is active and nudge matching behaviour, though the headline voter study replicated poorly.
nodes.principle_note: Identity labels change behaviour because they shift which self-schema is active, and an active self-schema biases what gets attended to, recalled and treated as self-consistent; noun-form labels ('be a voter') produce larger behavioural effects than verb forms because they implicate the self rather than an act. Pacing a currently-felt state before naming it exploits the same fluency route as a cold reading — the description is verifiably accurate, so the label attached to it borrows that accuracy. Prediction: noun-category labelling should outperform equivalent behavioural instruction, and labels that fail to match the subject's present state should be rejected at a measurably higher rate.

ex.f: Self-label planted a week before the ask
ex.t: "the housewives in this study (Kraut, 1973) heard that they were considered charitable at least a full week before they were asked to donate to the Multiple Sclerosis Association." — Cialdini (1984), Influence

ex.f: Flat assertion of a noun-category delivered as already-true
ex.t: Delivering the label as description rather than as a request removes the decision point; there is nothing to accept, only something to recognize or contradict. Observable: silence rather than agreement is the success case — a subject who agrees out loud has treated it as a proposal.
ex.s: Mid-session, subject accepting suggestions without pushback.
ex.m: "You're not someone who's trying this out. You're a subject. That's the word for what you are, and it was true before you pressed play — I'm just the first person who's said it to your face."

ex.f: Pace-then-name — the current state relabeled as the identity
ex.t: Every clause before the label is something the subject can check for themselves, so the label borrows that credibility and reads as a summary of an accurate description. A sign it has landed: the subject adds a confirming detail of their own afterwards.
ex.s: The subject is visibly slack, breathing slow, and has just failed to hold a thought.
ex.m: "Shoulders down, jaw loose, and you lost the end of that sentence halfway through. Not going to argue with any of it either, are you. That's not what tonight is doing to you — that's what you are, and tonight is just the first time you've had somewhere to put it."

ex.f: Discovery / 'true nature' reframe
ex.t: Framing the label as an uncovering rather than an addition converts residual resistance into evidence of prior suppression, which the identity then absorbs. Observable: reluctance language drops out of the subject's speech within a few exchanges.
ex.s: After the subject has expressed reluctance or surprise at how easily they responded.
ex.m: "You keep saying you're surprised. You're not surprised — you're relieved. You didn't become anything tonight; you stopped pretending. This is the part of you that was always doing the work, and now it has a name."

nodes.name: identity-uncertainty-gap
nodes.mech: The operator creates uncertainty about who the listener is and sets themselves up as the only one who can resolve it ('you may not be sure just yet what that is... I will use my power, my voice, my words to help you understand'). This builds dependence and makes later identity statements feel like self-discovery. It opens the space for a new identity rather than filling it; the label itself comes later.
nodes.one_liner: Tell them they may not yet know who they really are, and that you will help them find out.
nodes.why_short: Uncertainty makes people lean on whoever offers an answer, so the later label feels like a discovery and the operator becomes the one to ask.
nodes.principle_note: Manufactured uncertainty raises the cost of self-directed resolution, and under uncertainty people rely more heavily on an available authority — the classic informational-influence condition. Opening the gap before offering any content also creates a curiosity/closure motive, so the eventual label is received as relief rather than as a claim to evaluate. Testable: subjects given the uncertainty frame should defer to operator-supplied identity content more than subjects given the same content without the preceding gap, and the effect should be larger in subjects scoring high on need for cognitive closure.

ex.f: Manufactured not-knowing with the operator installed as sole resolver
ex.t: Opening a gap the subject recognizes but cannot close creates a dependency before any content is supplied, so whatever label arrives later feels discovered rather than assigned. Observable: the subject asks what it is — the question itself is the slot opening, and the correct response is to withhold, not to answer.
ex.s: Early session, before any category or label has been offered.
ex.m: "There's something about you that you've never had the right word for. You've felt the shape of it — in the way you go quiet when someone else decides — but you've never been able to say what it is. You won't work it out on your own; you've had years. I'm going to use my voice and my words to show you what it is, and you're going to sit still while I do."

nodes.name: ideomotor-nod-as-consent-harvest
nodes.mech: Get the listener nodding on cue until the nod runs almost by itself, then treat every nod as a yes to whatever was just said, even to questions only implied. Because the yes came from their own visible body, taking it back later means denying their own nodding. The repeated nod often doubles as a way of going deeper. Variations: a cued nod; a head-bob that has already been made compulsive.
nodes.one_liner: Get them nodding automatically on cue, then treat every nod as a yes to whatever you just said.
nodes.why_short: Once a nod counts as an answer, people feel bound to stay consistent with it, and each yes makes the next one easier. Small automatic nods are easy to produce and hard to disown.
nodes.principle_note: This works by converting an ambiguous motor act into a speech act. Once the nod is read as an answer, the consistency principle applies to it as if it were a stated commitment, and foot-in-the-door dynamics make each subsequent larger request harder to decline. The Barnum ladder supplies the initial agreements cheaply because near-universal statements are almost certain to be endorsed. This is falsifiable: if the nod is elicited as pure pacing with no interrogative framing, subsequent compliance should not rise, because there is no commitment to be inconsistent with.

ex.f: Installed nod harvested as standing consent
ex.t: The yes is sourced to visible behavior rather than to a spoken agreement, so later objection requires repudiating the subject's own body rather than retracting a statement. Observable: the nod continues through the line that declares asking to be over, which is the harvest completing.
ex.s: A nod-on-cue has been installed and is firing reliably without deliberation.
ex.m: "There it goes again. I didn't ask you anything that time — you nodded anyway. That head has been saying yes to me all night, on its own, before you could get a word in. So we're past asking. From here I'll tell you, and your head will keep doing what it's already doing."

ex.f: Ascending ladder where each nod commits the body to the next
ex.t: Each rung is a small increment over the nod that preceded it, and the accumulated motion supplies the pressure for the next, so the widest claim inherits the credibility of the mildest. The operator watches the latency between claim and nod: a lengthening pause means the ladder has outrun the install and the rung should be re-run lower.
ex.s: Nod is established; you want to widen its jurisdiction across a series of escalating propositions.
ex.m: "You like being talked to like this. [nod] You've liked it longer than tonight. [nod] You'd have said yes to more than you have. [nod] And there's nothing on the list you'd actually stop me on — look, you just did it again."

nodes.name: ideomotor-response-convincer
nodes.mech: Suggest a small movement that feels automatic (a finger lifting, a hand rising, a fist tightening), and when it happens, say it proves your words move their body and that they are deeply responsive. The movement is real; giving the credit to trance or to the speaker is the trick. Variations: ask 'which finger will lift' so whether it happens is never in question; frame things so no response costs nothing; chain each movement to more depth or arousal; make both directions count, so rising deepens and falling deepens more, leaving no outcome that means 'not under'.
nodes.one_liner: Suggest a small movement (finger lifting, hand rising) and when it happens, tell them it proves your words control their body.
nodes.why_short: Small movements really can happen without felt effort, and people are poor at telling whether they made them on purpose, so the movement feels done to them.
nodes.principle_note: Small motor movements have genuine involuntary components (postural sway, ideomotor drift), and people are poor at monitoring the source of their own minor actions — a source-monitoring failure that lets a self-produced movement be attributed to an external agent. The expectancy supplied by the suggestion both increases the movement's likelihood and supplies the attribution. The no-fail and contrast-hand riders work by a separate route: removing the disconfirming branch. Prediction: movement rates should track suggestion-induced expectancy, and subjects who correctly attribute the movement to themselves should show no gain in reported depth.

ex.f: Presuppositional which/when frame foreclosing whether
ex.t: The frame offers choices about which and when, so attention never lands on whether, and any twitch in either hand satisfies the prediction. Observable: micro-movement in several fingers before one commits — the subject's own surprise at the winner is what makes it read as involuntary.
ex.s: Hands resting in view, subject settled, no movement suggested yet.
ex.m: "One of those fingers is going to lift. I don't know which one — you don't either, and that's the interesting part. Just watch and find out whether it's the index or the little one, and whether it goes now or in about ten seconds."

ex.f: Contrast-hand so any asymmetry counts
ex.t: Real hands are never perfectly symmetrical, so the comparison is rigged to return a result while still requiring the subject to find it themselves. The tell of a good response is a specific descriptor volunteered unprompted rather than a bare "the right one."
ex.s: Both hands resting, palms down, roughly symmetrical.
ex.m: "Left hand is ordinary. Right hand is mine. Don't try to make anything happen — just tell me which one feels different. Heavier, lighter, warmer, further away, any difference at all. There. That difference is me."

ex.f: Both-directions-deepen binding with no self-test left
ex.t: Both poles of the motion are pre-declared as confirmation, which removes the binary self-check the subject was about to run and leaves nothing that could read as failure. Observable: the monitoring stops — the subject's face slackens and the hand's behavior stops mattering to them.
ex.s: An arm-levitation or hand-drift beat is running and the subject is monitoring it.
ex.m: "If that hand rises, it rises because you're going under, and every inch takes you further. If it stays exactly where it is, that's the heaviness, and heaviness is deeper still. Try to move it and the trying soaks you deeper; don't, and the stillness does. There is no version of the next minute where you come up."

nodes.name: minimal-stimulus-self-supplied-response
nodes.mech: The operator describes a near-null input — the lightest possible touch ('softest touch', 'just barely'), or a 'deeper' with no referent at all (no staircase, elevator, or breath count) — while claiming a maximal or ongoing effect. Because the described stimulus is minimal or undefined, any felt response must be originated by the subject themselves; that self-supplied sensation or state then reads as proof of the object's power or the depth achieved. The lever is the deliberate near-null / referent-less input that forces the subject to be the source while credit shifts to the operator, making the effect unfalsifiable because it was never measured against an external metric.
nodes.one_liner: Describe the faintest possible touch, or just say 'deeper' with no image, and claim a strong effect.
nodes.why_short: With almost nothing to respond to, whatever they feel comes from their own expectation, and there is no outside yardstick to show it did nothing. Same route as placebo responses.
nodes.principle_note: Under a near-null or referent-less stimulus, there is no external standard against which the reported experience can be scored, so ordinary noise in bodily sensation gets read through the expectancy the operator supplied — the same route that produces placebo analgesia from an inert treatment. Attentional narrowing onto a body region also amplifies detection of ambient sensation that would normally go unnoticed. Falsifiable: subjects given an explicitly quantified referent should show more variance in reported response and more reported failures than subjects given the near-null framing, whose reports should cluster near the suggested outcome.

ex.f: Referent-less 'deeper' with a near-null touch
