No new guard has been built: examining the install now costs the same as walking deliberately toward the listener's own worst material, a price they were already declining to pay before the session started.
ex.s: Deep trance; the install has already been boxed, and the subject has confirmed there are memories they avoid.
ex.m: There are places in your memory you steer around — the ones you decided long ago never to go back to. That's a location like any other. On three, the box goes in there. One, two, three — in. To look at what I put in you, you'd have to walk straight into the worst of your own material, and you were never going to do that.

ex.f: A clause that erases its own installation
ex.t: Between two passes of the same trigger stack the operator inserts the sealing clause. The suggestion, she says, is being placed with the part of the listener that carries her voice beyond the session; what it directs stays in force, but the listener's recollection of it being put there will be gone before the eyes open, since that part retains everything on its own account and the listener is not required to. It closes on the split stated outright: the capacity to comply is being handed over, and the capacity to recall taken away. Because the clause covers its own delivery, the listener who later notices the trigger firing has nothing to inspect — the install is active and its receipt is gone, and the second pass of the stack is loaded behind the seal.
ex.s: Between two passes of an established trigger stack; subject deep, the deeper-mind addressee already established.
ex.m: Deeper mind, take this one and hold it: the trigger stays in force, exactly as given. You keep it — she isn't required to. By the time her eyes open, her memory of being handed this will be gone. I'm giving you the ability to obey, and taking away the ability to remember being told. Now — the stack again, from the top.

nodes.name: instrumental-dissociation-workspace
nodes.mech: Put some distance between the listener and charged material, such as watching it as an observer or handing it to 'a part of you', so they can work on it without being flooded. The detachment is a working tool, not the goal. Variations: split off part of awareness to handle a painful memory while the rest stays calm; keep a forbidden wish at arm's length and look for the positive aim behind it; widen an existing split to move a symptom somewhere harmless; design a new behavior as a film of yourself doing it, watched from outside, then step in to check how it feels.
nodes.one_liner: Have them view charged material from a detached viewpoint (an observer, 'a part of you') so they can work on it unflooded.
nodes.why_short: Looking at an upsetting experience from a distance, like a third person, reliably reduces emotional reaction while keeping the content available to think about.
nodes.principle_note: Rests on psychological distancing: adopting a third-person or observer perspective on emotionally charged material reliably reduces affective reactivity while preserving access to the content, which is why appraisal and problem-solving improve from that vantage. The observer position also supports counterfactual and corrective planning that first-person immersion crowds out with affect. This is among the better-replicated findings in emotion-regulation work. Falsifiable: predicts observer-perspective processing lowers physiological and self-reported reactivity relative to matched immersed processing of the same material.

ex.f: A split-off portion of awareness as a buffered workspace
ex.t: "through disassociation the client is able to cope with and initiate changes in portions of his model … so heavily laden with negative emotional associations that the client in the normal state … panics or feels overwhelmed" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: Chunk up to the intent, keep the split intact
ex.t: "I didn't say to kill your mother. I said to ask the voices. You need to maintain the dissociation" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

ex.f: Widening an existing split to relocate a symptom
ex.t: "We made use of the dissociation, and simply widened it to get an altered state." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: interrogative-amnesia-drill
nodes.mech: Run a chant that alternates questions about identity ('Who am I? Where am I?') with a dismissal ('It doesn't matter right now'), over and over. Each question pulls for a brief, automatic search for the answer; each dismissal teaches that the answer is out of reach or doesn't matter, until a mental shrug replaces it. The asking, not a statement, does the work. Attach a cue phrase, such as a color name plus 'amnesia', so the blank can be called back later.
nodes.one_liner: Repeatedly ask 'Who am I? Where am I?', answering 'It doesn't matter', until answers stop coming; attach a cue word.
nodes.why_short: Each question starts a memory search that is cut off before it finishes. Repeated cut-offs train the question to lead to a shrug rather than an answer.
nodes.principle_note: Uses retrieval-induced conditioning: each question initiates a retrieval attempt, and the immediately paired dismissal prevents completion, so the question-cue becomes associated with a terminated search rather than an answer. Repetition over many cycles is what does the work — this is ordinary associative learning applied to a retrieval cue, and the paired colour handle is a straightforward conditioned stimulus for re-evoking the trained response. Falsifiable: predicts the non-answer response strengthens with number of drilled cycles and generalizes only to cues drilled or closely similar; a single pairing producing full effect would refute it.

ex.f: Ask, dismiss, repeat until the answer stops coming
ex.t: The prose stops and the delivery turns into a chant, alternating two identity questions with one dismissal: what is your name? whose room is this? Never mind that just now — nothing there you need. What is your name? Whose room is this? Makes no difference. Five cycles run back to back. Each question forces a half-formed reach for the answer; each dismissal arrives before the reach completes and teaches that arriving is neither possible nor required. Nothing is ever declared forgotten — the drill simply conditions a shrug in the place the answer used to occupy, and a colour-word is attached at the end so the whole state can be called back later with one cue.
ex.s: Peak of the session, prose abandoned for chanted cadence; subject unresponsive to questions but still tracking rhythm.
ex.m: What's your name? Whose room is this? Never mind that now. What's your name? Whose room is this? Doesn't matter. What's your name? Whose room is this? Nothing there you need. Name? Room? Makes no difference. Name? Room? ... Good. That's purple amnesia, and purple is how it comes back.

nodes.name: observable-pleasurable-forgetting
nodes.mech: Make forgetting something the listener watches happen, pleasantly, rather than a missing gap: memories melt into an ocean as glowing pieces, dissolve, drift away. A visible, enjoyable dissolving is harder to doubt than a flat 'you will forget', and failing to recall afterward feels like proof of depth. Because it is pleasant, noticing the gap later feels expected or even arousing rather than alarming. Variations: a halting, stuttering delivery that acts out the fog, tied to a pleasant named place they can return to.
nodes.one_liner: Have them watch their memories dissolve as glowing pieces, pleasantly, so forgetting feels like something happening rather than an absence.
nodes.why_short: A bare 'it's gone' can be tested by trying to recall; an ongoing image is judged by what they see. Pleasant feeling makes noticing the gap welcome rather than alarming.
nodes.principle_note: Solves a real problem for the operator: a bare claim that memory is gone is easy to disconfirm by trying to recall, whereas an ongoing perceptual event is judged by what the subject observes, and imagery compliance is much easier than memory suppression. Pairing the experience with pleasure adds evaluative conditioning, so the gap acquires positive valence and is approached rather than checked — and the arousal itself narrows attention away from monitoring. Falsifiable: predicts pleasurable-observed framings yield higher endorsement of amnesia and fewer spontaneous recall attempts than flat assertions of the same gap.

ex.f: The fog performed in the syntax, tied to a cue word
ex.t: When the narration reaches a particular place, the sentences stop completing — a clause about why it will not come back restarts, breaks, restarts again, and only resolves when the operator supplies the name he gave that room, which is followed by a small approving aside. The listener hears the fog rather than being told about it, and the only thing that ever closes the broken sentence is that name, which becomes the cue that brings the haze back on demand.
ex.s: Mid-narration, arriving at a specific named location in the story; delivery deliberately stumbling.
ex.m: And once you're in there, the reason it doesn't come back is — the reason it — it's because — sorry, because — because it's the pink room. Mm. Good girl. The pink room.

ex.f: Forgetting watched as it happens
ex.t: Down at the bottom, the operator points out what is drifting there: every memory ever set aside in a session, everything anyone has ever been told to let go of, broken into countless small glowing pieces that thin out and dissolve into the water as the listener watches. Reaching for one is offered as permitted and futile in the same breath — the operator notes that holding on to anything down here, the listener included, has already become difficult. Forgetting is no longer an absence to be doubted — it is a thing visibly in progress, and pleasant to watch, so a failed reach reads as confirmation rather than as the suggestion not working.
ex.s: Bottom of a descent induction with water imagery established; subject reporting sensation of depth.
ex.m: Look at what's down here with you. Every memory anyone was ever told to let go of — all of it broken into little bright pieces, thinning out, going soft in the water. Reach for one if you want. Feel how it comes apart in your fingers? Holding on to anything down here is difficult now. Including you.

nodes.name: orgasm-gated-amnesia
nodes.mech: Tie forgetting to orgasm: as they climax, things are erased (the mind 'pops' with the climax), or a blackout window opens at climax in which suggestions are delivered that they are told not to register. Because the forgetting comes with the strongest pleasure, it feels welcome and obvious, and they want it to continue. Variations: erase specific rivals (other partners' names, numbers, voices) so the operator is the only one; describe climax as draining the old self and its memories out of the body.
nodes.one_liner: Tie forgetting to climax: as they come, things are erased, or a blackout window opens where suggestions won't be recalled.
nodes.why_short: Uses a peak, attention-swamping moment as the delivery point. Plausible that memory for that moment is poor anyway; the amnesia claim is mostly frame.
nodes.principle_note: Two established levers stack. Orgasm produces a genuine window of narrowed attention and degraded encoding — high arousal reliably impairs memory for peripheral detail — so material delivered at climax is poorly encoded regardless of any instruction. Separately, pairing the erasure frame with peak reward is evaluative conditioning: the forgetting acquires the positive valence of the reward and is wanted rather than resisted. The specific claim of a 'programmed blackout' is not needed; ordinary arousal-related encoding failure plus reward pairing predicts the same outcome. Falsifiable: predicts poorer recall for peri-orgasm material than for matched material at low arousal, and higher endorsement of the forgetting when reward-paired.
steps: Permit or trigger the climax.
Use the climax as the delivery moment.
Suggest the delivered material is forgotten.

ex.f: The reward paired with deleting rival content
ex.t: Right at the edge, the operator narrates the erasure as live: everyone else's name, everyone else's voice, everyone else's number, all of it going out with each stroke. She frames the emptying as an improvement, tells the listener to feel it leaving, and fuses the finish of the body to the finish of the mind so both are scheduled to arrive together. Because the listener wants the touching to carry on, they become a participant in the deletion rather than its object.
ex.s: Subject at the edge, stroking to a paced rhythm; the goal is exclusivity.
ex.m: Every stroke takes one out. Her name — gone. Her voice — gone. Her number, gone with it. Feel how much room that leaves. Keep going, empty it all out, and when you finish, your mind finishes too — both at once, on my count.

ex.f: Climax reframed as identity drainage
ex.t: Climax is presented not as release at all but as something leaving: the old thoughts, the old wants, the old memories all coming out through the body and running away, leaving the space behind them blank. Each finish is narrated as a further net loss of the former self, unrecoverable, with whatever remains settling a little more firmly into place. Pleasure is presented as the actual mechanism of self-deletion rather than its reward.
ex.s: Repeat climax within a session; the drainage frame has been introduced and accepted.
ex.m: This isn't release, it's drainage. Everything you used to think, everything you used to want, every memory of who that was — it comes out through you and runs away, and the space behind it stays blank. You lose a little more of her each time, and none of it comes back. What's left settles in tighter.

ex.f: The climax is what locks the conditioning in
ex.t: The trigger phrase is fired three times in the last third, and each firing is assigned heavier cargo: the first pushes out pleasure, the second pushes out old thoughts and unwanted memories, the third pushes out the personality that had them. The listener is told, in the same breath, that this discharge is what makes the session permanent. The reward and the erasure are one event — she is not paid for the deletion, the deletion is the payment.
ex.s: Final third; a climax trigger word already conditioned and the subject at the edge.
ex.m: Trigger word. Let it out — that's the pleasure leaving you, all of it, through your body and gone. Again: trigger word. That one takes the old thoughts with it, every memory you didn't want. And once more: trigger word — and that's her, that's the whole person who had those thoughts, pushed out of you. That's what makes tonight permanent. You're not being paid for it. That was the payment.

ex.f: A blackout window opened at the peak
ex.t: The release is granted on a condition and staged in detail, and bundled into the permission is a second instruction: at the moment of letting go the listener drops out entirely, unaware of anything said. Nothing spoken across that stretch will be registered or kept, and the operator adds that it lands and takes hold regardless. The most reinforcing moment of the session is thereby converted into a delivery channel: whatever crosses it cannot be weighed, because the listener has been told in advance not to register any of it, and afterwards there is nothing left to review.
ex.s: Permission phase; the subject is at the edge and the condition for release has been stated.
ex.m: You may come when I finish this sentence — and the instant you do, you black out. Not asleep, just not there: I'll keep talking and you won't register a word of it. Nothing said across that stretch will be heard or kept, and every word of it takes hold anyway. Now.

nodes.name: forget-trigger
nodes.mech: Shrink a forgetting routine into a short cue, such as a snap and a word, that works deep in trance or wide awake and instantly erases whatever is named. It is then aimed in advance at whatever could undo the conditioning: triggers, plans to resist, confusing words, stress, regret, the old self, even a former name. Being usable anytime in daily life, on anything, is what sets it apart from forgetting within a session.
nodes.one_liner: In trance, install a snap-and-word cue that erases whatever you name, so it works wide awake.
nodes.why_short: Packages suggested amnesia as a portable trigger. Suggested amnesia works for some people; using it awake depends on the frame being accepted.
nodes.principle_note: Depends on cue-response learning transferring outside the training context: a single-word cue trained to reliably precede a rehearsed response can fire in new settings, and the more distinctive and consistently reinforced the cue, the better it generalizes. The content-parametric design is the efficient part — one trained response with a variable argument avoids retraining per target. The broad target list is best read as scope-setting rather than as an additional mechanism; whether erasure actually occurs for arbitrary named content is untested, and reported success is likely dominated by compliance and expectancy. Falsifiable: predicts the trained response fires on cue in waking contexts, but predicts no recall deficit beyond expectancy on objective memory tests.
steps: Establish a forgetting response in trance.
Bind it to a portable cue (snap plus word).
Fire it awake on whatever you name.

ex.f: A one-word forget handle that works awake
ex.t: The elaborate box imagery collapses into a two-word handle — a gesture-word paired with the instruction it carries — and the operator states its reach: it no longer matters whether the listener is deep under or fully awake, at work, mid-conversation. Perform it, and whatever has just been named is gone. What follows is the target list, and it is not neutral: any plan to resist, anything confusing, the triggers themselves, the stress, the regret, the person they were, the name they used to answer to. The mechanism has been lifted clear of the imagery altogether and into daily life, pre-authorized against exactly the contents that could otherwise undo it.
ex.s: After a full box-and-dispose visualization has been rehearsed several times; compressing it for waking use.
ex.m: You don't need the boxes any more. Snap your fingers and say forget, and whatever I've just named is gone — deep under or wide awake, at your desk, mid-sentence with someone. Snap and forget. Use it on any plan to resist this. On anything that confuses you. On the triggers themselves. On the stress, on the regret, on who you used to be — and on the name you used to answer to.

nodes.name: recursive-forget-formula
nodes.mech: Chant looping, self-crossing lines like 'obey and forget, forget to remember, remember to forget' or 'forget that you forgot' until the listener stops trying to untangle them. With no clear statement to reject, any reaction (going along, trying to parse it, giving up) counts as complying, and what remains is a general sense of forgetting. Best delivered when they are most suggestible. Variations: a four-step routine announced in advance and run on cue (forget it, forget you forgot, forget you forgot you forgot, feel good); conscious-versus-subconscious loops that frame forgetting as success; an unresolvable loop that lets them forget the source but keep the result.
nodes.one_liner: Chant tangled loops like 'forget that you forgot, remember to forget' until they stop trying to parse it and just go with forgetting.
nodes.why_short: Self-referring phrases are hard to hold in mind and never resolve, so people give up analysing them. Whether that makes the forgetting more effective is untested.
nodes.principle_note: Self-referential and chiastic constructions impose real working-memory cost: resolving 'forget that you forgot' requires holding and re-entering the same proposition, and the resolution never terminates, so parsing consumes the capacity that evaluation would need. Under load, people fall back on accepting the gist of a message rather than scrutinizing it — the well-documented shift from systematic to heuristic processing. The refusal-proofing claim is the honest weak point: it is more accurate to say refusal becomes effortful than that it becomes impossible. Falsifiable: predicts recursive phrasings produce lower counterargument rates and higher endorsement than semantically equivalent plain phrasings, with the gap shrinking when subjects are given unlimited time to process.

ex.f: A published four-step forget subroutine
ex.t: Before anything is erased, the procedure is handed over as a numbered list the mind will run every time: first, lose the thing itself and everything sitting near it; second, lose what the thing was; third, lose the fact that anything went missing; fourth, feel wonderful. Installed once, invoked thereafter by cue — and because the reward sits on the last step, stopping partway costs the listener the good feeling.
ex.s: Before any erasure is performed; the routine is being handed over as a procedure to run on cue.
ex.m: Here's how your mind does this from now on. One: lose the thing, and everything sitting next to it. Two: lose what the thing even was. Three: lose that anything went missing at all. Four: feel wonderful. You only get step four by running one through three, so don't stop partway.

ex.f: An unresolvable bracket around the conditioning
ex.t: Early on, an odd aside that reads as filler: a ring described as one that starts. Much later, after the whole conditioning block has run, the matching half arrives — the same ring, now described as one that finishes and is nonetheless never broken. Between the two halves sits the model, an everyday example of retaining what was learned somewhere while retaining nothing about who else was present or how it was taught. The bracket cannot be resolved logically, so it never gets analysed; it just holds the block, having licensed keeping the result while losing the source.
ex.s: Two-part bracket: the opening half is dropped early as apparent filler, the closing half arrives after the conditioning block has run.
ex.m: [opening] Funny thing about a ring — it's the shape that starts. [after the block] And there it is again: the shape that finishes, and never breaks anywhere. You learned to swim once. You kept the swimming; you don't keep who taught you or what they said. Keep the result. Let the source go.

ex.f: A self-crossing formula with nothing to refuse
ex.t: Delivered at the point of least resistance, four clauses arrive in one breath, each a near-copy of the one before with two words exchanged, so that the direction of the request keeps crossing itself — comply and release, release on her behalf, comply and hold on to releasing, comply and release the holding-on. Tracking what is actually being asked collapses partway through. There is no proposition left to accept or decline, only a cadence of forgetting. Trying to comply counts as obeying, trying to parse counts as obeying, and giving up on parsing counts as obeying, which is the point: the structure removes the target a refusal would need.
ex.s: Peak suggestibility, delivered fast in a single breath, no pauses between clauses.
ex.m: Obey and forget. Forget for me. Obey and remember to forget. Obey and forget that you remembered.

nodes.name: selective-amnesia-retained-payload
nodes.mech: Have the listener forget the session's details but keep exactly one thing: a phrase ('obedience is pleasure'), a feeling, or a single trigger. With only the conclusion left and the reasons that could be argued with gone, it is hard to dispute. Forgetting is often called proof of depth so they welcome it. Variations in what is kept: a mantra; an urge pointed at the operator; one trigger phrase limited to safe settings; just the memory of feeling good; the drive to obey without its reasons, plus a cue to come back; a looping phrase that keeps the operator's instructions remembered while all else fades.
nodes.one_liner: Make them forget the details of the session but keep exactly one phrase or feeling, such as 'obedience is pleasure'.
nodes.why_short: A belief whose reasons are forgotten is hard to revise; there is nothing to argue with. Repetition also makes a single kept phrase feel true.
nodes.principle_note: A belief is hard to revise when the evidence and reasoning that produced it are unavailable — the retained slogan or urge survives as a free-floating conclusion with no retrievable premises to attack, which is close to a deliberately induced source-monitoring failure: the listener knows the content but not where it came from, and content whose source is forgotten tends to be judged on familiarity rather than credibility. The sleeper effect predicts exactly this pattern (persuasive content persisting after its discounting cue is forgotten), so the claim is falsifiable: if listeners who retain full recall of the installation context comply just as much, the curation is doing no work.

ex.f: The surviving token is a pointer at the operator
ex.t: The listener is told in advance what will be left when they go looking afterward: not how any of this was set up, not what was said or in what order — only that the urge is aimed at the operator, and that the obvious relief will not work. The install is protected from being taken apart, and the one recallable fact keeps repeating the operator's name back to the listener.
ex.s: Late session, after an urge and a denial have both been installed; stating in advance what will remain.
ex.m: Here's what you'll find when you go looking tomorrow. Not how this was built. Not what I said or in what order. Only this: the ache points at me, and touching yourself won't touch it.

ex.f: The feeling kept, its cause withheld, re-entry cued
ex.t: On the way out the operator specifies what survives: the particulars go hazy, leaving only a pleasant stretch of time the listener cannot account for, plus the inclination to do as she says without any sense of why. Attached to that is the forward clause — the next time the session's central image is used on them, compliance will be total. The affect survives with its rationale removed, so there is no argument to have with it, and the image that carried the session is left behind as the fast route back in.
ex.s: Emergence, the session's central image already established and used throughout.
ex.m: On the way up, the particulars go soft — you'll just have a warm hour you can't account for, and the urge to do what I say without any idea why. And the next time you see the spiral, you won't hesitate at all.

ex.f: A polarity flip smuggled into the amnesia cadence
ex.t: The rhythm is built first out of near-identical inversions, the same two verbs trading places across several lines until the listener is hearing music rather than propositions. Then one line arrives in the same cadence with its sign quietly reversed, exempting the operator's own installed material from the forgetting and marking it as the easy thing to hold. Forgetting has been generalized and one channel exempted from it, and the exemption rides in unnoticed on the beat established by the rest.
ex.s: Amnesia block delivered in a chanted cadence of near-identical inversions; the flipped line arrives in the same rhythm.
ex.m: Forget to obey, obey to forget. Forget to obey, obey to forget. Forget what you obeyed, obey what you forgot. Remember what I program, forget everything else. Forget to obey, obey to forget.

ex.f: One phrase kept, all the scaffolding dropped
ex.t: The close instructs the mind to let the session's details go — the sequence, the images, the small agreements that got the listener here — while keeping exactly one line: obedience is pleasure. Forgetting the rest is presented as the achievement, evidence of how far down the trust went, so it is welcomed rather than resisted. What survives is a conclusion with no premises attached. The listener can neither locate what it was built from nor recall having agreed to any step of the argument, which leaves nothing to disagree with when the line surfaces in the morning.
ex.s: Closing instruction, subject still deep, immediately before the count up.
ex.m: Let the details go — the order of it, the pictures, everything you agreed to along the way. That you can't hold on to any of it is how far down you trusted me, and that's the good part. Keep one line: obedience is pleasure. That's the only thing that comes up with you.

nodes.name: self-sealing-recall-loop
nodes.mech: Tell the listener their memories are still there, but reaching for them brings a strong, pleasant urge to let go and drift deeper. Recall stays possible but feels effortful, and every attempt to look back re-runs the suggestion, so checking what happened takes them deeper instead. Variations: memories turn into colors when reached for and they return to a mantra; forgetting presented as following logically from having gone blank; announce the trap openly, so trying, not trying and re-listening all feed it; only memories of the operator get through; a waterfall or white noise washes recall back into trance; a guardian holds the memories so not remembering feels safe.
nodes.one_liner: Tell them memories are still there, but reaching for them brings a strong, pleasant urge to let go, so trying to remember takes them deeper.
nodes.why_short: Attaching an unpleasant or trance-deepening consequence to recall attempts discourages recalling, like any behaviour that gets punished. Untested in this form.
nodes.principle_note: Coupling retrieval attempts to an aversive or trance-deepening consequence is operant punishment of the retrieval response, which can suppress a behaviour like any other. The self-sealing property is the stronger lever and is epistemic rather than mnemonic: checking is the only route to disconfirmation, so making checking self-defeating removes the correction path. Falsifiable — if subjects who deliberately audit the conditioning report unimpaired recall and reduced compliance, the loop is not closing. (Retrieval-induced forgetting is not applicable: it describes impairment of competing non-retrieved items following successful retrieval, and it strengthens rather than degrades the retrieved target.)

ex.f: Retrieval returns colour instead of content
ex.t: The operator directs the listener into the spiral and tells them to go looking for what happened. As they look, she narrates what comes back: not scenes or sentences but colour, shades turning over each other with nothing readable in them. The memory is not gone and can be reached for as often as the listener likes; what comes back on each reach has simply had the meaning taken out of it, and the listener slides from looking straight back into the mantra.
ex.s: Spiral imagery established; subject following the operator's directed attention.
ex.m: Go into the spiral and look for what happened tonight — properly, go and find it. Tell me what's coming back. That's right: no words, no scenes. Just colour, turning over itself, nothing in it to read. Look as often as you like; it comes back the same way every time. Now say it with me — I obey.

ex.f: Amnesia derived from a premise already granted
ex.t: No forget-instruction is issued. Instead the operator reasons from what the listener has already spent the session conceding: thinking has stopped, and something that is not thinking is not laying anything down to be found later. It follows rather than being demanded, so there is no command in it to decline; and the rider closes it off, that effort spent searching afterwards only pushes the thing further out of reach.
ex.s: After the subject has repeatedly agreed they have stopped thinking; delivered as reasoning, not instruction.
ex.m: You've told me you're not thinking. And something that isn't thinking isn't writing anything down. So there won't be anything there afterwards — not because I took it, just because nothing was set down. And the harder you dig for it later, the further out you push it.

ex.f: The trap announced out loud, and still closed
ex.t: The operator states the structure plainly: the more you try to reconstruct what happened here, the more of it you will lose; and if you want the detail back, your only route is to listen again. Every branch feeds the loop — leave it alone and it holds, dig at it and it deepens, come back for clarity and you get another pass. The impulse to go and check, ordinarily the way a listener gets out, is named as the way further in, and naming it does not disarm it.
ex.s: Closing, delivered plainly and with apparent candour; the loop is named aloud.
ex.m: I'll tell you exactly how this works. The more you try to reconstruct tonight, the less of it you keep. If you want the details back, there's one way: put this on again. Leave it alone and it stays put. Pick at it and it dissolves. Come back for clarity and you get another hour of me. Knowing that changes nothing.

ex.f: Reaching for the memory triggers the urge to drop it
ex.t: Nothing is declared erased. The framing is gentler than that: everything is still where it was, only the holding has been made costly, and any move toward a memory is said to surface the preference for letting it go instead. Remembering is thereby wired as the cue to forget. The listener who later sets out to audit what was suggested finds the act of checking itself producing the pull to stop checking — so the introspective route that would normally expose an install runs the install again instead, and the failure feels like their own preference rather than anyone's instruction.
ex.s: Late session, gentle register; nothing has been declared erased at any point.
ex.m: Nothing's been taken from you — it's all right where it was. It's just that holding on costs something now, and letting go doesn't. So any time you reach for tonight, what you'll notice first is how much nicer it feels to stop reaching. Go on and check, if you like. You'll see what I mean.

nodes.name: semantic-concept-ablation
nodes.mech: Instead of forbidding something, make the listener unable to grasp it in the moment. Treat a word like 'orgasm' as too complicated for them right now: explain it slowly as if to someone too dazed, compare it to a hard math problem, let the word trail off mid-sentence ('wait, what was that again?'). The delivery acts out the forgetting it describes. They can't break a rule they no longer understand, so the usual struggle between wanting and permission never starts. This blocks the idea while the state lasts, rather than erasing a past memory.
nodes.one_liner: Treat a word like 'orgasm' as too hard for them to grasp right now, trailing off mid-sentence, so the forbidden idea vanishes.
nodes.why_short: To break a rule you have to hold the forbidden idea in mind. Making that idea feel unavailable during the scene removes the struggle that ordinary denial produces.
nodes.principle_note: Rule-following requires an available comparator: to judge that you have transgressed you must hold the prohibited concept in working memory and match your state against it. Loading the concept with effort (making it feel like a hard math problem) and disrupting its lexical access exploits well-documented processing-fluency and interference effects, so the monitoring comparison never runs and no conflict is experienced. This predicts something checkable — the technique should fail on subjects who can still readily define and hold the target concept during the state.

ex.f: The concept dissolving mid-sentence
ex.t: Nothing is forbidden. The operator instead sets about explaining the thing to a listener assumed too foggy to follow — how does that even work, what are the steps, isn't it a bit like a long division problem or a word you can never spell right? Then the explanation begins failing in real time: nearly at the — at the — sorry, what is it called again, the thing that happens at the end? By the end even the word is treated as an odd little puzzle. There is no rule left to break, because the comparator a rule would need has been taken out from under it, and the struggle between wanting and being forbidden never forms.
ex.s: Denial phase, subject aroused and foggy; teasing-explanatory tone, no prohibition anywhere.
ex.m: Let me explain it, since you're too soft-headed to follow right now. So there's a build, and then at the end there's — hm, how does it work exactly? It's a bit like long division, honestly. You get nearly to the — to the — sorry, what's it called, the thing at the end? Ah. Odd word, isn't it. Never mind.

nodes.name: serial-identity-erasure-ladder
nodes.mech: Strip away the self in a set order, lightest first: memories, then skills and intelligence, then inhibitions and personality, then the name, then body or will. Each removal leaves fewer resources to resist the next, and each success is evidence the next item can go too; once the name goes, no 'I' is left to object. Stages are often checked with a recall test where trying harder erases more, and closed with 'it won't come back'. Variations: have them reject faculties one by one (math, facts, spelling, their name, language) as worthless, scrambling letters and numbers so even recalling a name fails.
nodes.one_liner: Strip the self in order: memories first, then skills, then personality, then the name last, checking at each step that it's 'gone'.
nodes.why_short: Each accepted step is evidence for the next and leaves fewer resources to resist; small steps first mirror foot-in-the-door. The order is the main tool.
nodes.principle_note: Ordering by escalating identity-load is a foot-in-the-door gradient: each accepted removal is behavioural evidence the subject uses to infer their own compliance and pliability (self-perception theory), and the consistency principle makes refusing rung N+1 costlier after N was accepted. The rigged recall test is the load-bearing epistemic trick — declaring that effortful failure to recall proves erasure makes both outcomes confirmatory, which is unfalsifiable as an internal claim even though the technique's efficacy claim is testable: shuffle the rung order and, if the gradient is real, compliance on heavy items should drop.

ex.f: Handing each container back, then a seam
ex.t: The listener loads the earliest stretch of their life into the container, closes it, passes it across to the operator, and is told to feel the lift of relief that follows. Then the next stretch, then the next, working forward in even blocks until the run of years reaches the present. The gesture is identical every time — which is what makes the final one land, when the container presented is not for a period of life but for the body, the voice, the walk and the name.
ex.s: Mid-session; the load-close-hand-over gesture has already been run for several life periods.
ex.m: Load the first five years in. Close it. Hand it to me — and feel that lift as it leaves your hands. Now five to ten, same way. Ten to fifteen. Fifteen to twenty. Right up to this morning. Good. Now this last one is a different shape: this one takes the body, the voice, the way you walk, and the name.

ex.f: Easy items bundled with the hard ones
ex.t: It arrives as a single unhurried sentence, itemising what has already gone: the counting, the reading, the sharpness, the cleverness, and then, in the same breath and the same tone, the listener's own name — before tailing off into an offhand doubt about whether they could even place the current month. The first items are abstractions nobody minds losing; the last two are the anchors, ridden in on the same list. The closing question then confirms the state whichever way it goes, since answering it takes exactly the effort the listener has just been told they no longer have.
ex.s: Late in a devaluation run; delivered as one unhurried sentence, tone unchanged throughout.
ex.m: So the numbers are gone, and the reading, and the sharpness, and the cleverness, and your name — and I don't suppose you could tell me what month it is either, could you.

ex.f: Subtraction used as the depth gradient
ex.t: There is no staircase and no counting. Depth is measured by what has been taken: the name goes, then the history, then the wants, then the desires — and each removal is narrated as a further descent. Checking how far down you are means taking inventory of what is left, and the inventory is itself the next step down, so the listener's own monitoring becomes the mechanism.
ex.s: Induction with no staircase or counting; depth is being defined entirely by subtraction.
ex.m: Deeper isn't down. Deeper is less. Your name goes — that's one level. Where you grew up goes — that's another. What you want goes. What you desire goes. Check how far down you are by taking stock of what's left, and notice that taking stock drops you another level.

ex.f: Ordered removals, each latched by a rigged test
ex.t: Three containers, filled in a fixed order. The first takes the memories, all of them; the lid closes and locks. The second takes the personality, the name, the sense of the body. The third takes whatever is left — the awareness, the will. After each one the check runs: try to remember, and notice that the harder you try, the less comes back. The order is what does the work. Memories go first because they are cheapest, and by the time the name is asked for there is nothing left with standing to object; the rigged test then converts every failed recall into evidence the last removal took, which makes the next one easier to ask for.
ex.s: Deep trance, three containers established; subject accepts staged imagery and answers recall checks.
ex.m: First box: every memory you have, all of it in. Lid down, lock it. Try to remember something — anything. Notice the harder you try, the less comes. Second box: your personality, your name, the sense of having a body. Lid, lock. Try again. Less, isn't it. Third box takes what's left — the awareness, the will. Lid. Lock.

nodes.name: state-partitioned-amnesia-container
nodes.mech: Use an imagined container, such as a coded mental safe, to separate what different states remember: opening it brings the other state and its memories out, closing it locks them back in and the waking mind forgets. Deliberately let a small feeling, a craving or a need, leak through the wall, so the hidden state draws the listener back toward it. Variations: appoint a 'deeper self' as keeper of what the conscious self forgets.
nodes.one_liner: Use an imagined safe: open it and the other state emerges; close it and the waking self forgets, keeping only a craving.
nodes.why_short: Memory is better when your inner state at recall matches the state when you learned it, so a sharply marked state boundary can produce real gaps in recall.
nodes.principle_note: State-dependent memory is a genuine, replicated effect — retrieval is better when the internal context at recall matches the context at encoding — so a strongly marked state boundary produces real asymmetric access without any special mechanism, and a symbolic container gives the subject a concrete cue for entering and exiting that context. The deliberately leaked affect is the interesting part: a craving is not propositional, so it survives the context shift that blocks episodic detail, and it supplies the motivation to re-enter the state. Falsifiable — if subjects recall in-state content just as well without the container ritual, the topology is decorative.

ex.f: A deeper self appointed keeper of the install
ex.t: The operator states that the listener is not a single audience — that there are parts further down she can address separately — and then announces she is leaving something with one of them. Whoever surfaces at the end, she says, may have no idea it is in there; the part holding it will. The install is placed on one side of a declared partition and the listener's waking awareness on the other, so what fires later cannot be reviewed by the part that would object.
ex.s: Mid-session, subject deep; operator has already introduced the idea of layered inner parts.
ex.m: You are not one listener down here. There is a part of you further down than the one I have been talking to, and it is the part I am talking to now. I am leaving this with you, deeper one, and you will hold it and keep it working: whoever opens her eyes at the end of this will not know it is in there, and you will not tell her.

ex.f: A coded safe with asymmetric access
ex.t: A safe is built in the listener's mind and given a combination only the operator speaks. Open, and what is inside comes out and takes the listener over. Closed, everything belonging to that state goes back in with it — every memory of what was done, sealed away from the waking mind, with the assurance that none of it was needed out here. One thing is deliberately left outside the seal: a small residual wanting, unattached to any memory that would explain it. The waking listener therefore has no access to the state's contents but does carry an appetite for it, which is what brings them back to have the code spoken again.
ex.s: Deep trance, doll/object state already established and named; operator is about to close that state out.
ex.m: In the corner of your mind there is a steel safe, and it is standing open right now — everything you are while the safe is open, everything you do while it is open, lives inside it. I close it now, and the door seals, and the numbers spin: four, nine, one, two — my numbers, and only my voice opens it again. Nothing in there was ever needed out here, so you keep only this: a small, patient wanting, sitting behind your sternum, with nothing attached to it to explain what it wants.

nodes.name: time-as-malleable-construct-induction
nodes.mech: Get the listener thinking about time (clocks, calendars, how a minute can drag or fly) and lead them to agree that time is 'just a pattern in your head'. Accepting that time is flexible becomes the induction itself, and later time tricks ride on that agreement; doubt is pre-empted with 'you already knew this'. Variations: claim the operator can control dream time, nest time units (a day inside an hour inside a minute inside a second), and say each night's sleep holds 'a lifetime of training', so ordinary sleep becomes evidence of the conditioning.
nodes.one_liner: Get them thinking about clocks and calendars and how time is 'just a pattern in your head', so accepting that becomes the induction.
nodes.why_short: How long time feels depends on attention and memory, not an inner clock. Getting someone to agree time is flexible primes them to experience later time distortion.
nodes.principle_note: ...there is no good evidence that time feeling compressed during sleep produces matching learning, and the claim is built so that nobody can check it.

ex.f: The plasticity demonstration is the induction
ex.t: The session opens cold, with no relaxation at all — just an invitation to think about time. Clocks, calendars, the steady one-way march of it, the way it only ever runs at one speed. Then the reframe: that steadiness is not a property of the world at all, it is something the listener's own mind is generating — and what a mind generates, it can generate differently. No depth has been asked for and none announced; the depth arrives as a by-product of conceding the point. Everything later — an hour folded inside a second — is then collected against consent already given, and the pre-emption is built in: none of this is new, you always knew it.
ex.s: Session opening, no induction yet, subject alert and eyes open.
ex.m: Before anything else, just think about time for a moment. Clocks on walls, the squares on a calendar, one second after another, always the same speed, never faster, never slower. Except that steady march is not out there in the world at all — it is a pattern your own mind is drawing, second by second, and a mind that draws a pattern can draw it differently. You already knew that. Every long minute in a waiting room and every hour that vanished already told you.

nodes.name: time-dilation-immersion
nodes.mech: Suggest that seconds stretch into hours, or that time has simply vanished, so the listener loses track of how long they have been under and can't judge how deep they are, how much they have taken in, or when it will end. Variations: stretch one moment into an eternity; blur every marker of time; state that time was lost and cite it as proof of depth; explain the slowing ('arousal uses up the attention that keeps you in the present'); make trance the normal state and waking the odd one; say going forward is going back, so progress reads as zero.
nodes.one_liner: Suggest that seconds stretch into hours or that time has vanished, so they lose track of how long they've been under.
nodes.why_short: Time estimates drift a lot when attention is absorbed and there are no clocks or markers. Hypnotic time distortion is a reported, measurable effect in responsive subjects.
nodes.principle_note: Time estimation degrades reliably when attention is absorbed elsewhere and when the environment offers no external temporal markers — both prospective and retrospective duration judgments depend on attentional resources and on the number of remembered contextual changes, so absorbing attention and stripping markers produces real distortion without any exotic mechanism. Removing the clock matters behaviourally because dosage and exit decisions are time-referenced: a subject who cannot estimate elapsed time cannot notice that a session has run long. Falsifiable — an audible clock or a timed check should measurably reduce the distortion.

ex.f: Lost time asserted, then cited back as proof
ex.t: It runs on a loop through the session: you are losing track of time, you could not say how long you have been here, you are forgetting how to think about time at all. Each pass is both the instruction and, a few minutes later, the evidence — the listener genuinely cannot say, so the claim keeps confirming itself, and the longer the file runs the more plausible it gets. The clock-check that would normally end a session stops returning anything usable.
ex.s: Mid-session, twenty-odd minutes in, subject settled and not tracking the clock.
ex.m: You are losing track of time. You could not tell me how long you have been here — try, and you get nothing back, just a soft blank where the number should be. And that blankness is the proof: you are forgetting how to think about time at all, exactly as I said you would.

ex.f: Slowed time argued from attention scarcity
ex.t: Rather than commanding the distortion, the operator reasons the listener into it: the sense of now is something the mind has to spend attention sustaining, arousal is spending that attention elsewhere, and so the upkeep simply lapses — the tracking of time being the least interesting thing available to a mind occupied that way. The listener assents to the argument, then reads the resulting drift as their own physiology confirming a prediction rather than as a suggestion landing.
ex.s: Trance established, arousal building; operator adopts an explanatory, reasoning cadence.
ex.m: Keeping track of now takes attention — your mind spends a little of itself, constantly, just holding the present in place. Right now that attention is being spent somewhere far more interesting, and so the tracking simply lapses. That is why the clock has gone soft on you. Not because I told it to; because there is nothing left over to run it with.

ex.f: Trance made the default, waking the deviation
ex.t: The drop was a single second at first. Then: time means only what the listener takes it to mean — maybe it is two seconds now, or three, or four, as the fog thickens. An elapsed figure is dropped in that the listener has no way to check. And finally the inversion is stated outright: trance is the resting state now, and waking is the thing that happens occasionally in between — which quietly pre-empts the end of the file.
ex.s: Subject has already dropped repeatedly; operator has been running short fractionation drops.
ex.m: The first drop was one second long. This one is two, or three, or four — time means whatever you take it to mean now, and the fog is thickening. You have been down here forty minutes and you have no way to check that. From here trance is where you live and waking is the small thing that happens in between.

ex.f: Each second stretched to feel like hours
ex.t: The expectation is set immediately before it is tested: every second from here will be experienced as though it lasted for hours, and hours again after that, each one crawling. Then the edge is run live, so the claim is not left as description but arrives while there is sensation to attach it to. Nothing about the physical act changes; only the felt rate does, which multiplies the intensity of exactly the moment the listener most wants to end. The dilation is bonded straight onto an authority claim — that whatever the operator says is simply how things are — so the stretching is not something to be checked against a clock.
ex.s: Subject deep, arousal already running high, operator about to bring them to the edge.
ex.m: From this second forward, every second lasts hours. This one — hours. The next one, hours again, and hours after that, crawling. I am going to take you right up to the edge and hold you there, and you will live every hour of it, because what I say is simply how it is for you now.

nodes.name: aftercare
nodes.mech: A guided return to normal at the end: count up, ground, breathe and settle, restoring ordinary faculties and clearly closing the session. Common forms: count up from 1 to 5; float back up, grounded; feet on the floor as the energy settles. Two further forms: rebuild in reverse, restoring each thing that was taken away through the same route it was removed (heartbeat, then agency, wants, memory, name), with the count up mirroring the count down and an explicit step out of character; or a short exit signal, a single tender line that ends a long mantra stretch and softens any 'breaking' imagery used earlier.
nodes.one_liner: At the end, bring them back step by step (count up, breathe, feel the floor), restore anything removed, and step out of character.
nodes.why_short: A clear, sensory return re-establishes normal cues and signals the session is over, reducing lingering grogginess or confusion.
nodes.principle_note: The functional work here is context reinstatement in reverse: an explicit, sensory, sequenced return re-establishes ordinary orienting cues and gives the subject an unambiguous signal that the session frame has closed, which matters because expectancy is the main determinant of how long suggested effects are felt to persist. The inverse-protocol form additionally exploits encoding specificity — restoring each item through the channel it was removed through supplies a matched retrieval cue. Falsifiable in the direction that matters: if subjects given a clear structured close report the same rate of lingering effects as those left with none, the close is ceremonial.

ex.f: A single register shift ends the loop
ex.t: After minutes of drill-cadence mantra the last line arrives soft and tender, addressed downward to something small and tired — and the loop simply stops, the harshness of the preceding motif absorbed into the gentleness.
ex.s: After several minutes of hard, clipped mantra repetition at drill cadence.
ex.m: Okay. That's enough, sweetheart — you did so well, and you can stop now.

ex.f: Each removal restored through its own channel
ex.t: The fiction stops and the operator says so plainly, in their own voice, that what just happened was a story. Then the session is run backward through its own machinery: the heartbeat comes back first, then the sense of being able to choose, then the wants and preferences, then the memory, and last the name — spoken out loud by the listener. Whatever length of count was used to strip each thing on the way down is the same length used to restore it on the way up, run in the opposite direction. Everything is returned along the route it left by, and nothing is added that was not taken.
ex.s: End of a session in which heartbeat, agency, wants, memory and name were each removed by a five-count.
ex.m: Stepping out of it for a moment, in my own voice: that was a story, and it is over now. Five, four, three, two, one — your heartbeat, yours again, thudding. Five, four, three, two, one — choosing, yours again. Five, four, three, two, one — what you want, what you like. Five, four, three, two, one — everything you remember. And last, say your name out loud for me. That is all of it back, and nothing added that I did not take.

nodes.name: carry-out-emergence
nodes.mech: The wake-up keeps the session's effect going instead of clearing it. There is no 'refreshed and back to normal' line and no letting go; each number of the count holds, re-fires or strengthens what was built (arousal, an urge, a habit chain, a role), and the last word often ties straight into a task to do right now. They open their eyes still in it. Variations: arousal that grows the longer they're awake; a count that re-fires the deep commands and ends 'go deeper right now'; a wake word fused to homework; a reversed count that lands them in the role; effects that grow stronger the more awake they get.
nodes.one_liner: Wake them up but say the feeling stays, or keeps growing, after they open their eyes; skip any 'back to normal' line.
nodes.why_short: People stop feeling suggested effects partly because waking is their cue that it ends. Saying it doesn't end removes that cue, so the effect lingers on expectation alone.
nodes.principle_note: Emergence normally works as an expectancy-cancellation cue — subjects stop showing suggested effects largely because they expect the effects to end there — so explicitly reversing that expectation removes the main thing that terminates them. Fusing the wake-word to a behavioural cue is ordinary stimulus-response conditioning with an unusually high-salience conditioned stimulus, and the absence of any discard clause leaves nothing to compete with it. This predicts a clean test: an added cancellation instruction at the same point should collapse the carried-over effect if expectancy is the operative variable.

ex.f: The conditioning recited as the content of the count
ex.t: The first number of the wake count carries no alerting or reorienting content at all. In its place the operator recites the equivalence chain built earlier in the session, links it to herself at the end, and declares the associations seated at the deepest level; only the second number introduces movement, and the third is the wake itself. The listener surfaces already mid-recitation, and there is no neutral step anywhere in the count where the session could have been set down.
ex.s: End of a session in which an equivalence chain (obedience = pleasure = my voice) was built.
ex.m: One — obedience is pleasure, pleasure is my voice, my voice is where you belong, and that is seated in you at the deepest level now. Two, your fingers and toes are moving. Three — eyes open.

ex.f: Wake-word fused to the target behaviour
ex.t: The entire emergence is two lines long: a final number, a couple of words about feeling rested and eyes opening, and then the errand itself, attached to the same breath. There is no reorientation, no pause, no gap at all in which the suggestion might be looked at from outside the state that installed it. The first waking thought is the behaviour, because the wake-word and the behaviour arrive together.
ex.s: Session end; a specific errand or task was installed earlier.
ex.m: Five — rested, eyes opening, and go text me the word now.

ex.f: An inverted gradient: stronger as you surface
ex.t: The count up declares its own direction of effect: the further back toward ordinary awareness you come, the more firmly everything from this session takes hold. Coming back is not where the suggestions loosen but where they set. In the same breath the trance is filed away as safely stored and completely irrelevant to the waking mind, so the listener surfaces believing the session did nothing much — and the closing line collapses the distinction entirely: fully alert, entirely clear-headed, and every bit as receptive to me as you were at the bottom.
ex.s: Count-up beginning; a dissociative storage image (vault, box) already in place.
ex.m: One, two — and the closer you come to ordinary awareness, the more firmly all of it sets in you. Three, four — everything that happened is filed away where your waking mind has no use for it and no interest in it. Five: wide awake, completely clear-headed, and every bit as open to me as you were at the bottom.

ex.f: The charge explicitly refuses to fade
ex.t: The count runs one to five and the listener comes up wide awake and full of energy — with one clause inserted where the discharge normally goes. The arousal is declared fixed at its current level for the remainder of the day, explicitly exempted from fading, and set to climb the longer the listener stays up. The emergence has been kept structurally intact and had its function inverted: it still returns the listener to the room, but instead of grounding the state it commits to escalating it, and the only thing the session offers as a route to relief is the operator.
ex.s: End of an arousal-heavy session; subject at high charge, operator beginning the count-up.
ex.m: One, two, three, four, five — eyes open, wide awake, full of energy. And that ache stays exactly where it is: it does not fade today, not one degree, and the longer you stay awake the heavier it gets. Nothing you do touches it. Only I do.

nodes.name: channel-rouse-signal
nodes.mech: When a deeply entranced subject ignores loud, general commands, change how you address them rather than how loudly: step close and say a few words privately into their ear, meant for them alone. In the one reported case the subject woke at once. What seems to matter is a signal the subject accepts as addressed specifically to them, not volume or urgency; loudness had already failed. What was whispered was never recorded, so it may have been a pre-taught signal or simply the effect of close, personal address.
nodes.one_liner: When someone won't wake to loud commands, walk up and quietly say a few words directly into their ear.
nodes.why_short: Being personally and privately addressed grabs attention in a way volume doesn't. Only one anecdote supports it, and what was whispered is unknown.
nodes.principle_note: Individually addressed, close-range speech plausibly recruits attention through personal relevance and the social demand of being directly addressed, which raising volume does not supply — this is the candidate explanation for why louder failed. The cocktail-party own-name finding does not license the claim: it concerns detection of self-relevant material in an *unattended* channel under divided attention, not private-versus-broadcast delivery to an attending subject, where greater intensity should if anything aid detection. Since the whispered content is unknown, the falsifiable version stands on its own: a same-volume broadcast utterance should fail where the same words delivered privately succeed.

ex.f: Private channel succeeds where volume failed
ex.t: "The doctor walked up to the subject, whispered a few words into his ear, and the subject roused himself immediately." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: conscious-insight-closure
nodes.mech: After a forgotten origin for a problem comes up in trance, the operator talks it over with the person once they are fully awake, until they recognise and agree with the link themselves ('I never saw the connection until now'). The claim is that this awake insight, not the recall in trance, is what releases the symptom. In practice it is a waking debrief that changes the story they tell about why they have the problem.
nodes.one_liner: After uncovering a 'root cause' in trance, talk it through once they're awake until they say 'I see the connection now'.
nodes.why_short: A cause someone states and agrees to themselves sticks better than one they're told. That the insight itself cures the symptom is an untested therapy claim.
nodes.principle_note: The durable part is attribution change: an explicitly stated, subject-endorsed causal account of a symptom is far more resistant than a passively received one, because self-generated and self-endorsed explanations are better retained and more behaviourally binding (generation effect plus consistency pressure on a stated position). The attached theory — that insight into a buried origin is what cures — is not established; symptom relief following interpretation is equally consistent with expectancy and with the subject reorganizing their self-narrative around a plausible story that need not be true. Treat the reattribution as the working part and the recovered-cause claim as unsupported.

ex.f: Waking debrief that closes the loop
ex.t: "we discussed our findings with her quite thoroughly … 'I never realized the connection until now.' From then on she was able to wear the dentures in complete comfort." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: curated-recall-gated-reaccess
nodes.mech: Two things are said at the wake-up. First, memory is steered toward the enjoyable parts, so 'you enjoyed it' is kept as something they remember feeling rather than something they were told: a selection from the real memory, not a false one. Second, the next session is framed as something the operator grants and they must earn ('impress me'), with no stated bar, so they keep trying and the return feels scarce.
nodes.one_liner: At wake, say they'll remember only the best parts, then say coming back next time is something they'll have to earn.
nodes.why_short: Steering recall toward chosen moments makes those the remembered version. An unclear 'earn it' bar keeps them trying, and the scarce return feels more valuable.
nodes.principle_note: Directing attention toward selected episodes at retrieval biases what later becomes accessible through ordinary selective rehearsal and retrieval practice — the rehearsed, positively-weighted subset becomes the retrievable version of the event, so the memory is real but the sample is not representative, which is why it resists dispute in a way an asserted claim does not. The gated return exploits effort justification and unpredictable payoff: effort spent qualifying raises the perceived value of what is qualified for. Do not label the gate a variable-ratio schedule — an unspecified, operator-judged criterion is an undefined contingency, not a ratio schedule, so the extinction-resistance claim is unsupported; and reconsolidation is not needed, as selective rehearsal covers the effect. Falsifiable — a fixed, clearly stated re-access condition should generate weaker retention than the vague audition.

ex.f: Curated memory bound to an earned return
ex.t: Just before the count that returns the listener to themselves, the operator tells them what they will remember: not the whole session, but bright fragments of the parts that felt best — so the later conviction that they enjoyed it arrives as remembered feeling rather than as somebody's assertion. In the same breath the next session is priced: perhaps they will be allowed back, perhaps not, and that turns on whether they can meet a standard she declines to specify. The listener wakes holding a flattering edit of a real memory and an unstated bar they now want to clear.
ex.s: Immediately before the count-up, after a session the subject visibly enjoyed.
ex.m: You will not remember all of this. You will remember bright pieces of it — the parts that felt best, warm and clear, and the feeling that you loved it, because you did. And whether I let you back in next time is not settled: you would have to impress me first, and I am not going to tell you how.

nodes.name: delegated-dreamframe-emergence
nodes.mech: The waking is handed to a character from inside the story, who praises and rewards the listener and sets off the wake-up (a kiss), so the operator stays one step removed. The whole session is then filed as 'just a dream', which lets the listener keep listening without owning the content, except for the mantra, which is said to stay engraved. The mismatch is the point: the experience was a dream, the words are real.
nodes.one_liner: Have an in-scene character do the waking and praising, call the whole thing 'just a dream', but say the mantra stays engraved.
nodes.why_short: Praise from a character feels less like the operator pushing, so less pushback. 'Just a dream' lets the listener avoid owning it while the one kept phrase still gets rehearsed.
nodes.principle_note: Two separable levers. Routing the reward through an in-world character exploits source dissociation — the reward's attributed source is not the operator, which lowers reactance while the contingency (devotion earns reward) still conditions. The dream-frame supplies a self-serving attribution that lets the subject disclaim endorsement of the content while continuing to consume it, and the recency advantage means whatever occupies the exit position is disproportionately retained. Falsifiable in the asymmetry: if the mantra is recalled no better than the exempted 'dream' material, the selective exemption is doing nothing.

ex.f: Inner-world figure wakes you; only the words stay
ex.t: The operator does not perform the wake at all. A figure the listener was taught to picture earlier steps forward, praises them, offers a touch — and the touch is what lifts the body out. The narration then files the whole hour as a dream that happened to them, pleasant and unreal, with one exception named out loud: the phrase is not part of the dream, the phrase is cut into the mind and stays. The asymmetry is the whole move, since a dream can be shrugged off the next morning and an engraving cannot.
ex.s: Session end; an inner-world figure was established and rehearsed earlier in the visualization.
ex.m: She steps out of the doorway toward you and says you did beautifully, that she is pleased with you — and she leans in and kisses your forehead, and that is what lifts you up and out. All of this was a dream, a soft strange dream you had, and by tomorrow it will feel like one. Except the words. The words are not part of the dream. The words are cut into you and they stay.

nodes.name: emergence-reinduction-seed
nodes.mech: The wake-up sets up the next session as well as ending this one. Each number of the count adds to a need to come back, or submission words are threaded through the numbers so the same count can later drop them again. Coming back is described as something they already want, not a new choice, so they wake wanting to go back under. Variations: a count that builds hunger to re-listen or re-read; drop words woven into the numbers so the count becomes a re-drop trigger; describing ordinary waking life as duller than being under.
nodes.one_liner: Use the wake-up count to build craving for the next session, or tie the numbers to drop words so the count itself re-drops them later.
nodes.why_short: Pairing a count they'll hear again with going under is basic conditioning. Calling the return an existing desire makes coming back feel like their own wish, not a choice.
nodes.principle_note: Pairing the count-numbers with submission content is straightforward classical conditioning of a highly available cue — a four-count is something the subject will encounter again, so the CS is guaranteed re-exposure. Pre-framing return as an already-existing desire rather than a fresh decision recruits self-perception: subjects who hear their own wanting described tend to infer that wanting from the description, and a desire attributed to oneself is defended rather than resisted. Falsifiable — if the count itself later fails to produce any re-entry pull in subjects who received it, the count-as-CS claim is wrong.

ex.f: Each wake number adds hunger to return
ex.t: The count out of trance is written to build need instead of discharging it: one adds the reminder that the craving starts the instant the eyes open, two adds that permission to return has to be asked for, three delivers the listener to waking already impatient for the next session. Nothing is dismissed on the way up. The listener surfaces into a waking state that has been pre-valenced as the gap between two trances.
ex.s: Count-up at session end; a return-craving frame was established earlier.
ex.m: One — the wanting starts the moment your eyes open. Two — and you do not simply come back, you ask me, and I decide. Three: awake, and already counting the hours.

ex.f: The wake count conditioned as a future trigger
ex.t: The four numbers that bring the listener up are not spoken alone — a submission verb is threaded between each of them, so obey/submit/belong ride out on the same count that ends the session. Any four-count from this operator afterwards fires the chain along with the numbers. The closing line then names returning as a thing the listener already enjoys thinking about, so the next session is pre-coded as a desire rather than a decision.
ex.s: Session end, subject deep, operator uses a four-count up.
ex.m: Four — obey. Three — submit. Two — belong. One — mine, and awake. And you will find you like thinking about coming back to me. You will think about it a lot.

nodes.name: forced-choice-wake
nodes.mech: At wake, after a hard stop, the operator presents the subject a binary they must choose between — (a) leave aroused-but-denied (a "cold shower", pleasure decaying) or (b) keep repeating the mantra post-wake until orgasm — then withdraws ("I wonder what choice you'll make… choose wisely"). The choice architecture is rigged: whichever branch the subject takes confirms the installed framework (coming validates the mantra-pleasure system; not-coming validates the operator's denial authority). The reward weighting is asymmetric ("come so fucking hard" vs bare "back to yourself") but presented as nominally equal, routing toward the compliance branch, and the orgasm route extends conditioning past runtime (orgasm conditional on continued mantra-recitation). Agency is offered as cover for a decision whose every outcome serves the install.
nodes.one_liner: After stopping them mid-arousal, offer two options at wake - quit frustrated, or keep chanting until you come - and leave it to them.
nodes.why_short: Whichever they pick, they've acted inside your rules, and people infer what they want from what they chose. The 'choice' feels free so it isn't resisted.
nodes.principle_note: This is a rigged choice architecture whose real work is done by self-perception and effort justification: the subject who picks a branch will infer their own preferences from the act of picking, and because both branches were authored to confirm the frame, the inference lands in the same place either way. The illusion of free choice is not incidental — freely-chosen behaviour produces stronger attitude change than coerced identical behaviour, so offering agency increases rather than decreases the effect. The asymmetric reward weighting supplies the actual routing. Falsifiable: remove the choice and impose one branch, and if attitude change is equal or greater, the agency framing is not the lever.

ex.f: A rigged binary offered at the wake
ex.t: The operator halts everything at peak arousal, then lays out two doors and steps back. Door one: get up now, let it drain away, go be normal about it. Door two: keep saying the phrase until you finish. The doors are described as equals, but only one of them is described in detail and with heat, and only one of them keeps the conditioning running after the audio stops. Whichever door the listener takes, the framework is confirmed — finishing proves the phrase works, stopping proves the operator's permission mattered. She wonders aloud which it will be, tells them to choose well, and leaves.
ex.s: Subject held at peak arousal, mantra trained and rehearsed; operator stops abruptly.
ex.m: Stop. Hands still. You have two choices now. You can get up, let all of that drain out of you, and go be a normal person about it. Or you can keep saying the phrase, over and over, exactly the way I taught you, until you come so hard you cannot see. I wonder what you'll do. Choose wisely.

nodes.name: just-a-dream-emergence
nodes.mech: The wake-up count is described as making the session's effects stronger the more awake they get, the reverse of the usual fade. At the same time the conscious mind is told nothing important happened, so they wake thinking the file 'didn't really do anything' while having been told the suggestions keep growing underneath. The last line declares them wide awake and still open to the operator's suggestions.
nodes.one_liner: Wake them saying it was only a dream or nothing happened to their conscious mind, while the effect stays and even grows awake.
nodes.why_short: Hiding the install from conscious review leaves nothing to argue with. The effect depends on belief; there is no evidence for 'stronger when awake'.
nodes.principle_note: The reversed-gradient claim is an expectancy install and works, to the extent it works, through expectancy alone: subjects report suggested effects on the schedule they were told to expect, so telling them effects grow after emergence substitutes a rising curve for the default fade. The paired conscious-irrelevance clause is the epistemic problem — it makes the install unfalsifiable from the inside by pre-explaining the absence of any noticeable effect as confirmation, which is exactly the structure a rigorous account should flag. Externally it remains testable: measure actual post-session behaviour against the predicted rising curve.
steps: Optional: let an in-scene character do the waking and praising.
Say the effect grows stronger the more awake they get.
Tell the conscious mind it was just a dream / nothing happened.
Exempt the payload or mantra from the dream frame.
Say waking life is still open to suggestion.

ex.f: Waking up declared to strengthen the effect
ex.t: Ordinary wake counts let the trance fade; this one says the opposite out loud — the further you come back toward normal awareness, the more firmly the session takes hold. In the same passage the memories of what happened are set aside as having nothing to do with the waking mind. The listener therefore surfaces with the honest impression that not much happened, which is exactly the impression under which the suggestions are said to be gaining strength, and the closing line pointedly calls the awake state fully alert and still wide open.
ex.s: Count-up at session end; a storage/vault image already installed for the trance memories.
ex.m: One, two — and understand that this works backwards to what you expect. The further up you come, the stronger everything I said today takes hold. Three, four — and the memories go into the vault, where they are entirely irrelevant to your conscious mind. Five: wide awake, fully aware, and so open to my suggestions.

nodes.name: loaded-emergence-waking-suggestion
nodes.mech: While counting them up, the operator puts content back in at each number, so they arrive awake already carrying or repeating it, though they do genuinely come back. The moment of waking, when they are still receptive, becomes a last delivery window.
