ex.f: A word paired with the payoff becomes self-reinforcing
ex.t: "just prior to pushing a child on a swing, the word 'swing' is emitted… the word 'swing' may eventually become an Sr" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Pair a distinct signal until it marks the response
ex.t: "Reinforcement is paired with the sound of the clicker so that the sound becomes a conditioned reinforcer." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Scale the treat, never the marker
ex.t: "If you want to express special enthusiasm, increase the number of treats, not the number of clicks." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Yoke praise to tokens so praise survives withdrawal
ex.t: "the token presentation should always be paired with social approval and verbal praise. This should increase the reinforcing effect of the social approval and serve to maintain behaviors after token withdrawal." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: differential-reinforcement
nodes.mech: Instead of punishing or ignoring a behaviour, reward something else: its absence, a lower rate of it, or a behaviour that can't happen at the same time. Which 'something else' you reward decides the outcome. Variations: reward a stretch of time without it (checked at the end, or at unpredictable moments; unused 'passes' turn into a bonus); reward it only while it stays under a limit; reward an incompatible behaviour (silence instead of noise, a slack leash instead of a taut one); offer several options at once where the wanted one pays best; make the alternative pay faster or more reliably so they drift toward it.
nodes.one_liner: Instead of punishing a habit, reward its absence, or a different behavior that can't happen alongside it.
nodes.why_short: Behavior shifts toward whatever pays best; making the alternative pay more lowers the old habit without removing all reward.
nodes.principle_note: Behaviour allocates across concurrently available options roughly in proportion to the reinforcement each yields — the matching law. That is why paying an alternative reduces the target without ever withholding reinforcement: the target's relative payoff falls even when its absolute payoff does not. The functional-assessment step matters because reinforcers are not interchangeable; an alternative only competes if it produces the same consequence the problem behaviour was producing, at lower response cost. Directly falsifiable: if allocation were insensitive to relative rather than absolute payoff, differential reinforcement would fail whenever the problem behaviour still worked at all — the graded-concurrent-choice results say otherwise.

ex.f: Per-response reset tightens the feedback
ex.t: "The second response, however, resets the time interval, providing a consequence for the problem behavior." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Pay the behavior only under a rate ceiling
ex.t: "delivers reinforcement… contingent on the number of responses within a period not exceeding a predetermined criterion." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: The ceiling made visible as a depleting card
ex.t: "No additional points were awarded if more than one box was left empty, because we wanted the children to use the opportunities." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Reinforce absence only at the sampling instant
ex.t: "reinforcement is contingent on the absence of the problem behavior at the exact time each interval ends … Occurrences of the problem behavior between those moments have no effect" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: precommitment-rule-governed-stakes
nodes.mech: While temptation is still far off and easy to resist, you arrange things so your later self can't easily back out: remove the option, or attach a cost to giving in. This is precommitment; it works because people discount distant rewards, so choices made early are less pulled by the quick payoff. Variations: an irreversible act in advance (locking away the cigarettes, Odysseus tied to the mast); a fixed penalty paid to a friend on any day you fail, held by someone trustworthy so it can't be waived; a delayed, unpleasant stake, such as money going to a cause you despise if you break the limit.
nodes.one_liner: While temptation is far off, lock in a choice or penalty in advance so your later self can't back out.
nodes.why_short: People value near rewards far more than distant ones, so preferences flip as temptation nears; deciding early catches the calm preference.
nodes.principle_note: People discount delayed outcomes steeply and, for many, hyperbolically, so the relative value of a smaller-sooner reward and a larger-later one reverses as the sooner one approaches — which is why a preference formed at distance predictably fails at close range. Acting on the contingency during the low-temptation window exploits that reversal: the choice is made while the larger-later outcome still dominates, and the act removes or prices the later defection. A third party holding the stake matters because self-imposed penalties are otherwise waivable by the same self that will want to waive them. Falsifiable: predicts commitment devices only help where preference reversal actually occurs, and that self-held, waivable stakes underperform externally held ones.

ex.f: Bind the future self while temptation is distant
ex.t: "Since the smoker is just about to have a cigarette, the value of a future cigarette is negligible, making it easy to shut the case" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: motivating-operation-engineering
nodes.mech: Before asking for a behaviour, change how much they want what it gets them: have them go without to raise the want, or let them have their fill to lower it. Nothing is given; only the wanting is moved, and every behaviour that earns that thing rises or falls with it. Variations: wait for a moment they already want something and teach right then; give one item that makes a second one necessary, then block the second until they ask; interrupt a routine where a needed piece is missing; pair a cue with wanting until the cue alone makes them want. Overdoing it, too full or too frustrated, backfires.
nodes.one_liner: Change how badly they want something first - deprive or satisfy them - then ask for the behavior that gets it.
nodes.why_short: How rewarding something is depends on current want; deprivation raises it and satiation lowers it, changing how hard people work for it.
nodes.principle_note: How reinforcing a consequence is right now is not fixed — deprivation raises it and satiation lowers it, and this momentary value change alters the rate of every behaviour that consequence maintains, independently of any learning about the response-reinforcer relation. That is the difference between wanting and having learned; the manipulation is antecedent, nothing is delivered. Conditioned versions work by the same Pavlovian logic that builds conditioned reinforcers: a cue reliably correlated with a value-altering state comes to reproduce the value change. Falsifiable and routinely tested — free-operant rates should track deprivation state with the contingency held constant, and they do.

ex.f: Capture the motivation or contrive it
ex.t: "capturing the MO value change as it occurs naturally and (2) creating the MO by generating some change that alters the value of a consequence" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Engineer the antecedent that inflates the value
ex.t: "give the child some salty foods to increase the value of drinks" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Interrupt the chain to make the missing link valuable
ex.t: "By interrupting the chains at the point at which these additional objects (or actions) are needed, practitioners can momentarily establish them as reinforcers and contrive opportunities to teach a wider variety of mands" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: contriving a value change via a staged antecedent
ex.t: A learned motivating condition can be created on demand: introduce a stimulus that, by learning history, raises the value of some other thing. A low-battery warning makes a charger valuable; a parking meter makes coins valuable.

nodes.name: noncontingent-reinforcement
nodes.mech: Give the reward a problem behaviour was earning for free, on a timer, whether or not they do it. With the payoff already coming, the behaviour has no job left. For this to work the free reward has to beat the earned one (more of it, better, more often than before), and it usually goes together with no longer rewarding the behaviour; if free and earned merely match, they keep working for the earned one. Variations: handing out breaks from a demand on schedule, before they act out, so the task feels interruptible and acting out stops paying.
nodes.one_liner: Give the reward a behavior was chasing on a timer for free, so acting out no longer earns anything extra.
nodes.why_short: If the payoff comes anyway, the behavior has nothing to produce; it only works if the free supply beats what acting out used to earn.
nodes.principle_note: If the reinforcer that maintained a behaviour arrives freely on a clock, the behaviour no longer produces anything the subject does not already have — both because the response-reinforcer contingency is degraded and because free delivery satiates, lowering the reinforcer's momentary value. Which of those two does the work is not fully settled, but the practical consequence is well replicated. The competition guard is the falsifiable core: the account predicts that NCR fails whenever the free source does not out-compete the earned one in rate, amount or quality, and that failure mode is exactly what is observed when schedules merely match.

ex.f: Free breaks on the clock, not on the behavior
ex.t: "the therapist used an initial FT 10-sec schedule for escape, meaning that the student had a break from the instructional requests every 10 seconds" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: reinforcement-extinction
nodes.mech: Find what a behaviour is getting them, then make sure it no longer gets it, from every source, every person, every time, and it fades. Nothing unpleasant is added; the payoff is simply removed. Expect a burst: it gets worse, varies, or turns angry before fading, and may return later; giving in even once teaches a bigger, more stubborn version, so hold steady. Variations: block escape so it no longer gets them out of a demand; state the rule flatly and disengage so it earns no attention; mask the sensation when the behaviour rewards itself; stop paying a chain's final payoff so it collapses backward.
nodes.one_liner: Find what a behavior is getting them and make sure it no longer gets it, from every source, every time.
nodes.why_short: Behavior that stops paying off declines toward baseline; expect a temporary burst first, and intermittent slip-ups keep it alive.
nodes.principle_note: Behaviour persists because it produces a consequence; break that relation and the rate declines toward baseline — this is the most heavily replicated finding in operant work. The characteristic side effects fall out of the same account: the burst and response variation are what an organism does when a previously reliable contingency stops paying (try harder, try differently), and partial reinforcement histories slow extinction because the subject has already learned that non-payment does not mean the contingency is gone. The account is falsifiable at the point that matters operationally — it predicts extinction fails if any maintaining source is left live, which is why incomplete enumeration reliably produces no decline at all.

ex.f: Enumerate every source before withholding any
ex.t: "withholding one source of reinforcement may have minimal or no effect on behavior." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Block the exit so escape stops paying
ex.t: "placed on extinction (escape extinction) when those behaviors do not produce a removal of the aversive stimulus, meaning that the individual cannot escape from the aversive situation" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Break the contingency at the sensory channel
ex.t: "adding lima beans to the vomit... the vomit did not taste as good, and the positive sensory consequence was masked." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Withhold all reinforcement for the response
ex.t: "Extinction (withholding all reinforcement for a previously reinforced behavior) produces a decrease in response rate to the behavior's pre-reinforcement level." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: self-management-self-administered-contingency
nodes.mech: The tracking, and often the rewards, are moved into the person themselves, because they are the only one present everywhere, including private thoughts and places no one else can watch. Simply recording one's own behaviour often changes it. It only works if their self-record is honest. Variations: recording at the moment it happens, such as a tally or a chart on the mirror; checking their record against an outside observer's and rewarding accuracy, then fading the check; doing something earlier, while temptation is weak, that changes what they'll do later; scoring their own work against an answer key and giving themselves the consequence.
nodes.one_liner: Have them track their own behavior, and optionally set and give themselves the reward, instead of you doing it.
nodes.why_short: Just recording behavior changes it a little; self-rewarding works when the self-monitoring stays honest, which is the weak point.
nodes.principle_note: Two separable effects. First, self-monitoring alone changes behaviour by reactivity: measuring a behaviour makes it salient and evaluable against a standard, and rates shift even with no consequence attached — the effect is real but typically modest and decays as monitoring lapses. Second, self-delivered consequences work to the extent the self-report is accurate, which is why accuracy-matching against an independent observer is trained separately; the honest-self-monitoring premise is the weak joint, not an incidental caveat. Falsifiable: predicts self-management effects shrink as recording accuracy degrades, and that reactivity-only interventions fade faster than externally verified ones.

ex.f: Score your own work and deliver your own consequence
ex.t: "students who have been taught to evaluate their own performance and provide their own feedback in the form of self-delivered rewards and error correction… are not dependent on the teacher's direction" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: The self is the one agent present everywhere
ex.t: "What behavior change agent can go with the student to every necessary lesson, at all times…? The student's own 'self' can always meet these specifications" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Reinforce accurate self-recording, not the behavior
ex.t: "Brian was taught to monitor his own behavior and to match his self-recordings to the recordings of his teachers. Accurate self-recording resulted in teacher praise" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: The subject holds all four contingency roles
ex.t: "A self-contract is a contingency contract that an individual makes with herself, incorporating a self-selected task and reward as well as self-monitoring of task completion and self-delivery of the reward." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: shaping-successive-approximation
nodes.mech: Build a behavior they don't do yet by rewarding small steps toward it. Start by rewarding something they already do that is a little like the goal, first bar at or just below their usual level. Once steady, reward only a slightly closer version, so the old one fades. Keep steps small, each bar winnable, and rewards frequent. If performance falls apart, go back to the last step that worked; a dip then recovery is normal. Variations: raise the bar on one quality at a time (how long, how fast, how exact); set each new bar from their recent typical tries; end with a free reward.
nodes.one_liner: Reward the smallest step toward the behavior you want, then only reward a slightly closer step, inching forward; back up if it falls apart.
nodes.why_short: Rewards shift the whole spread of someone's responses toward whatever gets paid. Paying only the best attempts, while older versions go unrewarded and fade, walks the behavior somewhere it never was before.
nodes.principle_note: Reinforcement acts on a distribution of responses, not a single one, so paying the upper tail of that distribution shifts the whole distribution in that direction while unpaid variants extinguish — response variability supplies the raw material each step. Gradualness is load-bearing because a criterion set beyond the current distribution's reach means nothing gets reinforced and the behaviour extinguishes instead of advancing, which is exactly why criteria keyed to the subject's own recent performance band outperform fixed ones. Falsifiable and tested: the dip-and-recover pattern following a criterion raise is predicted by this account, and criteria set outside the achievable band predictably collapse responding rather than slowing it.

ex.f: Advance in small steps; drop back on deterioration
ex.t: "If a behavior deteriorates, quickly revisit the last successful approximation or two" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Each stabilized class replaced by a closer one
ex.t: "The gradually changing criterion for reinforcement during shaping results in a succession of new response classes … each one closer in form to the terminal behavior than the response class it replaces" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Hold the form, narrow the acceptance window
ex.t: "each toss that is near the person (e.g., within 2 meters) will be praised… As students become more accurate, the area is reduced so that the terminal behavior—tosses within arm's length… is achieved… the form of the toss remains the same." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Capture a twitch, then walk the window forward
ex.t: "any hand or finger movement, even a twitch, would be reinforced. Subsequently, successive hand or finger movements toward the spoon would be reinforced... whereas other behaviors would undergo extinction." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: unconditional-antecedent-consequence-logging
nodes.mech: The operator keeps a running log of every relevant trigger and every consequence each time it happens, whether or not the target behavior happened too, next to a record of the behavior itself, usually on a simple coded sheet by time slot or count. Because the times the trigger came without the behavior are written down as well, the log later shows whether the trigger really predicts the behavior or only seems to. It is record-keeping, not something done to the subject.
nodes.one_liner: Write down every trigger and consequence whenever it happens, even when the behavior did not, so you can see what actually drives it.
nodes.why_short: People see patterns in coincidences and forget the times the cue happened without the result. Logging everything gives you the missing counts, so you can tell a real cause from a fluke.
nodes.principle_note: Humans (and clinicians) systematically infer causation from co-occurrence while ignoring the cells of the contingency table where the cue occurred without the outcome — the classic illusory-correlation error. Logging antecedents unconditionally forces the base rate into the record, so a spurious pairing can be shown false by the data rather than defended by memory. Falsifiable prediction: observers using unconditional logs should produce contingency estimates closer to the true delta-p than observers using behavior-triggered logs on the same event stream.

ex.f: Log the events whether or not the behavior fires
ex.t: "The targeted environmental events (antecedents and consequences) are recorded whenever they occur, regardless of whether problem behavior occurred with it." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: authority-diffusion-plurality
nodes.mech: Take away the single person the listener could push back against. Instead of one hypnotist giving orders, the authority is spread out, handed to peers, or disguised as friendship, so resistance has no clear target. Variations: split the operator into several voices or figures who all keep working; slide from 'my voice' to 'the voices' to 'our voices', drawing the listener's own inner voice in; have imagined trusted friends say the words; speak as a fellow subject already changed by the process, or as a messenger for an absent boss; keep real control while presenting it as partnership or shared fate.
nodes.one_liner: Make it so there is no single hypnotist to push against: several voices, 'we' instead of 'I', or you posing as a fellow victim.
nodes.why_short: Pushing back needs someone to push against. Spreading the voice across many figures, or posing as a peer, leaves resistance without an obvious target, so the content gets less scrutiny. Untested in this setting.
nodes.principle_note: Resistance is a targeted act: reactance is aroused by an identifiable agent perceived as constraining freedom, and counterarguing requires a source to argue against. Distributing, disguising, or demoting the operator removes the addressee, so the persuasive content is processed without the source-directed scrutiny that normally accompanies a recognised influence attempt; the peer or renounced-authority framing additionally lowers perceived persuasive intent, which is the strongest known suppressor of defensive processing. Falsifiable: plural/peer-framed delivery of identical content should yield fewer counterarguments and lower reported reactance than the same content from a single named authority.

ex.f: Self-reference pluralized from I to the voices
ex.t: Nothing changes in the recording except the pronouns: what began as one speaker's instructions becomes "the voices" a few minutes in, and then "our voices," with the listener handed a first-person line about obeying them. No second speaker ever appears — the plurality is purely grammatical. A listener framing a rebuttal finds the thing they meant to argue with has already moved to a plural nobody, and their own inner voice has quietly been enrolled into the set.
ex.s: Several minutes in, single-speaker recording; the pronoun shift is the only change and no second speaker ever appears.
ex.m: You've been listening to my voice. [later] Listen to the voices now — the voices are easier than thinking. [later] Our voices are in there with yours, and you can't tell which of us is which any more. Say it with us: I obey the voices.

ex.f: Listener populates the group that does the talking
ex.t: The operator never claims the position of the one doing the work. Instead the listener is asked to picture a room of people they already trust, talking around them, and the actual suggestions are attributed to that conversation. The group is left deliberately blank so the listener fills it with whoever they would genuinely defer to, and the demotion to listener-only feels like the natural shape of the room rather than something imposed by a speaker.
ex.s: Early; subject imaginative and able to populate a scene, operator explicitly stepping out of the source position.
ex.m: Picture the room you're most comfortable in, and put the people you trust most in it — you choose who, I don't need to know. They're talking around you, not to you, the way people do when you're half asleep on the couch. And what they're saying is that you've earned a rest from deciding things. Listen to them say it.

ex.f: Operator functions split across simultaneous figures
ex.t: Three figures are introduced, and the jobs a single hypnotist would normally do are divided between them: one arouses, one commands and restricts, one binds and elevates. They act in sequence and then all at once, each addressing a different layer — body, gaze, mind. There is no hypnotist to push back at, only a room with three of them, so a listener who mentally refuses one is still being worked on by the other two, and none of them has to relent for the others to escalate.
ex.s: Imagery-capable; three figures are introduced by function and then act simultaneously on different layers.
ex.m: There are three of us in here with you. The one on your left works your body — feel her hand on your thigh. The one in front holds your eyes and tells you what to do: don't look away. The one behind you handles your mind, and she's already started. Refuse any one of us and the other two carry on without pausing.

nodes.name: borrowed-reflex-recruitment
nodes.mech: Instead of building trust or momentum from scratch, attach the session to something that already works for the listener, so it inherits that pull. Variations: use their nightly falling-asleep as the induction vehicle; use their existing arousal at hypnosis as fuel; recall a real, pleasant memory of going under anaesthesia and say 'this feels so similar'; tie the effect to a sensation they genuinely felt before, and quietly test it in small graded steps before any irreversible step; borrow a shared ritual such as New Year's resolutions, ruling out similar ones; place new suggestions among ones visibly already working, so they borrow that credibility.
nodes.one_liner: Hook the session onto something that already works for them: their bedtime routine, a real memory of anaesthesia, a feeling they've had before.
nodes.why_short: Feelings and expectations attached to a familiar, trusted thing spill over onto whatever is linked to it. Riding an existing habit means you do not have to build momentum from nothing.
nodes.principle_note: Feelings and expectations attached to a trusted source spread to whatever is regularly paired with it or sits next to it, and this happens largely whether or not the pairing makes logical sense. This is known as evaluative conditioning, along with the transfer of expectations. Attaching a new suggestion to a habit that already runs smoothly, a real memory, or a suggestion the person can feel working also makes it easier to process, and that ease is often mistaken for truth. This could be shown wrong: the same suggestion should be accepted more when placed among suggestions that visibly work than when given on its own.

ex.f: The listener's kink recruited as the engine
ex.t: Between the induction and the deepener, the operator pauses to explain that the listener's existing arousal at being hypnotized is not something to be embarrassed about — it is evidence of unusual imaginative capacity, and the very reason they will be good at the skill about to be trained. A possibly-shameful reflex is relabeled as a talent, and in the same breath conscripted as the power supply for the ostensibly non-erotic work that follows.
ex.s: Pause between induction and deepener, non-erotic framing on the surface; subject's arousal at being hypnotized is already evident to them.
ex.m: You get turned on by this — by being put under. Don't be embarrassed about it; that response is a sign of an unusually vivid imagination, and it's exactly why you're going to be good at what I'm about to train you in. So let it build, and we'll run the work on top of it.

ex.f: Trance mapped onto the nightly sleep reflex
ex.t: Rather than building a state from nothing, the operator opens by telling the listener to get comfortable exactly as though they were going to bed, and asserts that entering the state takes no effort for the same reason falling asleep takes none. The listener is asked only to close their eyes and keep listening; the heaviness, the drifting and the slipping under are all borrowed from a reflex they perform every night and cannot fail at. There is nothing left to check whether it is working yet, because the process being invoked is one nobody has ever had to try at.
ex.s: Opening lines, before any induction proper; subject lying down at night, eyes not yet closed.
ex.m: Get comfortable exactly the way you do when you're going to bed — same pillow, same position, lights the way you like them. You don't have to try to go under, any more than you have to try to fall asleep; it happens to you, it always has. Close your eyes and keep listening. That's the whole of your job tonight.

nodes.name: collective-social-proof-enrollment
nodes.mech: Show the goal state as the normal, happy condition of a group who already went there, so giving in feels like joining friends rather than obeying the operator, and holding out feels lonely. Variations: a 'we' who say they are happier, with the listener cast as the last holdout; a background chorus already repeating the phrases the listener will say later, which can also voice the harshest claims deniably; a pronoun split where 'we' carries beliefs and 'you' instructions; overheard or watched scenes of others already living it; 'you will soon be one of them'; an open invitation to join people already changed.
nodes.one_liner: Present a happy group who already went where you want the listener to go, so giving in feels like joining them, not obeying you.
nodes.why_short: People judge what is normal and safe by what similar others do, most strongly when uncertain. Refusing then means staying alone outside a happy group rather than standing up to one person.
nodes.principle_note: Descriptive norms are among the most reliable levers on behaviour: people infer what is correct and safe from what similar others are doing, and this effect is strongest under uncertainty — exactly the state an induction produces. Reframing compliance as joining also converts the cost of refusal from 'obeying a stranger' into 'excluding myself from a group', and the aversiveness of social exclusion is well documented. Falsifiable: compliance should drop measurably if the cohort is described as unhappy or dissimilar to the listener, which a pure obedience account would not predict.

ex.f: Overheard peer gossip inverts recruitment into application
ex.t: For the first several minutes nobody addresses the listener at all: a handful of voices chatter to each other about the venue's rules — what gets you in, what gets you thrown out, how long it took them to qualify. The listener is positioned as an eavesdropper, so the value system arrives as ambient fact rather than instruction, and the scarcity talk flips the dynamic entirely: by the time an operator finally speaks, the listener is no longer being recruited, they are auditioning.
ex.s: First several minutes of the session; nobody addresses the subject at all, who is positioned as an eavesdropper.
ex.m: "She doesn't get in — did you see her? Still thinking about it at the door." "It took me four months to get in. Four." "You have to actually want it, that's the whole test. They can tell." "God, I'd never go back. Can you imagine going back?"

ex.f: Pronoun division of labor conscripts a we
ex.t: The pronouns are sorted by job. Beliefs and identity claims are always carried by the collective first person — what the group has come to believe, how it presents itself, what it has become. Concrete instructions are carried by the second person. A rare singular first person surfaces only long enough to establish that the speaker went through this too and is not above the listener. The harshest content arrives inside the collective voice, so it never reads as one person telling another what to do.
ex.s: Mid-session; pronouns are assigned by job — collective for beliefs, second person for instructions, one rare singular to establish peerhood.
ex.m: We don't argue with instructions any more — we found out how much lighter it is not to. Put your hands flat on your thighs and leave them there. We like being told; we stopped pretending otherwise a long time ago. Breathe out slowly. I was the last one in, so I know exactly how you feel right now.

ex.f: A phantom chorus pre-seeds the mantra
ex.t: The listener is told there are other voices behind the operator's — prior devotees, still chanting — and the phrases they are supposedly chanting are spoken aloud well before the listener is asked to say anything. When the demand to recite finally arrives, the words feel recognized rather than issued. The same chorus also carries the most coercive claims, so the operator never has to say them in her own first person.
ex.s: Before any recitation is demanded; the chorus is asserted as an audible presence behind the operator's voice.
ex.m: Behind me there are others — the ones who came before you, still going, still chanting. Listen: empty is better, empty is better, obey and be empty. They've been saying it since before you pressed play. And they're saying something you won't say yet: that you were never going to leave.

ex.f: An already-converted cohort reports being happier
ex.t: The speaking voice is a plural one, and it is specific about who it is: a group that used to be exactly where the listener is now, went through the change, and is measurably better off for it. Their self-deprecation about the old life is spoken in chorus, and inclusion is offered as the reward rather than obedience demanded as the price. What the listener is invited to weigh is not whether to submit but whether to keep standing outside a room where everyone else is happy — the cost of refusing becomes social isolation, and the frame never has to argue that the change is good.
ex.s: Plural voice speaking throughout; subject positioned as the only one still outside.
ex.m: We were where you are — arguing with our own heads at two in the morning, exhausted from it. We're not any more, and we're happier. Nobody here is going to make you do anything. We'd just rather you were in here with us than out there on your own, still doing all that thinking.

nodes.name: competence-harvest-installation
nodes.mech: Instead of arguing or teaching a disputed concept, the operator elicits a domain where the subject is expert and automatic (gear-shifting, tire-listening, engine gauges), actively surfaces the subject's own out-of-awareness access to it in real time, then renames that lived experience AS the concept. Acceptance of the familiar, undeniable domain carries acceptance of the concept because it now arrives as the subject's own knowledge rather than the operator's claim; the subject holds the new frame as lived knowledge with no didactic teaching, and the borrowed domain can be extended into a signal channel.
nodes.one_liner: Ask about something they do expertly without thinking, get them to notice it, then call that 'the unconscious' or whatever idea you're teaching.
nodes.why_short: People don't argue with their own lived experience. When a new idea arrives as a name for something they just felt, it feels like their own knowledge rather than your claim.
nodes.principle_note: People remember things they produce themselves better than things they are told, and resist arguing with them more (the generation effect). People also rarely argue with their own remembered experience. Drawing out a real experience and then giving it a new name lets the disputed idea borrow the standing of something the person saw for themselves. This could be tested against an outside measure: the same idea given as a plain analogy, without drawing out an experience, should be remembered less well later and disputed more in a controlled comparison. How the technique is defined is not itself evidence that this explanation is right.

ex.f: Harvest a real expert experience, then rename it
ex.t: "There are parts of you that know how to shift gears and listen for load shifts… so you don't have to consciously think about those things." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: concede-the-defended-topic
nodes.mech: The operator opens on a genuine shared-identity hook (a real common experience), then explicitly concedes and disclaims the topic the subject is defensively expert in ("it won't be about flowers... you know more than I do... that isn't what you want"), while naming the subject's actual unmet want. Flattering the expertise and surrendering the defended topic removes it from contention so the subject stops guarding it; naming the true want redirects the motivational search inward toward relief, and rapport forms as the suspicion of angling dissolves.
nodes.one_liner: Admit up front that they know more about their pet topic than you and that you won't argue it, then name what they really want.
nodes.why_short: People brace to defend the topics they care about. Openly giving up that topic removes the expected attack, so they relax, and naming their real want turns their attention toward relief.
nodes.principle_note: Defensive processing is topic-specific: when a subject expects an attack on a domain they are invested in, they pre-load counterarguments; explicitly disclaiming that domain removes the anticipated threat, and the relief lowers the persuasion-knowledge guard. Naming an unmet want simultaneously exploits the fact that a stated need directs attentional and motivational search toward relief. Falsifiable: subjects should show fewer counterarguments and higher rapport ratings after an explicit topic concession than after equivalent-length neutral small talk.

ex.f: Concede the topic the subject is expert in
ex.t: "it won't be about flowers because you know more than I do about flowers. That isn't what you want." — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

nodes.name: manufactured-insufficiency-treadmill
nodes.mech: Grants a small acknowledged success then immediately revokes its sufficiency ("that's it... but you still get distracted don't you... so let's take you deeper"), so each compliance becomes the pretext for going further; the operator owns the standard for "focused enough" / "deep enough", so the listener can never reach a stable "done". Success is spent as evidence of inadequacy, generating continuous downward pressure justified by the listener's own asserted shortcoming — compliance earns more depth, not satisfaction.
nodes.one_liner: Praise them for going deep, then say they're still not quite deep enough, so every success becomes the reason to go further.
nodes.why_short: Whether effort feels like enough depends on the standard it is judged against. If you own the standard and keep moving it, the listener never reaches 'done' and keeps chasing.
nodes.principle_note: This exploits the fact that satisfaction is judged against a reference standard rather than an absolute, and whoever controls the standard controls whether effort ever feels sufficient — the same structure as a shifting-goalpost or moving-baseline schedule. Intermittent partial reinforcement (the granted success) sustains responding far better than either consistent reward or none, so effort persists while the terminal state stays out of reach. Falsifiable: if the listener is given an externally fixed, operator-independent criterion for 'deep enough', the escalation should stop; if it continues regardless, the account is wrong.

ex.f: Grant the success, then revoke its sufficiency
ex.t: The operator acknowledges that the listener responded — that's it, that's right — and in the same breath withdraws the credit: they are still drifting, still not taking it in properly, so they had better go further down. The compliance just demonstrated becomes the evidence that more is required. Because the operator alone decides what counts as focused enough, no amount of complying ever lands on "done"; every success is spent immediately as proof of a shortfall.
ex.s: Immediately after a visible compliance — a response, a settle, a slowed breath the operator has just acknowledged.
ex.m: That's it. That's right — that's exactly what I wanted. And you're still drifting off it, aren't you, still not quite taking it all the way in. Which means you're not deep enough yet. So down further for me.

nodes.name: own-acts-surrender-ledger
nodes.mech: The operator enumerates or annotates the listener's genuine recent acts — purchasing, browsing, fetching a garment, adopting a posture, obeying setup instructions, sustained engagement, even a single compelled motion — and re-labels each as an instance of the target state (surrender, obedience, vulnerability, love, devotion), openly and contemporaneously. Because the cited proofs are the listener's own real behavior they are hard to repudiate; the perceived baseline shifts from zero to already-surrendered, future resistance now feels like self-contradiction (sunk-cost/complicity), and skeptical mode becomes harder to enter. Registers span retrocausal compliance/surrender ledgers, posture-as-consent ratchets, waking-compliance relabeled as automatic-obedience, a compliance act laundered into "natural" baseline desire, a symptoms-to-diagnosis interpretive frame, a single compelled motion re-narrated as a chain of consensual obedience acts, and a lure-reveal that rebinds self-generated pursuit to the operator.
nodes.one_liner: List things they really did tonight (pressing play, getting comfortable, following setup) and name each as proof they've already been surrendering.
nodes.why_short: People work out what they feel partly by watching what they do, especially when inner signals are fuzzy. The acts really happened, so they can only dispute the label, and backing out now feels inconsistent.
nodes.principle_note: Self-perception theory: people infer their own attitudes by observing their behaviour, especially when internal cues are weak or ambiguous — which trance deliberately produces. Because the cited acts genuinely happened, the subject cannot dispute the evidence, only the label, and the consistency principle then makes contradicting the inferred state costlier than continuing to act on it. Falsifiable: the technique should fail or backfire when the cited acts have an obvious situational explanation the subject can point to, since a salient external cause blocks the dispositional inference.

ex.f: Consumer behavior flattened into acts of power transfer
ex.t: The operator reads out a list of things the listener has done — visiting the site, watching the free material, downloading the file, following the undressing instruction — and attaches the same clause to every item: each one was an act of handing over power. Ordinary consumer behavior sits in the list alongside deliberate submission, undifferentiated. The listener is told to realize how far along they already are rather than to decide anything, so the next request is framed as continuing rather than starting.
ex.s: Mid-session; the subject has a real history with the material — site visits, free files, a download, a followed instruction.
ex.m: Count them with me. You found the site: that was you handing over a piece of power. You listened to the free ones: another piece. You downloaded this: another. You took your clothes off when I told you to, ten minutes ago: another. Look at how much of it is already mine. You're not deciding whether to start — you're a long way in.

ex.f: Waking setup compliance relabeled as a trait
ex.t: Before any induction the listener is sent to fetch a small item, then told how to arrange themselves and where to put their hands. Once all of it is done the operator stops and points out that every one of those instructions was followed at once, with no trance involved at all — which is offered as proof that compliance is simply how this listener works. A baseline is thereby established before any depth exists, and everything that follows only deepens something the listener has already accepted as a fact about themselves.
ex.s: Pre-induction, subject fully awake; a fetch instruction, a posture instruction, and a hand-placement instruction have all just been completed.
ex.m: Stop a moment. You got up and fetched it because I asked. You arranged yourself the way I described. Your hands went where I put them. All of that with your eyes open and nothing in your head but my voice on a speaker — no trance anywhere. That's not something I did to you. That's just how you work.

ex.f: One compelled motion renarrated as many obediences
ex.t: The listener is told they are already moving before they noticed deciding to — a single compulsion, openly described as such. The journey then passes through a series of doorways and stairs. At the destination the operator re-narrates the whole trip: every threshold, she says, was a separate command the listener chose to follow, and only that repeated obedience could have brought them here. One instruction has become a remembered chain of a dozen consented acts.
ex.s: Imagined journey through thresholds and stairs; the initial motion was framed as a compulsion the subject did not choose.
ex.m: You're already walking — you didn't decide to, you just noticed you were. Through the first door. Down the stairs. Through the second. [at the destination] Now look back at how you got here. Every doorway was a separate instruction, and you chose to follow every one of them. Twelve times you said yes tonight. That's the only way anyone arrives in this room.

ex.f: Recent real acts annotated as prior surrender
ex.t: Minutes in, the operator lists back three things the listener genuinely just did — the flicker of arousal while buying the recording, the reaction to the very first number spoken, the readiness with which a small setup instruction was obeyed — and labels each one, retroactively, as an episode of the state being installed. None of them were framed that way at the time. The listener now holds an evidence file about themselves that did not exist five minutes earlier, built entirely from their own behavior, which is much harder to dismiss than a claim the operator merely asserted. The state is presented as already true and simply being pointed out.
ex.s: A few minutes in; the subject has genuinely bought the recording, reacted to the first number, and followed one small setup instruction.
ex.m: Three things you already did tonight. There was a flicker when you paid for this — that was you surrendering. You reacted to the very first number I said, before I'd done anything — that was you surrendering. And you moved your hands where I told you without a pause — that was you surrendering. I'm not asking you to start. I'm telling you what you've already been doing.

nodes.name: preempt-objection-frame
nodes.mech: Before the listener can form their own objection to a coming change, hand them a ready answer to that exact objection, so it never takes hold. Variations: frame the change as an addition, not a loss ('this adds to you'); call an imposed rule a shared deal; admit you don't know everything; split a valued trait so they keep the part they care about and lose only the chore part ('you stay clever, you just stop doing sums'); answer 'but I don't feel any rope' by saying the mind is taken first and the body follows.
nodes.one_liner: Before they can object, say the objection's answer: 'this adds to you, it doesn't replace you', or 'your mind goes first, the body follows later'.
nodes.why_short: Whoever explains a change first sets how it is understood. If a harmless reading is already in place, the objection has less room to form and arguing back takes extra effort.
nodes.principle_note: Inoculation and forewarning research shows that whoever supplies an interpretation first sets the frame subsequent input is processed against; once a defusing reading is already held, the objection has no gap to form in and any counterargument arrives as the second, effortful move. The trait-partition variant additionally exploits the fact that identity threat is resisted only when the valued self-attribute is the thing at stake — leave that attribute intact and the threat does not register. Falsifiable: pre-empting an objection the subject was never going to raise should produce no benefit and may introduce the objection, which a generic 'more framing is better' account would not predict.

ex.f: Imposed contingency described as a shared exchange
ex.t: "children view contracting as a behavior-exchange process shared by all members of the group, not as something adults impose on them" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Positioned as an addition, never a replacement
ex.t: "this relaxation … is going to be used in addition to all the aids that medical science has invented … So this is going to be a wonderful plus to everything else." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

ex.f: Supply the benign reading before they invent a hostile one
ex.t: "if you make a change without establishing an explicit frame around it, that leaves the employees to make up their own frames" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: startle-back-disarm-ratchet
nodes.mech: Names the familiar jerking-back-awake experience near sleep, then asserts that here the pull-back gets monotonically harder each attempt while letting-go gets easier. This disarms the specific micro- resistance that keeps insomniacs awake (the startle-back): by framing each pull-back as strictly costlier than the last, any attempt to stay awake is reinterpreted as evidence sleep is winning — arousal/ vigilance pushed down with a one-way valve, and over-compliance becomes the success path.
nodes.one_liner: Name the jolt of waking as you fall asleep, and say each jolt here costs more than the last while letting go gets easier.
nodes.why_short: Trying hard to stay awake (or to fall asleep) keeps you alert. Framing each pull-back as harder and pointless makes the effort feel useless, so they stop fighting. Works only when they are already drowsy.
nodes.principle_note: Trouble falling asleep is kept going by a loop of self-monitoring in which the effort to sleep raises alertness, the effort paradox behind paradoxical-intention treatments. Framing each jolt back awake as more costly takes away the payoff of staying watchful, so the loop loses what keeps it going. This could be shown wrong in a specific way: the technique should only work when the body is already close to sleep, so failure when the person is wide awake is predicted, not explained away. One part of the usual claim is not part of this explanation: the idea that each jolt gets steadily harder is speculative decoration, and since any experience seems to confirm it, it cannot be tested and explains nothing.

ex.f: Each pull-back made costlier than the last
ex.t: The operator names the small jolt everyone knows — drifting off, then snapping back — and then states a rule about it: in here, each snap back costs more effort than the one before it, and each drift costs less. Nothing is forbidden; staying awake is simply priced upward on every attempt. The listener who tries once and finds it harder the second time has just produced the evidence the frame predicted, so the effort to stay awake becomes the proof that the drift is winning.
ex.s: Late-night listen, body genuinely near sleep onset; the subject has already twitched back once tonight.
ex.m: You know the little jolt — you start to go, and something snaps you back awake. In here that jolt costs more every time you use it. The second one is harder work than the first, the third harder than the second, and drifting gets cheaper on exactly the same schedule. Try it if you like. Notice how much more it took that time.

nodes.name: subtractive-fear-label-management
nodes.mech: Take the fear out of the name for the state, so a nervous or skeptical subject's defenses never switch on; you lower the stakes rather than building anticipation. Three ways: recast hypnosis as an everyday mood rather than a special condition ('how many moods have you had since you got up this morning?'), so being 'put into' something stops sounding alarming; leave the word out entirely and describe only the effect ('I'll teach you to relax'), so there is nothing to attach dread to; or swap in an impressive-sounding technical name, which adds a sense of authority while dropping the frightening word.
nodes.one_liner: Don't say 'hypnosis' to a nervous subject: call it an everyday mood, describe only the effect, or use a neutral technical name.
nodes.why_short: Loaded words call up fears before anything happens. Removing the word removes the cue. Caution: lab work found calling a procedure 'hypnosis' can increase responsiveness, so this helps mainly with frightened subjects.
nodes.principle_note: Labels activate schemas, and an activated threat schema recruits defensive appraisal before the content is even evaluated — the reason word choice measurably changes reported fear and compliance for identical procedures. Removing, softening, or swapping the loaded term denies the defensive schema its cue, and recasting the state as an everyday occurrence lowers perceived novelty, which reduces threat appraisal. Falsifiable: subjects given the unlabelled description should report lower anticipatory anxiety and higher responsiveness than subjects given the identical procedure labelled with the loaded term.

ex.f: Recast the state as an everyday mood
ex.t: "a state of mind is merely a mood, and I maintain that hypnosis is merely a mood." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

ex.f: Never speak the fear-loaded name
ex.t: "in introducing your patient to hypnosis, don't use the word hypnosis. Give the patient the benefit of the state without ever using the word. Why should you generate the fear associated with the word…" — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

ex.f: Swap the loaded term for a prestige euphemism
ex.t: "Patients expect--and want-a doctor to use esoteric, impressive terms… without introducing fear or a feeling of mystery" — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: withheld-frame-reveal
nodes.mech: Run the session under a harmless stated purpose the listener accepts, then use that acceptance to carry something it never covered, without asking again. Variations: reveal late, when they are deepest or past a point of no return (restrained, after climax, after waking), that it was conditioning all along, so their earlier participation reads as consent; set up a harmless-looking frame early (a fake anti-hypnosis safeguard, an empty-sounding rule, a rhythm they already agreed to follow) and later reveal or reuse it to justify the real suggestion.
nodes.one_liner: Run the session as something harmless, then reveal near the end, when they're deepest, that it was really conditioning all along.
nodes.why_short: After investing time and effort, accepting a new story about what you were doing is easier than admitting you were tricked. Timing the reveal when backing out is hardest strengthens this. Consensual fantasy only.
nodes.principle_note: Sunk participation is reinterpreted rather than repudiated: the consistency principle and effort justification make it psychologically cheaper to accept a revised account of what one was doing than to conclude one was deceived while continuing to participate. Timing the reveal after depth, restraint, or climax exploits the fact that the reappraisal window closes once the act is irreversible — there is no longer an action the reinterpretation could change. Falsifiable: revealing the true frame early, before commitment accrues, should produce refusal rather than acceptance; if late and early reveals worked equally, the sunk-cost account would be wrong.

ex.f: Disclosure timed to when exit is foreclosed
ex.t: The listener is walked through a benign setup and only once the scene has them fully secured does the operator explain, in a tone of friendly candour, what the session is actually for. The timing is the whole move: the same sentence delivered ten minutes earlier would be an offer that could be declined, and delivered here it is an update on something already underway. Withdrawing now would mean disowning the cooperation already spent getting to this point.
ex.s: Scene has been staged as a benign setup and the subject is now fully secured within it; disclosure lands only at that point.
ex.m: There — that's the last strap. Comfortable? Good. So I should tell you what tonight is actually for, now that we're here. I wasn't going to bring it up earlier, because earlier it would have been a question, and you'd have had to decide. It isn't a question now. It's just what we're already doing.

ex.f: Prior engagement re-read as evidence of identity
ex.t: Two-thirds of the way through, the operator announces that everything so far was the gentle version and pivots to heavier material — but frames the pivot as a deduction rather than a request. The listener chose this recording, and stayed with it this long; that behaviour, the operator says, is what tells them what the listener is. Declining now would require explaining away twenty minutes of one's own attention, which is more work than accepting the label.
ex.s: Two-thirds through; the subject has stayed with the recording for twenty minutes and the pivot to heavier material is framed as a deduction.
ex.m: Everything up to here was the gentle version. I'm not going to ask whether you want the rest, because you already answered — you picked this file out of everything you could have picked, and you're still here twenty minutes later. People who aren't what you are turn it off in the first five. So we both know what you are. Let's get on with it.

ex.f: Disclosure after the fictional dose is metabolized
ex.t: The listener is handed something to drink in the imagined scene and drinks it, with no explanation attached. Forty lines later the operator reveals what it supposedly was and what it supposedly does — and adds that its effect is permanent because of how the substance bonds to the body. There is now no instruction on the table to refuse, only a past act to accept, and the claimed irreversibility is laundered through invented chemistry rather than asserted by the operator.
ex.s: Imagined scene; the subject was handed something to drink with no explanation and has already drunk it in the fiction.
ex.m: Empty glass. Good. [forty lines later] I should tell you what that was. It bonds to the tissue — that's why it doesn't wash out, why there's no back from it. It's already through you by now. There was never anything for you to agree to; you drank it forty lines ago.

ex.f: The stated game was never the real game
ex.t: Thirty minutes in, at the point of least critical capacity, the operator drops the frame the session was sold under: what was actually being run was something else, it has been running the whole time, and it is finished. The conditioning is then described in the past tense — not asked for, not offered, reported as an accomplished fact. Because the announcement comes after the participation rather than before it, the listener has nothing left to decline; everything they already did is retroactively re-labelled as the thing being announced. A second move closes the last gap: any objection is pre-answered by claiming the listener silently wanted it, evidence for which the operator alone can see.
ex.s: Thirty minutes in, at maximum depth; the session has run under a stated benign frame the subject accepted at the start.
ex.m: You can stop trying to relax now, because that was never what this was. What has been running for the last half hour is conditioning, and it's finished. It's not something I'm offering you — it's done, it's in, and it was in some minutes ago. And if part of you wants to object: I could hear that you wanted this from the first minute. You just couldn't hear it yourself.

nodes.name: addressable-construct-building
nodes.mech: Build the imagined thing so it can be found again later, not just enjoyed now: give it a place, a route, or a clear marker image. The return trip is the point. Having the listener help design it adds ownership, and a structure with room for more (many doors, a chain of images) hints at more to come. Variations: a door bearing their own name at the end of a hallway of rooms; a few vivid, frozen images of a future self, tied to the senses, built ahead of a later ritual.
nodes.one_liner: Build an imagined place or image with an address, like a door bearing their name, so you can send them back later.
nodes.why_short: Memories come back more easily when they have a clear cue and a location. A named door or a fixed image works like the memory-palace trick, giving the later return a handle to grab.
nodes.principle_note: Memory retrieval depends on having a usable cue and a route to the trace; giving an imagined object a location, a name, or a discrete image builds exactly the kind of distinctive, spatially-indexed handle that supports later reinstatement — the same reason method-of-loci mnemonics outperform undifferentiated rehearsal. Self-authorship of the object adds the generation effect and raises subsequent investment in it. Falsifiable: an equally vivid but unaddressed scene should be significantly harder to re-evoke on later cue than an addressed one, and if re-evocation rates are equal, addressability is not doing the work.

ex.f: Three frozen future-self images built before use
ex.t: The listener is asked to compose three still pictures of their own successful future self — one a week out, one a month, one a year — each held frozen and pinned to specific sensory detail. Nothing is done with them in the moment; they are constructed as handles for a later ritual to address. Because the listener authored the images themselves, the investment in them is their own.
ex.s: Subject composed and imaginative; three still images are being constructed as anchors for a later ritual, with nothing done with them now.
ex.m: Make me three photographs of yourself. The first is you a week from now — where are you standing, what's in your hand, what's the temperature of the room? Hold it still. The second is you a month from now: what are you wearing, what can you smell? Hold it. The third is you a year from now — one sound, one texture. Hold all three. We aren't using them tonight; we're building them.

ex.f: A named door in an installable hallway
ex.t: The suggestion is not offered as a feeling but given an address. The listener is walked to a freestanding door marked with something that belongs only to them, then into a corridor lined with other doors, each said to open onto a different idea or a different part of the self, before choosing one and entering the room behind it. Because the suggestion now has a location and a route, it can be walked back to later rather than merely remembered. The corridor does a second job: by showing many doors and using only one, it implies more can be added later.
ex.s: Imagery-capable and mid-depth; the object is to be built for later re-navigation, not inhabited now.
ex.m: In front of you, a door standing on its own, and on it something written that belongs only to you — your name, in your handwriting. Open it: a corridor, doors down both sides, each one opening on a different room of you. Count seven along on the left and go into that one. Learn the way. You'll be coming back here, and this is the route.

nodes.name: causal-attribution-to-external-agent
nodes.mech: Name something outside the listener as the cause of the change ('the relaxing agent will do the rest'), something that isn't actually taken or used up. Their will then has nothing to push against, and there is no effort for them to succeed or fail at. Because the cause seems external and objective, the effect holds up when they look inward and question it.
nodes.one_liner: Tell them something outside them is causing the change, like 'the relaxing agent will do the rest', so they don't have to try.
nodes.why_short: Suggestions work best when the effect feels like it just happens. An outside cause gives the feeling a source other than the self, and removes any chance of trying and failing.
nodes.principle_note: Suggestion works best when the response feels like it is happening by itself. Naming an outside cause gives the listener somewhere to place sensations that actually come from expectation and focused attention. Taking the self out as the one doing it also removes the chance of trying and failing, which is the main way suggestions collapse. It can be tested only as the belief forms: people given no outside cause should report more sense of effort and respond less often than people given one. Whether the effect lasts after the named cause is debunked is not a fair test, because a mistaken attribution, once formed, often survives being disproved.

ex.f: A named agent does the relaxing
ex.t: "when I swab it, just stay relaxed and the relaxing agent will do the rest" — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

ex.f: An inert carrier plus a plausible cover story
ex.t: "They put the anesthesia right into the alcohol now—and when I swab you with this, you'll become completely anesthetized." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

ex.f: An imagined device retroactively explains the fog
ex.t: After the induction has already blurred the listener's thinking, the operator introduces a worn object fitted to the head and states that its workings are the reason thoughts are hard to form now. The cognitive fog was produced by the preceding twenty minutes, but it arrives with an external explanation attached, so the listener's own experience reads as confirmation of the device rather than of the induction. The same frame is then extended to the limbs, so stillness and dullness share one imagined cause.
ex.s: Twenty minutes of induction have already produced real cognitive fog; the external object is introduced only now.
ex.m: There's something fitted over your head — snug, warm at the temples, humming faintly. That hum is why the sentences won't finish; it isn't you, it's the field. Notice how hard it is to hold a thought — that's it working. It reaches down the arms and legs too, which is why they're so still and so dull.

ex.f: Control reified as a fluid that must drain
ex.t: The operator asserts — never hypothesises, never hedges with a simile — that conscious control is a substance held inside the body, and that the body has outlets through which it leaves. The grammar makes it mechanical: given an outlet, draining follows as a consequence rather than as a choice. Letting go is thereby demoted from an act the listener might fail at to a physical process already underway that they are merely invited to notice.
ex.s: Mid-induction; the assertion is made flatly and mechanically, with no simile and no hedge.
ex.m: Conscious control is a fluid, and it collects in the body. Your palms are open, and it runs out through them. It leaves through the soles of your feet. It isn't something you're doing — a container with an opening in it drains, that's all. You can just notice how much has already gone.

nodes.name: concrete-externalization-parked-faculty
nodes.mech: Reifies an internal faculty (the analytical mind, memory, resistance, bodily agency, or the self- model) as a concrete external object and relocates it out of the body so it can be set aside, watched, contained, or handed off. The parked object remains intact and retrievable in principle; the move quiets or dissociates by giving cognition a spatial 'away' model rather than by destroying, throttling, or attributing causation elsewhere. Variants differ by what is externalized (mind vs memory vs resistance vs body), by portability (carry-case, return promise), by who handles the extraction (listener vs operator-as-physical-agent), and by whether an observer/viewed split is staged, but all share the intact-parked-object surface.
nodes.one_liner: Have them picture their thinking mind as a small case, take it out, and set it on a shelf where it'll wait for them.
nodes.why_short: 'Stop thinking' fails because checking whether you've stopped is more thinking. A pictured object with a place is easy to hold and easy to ignore: the mind is 'over there' now.
nodes.principle_note: Cognition recruits spatial and object schemas readily, and an imagined object with a location is easier to hold, manipulate, and ignore than an abstract process — externalising a faculty converts 'stop analysing' (an intention that fails because monitoring it re-invokes it) into 'the box is over there' (a stable percept requiring no suppression). This sidesteps the ironic-process problem, where trying not to think of something increases its accessibility. The retrievability promise likely matters by reducing threat, which lowers resistance to the move. Falsifiable: instructing subjects merely to suppress the faculty should yield more intrusions than externalising it, per the ironic-process prediction.

ex.f: Operator reaches in and holds the faculty
ex.t: Instead of asking the listener to set anything aside, the operator steps inside the imagery as a physical handler: a hand reaches in, takes hold of the analytical faculty, and draws it out to a place where it can only watch. The listener is left observing two figures — one lodged outside and objecting, one still in the body and cooperating — and told that re-entry is the operator's to grant. Whatever the evicted half thinks is thereby pre-classified as not the listener's real response.
ex.s: Operator has stepped inside the imagery as a physical handler; subject is deep enough to accept a staged observer/participant split.
ex.m: Hold still — I'm going to reach in and take hold of the part of you that keeps checking. There. I'm lifting it out, and I'm setting it over there, where it can watch and nothing else. Look: two of you now. That one's outside the glass, saying no. This one's here in the body, doing as she's told. And that one doesn't come back in until I put it back.

ex.f: Memory restaged as machinery watched from above
ex.t: The listener is floated down inside their own head into an installation of humming equipment, and told this is where remembering is carried out. They are positioned above it, watching. Recall stops being something the listener does and becomes a facility they observe — which is precisely the distance the operator needs, since a facility can be reached and operated, and the listener never notices the distance was installed rather than found.
ex.s: Interior imagery established; the subject is being floated down inside their own head and positioned above the machinery.
ex.m: Down through the top of your skull and into a long room full of humming equipment — cabinets, spools, indicator lights going amber to green. This is where remembering gets done. You're on the walkway above it, looking down. Watch the machines do it. You aren't remembering anything; they are, and you're up here watching them work.

ex.f: The thinking mind packed away and set down
ex.t: At a threshold in the imagery the listener is told the thinking mind is now a portable object they are holding, and that it can be left here while they go on. An unperformable instruction to stop thinking is replaced by a single discrete physical act that can be completed, after which the absence is described as an accomplished state rather than an ongoing effort. The promise that the object will be waiting on the return trip is what makes the handover acceptable: the surrender is framed as a loan, not a gift, so the safety objection never fires.
ex.s: At a threshold in the imagery — a doorway, a stair, a boundary the subject is about to cross.
ex.m: Before you go through, look at what's in your hands: your thinking mind, and it's a small case with a handle. Set it down here on the shelf beside the door. There — done, and it's not with you any more. It'll be sitting exactly there when you come back for it, so you don't need to keep an eye on it.

nodes.name: consummation-as-trance-threshold
nodes.mech: Use the listener's own building desire to take them down, so the drop feels self-caused, not imposed. Build a craving inside the fantasy, then define the moment it is satisfied as the moment they go under. Variations: one act of finally tasting the craved thing (sucking a finger, eating a treat) is the drop; the instant it happens, recast it as a trap already sprung ('you consumed it, now it consumes you'); or make them chase the drop, a lure just ahead or clothing coming off one piece per step deeper, so each step down is wanted, and later recast that chasing as devotion to the operator.
nodes.one_liner: Build a craving for something imagined, then say that the moment they finally taste or take it, they drop.
nodes.why_short: When the drive comes from their own built-up wanting, the drop feels self-chosen. People credit motives to themselves more when no outside push is obvious.
nodes.principle_note: Motivation that the subject can feel as their own is attributed internally — self-perception and the overjustification literature both show that a salient external inducement licenses the discounting of one's own desire, while its absence produces stronger internal attribution. Building appetite inside the fiction means the subject observes themselves wanting and moving forward, so the resulting descent gets credited to their own volition rather than to compliance. Falsifiable: if the operator explicitly claims credit for producing the craving at the moment of consummation, the self-attribution should weaken and reported non-volition should drop.

ex.f: Completing the craved act is the drop
ex.t: A long stretch of the script is spent making the listener want one small imagined taste, with it always held just out of reach. Then it is granted — and its completion, not a count and not a command, is named as the moment of falling. Because the listener has been made to want it, the descent arrives as the consequence of something they were straining toward, so the trance reads as self-administered rather than imposed.
ex.s: Late in the session; a small imagined taste has been built up and held just out of reach for several minutes.
ex.m: It's right at your lips now, and you've wanted it since I first mentioned it. Take it — close your mouth around it, taste it properly. And the moment it's gone, so are you: swallowing it is the falling. There. All the way down, because you wanted it.

ex.f: The consummation re-narrated as a closed trap
ex.t: The listener is walked up to a treat they have been made to crave and told to take it — and in the same breath the direction of the verb is flipped: the one who consumed has been consumed. The recognition is delivered after the act rather than before it, so noticing the trap is itself scheduled as part of the trap, arriving as evidence rather than as an exit. Agency is inverted at the precise instant the listener was most actively choosing.
ex.s: The craved treat is granted and taken; the re-narration lands in the same breath as the act, not before it.
ex.m: Take it. Put it in your mouth, swallow it — good girl, you ate it. And now notice which way round it went: the thing you swallowed is the thing that swallowed you. You didn't take it, it took you, and you reached for it yourself.

nodes.name: covert-arousal-weld
nodes.mech: Link arousal to a target without ever saying so, by letting one word, rhythm or 'yes' slide from harmless to sexual. The listener feels one continuous build, never a separate link they could refuse. Variations: a chore described with a verb and rhythm that match a sexual act, so the action slides from floor to shoes to body; one word whose meaning quietly shifts across the session; a double-meaning phrase such as 'come to me'; get a broad yes to pleasure first, then narrow it to the specific pairing.
nodes.one_liner: Link arousal to something by sliding a shared word or rhythm from the harmless to the sexual, never saying 'this will arouse you'.
nodes.why_short: Feelings can attach to things paired with them even when the person doesn't notice the pairing, and noticing a persuasion attempt is what triggers pushback. Whether learning without awareness happens at all is debated.
nodes.principle_note: Evaluative conditioning is one of the few learning effects that operates without contingency awareness — pairings can shift valence even when the subject cannot report the pairing, and awareness of a persuasive linkage is precisely what triggers correction. By carrying the link on a shared motor program, a sliding referent, or a pun, the operator gets the pairing without the announcement that would let the subject discount it (the persuasion-knowledge correction). Falsifiable and testable in principle: making the linkage explicit should reduce the arousal transfer relative to the covert version; if explicit statement worked as well or better, the covertness would be doing nothing.

ex.f: One word held fixed while its referent moves
ex.t: A single anatomical word is repeated until it is saturated with pleasure, initially pointing at the listener's own body. It is then used as a cue, and finally the same word is used with a different owner — someone else's — without any announcement that the referent has changed. The listener experiences one continuously escalating craving rather than a switch of target, and the switch rides across on a word already coded as pure reward.
ex.s: A single anatomical word has been repeated until saturated with pleasure, initially pointing at the subject's own body.
ex.m: Cock. Your cock, the word alone makes it throb — cock, cock, feel it every time I say it. Now the word is the trigger: hear cock and the pleasure comes whether you're touching or not. Cock. There it is. His cock. Cock. On your knees for it. Cock.

ex.f: A pun that collapses two meanings into one
ex.t: The operator establishes herself as somewhere the listener is travelling toward, then repeats a short phrase that means both approaching her and reaching climax. The phrase is never explained; it is simply used often enough, and at high enough arousal, that the two senses stop being separable. What would be a bald instruction — feel devotion when you climax — is delivered instead by grammar, so no linkage is ever stated and none can be refused.
ex.s: High arousal, subject approaching climax; the operator has already been established as a destination being travelled toward.
ex.m: I'm at the end of the corridor and you're walking toward me. Come to me. Closer — come to me. You're nearly here, and you can feel it building. Come to me. Come to me now, all the way, don't stop until you reach me.

ex.f: A broad yes funneled onto one narrow pairing
ex.t: First the operator floods the frame with pleasure in the broadest possible sense — every kind imaginable, nothing to disagree with. Then, at a single seam marked only by a contrastive conjunction, the diffuse assent is narrowed to one specific pairing: this particular focal image will now produce this particular appetite. The general yes was easy to give; the specific pairing is carried in on its back and never separately offered.
ex.s: A broad, unobjectionable assent to pleasure has just been given; the narrowing rides one contrastive conjunction.
