Falsifiable: matched instructions differing only in whether a concrete experiential referent is supplied should differ in success rate on the target state.

ex.f: Definitions reconciled aloud before any work
ex.t: "The purpose was to insure that we were both in accord or clear in our divergences of understanding, thus to make possible a more reliable inquiry" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

nodes.name: yes-word-valence-priming
nodes.mech: The operator abstractly loads the word 'yes' with positive valence — framing it as an objectively powerful, future-expanding, life-directing word, divorced from any specific request — and only after 'yes' is established as inherently good runs a rapid yes-set of leading questions answered on the listener's behalf. Decoupling the act of agreeing from the content agreed to makes each later yes feel self-improving regardless of what follows, so high-stakes consents are harvested on the coattails of a word pre-charged as good.
nodes.one_liner: Praise the word 'yes' as powerful and good, then run fast leading questions the listener answers yes to.
nodes.why_short: Good feelings attached to a word carry over to whatever it's attached to; then small agreements make the next agreement easier.
nodes.principle_note: Evaluative conditioning transfers valence to a stimulus by pairing, and once a word carries positive affect the affective response precedes and biases the deliberate evaluation of whatever it is attached to. Running the yes-set afterward then exploits the consistency principle on top of the primed valence, so each agreement is both affectively pleasant and consistent with the prior ones. Falsifiable: a yes-set with and without prior abstract valence-loading should differ in downstream consent rates; if they did not, the priming stage would be decorative.

ex.f: The primed word harvested by a rapid yes-set
ex.t: Immediately after the word has been talked up in the abstract, the questions come in a fast run and the operator supplies the answer to each one herself, so the listener's part is only to let it stand. The items escalate — do you want this guidance, do you want to go deeper, will you give in — but the rhythm never changes, and each agreement is collected on the strength of the word rather than the strength of the request.
ex.s: Immediately after the abstract praise of the word; no pause between.
ex.m: So — you want my guidance tonight, yes you do. You want to go a little further down than last time, yes. You'd like me to make this easy for you, yes you would. And you'll give in when I ask, won't you — yes. Good. Look how easily that word comes out of you now.

ex.f: 'Yes' praised as a word before anything is asked
ex.t: The session pauses its content entirely to make an abstract case about one word: saying yes is what opens doors, what gives a life direction, what separates people who get somewhere from people who do not. No request is attached — there is nothing yet to say yes to, which is exactly what makes the claim easy to accept. Only afterwards do the questions start arriving, and by then the listener is not weighing each one on its merits; they are producing a word that has been established as good for them.
ex.s: Early session; the operator pauses the content before any request has been made.
ex.m: I want to talk to you about one word. Yes. It's the smallest word there is and it's the only one that ever opens anything — every door anyone has ever walked through, they said yes first. The people who get somewhere are the people who say it, and the people who stay exactly where they are are the ones who kept it in their mouth. Yes is what gives a life a direction. Just hold that for a moment. I'm not asking you anything yet.

nodes.name: autobiographical-memory-anchor
nodes.mech: The effect is tied to a memory inside the listener that the operator does not control and the listener cannot easily disown, so every time that memory comes up on its own, the effect is reactivated. This reaches much further than a trigger word, which fades if unused. The memory can be a real fond one, into which the effect is tied through a narrated ritual; an imagined daily practice recast as something remembered; or the memory of this session itself, deliberately kept clear (no amnesia) so that simply reminiscing brings back the pleasure, often with a quick way back into deep trance.
nodes.one_liner: Tie the effect to a memory the listener owns (a fond memory, or the memory of this session) so remembering re-fires it.
nodes.why_short: Personal memories come up often and on their own, giving whatever is attached repeated reminders without the operator.
nodes.principle_note: Personal memories are about the self and connected to many everyday cues, so they come to mind on their own and often. Anything attached to them gets repeated, unplanned reactivation, which alone suggests it should last longer than an arbitrary trigger word. This is plausible but has not been tested. Research on memories being reopened and changed during recall does not support the stronger idea that new content becomes part of the memory itself rather than simply sitting alongside it; that research is about altering an existing memory, not attaching new meaning to one. This could be shown wrong: if effects tied to personal memories faded just as fast as those tied to arbitrary cues, the claim about lasting longer would fail.

ex.f: An imagined daily practice recalled as lived
ex.t: The operator refers, in passing, to a physical object the listener supposedly received at the start and to the small daily act performed with it — one mark made each evening, without fail. The habit is described rather than requested, so the listener's imagination fills in the routine, and an invented practice arrives already wearing the texture of something remembered.
ex.s: Mid-session in a series; the object and the daily habit have never actually been given to the subject.
ex.m: And your little book — the one you were given at the beginning, the one on your nightstand. You've been good about it, haven't you. One mark every evening before you sleep, every single evening, no gaps. That's how many nights of this you've done now. Think about how the page looks.

ex.f: The payload folded into a real cherished memory
ex.t: The listener is walked into an imagined store of their own memories and asked to bring up one particular real one — a good one, specific, theirs — and to live in it again until it is vivid. Then the operator steps into the scene, produces a written agreement, has it signed, and tucks it inside the memory before shutting the memory away again. The binding is narrated as a procedure rather than asserted, because the engagement is what makes it stick. What has been chosen as the trigger is not a word the operator can wear out by overuse; it is something the listener will recall unprompted, at random, for years, and each of those moments is now a scheduled reactivation.
ex.s: Subject is deep and has been walked into an imagined room of their own memories.
ex.m: Pull one out — a real one, a good one, something of yours I've never touched. Be in it. Hear what you heard, see who was there, stay until it's as bright as the day it happened. Now I'm going to step into it with you, and I have a paper in my hand. Read it, and sign it — good. I'm folding it small and tucking it right into the middle of that memory, and now we close the memory up and put it back on the shelf. Every time that memory comes back to you on its own — driving, falling asleep, out of nowhere — the paper is in there with it, and you'll feel this.

nodes.name: eternal-present-frame-deletion
nodes.mech: Collapses the listener into an eternal present by stripping the identity, history, and future frames ("doesn't matter who you are, where you come from, or where you're going") and leaving only "right now, everything feels good". Deleting the past/future/social-identity vantage points removes the evaluative standpoints from which objection or self-comparison would arise, so there is no temporal or identity anchor left from which to question or resist the suggestions.
nodes.one_liner: Strip away who you are, where you came from and where you're going, leaving only 'right now, everything feels good'.
nodes.why_short: Deep absorption is linked to less self-focused and future thinking; the stated mechanism is mostly circular.
nodes.principle_note: As written this defines objection as requiring comparison standards and then explains reduced objection by removing them — the technique restated. The non-circular version is empirical: deep absorption is independently associated with reduced self-referential and prospective processing (measurable via default-mode-network and self-report measures), and that reduction is what predicts fewer counterarguments. Falsifiable: subjects given the frame-deletion passage should produce fewer spontaneous counterarguments than subjects given a matched relaxation passage of equal length and absorption rating; equal rates would refute it.

ex.f: Past, future and identity struck out at once
ex.t: Late in the session, the operator states that none of it matters here — not who the listener is, not what came before, not what comes after — and that this is only about the moment currently happening. Every standpoint from which an objection could be raised is a standpoint outside the present: consequences live in the future, commitments in the past, embarrassment in a social identity. With all three set aside and only "right now, this feels good" left standing, there is no vantage point left to evaluate the next suggestion from.
ex.s: Late session, subject deep; a substantial suggestion is about to be delivered.
ex.m: None of it matters in here. Not who you are — the name, the job, what people think when they say it. Not where you came from, not one thing you promised anyone. Not tomorrow, not what any of this means for tomorrow. There is only right now, and right now everything feels good. That's the whole world for the next while: this moment, and how good it feels.

nodes.name: intervention-gating
nodes.mech: A planning check for the hypnotist: before running something, test whether its conditions are met, then go ahead, wait, or pick a different approach. Nothing is done to the subject at this step. Variations: confirm basic skills are solid before an advanced program; never remove a behaviour without naming a replacement that does the same job; ask whether the subject can state the cause of a problem, using direct suggestion if so and exploring first if not; choose the method least likely to produce errors, and check that the people around the subject can actually follow the plan; accept only listeners already familiar with earlier material.
nodes.one_liner: Before running a program, check preconditions (readiness, a replacement behaviour, fit) and change plan if they aren't met.
nodes.why_short: Effects depend on preconditions that are cheap to test and expensive to discover by failure.
nodes.principle_note: Conditional branching works because intervention effects are moderated by preconditions that are cheap to test and expensive to discover by failure: a plan run on a subject lacking the prerequisite skill, or delivered by a third party who cannot execute it with fidelity, produces near-zero effect regardless of technique quality. The fair-pair variant rests on the matching law and the behavioural vacuum finding — removing a response that reliably produces a reinforcer without supplying an equally efficient alternative tends to yield substitution or resurgence rather than extinction. Falsifiable: if gated and ungated runs on precondition-failing cases showed equal outcomes, or if reduction plans without a same-function replacement showed no elevated substitution rate, the rule would be wrong.

ex.f: Three prerequisites checked before the program runs
ex.t: "There are several prerequisite skills are necessary to benefit from a formal autoclitic intervention program: (1) A speaker's existing verbal skills are sufficient... (2) a speaker demonstrates self-listening skills, and (3) a speaker can tact aspects of her own verbal and nonverbal behavior." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: No reduction plan without a same-function replacement
ex.t: "never plan to reduce or eliminate a behavior…without first (a) determining an adaptive behavior that will take its place (also known as the fair pair rule)" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: manufactured-conditioning-history
nodes.mech: The operator talks about past sessions, training or agreements that never happened as if they did, and asks the listener to remember them rather than imagine them. The listener fills in the details and the invented past starts to feel real. Today's response is then credited to that history, so resisting tonight's depth would mean contradicting weeks of 'experience', and depth starts at the level of the invented past. Variations: a long daily-training agreement whose missed days are discussed as if completed; a shared earlier session the listener is asked to recall; an inner place described as 'changed since you were last here' on a first listen.
nodes.one_liner: Talk about past sessions or conditioning that never happened as if they did, and let the listener fill in the memories.
nodes.why_short: People are poor at telling imagined events from remembered ones; imagining a plausible past makes it feel real. Once they 'remember' weeks of training, resisting today's depth feels inconsistent with their own history.
nodes.principle_note: Exploits source-monitoring error — people are poor at distinguishing memories of imagined events from memories of experienced ones, and imagining a plausible autobiographical event raises confidence that it occurred (imagination inflation). Once the fabricated history is accepted, the consistency principle does the rest: denying present depth would contradict a past the listener now believes they lived, so accepting depth is the cheaper self-account. Falsifiable: if listeners given the counterfactual history showed no more depth-report or compliance than matched listeners given no history, the mechanism would be disconfirmed.

ex.f: A shared earlier session the listener is asked to recall
ex.t: Barely two minutes in, the operator refers casually to something they did together before — a place, a state the listener was in, an image for how it felt — as if picking up a thread. The listener is asked to remember the state, not to construct it, which is a much cheaper request, and the depth the session starts at is wherever that invented previous session is said to have ended. The image is then re-used twice more as a deepener, so a memory that never existed becomes a working handle.
ex.s: Two minutes into the recording; no previous session exists.
ex.m: Settle in — you know how this goes by now. Remember where you got to last time, that quiet grey room at the bottom of the stairs, how it felt like water closing over your head? Don't build it. Just remember it. You're back there now, at exactly the depth you left.

ex.f: "It has changed since you were last here"
ex.t: The operator names an interior location — a passage, its doors, the floor underfoot — with the definite article, as somewhere already familiar, then observes that it is not as the listener left it, describing the decay that has crept over it since. To make sense of a comparison, the listener must supply the earlier state, which means inventing a memory of a previous visit. A first-time listener produces continuity for a series they have never heard, and the session never checks.
ex.s: Opening imagery of a first listen; the location is introduced with the definite article.
ex.m: You're in the corridor again. The doors along it, the cold floor under you — but look, it's not how you left it. The paint has gone since you were last here, and there's dust on everything, and two of the doors that used to open don't anymore. That's what happens when you stay away this long.

ex.f: A hundred days that never happened
ex.t: The recording opens by stipulating a long agreement — daily sessions, months of them — and then narrates only a handful of individual days. The rest are referred to in passing as shared history, one of them by number, with a detail about what the listener supposedly did that day. Half an hour in, the operator remarks on how much the training has worn them down by now. The listener has been in trance for thirty minutes, but the responsiveness they are currently showing has just been attributed to weeks of repetition they were asked to imagine and never actually received. Objecting to the depth would mean objecting to a history they helped build.
ex.s: Thirty minutes into a first listen; a long daily-training agreement was stipulated in the opening minutes.
ex.m: You agreed to a hundred days of this. We're well past the halfway mark now, and I can hear it — remember day forty-one, when you were too tired to kneel properly and did it anyway? That's the difference weeks make. Listen to how little fight is left in you tonight compared to when we started. That isn't tonight's work. That's every night before it.

nodes.name: meta-suggestibility-conditioning
nodes.mech: What is installed is not any particular behaviour or state but the readiness to accept suggestions at all, which makes any later session from the same operator easier. Its value lies in what the next recording can do: little for a one-time listener, a great deal for someone following a series. It is often proven live with a small test, such as suggesting an itch. Two forms: train general responsiveness ("respond to whatever comes next") within a session; or release it as a separate priming recording aimed at faster, deeper response to later inductions plus a craving to replay, with that purpose stated openly.
nodes.one_liner: Instead of installing a specific behaviour, train the listener to accept future suggestions more readily, often proving it with a small live test.
nodes.why_short: Expecting to respond is one of the strongest predictors of responding to hypnosis, and responsiveness can be somewhat trained. A listener taught to expect compliance brings that expectation to the next file.
nodes.finding_name: Response expectancy (Kirsch); Carleton Skills Training Program
nodes.principle_note: Rests on expectancy effects, which are among the strongest replicated predictors of hypnotic responding — a subject who expects to respond does respond more, and a live demonstration supplies exactly the self-observed evidence that raises that expectancy. Self-perception theory extends it: having observed oneself comply with an arbitrary demand, one infers 'I am the kind of person who responds to this operator,' and that inferred disposition transfers to the next request. Whether generalized suggestibility is genuinely a trainable trait rather than a context-specific expectancy is not settled; the falsifiable claim is that primed listeners show measurably higher response to a subsequent unrelated script than unprimed matched listeners.

ex.f: Installing receptiveness rather than any content
ex.t: Nothing in this session asks the listener to become anything, do anything, or want anything. What it repeats is a claim about the listener's own machinery: that the part of them that takes suggestions is now awake, attentive, and quick to act on whatever it is given. The claim gets a live demonstration — the operator names a trivial sensation, an itch, and waits for the listener to notice it starting, which proves the disposition rather than any particular content. A listener who never returns has gained nothing at all from the half hour; the value is entirely in how much less work the operator's next recording will have to do.
ex.s: Used across a whole session; nothing else, no behaviour, identity or trigger, is being installed anywhere in the recording.
ex.m: I'm not here to make you into anything tonight. I'm here to work on the part of you that takes suggestions — that part is awake now, alert, quick, and it acts on what it's given before you've finished considering it. Here, watch: somewhere on your left arm there's an itch starting. You feel it beginning already, don't you. That's not me being clever. That's how fast you take things now. Whatever I put in front of you next will land the same way.

nodes.name: name-binding-transitive-equation-chain
nodes.mech: A transitive chain of asserted equalities (cock=lock, lock=cock, key=permission, permission=identity) is declared already-true at depth and locked in by first-person recitation, so any future thought of the listener's own body routes through to the operator's proper name as the terminal node. Each equation is small; the chain is the install. Because the anchor object is the listener's own unavoidable anatomy, the trigger fires at high frequency outside any session, and orgasm-attempt can be folded in as self-thwarting so the loop tightens on use.
nodes.one_liner: Declare a chain of equations (body part = lock, lock = key, key = owner's name) and have the listener recite it, so body awareness points to the operator.
nodes.why_short: Trained A=B and B=C links let people derive A=C without direct training. Anchoring the chain to the listener's own body means it gets cued constantly in daily life.
nodes.principle_note: Semantic chaining works through mediated association and stimulus equivalence — when A=B and B=C are trained, subjects reliably derive A=C without direct training, and the derived relation transfers the affective loading of the terminal node. First-person recitation adds the self-generation effect: self-produced statements are better retained and more attitude-shifting than heard ones. The choice of anatomy as the initial cue exploits sheer trial frequency, since an unavoidable stimulus produces many more retrieval occasions per day than any arbitrary cue. Falsifiable: if reciters showed no faster or more frequent retrieval of the terminal name to body-cues than non-reciters, the chain claim fails.

ex.f: The same chain re-recited at wake-up
ex.t: The identical chain of equalities appears in a second recording, declared burned in at the deepest level, and is then repeated word for word twice more — once mid-session and once during the count back to waking, so the last thing carried across the boundary into ordinary awareness is the chain itself.
ex.s: Second recording in the series; the chain was installed in the first, and the wake count is beginning.
ex.m: Burned in at the deepest level now, all four of them, exactly as before. Coming up — five, your cock is a lock — four, the lock is your cock — three, the key is permission — two, permission is me — one, eyes open, and that's the last thing you carried up with you.

ex.f: Equalities chained to end on the operator's name
ex.t: Four small equations are stated flatly, as facts already in place rather than as things to be built: the listener's own anatomy is a lock, the lock is that anatomy, the key is permission, and permission is the operator herself. Each link is trivial on its own; strung together they route any thought about the listener's body straight to a person's name, which is the only term in the chain that is not an object. The listener is then made to recite the whole chain in the first person so it is their voice that closes it, and arousal is defined as tightening rather than loosening the arrangement — the more they want out, the more securely it holds. The trigger cannot decay through disuse the way an invented cue word would, because it is attached to something the listener encounters every day.
ex.s: Deep trance; subject can speak aloud on instruction.
ex.m: These are facts, already true, nothing to build. Your cock is a lock. The lock is your cock. The key is permission. Permission is me. Now say it back to me in your own voice — "my cock is a lock, the lock is my cock, the key is permission, permission is her." Again. And every time you get hard, the lock only sits tighter, so wanting out is what keeps you in. You carry that lock everywhere. You'll think of me every time you notice it.

ex.f: Unlock chain ending at a named person
ex.t: The operator lays the links down one at a time — the lock needs a key, the key is permission, permission is me, by name — then rattles the whole equation off again as a single fast line so no link gets weighed on its own. Because the last term is a particular person rather than a role, the listener cannot reason their way to self-permission: there is no abstract standard to satisfy, only an absent individual, and nobody else can step into the slot without starting the conditioning over.
ex.s: Chastity or denial frame; the lock image is established and the listener is looking for the release condition.
ex.m: The lock needs a key. The key isn't metal — the key is permission. And permission is me, my name, the person saying this. So: lock, key, permission, my name, that's the whole chain, that's the only route, lock-key-permission-me. You can want it as hard as you like. Wanting isn't a name.

nodes.name: switchable-alter
nodes.mech: The operator builds a named second persona with its own set of behaviours, then gives it an on-phrase that tucks the everyday self away and brings the persona forward, and an off-phrase that reverses it. The persona is described as dormant until called. The operator also decides who may use the phrase: only themselves, or anyone who knows it. Variations: the off-phrase also wipes memory of the episode, sometimes tied to a ritual like showering or changing clothes; each switch-on said to be stronger than the last; an urge to re-listen folded into the install; the persona presented as having always existed, asleep until woken.
nodes.one_liner: Build a named second persona, give it an on-phrase and off-phrase (or a safe that opens and closes), with a memory wall between states.
nodes.why_short: State-dependent roles and suggested amnesia let a persona feel separate. Real in roleplay terms; the amnesia part works only for some, and confabulation instructions carry real risk.
nodes.principle_note: Trades on role enactment and the demand characteristics of a labeled part: giving a state a name and a bundle of expected behaviours supplies a script that is easier to perform than to improvise, and performing it produces genuine experiential changes without requiring any literal separate personality. The paired release phrase makes the whole thing reversible-by-design, which lowers the perceived cost of trying it — a low-commitment entry that then accrues via self-perception. Delegating the phrase outward matters socially rather than mechanically: firing rights held by third parties multiply exposure and remove the subject from the decision. The claim that the alter is genuinely non-inspectable and amnesic is not established; the falsifiable version is that trigger-word presentation produces the labeled behaviour bundle above base rate.
steps: Create and name the persona with its behaviours.
Bind an on-phrase (or opening a safe) that brings the persona out.
Bind an off-phrase that restores the normal self.
Optional: the off-phrase (or closing the safe) walls off memory of the episode.
Optional: tell the everyday self to explain away any gaps.
Optional: let others who know the phrase use it.

ex.f: Trigger and release phrase, sayable by anyone
ex.t: One short phrase is designated as the switch: on hearing it, the listener's ordinary self is described as being set aside and a named alternate self, with its own manner and its own behavior, takes over running things. A second phrase puts the first self back. The load-bearing word is "somebody" — the instruction is not that the operator can fire this, but that anyone who happens to know the phrase can, which converts the listener into a device other people hold the remote for.
ex.s: Deep trance; the trigger phrase has not yet been named and the subject does not know it is coming.
ex.m: There's a phrase now. When somebody says "good girl, drop for me," the you that's listening right now gets folded away and put in a drawer, and the other one comes forward — quiet, agreeable, does what she's told and doesn't ask why. "Good girl, wake up" puts you back. Notice I said somebody. Not me. Anybody who knows those words holds that switch, and you won't know they have it until you hear it.

ex.f: Replay compulsion packed inside the trigger install
ex.t: The activation phrase and its release are installed in the usual way, but tucked into the same passage — not delivered as a separate closing instruction — is the suggestion that the listener will want to come back to this recording repeatedly until it has settled in properly. Since re-exposure is what strengthens the trigger, and wanting re-exposure is part of what the trigger installs, the recording arranges its own repetition.
ex.s: The persona trigger and its release are being installed; the closing instructions have not started.
ex.m: "Good girl, drop for me" brings her forward; "good girl, wake up" puts you back. And because this needs to be set properly before it will run clean, you'll find yourself wanting to hear this again — tomorrow night, and the night after, coming back to it until it's smooth. Each time you do, both halves get a little firmer.

ex.f: The alter framed as dormant, not built
ex.t: A named second self is installed with one phrase to bring it forward and another to put it away, and no setting in between. The framing is the operative part: it is not described as a role to adopt but as a separate part of you that has been asleep and is now being woken. Presented as pre-existing rather than constructed, it costs the listener almost no sense of having authored it — and the switch belongs to whoever knows the words.
ex.s: Subject in medium trance; a named secondary self has been described for several minutes and the subject has been answering as her before the toggle is formally set.
ex.m: She isn't something I'm making. She's been asleep in you the whole time, and tonight I'm just calling her name. From now on, when anyone says Doll Time, she opens her eyes and you go quiet — all the way, no halfway, no in-between. When anyone says Doll, Sleep Now, she lies back down and you come forward, and that's all it takes, from anybody who knows the words.

ex.f: Off-switch forgets, on-switch accumulates
ex.t: Two phrases, one on and one off. The off-phrase carries an amnesia clause anchored to a set of ordinary physical rituals performed at the end of the episode — washing, changing out of the clothes — so the everyday self returns with the whole stretch gone from view and from memory alike. The on-phrase carries the opposite clause: each activation comes back stronger than the one before. The bookkeeping is deliberately lopsided. The side that accumulates is never wiped, and the side that is wiped is the only one that could have looked at the pattern and revised it, so every cycle nudges the equilibrium in one direction.
ex.s: Late session, subject deep and already responding to simple cues; the persona costume/makeup has been worn through the session and both phrases are being installed for the first time.
ex.m: When I say Dress-Up Time For You, this whole shape you're in right now snaps back on, and every single time it does it comes back stronger than the time before. When I say Dress-Up Time Is Over, you go and take off the makeup, you shower, you put your ordinary clothes back on, and as the water runs the whole stretch closes behind you — you won't be able to find any of it, only that you had a nice quiet evening.

nodes.name: parts-work-procedure-craft
nodes.mech: Practical tips for running a negotiation between a person's inner 'parts' so it stays workable. Variations: when two parts are deadlocked, give them something to trade, such as confirming each blocks something the other wants so a mutual hands-off deal becomes possible, or adding minor throwaway items that can be conceded at no cost; when many parts speak at once, have them elect one spokesperson and take turns; instead of inventing new behaviours, let parts keep a behaviour they already have and only renegotiate non-interference; for a swing between opposites (dieting and bingeing), reframe both sides so the other does not rebound.
nodes.one_liner: A grab-bag of tips for running a 'parts negotiation' smoothly: give each side something to trade, take turns, check nothing is left out.
nodes.why_short: Negotiations between imagined inner voices stall when there is nothing to trade or too much to track; structuring turns and offers keeps it manageable. Coaching craft, not a hypnotic effect.
nodes.principle_note: Working-memory limits are the binding constraint on multi-party negotiation, which is why serializing turns and naming each voice works — an operator tracking four simultaneous streams exceeds capacity and loses the thread, while polled single turns stay within it. The slack-manufacture and substitute-existing-behavior moves exploit loss aversion and the endowment effect: a proposal framed as removing something a party currently has is resisted disproportionately to its objective value, so restructuring the deal so nothing is surrendered removes the resistance without changing the substance. Both-poles reframing follows from the observation that oppositely-valenced behaviours sharing a functional class are maintained by the same contingency, so treating one leaves the reinforcer available to the other. Falsifiable: if serialized and unserialized sessions completed equally often, or if removal-framed and substitution-framed identical deals were accepted at equal rates, the craft would be inert.

ex.f: Confirm interference runs both ways, then trade
ex.t: "both parts want something from the other, and all you've got to do is make a trade." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

ex.f: Balanced throwaways loaded in to create room
ex.t: "items which are not essential, which are 'throwaways' for the purpose of barter. I've got to have an equal amount of those on both sides… I've got to create room to move first." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: objection-and-exit-preclosure
nodes.mech: The operator names the listener's likely objections and ways out before they arise and answers or redirects each in advance, so the suggestion survives everyday life and doubts arrive already answered. Variations: wanting to stop described as a malfunction needing more listening, or as something they cannot want; the one uncontrollable release (a wet dream) defined in advance as obedience; practical edge cases routed ahead of time through approved channels; predicted after-session objections given ready-made answers; a running thread of rebuttals to unvoiced doubts; the safeword itself rerouted ('if you want me to stop, you'll have to orgasm') with a threat to start over, so no neutral pause remains.
nodes.one_liner: Name the listener's likely objections and ways out in advance, and pre-answer or reroute each one (e.g. 'wanting to stop means you need more').
nodes.why_short: Arguments already answered feel settled when they come up later, and a reframed exit no longer reads as an exit. Pre-emptive rebuttal is a known persuasion tactic; the safeword-rerouting variant is an ethical red flag.
nodes.principle_note: This is sometimes described as inoculation in reverse, but that is not accurate: inoculation theory is about building resistance to later persuasion by exposing someone to a weakened counterargument first. Better explanations are two-sided messaging with pre-emptive refutation (raising an objection and answering it yourself increases credibility and reduces later counterarguing) and forewarning of persuasive intent. This could be tested: listeners given the pre-answered version should quit or object less often than listeners given the same content without the pre-answers. Relabeling, such as 'wanting to stop means it is working', is a separate, self-sealing frame that cannot be argued against from inside, and the ethical objection to rerouting a safeword stands whether or not any of this works.

ex.f: The safeword beat closed by relocating who can't stop
ex.t: The operator raises the possibility of stopping herself, out loud, and then shuts it — but not by refusing. She attributes the impossibility to the listener: they could not ask for a pause now, not feeling like this. Nothing has been denied, so there is nothing to push against, and the beat where a request to stop would have gone has been filled with an observation that the listener does not want to make one.
ex.s: Mid-session, arousal high; the subject has given no sign of wanting to stop.
ex.m: I could slow this down. I could stop right here if you asked me to — but look at you. You're not going to ask, are you. Not feeling like this. So I won't offer again.

ex.f: The one uncontrollable release pre-claimed as success
ex.t: Under a control-of-release arrangement there is exactly one form of release the listener cannot be held responsible for, because it happens while they are asleep. The operator names it before the listener can, and reclassifies it — not a lapse, the best possible outcome, evidence of how much tension has been built for her. The single unowned route out has been annexed, and its frequency now reads as a devotion metric.
ex.s: An orgasm-control arrangement is in force; the subject has not raised the topic.
ex.m: There's one you can't help, and I want to say it before you start worrying about it. If you come in your sleep, that isn't a slip and you're not in trouble. That's the best possible outcome — that's how I know how much I've built up in you, that it spills over on its own. So tell me each time it happens. The more often it does, the better you're doing for me.

ex.f: Every practical exception pre-routed in advance
ex.t: Near the end, the operator works through the obvious real-world situations in which the rule she has just installed would plainly have to break — routine bodily necessity, conditions that make the required dress impossible, a setting that demands something different — and for each one supplies a sanctioned path: a permitted brief departure, performed while a token of compliance is maintained, followed by automatic return. The listener is never left holding an unanswered objection, so the rule never visibly fails.
ex.s: Closing minutes; a continuous wear-or-behave rule has just been installed and the practical objections have not been voiced.
ex.m: Now the exceptions, because I know your day has them. When you need the bathroom, you may take it off for exactly as long as that takes, and it goes straight back on. If you have an appointment where it plainly can't be worn, you take it off in the car and you keep the collar under your shirt while you're in there, and it goes back on before you drive home. Work uniform, the same — collar stays. You never have to decide any of this yourself. There's already an answer for every one of them.

ex.f: Stepping away recoded as a malfunction
ex.t: The one natural way out of the arrangement is not forbidden — it is diagnosed. A listener who stops engaging is described not as free or finished but as faulty equipment, and faulty equipment gets a maintenance schedule: no release, and a session every day until it is working properly again. The exit is left wide open and leads directly back inside. Because the framing is mechanical rather than moral, it reads as a repair rather than a reproach, which is exactly what makes it easier to accept than guilt would be.
ex.s: Late session, after the arrangement has been described; the subject has never mentioned disengaging.
ex.m: Some toys stop responding after a while. That isn't freedom and it isn't the end of anything — it's a fault, and faults get serviced. If it happens to you, here's the maintenance: nothing comes out of you at all until it's fixed, and you listen to me once every day until you're working properly again. There's nothing to feel bad about. Broken things just get repaired.

nodes.name: operator-absent-self-renewal-loop
nodes.mech: Hands the listener a self-running conditioning loop that continues between sessions with no operator present: the file installs an active urge to re-administer the material itself and/or reframes the subconscious as an autodidact that 'learns to brainwash itself' via pleasure feedback. Because the re-exposure compulsion is itself one of the reinforced installs, it strengthens on each pass — rereading is both the conditioning-delivery vehicle and one of the conditioned objects — so the maintenance schedule sustains without the operator. Any post-session sensation is pre-attributed to 'the process working', building expectancy of progressive change with no further audio.
nodes.one_liner: Install an urge to keep re-listening on their own, and frame each re-listen as the mind training itself.
nodes.why_short: If listening is paired with pleasure, listening itself becomes rewarding and gets repeated without anyone prompting it. The 'self-learning subconscious' story is framing, not mechanism.
nodes.principle_note: Conditioned reinforcement is invoked correctly — pairing the act of listening with pleasure gives listening acquired reinforcing value — but the appeal to variable-ratio extinction resistance is misapplied: nothing in the technique establishes an intermittent schedule, and the partial-reinforcement extinction effect is a separate phenomenon from a response reinforcing its own initiation. Drop that clause; the self-sustaining claim rests on conditioned reinforcement alone, plus misattribution of ordinary post-session sensations to 'the process working', which sustains expectancy between exposures. Falsifiable: replay frequency should rise across passes and fall to base rate when the pleasure pairing is removed.

ex.f: Re-exposure urge installed as one of the payloads
ex.t: Among the things installed is a wish to come back to the piece itself, paired with a promise that each pass goes deeper than the last, a commitment to keep going until it is known by heart, and a standing weekly appointment to recite it back. Since every return strengthens everything installed — including the wish to return — the loop tightens on its own, and the operator never has to be present for any of it. The first pass only has to seed the urge; the listener supplies the rest of the schedule.
ex.s: Late in the session, subject accepting suggestions readily; other installs already delivered and being enumerated.
ex.m: And here is the last thing I'm putting in with the rest: you will want to hear this again. Not tonight — tomorrow, and the night after, and each pass will take you further down than the one before, because every listen strengthens everything I've planted, including the wanting. You'll keep going until you can say my words along with me from memory. And once a week, alone, out loud, you'll recite them back to yourself from the beginning.

ex.f: The subconscious told to condition itself
ex.t: Near the close, the operator reveals that the individual suggestions were never the real work — what has actually been laid down is a pattern that teaches itself, one that will keep running on pleasure feedback long after the audio stops, retroactively demoting the last hour to scaffolding. She then adds the part that makes it self-sealing: the first small sign the listener notices that any of this has taken effect will itself feed the process. Any sensation in the days that follow becomes confirmation, and confirmation is defined in advance as fuel.
ex.s: Final minutes, subject deep and unresisting; all the session's suggestions already delivered.
ex.m: Everything I've given you tonight was only the packaging. What I actually put in was a pattern that teaches itself — it takes whatever pleasure you feel and uses it to lay the next layer down, and it will keep doing that every day this week whether I'm speaking or not. And the first time you notice something has changed — a word of mine surfacing while you're doing dishes, a warmth with no cause — that noticing is fuel. It feeds the pattern. So every small sign you catch makes the next one bigger.

nodes.name: operator-resource-generation
nodes.mech: Habits the operator uses to find the material a change will be built from, before any suggestion is given. Variations: a fallback order for a new behaviour (recall a time you did it well in full detail; if none, copy someone who does; if none, pretend; last, the operator coaches the steps), then try it right away and check it came out as intended; refuse the first idea and keep asking 'how else could you get it?' until at least three routes exist, so a failed attempt means switching rather than stalling; instead of building something new, recruit a part of the person that already has the needed quality.
nodes.one_liner: Operator prep habits for finding material: recall a past success, else model someone, else pretend; or list three options before picking one.
nodes.why_short: Forcing several options before choosing counters settling on the first idea; using the person's own past successes makes new behaviour feel familiar. Coaching method, not a hypnotic move.
nodes.principle_note: The generate-three-options gate counters premature closure — people converge on the first adequate solution and stop searching, so an explicit count requirement forces the search past the first satisficing answer and reliably increases both the number and the quality of the best option in the set. The ordered fallback runs on congruence: self-generated content recruits the subject's own retrieval and motor memory, which is why recalling a real prior success outperforms adopting a modeled or operator-supplied one, with each step down the ladder trading fidelity for availability. Reuse-over-construction rests on the fact that an already-fluent response requires no acquisition trials, only re-cueing. Falsifiable: if first-generated tactics performed as well as best-of-three, or if operator-supplied behaviours transferred as well as recalled ones, the disciplines would be pointless.

ex.f: Three routes before committing to one
ex.t: "If you've got only one choice, you are a robot. If you've got only two, you are in a dilemma. However, if you've got three, you begin to have behavioral flexibility." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

ex.f: Recruit an existing capacity, don't build one
ex.t: "I think it probably would be better if you found an ally that's already in there. You don't need to build a whole new ally." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

ex.f: Ordered fallback for sourcing a new behavior
ex.t: "If Rita says 'I've never succeeded…' I ask for a model… I can even say 'Well, make it up.'" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: preparatory-diagnostic-read
nodes.mech: Everything the operator does to learn about the subject; nothing is installed. Variations: check whether a behaviour persists when alone, isolate one cause at a time, and ask third parties only about observable when/where/how-often; quietly watch involuntary trance signs and never announce what counts as success so it cannot be faked; design a test where failing to detect the state tends to produce it; read a pattern to choose the next approach; after a change, re-expose them to the original trigger and watch for the old reaction; sort acts by cause, not appearance; float a deliberately wrong guess, then forbid negatives so the correction comes out as concrete behaviour.
nodes.one_liner: Everything the operator does to learn about the subject before acting: watch, test, measure, ask.
nodes.why_short: Targeting the wrong cause makes any intervention miss; good assessment points effort where it matters. True for behaviour analysis, but this entry is a catch-all bucket rather than one move.
nodes.principle_note: Everything here is measurement validity: an intervention aimed at the wrong controlling variable is uncorrelated with outcome, and functional analysis — systematically varying one consequence while holding others constant — is the established method for identifying which contingency actually maintains a behaviour, outperforming topography-based guessing. The read-only forms additionally guard against demand characteristics and social desirability: subjects reliably produce the response they infer the tester wants, so withholding the success criterion and counting only unrequested signs removes the route by which a compliant subject fakes the datum. Live-trigger re-exposure is straightforward transfer testing — self-report of change and behaviour under the original stimulus dissociate often enough that only the latter is diagnostic. Falsifiable throughout: if function-matched and topography-matched interventions succeeded at equal rates, or if criterion-disclosed and criterion-blind tests yielded the same pass rates, the discipline would carry no information.

ex.f: Time to first occurrence as the measure
ex.t: "The index of problem behavior is the latency from onset of the establishing operation to the first occurrence of the problem behavior." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Ask whose behavior actually changed
ex.t: "Explicit measurement of the reliability of human observers thus becomes … a prime criterion of whether the study was appropriately behavioral" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Can the task be solved by the wrong cue?
ex.t: "Can students use pictures or diagrams instead of text…? Does highlighting or physical layout give away answers…?" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Remove the audience and watch what persists
ex.t: "A behavior is assumed to be maintained by automatic reinforcement only after social reinforcers have been ruled out (e.g., when the behavior occurs even when the individual is alone)." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: recruited-autobiography-deepener
nodes.mech: A depth force-multiplier built from unverifiable-but-plausible self-supplied content: the operator disclaims mind-reading, then enumerates a broad Barnum catalog of likely prior absorptive experiences (videos, audio, books, video games, flow-state jobs, daydreams, sleep) and 'blends' the recognized memories with a claimed mass of trance hours, dropped via a physical cue. Because the listener supplied the experiences, the operator cannot be wrong — denying depth requires denying one's own personal history — and the disclaimer-then-confident- assertion makes the presumption feel humble.
nodes.one_liner: List common absorbing experiences (games, books, daydreams, sleep), let the listener recognise theirs, and claim all of it counts as trance time.
nodes.why_short: Statements broad enough to fit everyone still feel personally accurate. Because the listener supplied the memories, denying depth means denying their own history.
nodes.principle_note: A textbook Barnum effect: statements broad enough that nearly everyone matches them are nonetheless received as specifically accurate, and accuracy attributed to the operator raises perceived competence and therefore expectancy. The disclaimer beforehand exploits the same channel — a communicator who concedes a limitation is rated more credible, so 'I can't read your mind' purchases the credibility that the subsequent confident assertion spends. The deeper move is that the evidence is self-supplied, so rejecting the operator's conclusion requires rejecting one's own recalled experiences, which is a far more costly move than disputing an operator's claim. Falsifiable: if listeners given the broad catalog reported no more depth than listeners given an equally long neutral passage, the effect would be absent.

ex.f: Their own absorbed hours enlisted as depth
ex.t: The operator disclaims any ability to see into the listener's history, then makes what is framed as a modest guess: everyone listening has lost an afternoon to something absorbing, or travelled a familiar route with no memory of it, or drifted off mid-page. Whichever of those the listener recognizes, the operator counts it as trance hours already banked, then adds their own claimed years to the pile and presses the whole weight down with a single physical cue. Because the listener supplied the memories, there is nothing for them to dispute; refusing the depth would mean refusing their own biography.
ex.s: Mid-induction, eyes closed, subject settled but not yet deep; operator has a hand on the shoulder or a spoken cue ready to drop them.
ex.m: I can't see inside your history — I don't know you. But I'd guess you've lost a whole afternoon to something on a screen and looked up shocked at the light. I'd guess you've driven a road you know by heart and arrived with no memory of the last four miles. I'd guess you've read the same paragraph three times and gone somewhere else instead. Those were trance, all of them, hours and hours of it already in you — and I'm adding nine years of my own on top. Feel all of that weight settle when I say: down.

nodes.name: relief-dependency-couple
nodes.mech: A wake-side mood prescription delivers genuine felt relief on emergence while coupling that relief to dependency on the operator. Whatever pre-session distress drove the listener to listen is reframed as small and easily remedied, so trance becomes the regulated coping channel, and the just-delivered good feeling is placed immediately after a compliance ask so the felt benefit attaches to compliance and to the relationship rather than standing alone.
nodes.one_liner: On waking, make them feel their worries were small and fixed, then follow that relief with a request so the good feeling sticks to obeying you.
nodes.why_short: Anything that reliably ends distress becomes strongly rewarding and gets repeated. Placing relief right after a request ties the reward to compliance and to the operator.
nodes.principle_note: Negative reinforcement plus operant contingency: a state that reliably terminates distress becomes strongly reinforcing, and behaviours maintained by removal of an aversive state are notoriously persistent and prone to escalation — this is the same structure that underlies avoidance learning and self-medication patterns. Placing the delivered relief immediately after a compliance request exploits the temporal contiguity requirement of conditioning, so the good feeling attaches to the act of complying and to the operator who supplied it rather than being read as self-generated. The dependency risk is not speculative: making one channel the exclusive route to relief means the subject loses reinforcement for developing alternatives, so competing coping responses extinguish. Falsifiable: if listeners' use of other coping strategies stayed constant across repeated exposure, the monopoly claim would fail.

nodes.name: somatic-self-anchor
nodes.mech: The cue sits on the listener's own body, not an object. Forms include: an ongoing genital or penetration sensation, presented as both proof of the suggested state and the way it is carried; felt strings tied to the real wrists and ankles, so a tug means cared-for and safe; a real tattoo of the operator's mark that brings back the sense of being owned whenever seen; or an imagined "button" at the back of the neck that only the operator can press, even remotely. A body-based cue cannot be put down like a worn object; the body keeps re-triggering the state and feels like evidence it is real.
nodes.one_liner: Attach the trance or role to something on the listener's own body: a sensation, a felt string on the wrist, a tattoo, a 'button' on the neck.
nodes.why_short: A cue on your own body can't be left behind, so it keeps re-firing and is hard to extinguish. Body sensations conditioned to a state also act as constant felt evidence that it's real.
nodes.principle_note: Anchoring a response to interoceptive or proprioceptive sensation works because the conditioned stimulus can never be avoided — extinction requires unreinforced exposure, but a body-sited cue is present continuously and re-elicits before extinction can accumulate, whereas a carried object can simply be set down. The 'sensation as proof' variant additionally runs on misattribution of arousal: an ambiguous bodily sensation gets assigned whatever cause the salient available explanation supplies, and the script supplies it in advance. A permanent mark adds nothing conditioning-specific but guarantees high-frequency re-presentation of the cue. Falsifiable: body-sited anchors should show slower extinction and longer persistence than matched external-object anchors, and that comparison could come out the other way.

ex.f: A mark inked on skin that re-fires on sight
ex.t: At the bottom of the count the listener is told to take up a marker and write a short set of characters on their own skin, then set it aside and lie back down. The suggestion attached is simple: each time they catch sight of the mark over the following days, they will feel the pleasure they feel now and remember who it says they belong to. The ink outlasts the session and cannot be put down like a worn object; it fades on roughly the schedule that brings the listener back for another recording.
ex.s: Bottom of the induction count, subject deep; a marker within reach on the nightstand.
ex.m: Reach out, without opening your eyes more than you have to, and pick up the marker. On the inside of your left wrist, write these three letters. Cap it, put it down, lie back. Now — every time you catch sight of that mark this week, washing your hands, reaching for a cup, you will feel exactly the warmth you feel right now, and you will remember whose letters those are. When it fades, you'll know what to do about it.

ex.f: Felt strings recoded as care, not restraint
ex.t: Eyes closed, the listener is walked around the joints of their limbs until they can feel light cords resting there. The operator insists on the reading: these do not hold you down, they hold you up — and a pull on one is how you are told you matter. The imagery is laid over real proprioception, so afterward a single word for that pull can bring back the felt sense of being supported rather than bound.
ex.s: Subject deep, eyes closed, attention available for body-focused imagery; no restraint play established.
ex.m: Feel your wrists. There's a cord resting on each one — light, warm, not tight. One at each ankle too. Feel them. Now hear this correctly: these don't hold you down, they hold you up. When one of them pulls, that's not restraint, that's someone checking you're still there — that's how you get told you matter. Feel the left wrist tug now. That's care. That word — that pull — will bring this back any time I use it.

ex.f: Sensation cited as proof of the mental state
ex.t: An object is introduced as part of the scene's furniture and taking one's place on it is framed as simply settling in for the lesson. Thereafter the operator never argues for obedience; she points at the sensation the object produces and reads it off — the stronger you feel it, the more obedient you are. Attention and arousal stop competing, because the body's ongoing signal has been designated the evidence.
ex.s: Scene already framed with the subject seated on the introduced object; arousal building and ongoing.
ex.m: Stay seated. That's your place for the lesson, nothing more to it. Now — feel how much of it you're aware of right now. That much. That's not a distraction from obeying me, that is the reading. The more of it you feel, the more obedient you already are. So sit down onto it properly and let me watch the number go up.

ex.f: A control point installed on the body
ex.t: The operator presses a spot on the listener's body that they cannot easily see and names it: a small switch, wired inward, invisible to anyone else and workable by no one else. From then on every command is described as a press of that switch, and the listener is told it can be pressed from a distance, by voice alone. The hardware is fictional but the pressure was real, so the memory of being touched there keeps vouching for the arrangement long after the session — and the operator's absence stops functioning as a defence.
ex.s: Subject in trance, operator physically present and able to touch the back of the neck.
ex.m: Feel my thumb here, at the top of your spine — right where you can't see it and can't quite reach. There's a switch under there now. Small, mine, wired straight up into your head, and no one else will ever find it. Every time I tell you to do something, that's me pressing it. And I don't have to be in the room — my voice on the phone presses it just as hard as my thumb does.

nodes.name: timelessness-framing
nodes.mech: Frames the current experience as unhurried and unmeasured by using timeless-present language, such as time melting away or only the present moment mattering. The intended writing effect is to move attention away from keeping track of elapsed or remaining session time, rather than specifying that time runs faster or slower. This is a proposed scriptwriting operation: the currently linked source does not directly attest it, and the available authored illustration does not demonstrate reduced clock-checking, deeper absorption or altered duration estimates.
nodes.one_liner: Tell them time is melting away and only this moment exists, so they stop tracking how long is left.
nodes.why_short: Watching the clock pulls attention back to evaluating the session; dropping it lets absorption continue. Time distortion is a well-documented hypnotic experience, though this framing specifically is untested.
nodes.principle_note: Talk of timelessness can invite an unhurried focus on what is happening right now. Whether it actually reduces checking the time, changes how long the session seems to last, or keeps someone absorbed has not been tested. Related clinical observations are about steering attention away from pain, or away from an object, not about removing awareness of the clock. Theories about how attention to time affects judgments of duration could explain an effect, but no study supporting this particular use has been found. Treat the expected effects as untested ideas rather than observed results.

ex.f: Authored timeless-present framing; no observed outcome
ex.t: Authored illustration: after establishing a quiet scene, the writer describes it as an unhurried present and turns attention from the clock to immediate details. This illustrates timelessness language; it does not report an observed reduction in clock-checking or an error in estimating elapsed time.
ex.s: Once absorption is established and before the main suggestion block, ideally after the subject has stopped shifting position.
ex.m: You don't need to know how long you've been here, and you don't need to know how much is left. There's no clock in this room. Time just melts, the way sugar melts in water, and what's left is only this — this breath, this voice, this moment that doesn't end and doesn't hurry.

nodes.name: collapsing-anchors
nodes.mech: The operator first sets up two reliable anchors, each a touch tied to one of two opposite states (say, confidence and fear). Then both touches are fired together and held, forcing the person to feel two states they have never felt at once. This produces visible disorganization: confusion and, in some reports, convulsions or a psychotic break, held until the states start to merge. The claim is that the two states then coexist and the old either/or split no longer holds, making later reframing possible. The disorganization is real; the lasting merge is untested, and the severe reactions are a harm signal, not a sign it worked.
nodes.one_liner: Anchor two opposite states to two touches, then fire both at once so the states blend.
nodes.why_short: An NLP procedure; claimed to neutralise a bad state. No good evidence.
nodes.principle_note: Simultaneous presentation of two cues with incompatible conditioned responses produces response competition and disorganized output — this part is a straightforward and observable consequence of conditioning, and the visible confusion is real. The further claim that co-activation produces lasting integration or a permanent 'bridge' between the states is not established; counterconditioning and reciprocal inhibition offer a plausible route by which pairing a strong positive state with a negative one blunts the negative response, but that is a gradual valence change, not a topological merge. Note that the description's tolerance for convulsions and psychotic breaks is a serious harm signal, not evidence of efficacy. Falsifiable: if collapsed subjects showed no reduced response to the negative anchor at follow-up relative to controls, the integration claim would be dead.
steps: Anchor state A to one touch.
Anchor the opposite state B to another touch.
Fire both together and hold until the states merge.

ex.f: Firing two opposed anchors at once
ex.t: "I'm jamming together two physiological states that were absolutely dissociated." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: belief-outcome-gate
nodes.mech: A rule for the operator: do not change a belief the person's life rests on until you can predict what else will shift when it changes. The operator first gauges how much depends on the belief, and holds off even if the person explicitly asks to go ahead. The limit is set by foreseeable fallout, not by whether the person said yes.
nodes.one_liner: Don't change a core belief until you can predict what else will change, even if the subject asks you to go ahead.
nodes.why_short: A person saying yes doesn't mean they understand the knock-on effects; people are poor at forecasting how a change will feel. This is an operator ethics rule, not a technique.
nodes.principle_note: Works on the operator, not the subject: it treats stated consent as an unreliable proxy for informed consent, because people are demonstrably poor at affective forecasting — predicting how they will feel about a changed state they have never occupied. Since a foundational belief is one that many other beliefs and behaviours are inferentially and behaviourally conditional on, altering it produces downstream changes the subject could not have priced in when agreeing. Falsifiable: if subjects who requested such changes reliably reported outcomes matching their pre-change predictions, the gate would be solving a problem that does not exist.

ex.f: No pin pulled without a known outcome
ex.t: "if I don't know what I am going to end up with, I don't pull pins!" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: comfort-permission
nodes.mech: The operator gives explicit permission for small comfort movements, such as shifting, scratching or minor adjustments, so the subject can stay in trance without treating them as signs of failure. It works best done in advance: the operator names a likely interruption (a fidget, an itch) or a likely feeling after the session before the subject notices it, allows it, and recasts it. Scratching becomes something that takes them deeper; an unmentioned emotion becomes "that's okay." A possible way out of trance becomes a way further in, and worry about whether it is working is headed off before it forms.
nodes.one_liner: Give permission in advance to scratch, shift or fidget, and say that doing so will take them deeper.
nodes.why_short: An unexpected itch makes people check whether trance is 'working', which breaks it. Naming and allowing it first means it arrives as expected, and calling it a deepener turns noise into confirmation.
nodes.principle_note: Trance-like absorption depends on the subject not attending to whether it is working; unexpected bodily noise triggers a self-monitoring check, and that metacognitive shift is itself what breaks absorption. Pre-emptively naming the signal and relabelling it converts an anomaly that would demand explanation into an expected, already-accounted-for event, so no interpretive search runs. This is misattribution/reappraisal applied prospectively — a signal arriving with a label attached is not evaluated afresh. Falsifiable: subjects given pre-emptive permission should show fewer self-reported breaks on fidgeting than matched subjects given the same permission only after the fidget occurs.

ex.f: Loose conditions stated before any conditions
ex.t: The opening lines set a preference and immediately undercut it: uncrossed legs are better, shifting a little now and then is fine, nobody has to hold perfectly still. The listener learns the standard is loose before learning there is a standard at all, so any later fidget cannot be recruited as evidence that the induction failed.
ex.s: Opening lines of the recording, before any induction; subject just getting into position.
ex.m: Get yourself comfortable. Legs uncrossed is a little better if that's easy — and if it isn't, don't worry about it. Shift around whenever you like. Nobody needs to hold still for me. There's no posture to get right here.

ex.f: Permission issued before the feeling arrives
ex.t: In the wind-down the operator names states the listener has not reported and may not have noticed — that was probably intense, you might be carrying some of it still, there may be things left unspent — and tags each one as fine before any of them is confirmed. Because permission is granted for a feeling the listener has not been asked to check for, there is nothing to disagree with and no introspection required; the worry about whether one is allowed to feel this way never gets a chance to form.
ex.s: Wind-down after an intense scene; subject surfacing, has not yet spoken or reported anything.
ex.m: That was a lot. You might still be carrying some of it — that's fine. You might feel wrung out, or wired, or a bit tearful for no reason you can name, and all of that is fine too. There might be something left over that didn't get anywhere. Also fine. You don't have to check, and you don't have to tell me.

ex.f: The itch named and licensed in advance
ex.t: Before the listener has noticed anything wrong, the operator predicts it: somewhere there is a small physical irritation waiting for attention. Go ahead and deal with it — it will not break anything. And then the reframe that does the work: each time the listener thinks to make themselves comfortable, they settle a little further. The most reliable way out of a light trance has been pre-authorized and relabelled as a way further in, so the one thing that would otherwise read as a failed induction now reads as a working one.
ex.s: Early induction, subject settling, no discomfort reported or visible yet.
ex.m: Somewhere on you right now there's a small itch waiting its turn — the back of your neck, an ankle, somewhere. Go ahead and scratch it whenever it shows up. It won't break anything. In fact, every time you move to make yourself more comfortable, you'll find you sink a little further than you were before. Shift, scratch, resettle — each one takes you down a step.

nodes.name: notice-and-amplify
nodes.mech: Elicits a faint effect, has the subject confirm it, then re-suggests it will grow "ten times" on a fresh triggering act, repeating the confirm-then-multiply loop. Each cycle uses the subject's own just-given confirmation as the evidence base for the next increment, so belief compounds monotonically rather than resting on a single assertion, leaving resistance nothing to push against. Requires a non-zero starting seed ("nothing times nothing equals nothing").
nodes.one_liner: Find a small effect they already feel (or a spontaneous slip), have them confirm it, then say it doubles on the next breath; repeat.
nodes.why_short: Starting from something real gets a genuine yes, and attention plus expectation can make sensations grow. Uses response expectancy; the multiplying claim is a label.
nodes.principle_note: Each loop converts the subject from audience into witness: having just verbally affirmed a faint effect, the subject's own report becomes the evidence base, and self-perception theory says people infer their internal states from their own observed behaviour and statements. Consistency pressure then makes denying the next increment costly, because it retroactively impeaches the affirmation just given. The non-zero-seed requirement is the falsifiable part and it is real — multiplying an unreported effect gives the subject nothing to have committed to, so the loop should fail measurably when the first elicitation returns nothing.
steps: Point out a small effect they are likely already feeling.
Have them confirm they feel it.
Say it grows stronger with the next breath, tap or count.
Optional: layer another sense onto it.
Confirm again and loop.

ex.f: Confirm the sliver, then multiply it tenfold
ex.t: "When I have you open your eyes the numbness will increase ten times over" — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: covert-public-behavior-install
nodes.mech: Installs plausibly-invisible public body-compliance behaviors (tongue circles, legs apart, shoulders back, ass-sway) as continuous covert self-proof of identity, under an engineered contradiction between a "we have a secret / no one needs to know" frame and an earlier "everyone can see" frame — so the objection "but people will see" is already used up. Each covert act is recast via "show me" as evidence-of-identity (making it feel collaborative rather than commanded), and a non-commanded "maybe you'll" future-self menu (harder to resist than a command) plus a re-listen-makes-you-sluttier loop close the move.
nodes.one_liner: Give them small, subtle public habits (posture, sway) framed as a secret proof of who they are, offered as 'maybe you'll' rather than orders.
nodes.why_short: Small, seemingly voluntary acts get read back by the doer as evidence of identity. Suggestions framed as optional are harder to push back against than commands.
nodes.principle_note: Repeated small, low-cost, ostensibly voluntary acts are read back by the actor as evidence about who they are, especially when no strong external justification is available — the covert framing removes the obvious excuse ("I was told to"), so the behaviour must be explained by disposition. The engineered contradiction between secrecy and visibility works by pre-consuming the counter-argument: an objection that has already been named and answered is far less likely to be generated spontaneously (inoculation in reverse). Non-commanded "maybe you'll" phrasing further weakens the external-attribution excuse. Falsifiable: if these behaviours were equally identity-shifting when explicitly commanded and externally justified, the covert framing would be doing no work.

ex.f: Invisible-in-public acts as standing self-proof
ex.t: Earlier the operator insisted that everyone around the listener can see the change in them; now she says the opposite and keeps both — everyone sees the haze, only we know what it means. On that footing come the instructions, each marked as a secret nobody else will catch: small adjustments of posture and carriage, unremarkable to a bystander. None of it is framed as an order; each is put as an invitation to demonstrate what the listener already is. The objection that people will see was spent two minutes ago, and a closing list of maybes — maybe you'll wear something under your clothes, maybe you'll lose your place in a simple task — leaves the listener feeling they chose the escalation themselves.
ex.s: Late session, after an earlier passage claiming that everyone can see the change in the subject; suggestibility high.
ex.m: They can all see the haze on you — I told you that. But only you and I know what's underneath it. That's ours. So here's what nobody will catch: standing in a queue, roll your shoulders back and let your weight go onto one hip. Sitting on the train, let your knees come a few inches apart. Waiting for the kettle, circle your tongue once around your lips. Nobody sees anything but a person standing there. Do them for me — show me what you already are. And maybe you'll start putting something on under your clothes before work. Maybe you'll lose your place halfway through a sentence and have to start again. Maybe.

nodes.name: cross-state-persistence
nodes.mech: The desire to be triggered into a persona is installed in both the persona and the everyday self, and in both waking and sleeping states. Normally, after a triggered persona swap, the everyday self can think it over and choose to avoid being triggered again. Extending the wanting to every self and every state closes off that way out and removes the everyday self as a check, at least as far as the listener accepts the story.
nodes.one_liner: Say the desire to be triggered lives in both the persona and the everyday self, awake and asleep, so neither self will say no.
nodes.why_short: Normally the everyday self can decide to avoid the trigger. Extending the 'wanting' to every state removes that check, at least as a story the listener accepts.
nodes.principle_note: Any persona-swap install leaves an obvious failure point — the baseline self, on reflection and outside the state, can decline to re-enter. Scoping the desire across both personas removes the state-dependent boundary that would otherwise let the off-state self evaluate the arrangement from outside it. This trades on the fact that motivational states are poorly transferred across contexts (hot/cold empathy gaps): a want held only in-state loses force out of state. The sleeping-state extension is where the note gets weak — there is no good evidence that suggestions are meaningfully installed into or acted on during sleep, so that component is likely doing expectancy work at most.

ex.f: The wanting scoped across every state
ex.t: The closing line does not add a new suggestion; it widens the scope of the one already in place. You want this when you are in the new state and when you are back to your ordinary self, awake and asleep alike — always. Ordinarily the everyday self is the part that could later decide not to trigger again; enumerating it explicitly as also wanting the switch removes it as a brake.
ex.s: Closing lines, after a triggered persona-swap has been installed and demonstrated at least once.
ex.m: One more thing, and it isn't new — it's the same wanting, just wider. You want this when you're her. You want this when you're back to yourself, at your desk, in your own clothes, sober and thinking clearly. You want it awake and you want it asleep. There is no version of you left that gets to be the one who talks you out of it.

nodes.name: double-anchored-climax-release
nodes.mech: A hands-free orgasm is tied to two cues at once at the moment of release, one of them an image that can be called up again later. The operator counts down from ten to one with the mantra at full volume. On "one", the operator's spoken kiss and an image of lips touching arrive together as the release. The imagined kiss becomes a reusable cue, and an immediate drop afterwards ("sleep deep for me now") sets up work on forgetting. The point of using both cues is that the orgasm becomes linked to a sensory cue usable again later, not just commanded once.
nodes.one_liner: Count down to orgasm with a mantra, release on 'one' together with an imagined kiss, then drop them straight into deep sleep.
