ex.s: Any point in a piece written entirely in ten-syllable rhyming couplets; the cadence does not change here, and does not change anywhere.
ex.m: The counting slows, the shoulders settle down, / your breathing finds a softer, slower sound; / there's nothing here that asks you to decide, / just let the metre carry you inside.

nodes.name: proximity-deepening
nodes.mech: Depth is coupled to shrinking spatial distance between the subject and an approaching stimulus or the operator — each increment of approach deepens the state, with release or maximal depth at contact. Demonstrated forms include an inbound light narrated as a felt countdown releasing into sleep at contact, and the operator's approaching footsteps binding per-step deepening fused to a fixation object; classic forms — a voice drawing closer, a chime approaching, a snap appearing closer with each snap — fit the same shape.
nodes.one_liner: Tie depth to something coming closer (a light, footsteps, your voice) so each step nearer takes them deeper, deepest on contact.
nodes.why_short: An approaching thing grabs attention and gives the listener a concrete, changing quantity to map their depth onto; expectancy turns 'closer' into 'deeper'.
nodes.principle_note: 'A readable expectation is a met expectation' explains any outcome and restates the technique — proximity is narrated, so depth is reported as tracking proximity. The falsifiable content is expectancy anchored to an externally supplied scalar: a continuously updating observable gives the subject a concrete quantity to map an otherwise unmeasurable internal state onto, and looming stimuli reliably capture attention. Falsifiable: if a static or receding stimulus with identical suggestion wording produced equal depth reports, the approach coupling contributes nothing.

ex.f: An approaching light as a felt countdown
ex.t: The operator tracks something bright on its way in — past the moon, into the upper air, through the cloud layer, closer with every clause, down and down toward the listener. Nothing counts and nothing is numbered, but the shrinking distance does the work of a countdown the listener can feel tightening. At contact the accumulated expectation is discharged in three words: it touches you, and you sleep.
ex.s: Induction proper; subject's eyes closed, attention placed on a point of light far overhead.
ex.m: There's a light above you and it's coming down. It's past the moon now. Now it's through the high cold air, now it's below the cloud, and it's getting bigger every time I speak — closer, closer, close enough to feel on your face. It touches you. Sleep.

ex.f: Each approaching footstep binds to depth
ex.t: The listener is left immobilised in the scene, and then footsteps start — unhurried, getting nearer. Each one is tied to depth: the operator narrates her own approach as the thing doing the sinking, one pace at a time. Here the depth-driver is not anything the listener does but the operator's proximity, so the state now rises and falls with how close she is rather than with the listener's effort. The attention is simultaneously pinned to the footwear making the sound, welding the fixation object and the deepener into one thing.
ex.s: Subject already immobilised in the scene and unable to turn; a fixation object (the operator's heels) is being introduced by sound.
ex.m: You can't turn around, so just listen. Those are my heels on the floor behind you — hear them? Every step I take toward you takes you down another layer. Nothing you do moves you now; I do. Closer. Deeper. Keep your attention on the sound of them and count me in.

nodes.name: scope-coupled-depth-titration
nodes.mech: Some hypnotic effects can be had in light trance if they are partial: a numb patch, forgetting a detail. Ask for the total version instead (complete numbness, forgetting the whole session) and the person, trying to comply, tends to go deeper to make it happen, rather than simply failing. So the operator can steer depth by asking for wider or narrower effects. This is a practitioner observation, not a tested finding.
nodes.one_liner: Ask for a total version of a phenomenon (complete numbness, complete amnesia) to push the person deeper rather than accept a partial one.
nodes.why_short: A total request gives no partial benchmark to fail against, so ambiguous experience gets read as success and reported as deeper trance. No real 'depth resource' is being recruited.
nodes.principle_note: Widening scope raises the demand characteristic without supplying a failure criterion: a total suggestion offers no partial-success benchmark against which the subject could score themselves as failing, so ambiguous experience is resolved in favour of success and reported as greater depth. This is an expectancy-and-interpretation account, not a claim that some depth resource is literally recruited — no such quantity is established. Falsifiable: if total-scope requests produced measurably higher failure and disengagement rates than partial ones rather than deeper reports, the titration claim is wrong.

ex.f: Widening the scope drags the depth along
ex.t: "Any effort to have a total amnesia resulted in a progression toward a deep trance" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

nodes.name: antecedent-manipulation
nodes.mech: Change a behaviour by changing what comes before it, not by rewarding or punishing what follows. First know why the behaviour happens, and make sure you control the situation. Then remove its reason: make a dreaded task easier so there is nothing to escape, make the avoided thing less unpleasant, remove the cue that starts the habit, or remove the means during a low-urge moment. No consequence is ever applied. Variations: swap the old cue for one that starts a preferred routine (ashtray replaced by the TV remote); remove rival rewards so yours stand out; stack weak cues until together they prompt the behaviour; physically block it before it starts.
nodes.one_liner: Change the behavior by changing the situation before it happens: make tasks easier, remove the cue, remove the means.
nodes.why_short: Behavior is prompted and motivated by its setting; take away the cue, the reason, or the opportunity and it simply occurs less, with no reward or punishment needed.
nodes.principle_note: Antecedent control is well established in applied behaviour analysis: motivating operations alter how reinforcing a consequence currently is, and discriminative stimuli set the occasion for responding, so editing either changes rate without any consequence being delivered. Its practical advantage is that it produces no extinction burst and no punishment side effects, because the response is never emitted to be consequated. Falsifiable per case by functional analysis: if removing the identified antecedent left response rate unchanged, that variable was not controlling the behaviour.

ex.f: Remove what the behavior needs to happen
ex.t: "ridding oneself of the items needed to engage in an undesired behavior is a good start" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Make the task non-aversive, escape loses value
ex.t: "problem behavior by all participants was reduced simply by making specific modifications to the instructional methods, without modifying the demands… by making the tasks less difficult and, thus, unpairing task demands with aversive properties" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: belief-gate-contingent-yoking
nodes.mech: Once the listener is suggestible, state one effect with total confidence and tie it to something they are already doing, using 'as long as': 'as long as you keep pretending you can't open your eyes, you will feel nothing.' Because the effect is fastened to an ongoing action, keeping up the action keeps up the effect, with no need to repeat the suggestion. The claim behind it is that the absence of doubt matters more than trance depth.
nodes.one_liner: Tie a suggestion to something they are already doing: 'as long as you keep your eyes closed, you will feel nothing.'
nodes.why_short: Keeping up the ongoing act becomes the proof the suggestion is still in force, so no new suggestion is needed; the conditional grammar makes doubt feel like breaking the act.
nodes.principle_note: Yoking an effect to an ongoing act exploits self-perception: the subject continuously observes themselves performing the behaviour and infers the accompanying state from it, so the evidence for the suggestion is regenerated every moment rather than needing re-delivery. The consistency principle adds cost to stopping, since ceasing the act would retroactively mark the sustained belief as false. The claim that 'absence of doubt makes belief operative reality' is a restatement of expectancy and is not independently established. Falsifiable: if the effect persisted equally after the subject stopped the yoked behaviour, the contingency is doing no work.

ex.f: One belief yoked to an ongoing act
ex.t: "So long as you keep pretending that you can't open your eyes, you will feel nothing... I have established selective thinking while your critical faculty was inoperative, and the result is complete anesthesia." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: response-cost-token-economy
nodes.mech: Discourage a behaviour by taking away part of a reward the person already holds (points, tokens, earned minutes) each time it happens. The fine must be immediate and cost something they value; it teaches nothing to replace the behaviour. Build up a stock first, announce fines in advance, and scale them to the offence. Oversized fines backfire: never let the balance run out or go below zero, or the person gives up. Variations: fine from a free bonus pool while protecting earned holdings; penalise refusing to pay; keep the ledger in the operator's hands; give rewards far more often than fines, so fines do not become attention.
nodes.one_liner: Take away some of an earned reward (points, minutes, tokens) every time the unwanted behavior happens.
nodes.why_short: Losing something you already own is a reliable punisher. It works only if the reserve exists, fines are immediate and proportionate, and the person never goes broke and gives up.
nodes.principle_note: Loss of an already-held resource is weighted more heavily than a forgone gain of equal size, so debiting a stockpile suppresses behaviour at a lower nominal cost than withholding an unearned reward would. The parameter constraints follow from the same account: if the reserve is drained or the token's net value goes negative, the token stops functioning as a reinforcer and the contingency collapses into general demotivation — which is why the effect should observably invert past the depletion ceiling rather than increasing monotonically with fine size.

ex.f: Provision the pool above baseline so it cannot run dry
ex.t: "increase the number of reinforcers 25% above the mean number of occurrences during baseline... mean number of disruptions per day is 20... establish 25 minutes of free time" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Stockpile a reserve before you can fine it
ex.t: "Positive reinforcers cannot be removed from a person who does not have any... the practitioner must ensure a sufficient reinforcer reserve" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: No debt: earnings must stay net-positive
ex.t: "Token loss should never be applied to a behavior if the learner does not have tokens. Students should not be allowed to go into debt... A learner should always earn more tokens than she loses." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Pre-commit the penalty before the failure
ex.t: "Do 50 sit-ups at 11:00 pm on Sundays for each day that I did not practice" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: count-up-return
nodes.mech: Bring the listener back to ordinary waking gradually, under the operator's lead, reducing trance step by step until they are fully oriented, with no suggestions carried out and no catch. This is the clean, benign exit. Variations: a count up from one to five, getting more awake with each number; reverse the journey used to go down (climb back up the stairs); sweep attention through the room, sounds, time of day and body position; a feeling of energy and warmth flowing back through the limbs.
nodes.one_liner: Bring them back up gradually, usually counting up, reorienting to the room and body, until fully awake.
nodes.why_short: A clear, expected ritual marks the end of the session and gives the listener steps to follow back to normal alertness; expectancy and reorientation do the work.
nodes.principle_note: Trance is largely a state of narrowed, absorbed attention sustained by the operator's ongoing framing; withdrawing that framing while supplying graded external-orientation cues (counting, breath, room, body) restores broad attentional scanning and reality-monitoring. The graded ramp works because reorientation is easier when it is scaffolded stepwise than when demanded at once — the prediction is that abrupt, unscaffolded termination leaves more residual disorientation than a counted or enumerated return.

ex.f: Full ramp: count, breath, body, eyes, room
ex.t: The exit is a bundle rather than a bare count: the operator asks for one deeper breath, invites the listener to shift the shoulders and stretch the hands, then counts upward while the eyes come open, and finishes by suggesting a slow look around at wherever the listener is actually sitting. Each element does a different piece of the return — breath and movement re-engage the body, the count paces it, the look-around restores orientation.
ex.s: End of session; a fuller reorientation is wanted than a bare count, subject still seated or lying.
ex.m: Take one good deep breath in — and let it go. Roll your shoulders, open and close your hands a couple of times. Now, one, two, three, four, five — eyes open. Take a slow look around at the room you're actually in, find the walls, find the light, and let yourself arrive back here properly.

ex.f: Sweeping awareness back through the room
ex.t: Instead of a bare wake cue, the operator walks the listener category by category through the ordinary world: notice the temperature of the room, notice whatever sound is nearest, notice what time of day it is, notice the weight of your own body against the chair. Each anchor is named, checked, and left behind. By the last one, attention has been rebuilt outward and the trance frame simply has nothing left holding it.
ex.s: End of session; return is being run by external-anchor enumeration rather than by counting.
ex.m: Notice the temperature of the room on your skin. Notice the nearest sound to you, whatever it happens to be right now. Notice what time of day it is out there. And notice the weight of your own body pressing down into the chair. That's four things back in place, and there's nothing left holding this.

ex.f: Energy returning through the limbs
ex.t: No numbers are used at all. The operator narrates warmth gathering in the chest and then moving outward — down through the arms until the fingers want to move, down through the legs until the feet feel solid on the floor — and describes the heaviness draining off as it goes. The return is driven entirely through what the body reports, and the listener arrives awake because they can feel themselves again, not because they were counted there.
ex.s: End of session; a somatic return is wanted with no numbers used at all.
ex.m: There's a warmth gathering in the middle of your chest — feel it start to spread. It's moving out along your arms now, all the way to your fingers, until they want to move on their own; go ahead and let them. It's going down through your legs, and your feet are finding the floor, solid. The heaviness is draining off you as the warmth arrives. There you are — all the way back.

ex.f: The counted ramp back up to waking
ex.t: The operator announces that a short climb will bring the listener back, then walks it upward, giving each number a job: the first, weight beginning to leave the arms; the next, sounds in the room becoming ordinary again; then the breath picking up its normal rhythm; then almost all the way back. On the last one the eyes open and the listener is told they are alert and clear-headed. Nothing is added on the way up and nothing is asked for at the top — the count exists only to change the state back.
ex.s: End of session, all content delivered; nothing is to be carried out and no charge remains.
ex.m: I'm going to count you up from one to five and you'll be fully awake at five. One — the heaviness starting to leave your arms. Two — the sounds around you becoming ordinary again. Three — your breathing back at its normal pace. Four — nearly all the way back, clear and steady. Five: eyes open, wide awake, alert and clear-headed.

nodes.name: emergence-negative-space
nodes.mech: Leave out the wake-up on purpose, so the session never formally ends and the line between trance and ordinary life is blurred. The goal is for suggestions to carry on outside the session rather than being contained by it. Variations: end without waking and hand the listener straight to the next recording; chain several 'final' transformations with no return to normal; loop the ending back to the opening line and call waking part of the dream; a count-up that intensifies the state instead of lifting it.
nodes.one_liner: Leave out the wake-up on purpose so the session never formally ends and suggestions bleed into ordinary life.
nodes.why_short: An explicit ending marks the session as a separate context; without it, nothing tells the mind the suggestions belong only to the session.
nodes.principle_note: Suggestions tend to be bounded by the context in which they were encoded; an explicit closing ramp marks the session as a distinct context and cues the retrieval boundary. Omitting the ramp removes that boundary marker, so suggested material stays contextually undifferentiated from waking life and is more likely to be retrieved outside the session. This predicts measurably greater carryover of suggested responses from arcs lacking a return ramp than from otherwise identical arcs that include one.

ex.f: Session stops with the hook still live
ex.t: The final line of the recording is not a wakener; it is the trigger phrase, fired once more, on what sounds like a wake-cue. No count out, no reorientation, no closing word about how the listener should feel now. Whatever was switched on stays on, and the listener carries it out of the session because nothing in the session ever turned it off.
ex.s: Final seconds of the recording; a trigger phrase was installed and rehearsed throughout.
ex.m: And now, wide awake — drop for me.

ex.f: Installs voiced inside a five-line wake
ex.t: The wake-up runs five lines total, and two of them are not wake-up lines: between the second and third count the operator restates the installed condition as present fact, then ends the recording on a fresh instruction for what the listener should do now that they are up. The loudest signal in the closing seconds is the install, and the last word is a command rather than a release.
ex.s: Session end; a condition (blankness, obedience, arousal) was installed during the body of the session.
ex.m: One. Two. Your mind stays soft and empty for me, exactly as it is now. Three. Four. Five — eyes open, and go do what you were told.

ex.f: Non-terminating series node handing off in-state
ex.t: Withholding the emergence ramp makes the state the default condition between files rather than something bracketed by each one, so trance becomes a place the subject lives in across sessions instead of visits. The operator observes it in aggregate: subjects report chaining files, and report not remembering having woken up in between.
ex.s: The final thirty seconds of a session that is one numbered instalment in an ongoing series; no count-up has been given.
ex.m: Don't come up. There's nothing to come up for. Stay exactly this deep, exactly this soft, and when you're ready — not before — reach out and start the next one. It picks up right here, right where you are now.

ex.f: Russian-doll chain of "final" transformations with no baseline
ex.t: Each nested layer forecloses the return path of the one above it, so no level ever resolves to baseline and in-trance content is post-dated into waking life. The operator reads it structurally — the arc has no line that undoes any layer — and observes subjects treating session-installed content as ordinary self-description afterwards.
ex.s: After a transformation suggestion has already been delivered and would ordinarily be released before waking.
ex.m: That was the last change — and underneath it, one more. Deeper than the last one, and this one is the real you, the one that was always underneath. And beneath that, deeper still, the final one. You don't go back up through them. There's no back up. This is where you live now.

ex.f: Inverted release contour — count-up that intensifies
ex.t: Occupying the emergence slot with escalation rather than release means the surface ritual of waking is performed while the release it normally carries is deleted, pushing persistence past the session boundary. The operator can see subjects emerge alert and oriented while reporting the suggestions feeling stronger after waking than during.
ex.s: At the position in the arc where an emergence count would normally run, with the subject at depth.
ex.m: Counting up now. One — it gets stronger. Two — stronger still, and it follows you. Three — eyes open, wide awake, and everything I said is more true out there than it was in here. Four. Five. Carry it.

nodes.name: erogenous-field-generalization
nodes.mech: Just before a promised whole-body orgasm, the operator spreads genital arousal outward: every inch of skin, the touch of the chair, the air, even the operator's words are declared to be sexual stimulation. Nothing is left as neutral sensation. This intensifies the coming orgasm and leaves no neutral place to rest attention and escape the arousal. Even listening to the script becomes part of the stimulation.
nodes.one_liner: Declare that every sensation (skin, chair, air, even your words) is sexual, so there is nowhere neutral to escape to.
nodes.why_short: Ambiguous touch is interpreted by the label on offer; while arousal is high, one global label turns ordinary input into arousal and removes any neutral place to rest attention.
nodes.principle_note: Interpretation of ambiguous bodily sensation depends heavily on the label available at the time, and expectancy plus attentional focus shape what is felt. Declaring all sensation erogenous supplies a single global label just as arousal is high, so ordinary tactile input is misattributed to sexual arousal, and removing any designated neutral surface removes the attentional escape route. It would be falsified if subjects reliably reported neutral tactile experience on undesignated surfaces during the induction.

ex.f: All sensation reattributed as sexual
ex.t: Before the promised finish, the operator widens the map: the sensitivity that used to belong to one place is declared to belong to the whole surface of the skin. Whatever the listener is resting against, the fabric they are wearing, the temperature of the room — each is named in turn and re-labelled as contact of the same kind. Then the operator turns the delivery itself into stimulation, framing the sound of the voice as another point of contact. There is now no direction attention can travel that is not arousing; looking away from it means looking at more of it.
ex.s: Just before a promised whole-body climax; arousal already high and the subject is stationary against a surface.
ex.m: That sensitivity you feel in one place — it isn't staying there. It's on every inch of your skin now. The chair against your back is touching you like that. The fabric on your thighs is touching you like that. The air on your throat is touching you like that. And my voice going into your ears is touching you like that too. There's nowhere left to look that isn't this.

nodes.name: foreclosed-emergence
nodes.mech: Make the ending feel like a free choice while quietly removing the option of genuinely waking up. Every route offered ends in a state the operator wants. Variations: a fork of 'choices' where each branch keeps them under; calling waking up just another stage of the dream; a count-up that arrives back where it started, so nothing actually changes.
nodes.one_liner: Offer a choice of endings where every option keeps them under, so there is no real way to fully wake up.
nodes.why_short: Choosing feels like freedom and increases commitment to the pick; people rarely notice the option that is missing.
nodes.principle_note: Choice architecture governs compliance as strongly as the options themselves: perceiving that one selected an option raises commitment to it, even when every branch led to the same place. Because people rarely audit the option set for what is missing, an absent baseline branch goes unnoticed while the offered pick supplies a sense of agency. Prediction: subjects given the rigged fork report higher felt choice than subjects simply told the outcome, despite identical end states.

ex.f: The wake count that arrives where it started
ex.t: Several times across the session the operator announces that the listener is coming up, runs a brisk count, and then describes the arrival state — and the description is the same one used for being under. Repeated often enough, the count stops marking a transition at all: awake and under become the same described place, and the listener has no moment at which the session can be said to have ended.
ex.s: One of several apparent wake-ups distributed across the session; the arrival state described matches the trance state exactly.
ex.m: Coming up now — one, two, three, and you're awake. Awake means soft, heavy, wide open, waiting for my voice. That's what awake is. Good. And now let's go down again — one, two, three, and you're under: soft, heavy, wide open, waiting for my voice.

ex.f: Waking redefined as part of the dream
ex.t: The operator alternates two opposed state-words back and forth, long past the point where either keeps a distinct meaning, then closes the loop by folding the waking term inside the other: coming out of it is reclassified as one more event occurring within the frame. The listener's most basic escape route, simply deciding to leave, has been redefined as a move that happens inside the thing it was meant to leave.
ex.s: Late close, after the two state-words have been alternated to the point of blurring.
ex.m: Asleep, awake, asleep, awake — you've stopped being able to tell which one I've just said, haven't you. Here's the answer: waking up is a thing that happens inside the dream. It's one of the events in it. So go ahead and wake, if you like. You'll be doing it in here, with me, where you already are.

ex.f: Choosing between exits that both stay under
ex.t: The close hands the listener their agency back as a decision between two ways to finish, and lets them settle it themselves. It is presented warmly, as though the listener is finally in charge of their own exit. What is never on the menu is the option of coming all the way up and being finished. Every branch on offer leaves the trance operative; the listener spends their restored authority picking which operator-favoured state to occupy.
ex.s: Close of session; the subject is told their agency is being returned to them, and offered a choice of endings.
ex.m: You get to choose how this finishes, and I'll take whichever you pick. You can drift off to sleep right here, still soft, still holding onto everything I've given you — or you can come up into your evening and go about it dreamy and open and easy to reach. Take your time. Whichever you want. Choose.

nodes.name: forward-dated-trait-authorization
nodes.mech: Asserts a standing, forward-dated permission — the operator may at any future point change the listener's likes, dislikes, needs, wants, desires — executing no trait change here but pre-licensing future scripts/sessions to do trait-level work without re-establishing authority each time. If accepted now, a later "you now love X" suggestion arrives pre-licensed, so resistance to it becomes resistance to a frame already agreed-to, which is harder than resisting a fresh imposition. The clause's value is realized in later sessions, not this one.
nodes.one_liner: Get them to agree now that you may change their likes and wants later, without changing anything tonight.
nodes.why_short: An abstract permission is easy to grant; once given, refusing a later specific change means contradicting yourself, which adds consistency pressure.
nodes.principle_note: Agreeing to a standing permission is a low-cost, abstract commitment, but once made it becomes the frame against which later concrete requests are judged — refusing a specific trait change then requires contradicting an already-accepted position, which carries consistency cost on top of the object-level objection. This is the foot-in-the-door structure applied to authority rather than behaviour, and it predicts higher acceptance of a later trait suggestion in subjects who accepted the blanket clause than in those who received the same suggestion cold.

ex.f: Standing permission to rewrite you later
ex.t: Nothing about the listener is altered in this session. The operator only states a standing term: whatever you are drawn to and whatever you avoid, whatever you want and need, are all subject to revision by me, at a time of my choosing. The clause is agreed to at a moment when it costs nothing, because it asks for no change today. Its value arrives months later, when some other session declares a new preference already in place — and the listener's objection has to fight a permission they already granted rather than a fresh demand.
ex.s: Mid-session, ownership frame already accepted; no trait change is executed here or anywhere in this file.
ex.m: One term, and then we move on. What you like, what you can't stand, what you want, what you need — all of it is mine to change, whenever I decide to, without asking you again. I'm not changing anything tonight. I'm just telling you the terms, and you're agreeing to them now, while they cost you nothing.

nodes.name: contingency-function-substrate-principles
nodes.mech: A principle rather than a move: what a stimulus does depends on how it is arranged, not on the stimulus itself. The same thing can reward, punish or motivate depending on when it starts and stops relative to the behaviour; a token can reward, fine, signal or prompt. And change is what counts: a sudden onset or offset controls behaviour, while a steady background condition does little. A consequence only works if its start is sharp enough to notice as following the action; a gradual change acts only as a mood or motivator.
nodes.one_liner: The same stimulus can reward, punish or motivate depending on how and when it is arranged; changes matter more than steady states.
nodes.why_short: In operant learning, function comes from the relationship between stimulus and behavior, and organisms respond to detectable changes, not constant background.
nodes.principle_note: These are statements of the operant framework's own definitions rather than empirical claims about a subject: function is defined by the response-consequence relation, so the same stimulus in different relations genuinely has different functions. The empirically contentful part — that behavioural control tracks stimulus change rather than standing states, and that a consequence needs a discriminable onset to be attributed to the preceding response — is testable and could fail: a gradually-onsetting event that nonetheless suppressed the response it followed would contradict the detectability bound.

ex.f: A token's function comes only from its relations
ex.t: "a token may serve multiple functions—reinforcing, punishing, discriminative, eliciting—depending on its relationship to these other events" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: One stimulus, three functions by arrangement
ex.t: "(a) a negative reinforcer if its termination increases behavior, (b) a punisher if its presentation decreases behavior, and/or (c) a motivating operation if its presentation increases the current frequency of behaviors that have terminated it in the past" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: future-pacing
nodes.mech: Declaratively projects a suggested response or state into future situations as automatic and inevitable (every time X, you will Y). Variations: unmarked grammatical slides that hand the listener's own rehearsal back as a forecast; a continuous future-tense stream that leaves the checking to the listener's future self; and future intrusive thoughts scripted in advance as the listener's own preference.
nodes.one_liner: Describe the future situation and tell them that, every time it happens, they will automatically respond this way.
nodes.why_short: Imagining a specific response in a specific setting links cue to action and makes the event feel more likely, much like forming an if-then plan.
nodes.principle_note: Explicitly imagining a specific response in a specific future context increases the likelihood of that response by forming a cue-response association and by raising the subjective probability of the event (imagined scenarios feel more likely once simulated). Naming the triggering situation supplies a concrete retrieval cue, which is why 'every time X' outperforms an unanchored prediction. It is falsifiable in the ordinary way: the forecast response can simply fail to appear when X occurs.

ex.f: Future-tense barrage with no checkpoints
ex.t: The operator lists change after change, all in the future tense, and never pauses to ask whether any of it is happening yet. Each claim is asserted as already underway before the previous one has been dwelt on, so verification is always deferred to a later self. The listener never gets the beat in which they could check one item against their body — and one thing that does feel slightly different later gets read as confirmation of the whole list.
ex.s: Mid-session; a long declarative run with no pauses, no checks, and no request for feedback.
ex.m: Your hands are getting lighter and they'll keep getting lighter. Your voice is going softer and it will stay softer. You'll find yourself standing differently. You'll notice you take up less room. You'll want less, and you'll be happier wanting less. You'll stop needing to finish sentences. All of it is already underway.

ex.f: The next session's thought scripted in advance
ex.t: The operator forecasts not just that the listener will return but exactly what the return will feel like from the inside — smoother, quicker, easier than this time — and then supplies the sentence that will arrive in their head some ordinary afternoon: a mild, curious wondering about when they can do this again. When that thought duly surfaces days later it presents as the listener's own idle preference, not as something that was written down for them in advance.
ex.s: Closing minutes, before emergence; the subject is being pointed at the next session.
ex.m: The next time will be smoother than this — quicker down, easier, less work for you. And sometime Wednesday afternoon, in the middle of something ordinary, a thought is going to turn up on its own: I wonder when I can do that again. Just a small, curious, pleasant thought. Yours.

ex.f: Imagining slides into predicting
ex.t: The opening asks only for imagination — picture the shop, picture how you would feel walking out. The listener builds the scene willingly, because it is only a game. Then, inside the same paragraph and without any marker, the grammar changes: what you might feel becomes what you will feel, and the operator confirms it as a forecast. The listener's own vivid rehearsal, produced with defences down, is handed back to them as evidence of what they are going to do.
ex.s: Early in the session; the subject has been asked only to imagine a scene and is building it willingly.
ex.m: Picture the shop — the doorway, the light inside, the shelf you'd go to first. Imagine how it might feel to walk out of there with it in your bag. Feel how easy that is. And that's how it will feel, Thursday, when you're actually standing there. That's your own answer, not mine — you just showed it to me.

nodes.name: inner-voice-medium-colonization
nodes.mech: Instead of planting a particular thought, the operator changes how thoughts sound: the listener's inner voice is said to be a different voice now (soft, girly, slutty, giggling, automatic). Every later thought, whatever it is about, comes through that voice and signals that the new identity is doing the thinking. This takes away silent inner speech as a private place to retreat to. It is sealed with a dare ('no matter how hard you try'): checking whether a thought is in the new voice means listening to the inner voice, which brings the new voice to mind and seems to confirm it.
nodes.one_liner: Tell them their inner voice now sounds different (softer, giggly) and dare them to try thinking in their old voice.
nodes.why_short: Checking for the new voice means imagining it, so checking produces it; the 'try and you can't' dare turns every check into confirmation.
nodes.principle_note: Attempts to monitor whether an intrusive quality is present require activating a representation of that quality, so checking tends to produce the very experience being checked for; the built-in 'no matter how hard you try' clause converts any monitoring into apparent confirmation. That self-sealing structure is precisely what makes this notably weaker as an evidential claim than it feels to the subject — the confirmation carries no information. The claim that inner speech has a fixed audible register that can be globally reassigned is itself unestablished; treat the durable-recoloring part as speculative.

ex.f: The inner monologue's voice replaced
ex.t: The operator does not supply a thought to think. Instead the register of thinking itself is reassigned: from now on, whatever crosses the listener's mind arrives sounding like someone else's voice rather than their own. And the clincher — however much effort goes into thinking in the old voice, the result comes out in the new one anyway. That last clause turns the only available test into a confirmation, because checking which voice a thought is in requires listening to the inner voice, and the listener has just been told what they will hear. Subvocal speech, the one channel that was never shared, stops being somewhere to retreat to.
ex.s: Identity install, deep trance; no specific thought is being supplied — only the register of thinking.
ex.m: Listen to the voice you think in. From now on that isn't yours — it's higher, softer, sillier, and it giggles at the end of things. Every thought you have arrives in it, whatever the thought is about. And go on, try to think one in your old voice. However hard you try, it comes out in hers. Check it and you'll hear her.

nodes.name: lexical-relay-semantic-lattice
nodes.mech: A predicate ending one line becomes the subject opening the next, handing a term forward like a bucket-brigade relay ("deeper" to "dumber" to "deeper"; "drop" to "drip" to "drop"), so a new equivalence is smuggled in one harmless handoff at a time. Across the chain this builds a closed cross-substitutable semantic lattice in which depth, stupidity, dripping and arousal all become substitutable nodes; once installed, triggering any single node later re-activates the whole conditioned cluster, so one cue fires the entire state.
nodes.one_liner: Chain lines so each ends on a word the next begins with (sink, soft, warm, sink) until the words all mean the same feeling.
nodes.why_short: Words presented together become associated, and chained pairs spread association along the chain; each tiny step is too small to object to.
nodes.principle_note: Repeatedly presenting two terms in immediate succession builds an associative link, and chained overlap lets association spread transitively so distant terms in the chain come to co-activate. Each handoff is individually small enough to pass without objection, which is a persuasion property rather than a memory one. Testable prediction: after the chain, presenting one node should speed or evoke responses to the others relative to unchained controls, and the effect should weaken if the pairs are presented out of order.

ex.f: Each line hands its last word to the next
ex.t: The listener repeats a chain in which the word that closed one line opens the next: sinking leads to softness, softness leads to warmth, warmth leads to sinking. Every individual handoff is a small, agreeable step, and no line ever asserts the big claim outright. But after the full circuit the terms have become interchangeable, and later on the operator only has to say one of them — any one — to bring the whole set back at once.
ex.s: Repetition drill, subject repeating aloud or subvocally after the operator; the chain must be delivered in order.
ex.m: Say them after me, in order. Sinking makes you soft. Soft makes you warm. Warm makes you sink. Sinking makes you soft. Again — and don't skip one, each word hands you the next.

nodes.name: manufactured-insufficiency-ratchet
nodes.mech: Just as the subject would reach 'enough', the operator raises the bar and uses their wish for approval so each attempt must beat the last. Satisfaction never arrives, effort and arousal keep climbing, and the habit carries over. One form: right after a likely success, mild disappointment ('you could have tried a little bit harder') and a push past the last attempt. Another: a depth 'pop quiz' where a cue is fired and the result is always declared not deep enough. Since depth is subjective, the test can't be passed; it also makes depth the listener's responsibility and casts the operator as judge, with a standing excuse to punish.
nodes.one_liner: Right when they succeed, say it wasn't quite enough and ask for more next time; or grade their depth and always find it lacking.
nodes.why_short: If approval is wanted and the bar keeps moving, satisfaction never arrives, so effort keeps climbing. A test that cannot be passed also casts you as the judge.
nodes.principle_note: Reward that arrives on completion produces satiation and stops driving effort; withholding the verdict of sufficiency keeps the goal unclosed, and unresolved goals retain motivational pull. Because the standard is subjective and controlled by the evaluator, no performance can close it, so effort persists while the evaluator accrues the authority that comes from being the sole arbiter. The falsifiable edge: chronically unattainable standards typically produce disengagement rather than escalation once perceived attainability drops far enough, so the ratchet should fail in subjects who conclude the standard is rigged.

ex.f: Dissatisfaction introduced at the point of success
ex.t: The listener completes the task and, in the moment they would normally feel they did well, the operator sounds mildly unimpressed: that was fine, but you had a bit more in you, didn't you? The next round is then aimed past the one just finished. The tone stays gentle enough that nothing feels like punishment, which is what lets it repeat — each time the listener reaches the standard, the standard has already moved, so approval stays one attempt away indefinitely.
ex.s: Immediately after the subject completes a task they performed well; the moment they would otherwise register success.
ex.m: Mm. That was fine. You had a little more in you than that though, didn't you. Let's go again — and this time I want past where you just got to, not back to it. I know you can. Show me.

nodes.name: massed-practice-rate-suppression
nodes.mech: The subject deliberately over-emits the undesired behavior far beyond any functional occasion (a compulsive checker performs the full 13-step ritual five times for every real check), attaching an effortful or aversive cost — satiation or response-cost, left unstated — so its future rate declines. A counterintuitive increase-emission-to-reduce-rate move.
nodes.one_liner: Make them repeat the unwanted habit far more than needed, on purpose, until it becomes tedious.
nodes.why_short: Effortful over-repetition makes the behavior costly and satiating, lowering its later rate; results are mixed and it can backfire for habits that strengthen with practice.
nodes.principle_note: Emitting a response far beyond its functional occasion, with effort or aversive cost attached, reduces its future rate — the standard accounts are satiation of whatever the response produces and the accumulating response cost of performing it. It is falsifiable and in fact fails in some domains: for behaviours maintained by their own practice effects, massed emission strengthens rather than suppresses, and outcomes for compulsive rituals specifically are mixed compared with exposure-and-prevention.

ex.f: Over-perform the habit to suppress it
ex.t: "Forcing oneself to perform an undesired behavior again and again… will sometimes decrease the future occurrences" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: monotonic-ratchet-one-way-valve
nodes.mech: Set rules so that every success makes the next step stricter, with no way back to an easier level. The tightening often continues without the operator: the listener pushes themselves to stay eligible for the reward. Variations: each repeat of a lasting rule must exceed the last (a longer chastity interval each time, 'twice means go further'); recordings that each point to stricter recordings; a chain of uncheckable claims ('twice as deep', 'you can always go deeper') where each accepted claim raises the starting point for the next.
nodes.one_liner: Set rules so every success makes the next step stricter and there is never a way back to an easier level.
nodes.why_short: Each accepted step becomes the new baseline, so consistency pressure and habituation push forward; with no reachable easier state, there is no natural moment to quit or object.
nodes.principle_note: Each accepted step becomes the new reference point against which the next is judged, so a demand that would have been refused from baseline reads as a small increment from the current position — and having complied, the subject already has a self-consistent reason to comply again. Removing any reachable easier state means no comparison ever supplies evidence that the sequence has gone too far, and the epistemic variant works because unverifiable claims give the subject no baseline against which to register the shift. Falsifiable: if subjects are shown the endpoint against their original baseline, refusal rates should rise sharply.

ex.f: Every step makes the next step stricter
ex.t: Look at what each rule in the session does on its second use rather than its first. The abstinence interval must be longer than the one before it. Completing the session sends the listener to further sessions, each carrying rules of the same shape. Succeeding at the drill twice in a row means going further in the same direction, never repeating at the same setting. Nowhere in the whole design is there a reachable position, however compliant, from which the next demand comes out smaller than the last — and because the tightening is written into the rules themselves, the operator does not have to be present for it to continue. Staying eligible is what makes the subject keep turning the screw on themselves.
ex.s: Rules segment, subject already compliant with a first round; the durable elements (interval, drill, follow-on listening) are being restated as standing terms.
ex.m: From now on, every lock is longer than the last one — if you held four days, the next is five, and there is no version of this where you go back to four. Each time you finish this recording cleanly, you queue the next one in the set, and each one in that set asks for a little more than this. And if you manage the drill twice without slipping, you don't get to repeat it at that setting — twice means you move up. That is the only direction the numbers go, whether I am here or not.

nodes.name: pseudo-orientation-in-time
nodes.mech: The subject is taken into a future where the current problem is already solved. The operator speaks of it in the past tense, as something that already happened, and asks the subject to remember the solution rather than hope for one, claiming to have forgotten the details and asking them to describe what they did. Assuming the solution exists and that the subject came up with it helps them produce new, workable ideas past the stuck 'I can't think of anything' point, while their expectations point at an outcome already achieved.
nodes.one_liner: In trance, send them to a future where the problem is solved and ask them to remember how they solved it.
nodes.why_short: Erickson's technique: imagining success as already past can surface ideas and raise expectation. Case reports only.
nodes.principle_note: Retrieval framing changes what is produced: asking someone to recall what they did recruits generation of concrete, self-authored, plausible content, whereas asking them to invent a solution invites the same evaluative filtering that produced the impasse. Presupposition also does work — the solution's existence is embedded in the question rather than asserted, so it is not the proposition under scrutiny. The claim is falsifiable and modest: past-tense recall framing should yield more and more specific solution content than hypothetical framing, with no implication that the retrieved plan is a genuine memory.
steps: Take them into deep trance.
Orient them to a future where it is solved.
Speak of the solution as already done.
Ask them to recall and describe what they did.
Optional (Erickson's form): amnesia for the session.

ex.f: Asking the client what the cure was
ex.t: "Will you recall for me exactly what you consider the most essential thing that I did which changed you?" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

ex.f: Recalling the solution you have not found yet
ex.t: "induce a deep trance and use a technique called 'pseudo-orientation in time'… 'Would you describe in detail what you did?'" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: rehearsed-pre-commitment
nodes.mech: A future contested act is rehearsed in detail and consented to upstream, while the listener's judgment is intact, so the decision arrives already made at the moment deliberation is stripped. Realized as explicit teaching plus honor-framing of an aversive motor routine (the withdrawal is banked before arousal peaks and runs on cue with no live decision), and as experiential inhabitation of a fantasized future state that pre-validates a protocol before it is requested.
nodes.one_liner: Before arousal or trance peaks, rehearse the hard step and get real agreement, so it runs on cue later without a decision.
nodes.why_short: People in a calm state underestimate how arousal will change them; deciding and rehearsing beforehand turns a hot choice into a cued routine backed by their own promise.
nodes.principle_note: Decisions made in a cool, low-arousal state are systematically different from those made in a hot state, and people underestimate how much arousal will shift their preferences. Committing and rehearsing the routine in advance converts a live deliberative choice into cue-driven execution of a pre-formed plan, and having given genuine consent adds consistency pressure at the moment of execution. It predicts that pre-committed subjects follow through at higher rates than equally-willing subjects who decide in the moment — and that the advantage shrinks as the rehearsal-to-execution cue match degrades.

ex.f: Inhabiting the future self who already agreed
ex.t: The listener is invited to imagine, in detail, the body of someone who has already gone months under the restriction being contemplated — how starved the nerves would be, how much a small touch would register. They inhabit that state vividly for several minutes before the restriction has been asked for at all. By the time the actual assignment is stated, the listener is not evaluating a proposal; they are agreeing to something they have already felt themselves wanting.
ex.s: Mid-session, good depth, subject responsive to imagery; the restriction has not been named or requested yet.
ex.m: Put yourself three months forward. Feel that body — every nerve on the surface starved, the seam of your clothes registering like a hand, your pulse audible in your ears when someone stands close. You have gone ninety days untouched and your skin has become one enormous ear listening for contact. Stay in that body. Breathe in it. Feel how much you want it, before anyone asks you for anything.

ex.f: The hard part taught and agreed before it hurts
ex.t: Rather than springing the unpleasant instruction at the moment it has to be carried out, the operator stops early and teaches it as a procedure: here is how the build works, here is the exact point at which your hands come away, here is what you will feel afterwards. The listener rehearses the movement mentally while they are still calm enough to weigh it, and the operator frames agreeing to it as something granted rather than demanded. When the moment finally arrives, arousal has removed the listener's capacity to deliberate — but there is nothing left to deliberate about, because the decision was banked half an hour earlier.
ex.s: Early session, subject calm and clear-headed, arousal not yet built; the aversive instruction will be needed much later.
ex.m: Before we start anything, I want to teach you the hard part while you can still think about it. Later, when your breath goes ragged and your hips start to lift on their own, your hands come away from yourself and rest flat on your thighs — that exact moment, no negotiation, because there will be no one home to negotiate with. It will ache, and the ache is the proof. I'm not ordering you to do it; I'm asking you to agree to it now, and you telling me yes right now is a gift you're giving me, not an obedience I took.

nodes.name: self-efficacy-tag
nodes.mech: Installs a belief about the subject's own future capability to re-access the trance state with increasing ease — a forward-directed suggestion framing return as a self-owned ability ("you can return whenever you wish"), emphasizing "can" over "must" so the subject, not the operator, holds the key to re-entry.
nodes.one_liner: Tell them they found the way down themselves and can return whenever they choose, easier each time.
nodes.why_short: Hypnotic response tracks expectancy; believing re-entry is their own skill raises the expectation of success and reduces anxious self-monitoring.
nodes.principle_note: Believing one is capable of producing a state raises the likelihood of producing it, both by reducing effortful monitoring for failure and via straightforward expectancy — and hypnotic responding in particular tracks expectancy and attitude toward the state more strongly than any trait-like susceptibility measure. Attributing the capability to the subject rather than the operator also engages self-perception: acting on the suggestion becomes evidence of one's own ability. Falsifiable: re-entry latency should be lower in subjects given the capability framing than in matched subjects given a neutral or operator-owned framing.

ex.f: Re-entry framed as the subject's own growing ability
ex.t: Framing re-access as a skill the subject owns builds a capability belief that survives the operator's absence and makes the next induction faster by expectancy alone. The operator observes shortened induction times on subsequent sessions and, in self-practice reports, subjects entering state without any operator input.
ex.s: During the emergence sequence, after the main suggestion block and before the count-up completes.
ex.m: You found your way down here yourself tonight, and you can find it again whenever you want to — sit down, close your eyes, take three slow breaths, and you'll be right back at this depth. It gets easier every time you do it, because you're the one who knows the way now. Not because you have to. Because you can.

nodes.name: self-observation-instrumentation
nodes.mech: Train the person to record their own behaviour accurately. Give the reward only when their own count matches an independent count, so honest reporting, not performance, is what gets rewarded. Then show the goal as a shaded band on a chart, so 'am I doing well enough?' becomes the simpler question 'is my dot inside the band?'
nodes.one_liner: Reward them only when their own count of their behavior matches yours, and show the target as a band on a chart.
nodes.why_short: Rewarding the score invites inflating it; rewarding agreement with an independent count makes honest reporting the thing that pays. A visual band makes self-judging easy.
nodes.principle_note: Behaviour follows the contingency actually in force, so making the reward depend on agreement between self-report and an independent count reinforces accuracy rather than performance — misreporting stops paying. The graphical band works by replacing a judgment (is this good enough?) with a perceptual discrimination (is the dot inside the shaded region?), which is faster and less variable across occasions. Falsifiable in an obvious way: if the independent check is removed or becomes predictable, reported scores should drift upward relative to actual performance.

ex.f: The standard drawn as a band on the graph
ex.t: "chart self-recorded data on a graph that showed the competitive standard with a shaded area"; "I'm not in the shaded area. I need to work faster." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Reward gated on agreement, not performance
ex.t: "If Brad's self-recorded data agreed with the teacher at a level of 80% or higher, he received his choice from a menu" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: split-self-unfalsifiability
nodes.mech: Tell the listener that their everyday self may feel unchanged, notice nothing, or forget, and that this is expected and fine, because the real change lives in a deeper part of the mind they cannot reach. That way any honest report ('I still feel like myself', 'nothing happened', 'I forgot') is already counted as confirmation, and the claim can never be checked or disproved from the inside.
nodes.one_liner: Say their everyday self will feel unchanged and that's expected, because the change lives in a deeper part they can't check.
nodes.why_short: Every possible report, including 'nothing changed', is pre-counted as confirmation, so the claim cannot be disproved by introspection and people rarely notice that.
nodes.principle_note: Pre-committing every possible self-report to the same conclusion removes the disconfirmation channel a person would normally use to check a claim, and people rarely notice that an explanation covering all outcomes has no evidential content — this is the same structure that sustains belief in unfalsifiable systems generally. It is reinforced by the fact that introspective access to one's own cognitive processes is genuinely poor, so "you cannot check this from the inside" is locally true enough to feel credible. Prediction that could fail: subjects given an explicit falsification criterion beforehand ("if X, the install did not take") should report the claim as less credible than subjects given the all-outcomes-confirm framing.

ex.f: Forgetting pre-explained as the deep part remembering
ex.t: Late in the session the operator stops addressing the listener as one person and starts addressing layers — telling them that the thinking part may well lose all of this, while a part further down keeps it. Every possible aftermath is now pre-assigned: remembering proves it took, forgetting proves it went deep enough to bypass the part that would have interfered.
ex.s: Late session, immediately before closing; subject deep, install already delivered.
ex.m: I'm not talking to you as one person anymore. The thinking part of you may lose every word of this by morning — it might keep nothing at all. The part further down keeps all of it. So if you wake and remember, that means it took hold. And if you wake with a blank where this hour was, that means it went past the part that would have interfered. There is no version where it didn't land.

ex.f: Awake on the surface, owned underneath
ex.t: The operator confirms out loud that the listener is fully awake now — and in the same breath states that underneath, something is still listening and still under instruction. Two selves are now on the table: anything the listener does freely belongs to the one that is awake, anything compliant belongs to the one that is owned. Reporting that one feels entirely ordinary stops being a defence, because it is a report from the self that was never the one in question.
ex.s: Emergence, subject just counted up, eyes open, alert.
ex.m: You're wide awake now. Fully alert, fully yourself, back in the room — and underneath that, something is still listening to me and still holding what I said. Anything you do freely today belongs to the awake one. Anything you do because I told you belongs to the other one. So when you tell yourself you feel completely ordinary, remember which of the two of you is talking.

ex.f: The surface self allowed to feel unchanged
ex.t: The operator concedes the obvious objection before the listener can raise it: the everyday mind will go on behaving like itself, with its own opinions and habits, and that is entirely fine. What has been changed sits underneath that, where the everyday mind cannot look. A listener who later notices that they feel entirely ordinary finds that observation already accounted for — it was named in advance as exactly what the surface was expected to report, so the report can never count as evidence against anything.
ex.s: Mid-session, install content about to be delivered; subject deep but not amnesic.
ex.m: Your everyday mind is going to stay exactly as it is — same opinions, same stubbornness, same taste in arguments — and that is correct. That is not the part I am talking to. What I am putting in goes underneath, where the thinking part has no window. So when you're back at your desk on Thursday and you notice you feel completely normal, completely yourself, nothing changed — that is precisely what the surface is supposed to report.

nodes.name: ubiquity-cued-covert-ratchet
nodes.mech: Make an unavoidable everyday social cue, like a simple hello, the unspoken starting point for a rising urge, without ever calling it a trigger. Because it is never named, each spike feels like the listener's own desire. Pair it with a fixed ladder of small commitments, from least to most, so each step sets a precedent for the next; a recited list of earlier steps refreshes them; and the repeating pattern invites the listener to keep climbing past the script's end.
nodes.one_liner: Make an everyday greeting the unspoken cue for a rising urge, and climb a ladder of small commitments with each one.
nodes.why_short: An unlabeled cue produces urges that feel self-generated. Small then larger commitments shift self-image step by step, and reciting earlier steps renews consistency pressure.
nodes.principle_note: Two mechanisms stack. A cue that is never labelled as a cue produces responses the subject cannot attribute to the cue, so the arousal or urge gets misattributed to endogenous preference — the standard source-monitoring failure that makes covert conditioning feel like one's own taste. The ordered ladder then exploits foot-in-the-door: each small accepted item shifts self-perception ("I am someone who does this"), and the recital of prior items refreshes the consistency pressure against lapse. Falsifiable: naming the cue explicitly beforehand should sharply reduce the felt-endogenous quality, and scrambling the least-to-most order should reduce acceptance of the terminal items.

ex.f: An everyday greeting wired as the escalation cue
ex.t: The session rehearses an ordinary few days ahead. Someone greets the listener in passing, and in that moment a wish arrives for the first small item on a list. The greeting is never called a trigger — it is simply narrated as the thing that happens just before the wanting, so the listener has no reason to connect the two and no way to avoid an everyday courtesy. The list runs in a fixed order from the least committing thing to the most, and after each addition the operator recites the running tally so far, keeping the earlier items live. By the time the demanding ones arrive, half a dozen prior yeses stand behind them, and the pattern is regular enough that the listener could keep extending it after the recording ends.
ex.s: Future-pacing segment; subject deep, comfortable with imagined near-future scenes; the item ladder has been drafted least-to-most committing.
ex.m: Picture Tuesday morning. Someone passes you in the corridor and says hey — and right then, in that half-second after, you find you want to wear the collar under your shirt. Wednesday, someone says hey at the coffee machine, and you want the collar, and you want to keep the plug in for the whole commute. Thursday: hey — collar, plug, and you want to text me the photo before you leave the house. Say the whole list back to me each time it grows, from the first thing to the newest thing, and keep adding to it after this recording ends.

nodes.name: autoclitic-training
nodes.mech: Teach someone to add phrases that comment on, qualify or steer their own speech ('I think', 'listen to this', 'that was SO big'). The hard part is that the thing being commented on is the person's own brief words, so timing matters. Variations: create a situation where they need the listener's attention, model the phrase, prompt it, then fade the prompt; teach them to respond to something they themselves just said; catch a qualifier they already use and reward that word specifically, not the whole sentence.
nodes.one_liner: Teach someone to add phrases that comment on or qualify their own speech, by setting up a need, modeling it, prompting, then fading.
nodes.why_short: Standard verbal-behavior training: create the motivation, show the form, reinforce it when it appears, and withdraw help gradually so it becomes spontaneous.
nodes.principle_note: Verbal behaviour is shaped by its consequences like any other operant, and reinforcement is most effective when it is contingent on the specific response component and delivered immediately — which is exactly why the in-vivo capture variant reinforces the modifier alone rather than the whole utterance. The difficulty is a real one about stimulus control: the controlling stimulus is the speaker's own just-emitted covert speech, which is transient and inaccessible to the trainer, so a supplemental prompt supplies discriminative control until the natural motivating condition can take over. Falsifiable: reinforcing the whole utterance rather than the modifier component should yield slower acquisition of the modifier specifically.

ex.f: When motivation alone fails, prompt then fade
ex.t: "The first condition consisted of contriving the EO alone, which was ineffective... the second condition involving the contrived MO plus an indirect supplemental verbal prompt resulted in successful manding" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Contrive the motivation, then model the form
ex.t: "Teaching autoclitic mands involves capturing or creating the relevant MOs and using ABA teaching procedures"; "a louder voice or a certain phrase may function as an autoclitic mand to prompt a listener to attend better" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: coercion-as-caregiving-reframe
nodes.mech: Every physical restriction or coercive fact (strapping to a bed, gas mask, cuffs, bound hands) is introduced and immediately reframed as protective caregiving ("for your safety", "to keep you comfortable"), with the imposition and its benevolent rationale narrated in the same breath. By never letting the coercive fact stand unframed, the listener's interpretive frame for involuntariness flips from threat to comfort; the body's alarm response is starved of a coherent threat-narrative to attach to, so helplessness reads as being-cared-for.
nodes.one_liner: Introduce each restraint and, in the same sentence, explain it as care: 'so you can rest', 'so you don't hurt yourself.'
nodes.why_short: How a bodily state feels depends on how it is labeled; a caring explanation given at the moment of restriction steers the reading away from threat.
nodes.principle_note: Emotional experience depends on how an ambiguous bodily state is labelled and appraised, so supplying a benevolent interpretation alongside the restriction makes the same sensation more likely to be read as care than as threat. The basis should be appraisal and labelling, not misattribution of arousal — nothing here transfers arousal from a hidden source. Falsifiable: delaying the caregiving frame until after the restriction is felt should produce more alarm and less comfort-reading; note that this predicts an effect of order, not that first appraisals are generally irreversible.

ex.f: Each restraint narrated as care in the same breath
ex.t: No restriction is ever stated on its own. A limb is secured — because we need you to stay still and rest. Something is fastened across the body — so you cannot come to harm again. A piece of equipment is fitted — it will keep you comfortable while we work. Each coercive fact arrives already wrapped in its reason, so the listener never gets the unframed second in which alarm could take hold. The body registers that it cannot move, finds only a caretaking story to attach that to, and files being held down as being looked after.
ex.s: Restraint-scene narration; subject in trance, receptive to sensory description, each restraint being applied in sequence.
ex.m: I'm bringing your right wrist up to the rail and buckling it there — because you need to stay still and let yourself rest. Now the strap across your hips, snug, so you can't roll off and hurt yourself again. And this last piece over your nose and mouth, sealing warm against your face; it'll keep your breathing easy while we work. Nothing to hold up, nothing to manage. I've taken care of all of it.

nodes.name: cost-to-virtue-valence-flip
nodes.mech: Take something the person already sees as a flaw, cost or problem and give it a new meaning, so it loses its sting or becomes something they embrace. Variations: recast an embarrassing admission (being wrong, relying on shortcuts) as a virtue tied to an identity they want ('the mark of a true scientist'); place the complained-about behaviour inside something they value (a child's defiance as the independence the parent hopes for), using a leading question; split a conflict into 'what I meant' and 'what you heard', so a clash of wills becomes a fixable misunderstanding.
nodes.one_liner: Take something they already see as a flaw or cost and relabel it as a virtue or a misunderstanding.
nodes.why_short: Feelings about a fact depend on its meaning; a new frame, especially one tied to an identity they want, changes the charge without changing the fact.
nodes.principle_note: Preference and affect track the frame an object is presented in more than the object's fixed properties, so relabelling meaning changes evaluation without changing facts — the core finding of framing research and of cognitive reappraisal, which reliably lowers negative affect. The virtue-flip variant adds self-consistency pressure: once accepting the relabel is identity-affirming, rejecting it costs self-concept, which is more expensive than accepting. Falsifiable: if reappraisal worked purely by distraction, an equally distracting irrelevant statement would work as well; it does not.

ex.f: Concede the objection, then flip its valence
ex.t: "They are the most popular prompts precisely because they are the most reliable ones"; "there is nothing inherently wrong with the shortcut approach" — Cialdini (1984), Influence

ex.f: A costly admission relabelled as a virtue
ex.t: "new findings are not problems; they are opportunities for further investigation and expanded understanding" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: removal-from-reinforcement-timeout
nodes.mech: Discourage a behaviour by cutting off access to rewards for a short time whenever it happens, while the person stays present (time-out), rather than fining them or adding something unpleasant. It only works if ordinary time is rich in rewards, so losing them hurts. Keep it short, apply it every time, and end it only after a stretch without the behaviour. Plan from the start to replace it with rewarding alternatives. Variations: ignore the behaviour or remove one specific reward; let them watch others earn what they cannot; take an item away briefly and return it after the wanted response; allow the behaviour only in a dull, inconvenient place.
nodes.one_liner: When the behavior happens, cut off access to rewards for a short time while they stay in the room.
nodes.why_short: Losing access to good things after a behavior makes it less likely; it works only when ordinary time is rewarding enough that the loss stings.
nodes.principle_note: Removing access to reinforcement contingent on a response lowers that response's future frequency — negative punishment, one of the better-replicated operant relations. Everything else in the design follows from the fact that punishment strength is relative, not absolute: the procedure only bites if the time-in environment is richer than the time-out one, which is why an impoverished baseline nullifies it, and why release must be gated on absence of the behaviour or the exit itself becomes the reinforcer for the behaviour that got the subject removed. Falsifiable and in fact tested: equalize the richness of time-in and time-out and suppression should disappear.

ex.f: Watching others earn while barred from earning
ex.t: "planned ignoring, terminate specific reinforcer contact, contingent observation, and partition/select space time-out"; "repositioning occurs so that observations of ongoing activity continue, but without reinforcement" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: illusory-choice-authorship
nodes.mech: Make going along feel like the listener's own decision, so there is nothing to resist. Variations: offer choices that all lead to the same outcome and praise the pick ('wise choice'), so they choose only how, never whether; give them a three-step task (want it, expect it, watch it happen) so whatever happens feels self-produced; credit their continuing to an inner pull and a 'secret about you' that going deeper will reveal, so obeying feels like curiosity rather than submission.
nodes.one_liner: Offer choices that all lead where you want, then praise their pick, so going along feels like their own decision.
nodes.why_short: Feeling you chose raises commitment and lowers resistance, and people rarely check whether the options actually differed.
nodes.principle_note: People infer their own attitudes and motives from observing their behaviour and the apparent absence of external pressure, so an act that appears self-chosen is internalized while an identical act attributed to coercion is not — the insufficient-justification result underlying self-perception and dissonance work. Relocating agency also removes the target of reactance: resistance is aimed at a perceived constrainer, and a subject who cannot locate one has nothing to push against. Falsifiable: making the convergent structure of the choice visible ("both options lead to the same place") should collapse the felt authorship and restore resistance.

ex.f: Both turns approved as the wise choice
ex.t: At the end of the corridor the listener is told to pick a door — left or right — and given a pause long enough to genuinely decide. Whatever they picked, the next line congratulates them on choosing well, and the narration continues down a single path that was never going to branch. The listener has just exercised judgement and had it approved, which makes the next instruction easier to take; they have no way to notice that the corridor only ever had one continuation.
ex.s: Deepener; subject following a corridor visualization, responsive to imagery.
ex.m: At the end of the corridor there are two doors, one on your left and one on your right. Choose one now. [pause, four seconds] Wise choice — I thought you'd pick that one. Push it open and step through, and the stairs on the other side go down.

nodes.name: imagined-is-real-licensing-rule
nodes.mech: Early on, state a general rule of the form 'the deeper the trance, the more X becomes possible or true', presented as a plain fact about how minds work so it is accepted rather than obeyed. This lowers the bar before the content that depends on it arrives. One form: 'the deeper you go, the more the mind experiences the imagined as real' makes the operator's later imagery feel like real experience. Another credits depth with lifting a limit ('because you're so deep you can expand your limits to feel more pleasure'), recasting the listener's own protective restraint as the thing in the way.
nodes.one_liner: Early on, state as a plain fact that the deeper they go, the more imagined things feel real or limits fall away.
nodes.why_short: Stated as how trance works rather than as a command, it is accepted rather than resisted, and raises expectancy for the experiences that follow.
nodes.principle_note: Expectancy is one of the best-demonstrated drivers of hypnotic response: people told an effect is a normal part of trance report it more than people who weren't told. Presenting the rule as a neutral fact about how minds work, rather than as an instruction, matters because people judge factual claims by whether they sound plausible, not by whether to comply, and a plausible general rule gets less scrutiny than a direct demand. The specific suggestions that follow then borrow their authority from a premise already accepted. This could be tested: delivering the same suggestions without the earlier general rule should produce less vivid experiences or lower reported limits.

ex.f: Depth licenses the imagined to count as real
ex.t: Early on, before anything worth resisting has been described, the operator drops in a general remark about how the process works: past a certain point the mind stops sharply separating what it pictures from what it takes in. It is offered as information, not as an instruction, so there is nothing to comply with or refuse; the listener simply accepts it as true. A small test sensation is named and duly reported as getting stronger, which counts as proof of the rule. Everything the operator describes from then on arrives already set up to be felt rather than merely pictured.
ex.s: Early, just past induction; subject relaxed, no payload imagery delivered yet.
ex.m: Here's a thing about trance that people forget.
