The deeper you go, the less your mind bothers to separate what it pictures from what it takes in — past a certain point it just stops keeping them in different drawers. That's not something I'm doing to you, it's simply how the machinery runs. So: put your tongue against something cold and metallic. Feel it get colder the longer you hold it. Notice that it got more definite, not less — that's the mechanism doing its job.

nodes.name: contingency-discriminability-design
nodes.mech: Decide whether the person can tell which actions get rewarded. Make it unpredictable to keep them behaving the wanted way everywhere: random rewards (dice, raffles) across many settings so no moment is safely 'off'; rewards after an uncountable number of responses, which prevents pauses; in groups, keep secret which person or behaviour counts until afterwards. Or make it obvious so the behaviour attaches to the act rather than to guesswork: define it with clear examples and non-examples, post the rules where they stay visible, and give a reminder near the end. Variations: reward less often before a test so they cannot tell practice from test.
nodes.one_liner: Choose whether they can tell which actions get rewarded: make it unpredictable to keep them responding everywhere, or obvious to teach fast.
nodes.why_short: Unpredictable (variable) reward schedules produce steady, persistent responding; clear contingencies speed learning. Detectability is the dial.
nodes.principle_note: Variable-ratio schedules, where rewards come after an unpredictable number of responses, produce steady, high-rate responding and strong resistance to extinction. Fixed schedules produce a pause after each reward, and that pause comes from the fixed requirement itself, not from the person counting. The transparent option works by a different route: clearly marked cues and stated rules reduce ambiguity, so behaviour is guided by the act rather than by guesswork. This could be tested: switching from a variable to a fixed ratio at the same reward rate should introduce pauses after rewards, which separates this explanation from the simpler idea that randomness is exciting.

ex.f: A game device decides what pays off
ex.t: "a game-like procedure for randomly determining which green behaviors, emitted where and when, will earn what rewards" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Spread the payoff so no instance is safe to skip
ex.t: "When you can't tell which of several green behaviors performed exactly where or when will produce a reward, the best strategy… is acting green in every way, everywhere, all the time" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: protective-role-conscription
nodes.mech: The listener is assigned a non-trancer in-fiction identity (a new guard outside the cell) talked at by a chained, weak, distant captive; hypnotic content then lands while the listener wears a "not the one being hypnotized" costume. Resistance-monitoring is routed onto the fictional protective character, so movement toward danger reads as story-progression not escalation; the frame's safety is illusory by design, and a later chains-fake reveal retroactively recodes every "safe" earlier moment as already inside the trap.
nodes.one_liner: Cast the listener as a guard watching a weak captive, so the trance content lands while they think they're safe; later reveal they weren't.
nodes.why_short: Casting yourself as an onlooker lowers personal threat monitoring; the reveal reinterprets earlier 'safe' moments, which memory tends to rewrite.
nodes.principle_note: Monitoring for personal threat is triggered by construing oneself as the target; assigning a bystander role redirects that monitoring onto a fictional other, so the suggestions arrive without the scrutiny normally applied to a direct address. The later reveal exploits hindsight-style retroactive reconstruction — new information about the situation rewrites memory of how safe the earlier moments felt, so the subject cannot recover the original sense of having been outside the frame. Falsifiable: subjects given the bystander role should show lower rates of explicit challenge to the same suggestion than subjects addressed directly.

ex.f: A bystander role worn as a costume
ex.t: The opening minute never addresses the listener as a subject at all: it casts them as the one standing watch, on the safe side of the bars, while a restrained and obviously weaker speaker pleads to be heard from across the room. Every request that follows is a story beat rather than an instruction — step nearer, look this way, just listen — so the listener's guard is mounted on behalf of a character they are playing instead of on their own behalf. Suggestion lands the whole time, because the costume says the person being worked on is somebody else. Near the end the restraints are revealed to have been decorative, and the safety they supplied was never real; retroactively, every earlier moment the listener spent feeling like the guard was already a moment spent inside the trap.
ex.s: Opening minute, before any induction language; the listener has not yet been addressed as a subject.
ex.m: You're the new one on the night watch, and you're on the safe side of the bars. The thing in the cell is chained at the wrist and the ankle and can barely lift its head — you can hear how thin the voice is. It's asking you to come one step closer so it doesn't have to shout. Just one. You're not doing anything, you're just listening to it talk.

nodes.name: scaffold-fade-control-transfer
nodes.mech: Add a temporary helper that reliably produces the right response, such as an instruction, a demonstration or hand guidance, then remove it gradually so the natural cue alone comes to produce it, with few mistakes. The helper must actually be removed, or the person comes to depend on it. Variations: start with full assistance and step it down; start with a light hint and add help only if needed; exaggerate the target cue and slowly fade it to normal; wait a little longer before each prompt so they answer first; taper a support (tokens, dense rewards) on a planned schedule; model a word, reward the copy, then fade the model.
nodes.one_liner: Add a helper (instruction, demonstration, hand guidance) that gets the right response, then remove it gradually until the natural cue alone works.
nodes.why_short: Gradual withdrawal transfers control from the prompt to the real cue with few errors; removing it abruptly or never removing it leaves dependence on the prompt.
nodes.principle_note: A response reliably occasioned by an added prompt does not thereby come under control of the natural cue; control transfers only if the prompt is attenuated gradually enough that the response continues to occur and be reinforced in the prompt's near-absence. Fading works because the learner never experiences the error, and the extinction of the prompt's discriminative function is gradual rather than abrupt. The failure mode is a direct prediction of the same account: leaving the support in place means the support retains stimulus control, which is exactly what prompt dependence is. Falsifiable: an abrupt withdrawal should produce more errors and lower retention than a graded one, holding total training constant.

ex.f: Add a prompt that evokes the response, then fade it
ex.t: "Prompts are supplementary antecedent stimuli used to occasion a correct response in the presence of the natural SD" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Errorless transfer by superimposing then fading
ex.t: "first superimposing a white vertical line on the green light (SD)... Finally, the amplitude of the red and green lights was reduced gradually until only the vertical and horizontal lines remained" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: ambient-maintenance-reframe
nodes.mech: Before the listener does something that would normally end trance, say in advance that it fits with staying in trance, so the act isn't taken as a signal to wake. In the longer form, trance becomes a lasting background state carried while moving, working or being interrupted, with a real automatic wake-up kept for emergencies. In the one-off form, before asking for a single act like opening the eyes or baring an arm, the operator says nothing done here 'will bother or disturb you' and calls going back to it continuing 'the game', so pain relief or absorption survives the interruption.
nodes.one_liner: Before they open their eyes or move, say that doing so won't disturb the trance, or that trance can run in the background all day.
nodes.why_short: Whether opening eyes ends trance depends on what the person expects it to mean; pre-labeling it as compatible removes the cue to wake.
nodes.principle_note: Whether an event is read as ending a state depends on the interpretive frame available at the moment it occurs, and a frame supplied in advance pre-empts the alternative reading — the subject has no unclaimed interpretive slot in which "my eyes are open, so I must be awake" can form. This is expectancy operating on state attribution rather than on sensation: subjects told an act is compatible with trance report continued absorption more than subjects given no such framing. Falsifiable: withholding the pre-frame until after the disruptive act should produce more reports of the trance having broken.

ex.f: Trance inverted into a background layer
ex.t: The recording opens by cancelling every rule the listener expects: stay standing, keep your eyes open, keep working, keep moving around. Trance is presented not as somewhere you go but as a thin layer you keep running underneath ordinary activity — so getting up, being spoken to, or switching tasks no longer counts as breaking it. A genuine exit is armed alongside it: any real emergency wakes the listener fully and at once, and interruptions can be paused and picked up again.
ex.s: Opening of a maintenance/re-entry recording; subject has prior trance experience and is upright, mobile, likely mid-task.
ex.m: Don't lie down and don't close your eyes. Stay standing, keep the dishes going, keep the window open. This isn't a place you go — it's a thin layer you leave running underneath whatever your hands are doing, so getting up, answering the door, or being talked to doesn't break it and never has. If anything real happens — a smoke alarm, someone needing you — you snap fully awake at once and this drops away completely. Otherwise it stays on in the background, and you can set it down and pick it back up whenever you like.

nodes.name: authority-scope-hardening
nodes.mech: Take authority the operator already has and make it permanent and unchallengeable, so it outlasts the session and closes off ways to question it. Variations: declare the operator beyond objection and waive the listener's right to complain; name other authorities in their life and rank the recording's voice above them; upgrade a one-session effect into a lasting power the operator can use any time; at the extreme, a belief that the operator exists in the world whether or not the listener is listening, tied to an outside reminder symbol.
nodes.one_liner: Declare your authority permanent, beyond objection, and above any other authority in their life.
nodes.why_short: Mostly rhetorical framing; any power comes from consistency pressure once accepted and from fantasy appeal. No tested mechanism makes such clauses stick.
nodes.principle_note: Authority influences compliance most strongly when its legitimacy is treated as settled background rather than as a proposition under discussion, so foreclosing the challenge routes — who may evaluate, what outranks, how long it holds — removes the occasions on which the claim would come up for review. Assertions about scope also escape scrutiny more easily than assertions about the present, because they make no immediately checkable prediction. Falsifiable: explicitly inviting the subject to evaluate the operator's standing should reduce later compliance relative to a condition where the evaluability waiver stands unchallenged.

ex.f: Evaluability axis: objection waived by clause
ex.t: Buried in legalese, one clause declares the operator flawless by definition and therefore beyond any need or possibility of correction, while the listener signs away every present and future ground for complaint. A second clause lets the operator rewrite any term at any time, without reason. The document looks bilateral and is structurally impossible to invoke in one direction: the listener is not merely losing the argument, they have surrendered standing to open one.
ex.s: Contract/agreement segment, read aloud in legalese register; subject already accepts the operator's authority.
ex.m: Clause seven: the operator is held to be without fault in all matters arising, and accordingly no correction, remedy, or amendment may be sought against her by you. Clause eight: you waive, presently and for all future time, any ground of complaint, whether known to you now or discovered later. Clause nine: the operator may alter any term of this agreement at any time, at her discretion, without notice and without stating a reason. Read it back to me.

ex.f: Precedence axis: real-world authorities subordinated
ex.t: The recording names the competition before the listener can: you may already answer to someone in your own home, someone whose word you take seriously. That is set aside in a sentence — whatever they tell you, this voice is the one that trains you. The conditioning is thereby insulated against being overwritten by an actual partner's instructions, and the listener is licensed to keep running it whether or not anyone in their life asked for it.
ex.s: Mid-session, install already accepted; the subject has a real-world partner or authority figure whose instructions could compete.
ex.m: There may already be someone in your house whose word you take — someone you kneel for, someone whose rules you follow. Keep following them. But understand the order of things: they run your evenings, and I run what happens between your ears. Whatever they tell you about this, my voice is the one that trains you, and you run these recordings whether or not anybody asked you to.

ex.f: Persistence axis: an effect upgraded to a standing capability
ex.t: Having gotten the listener to accept that their thinking went quiet a moment ago, the operator stops describing the present and starts describing herself: if it can stop, then stopping it is something she is able to do, at will. Nothing further is asked for. The point of the session, she adds, was only to establish that the capability exists — not to exercise it on this occasion. A listener who could have refused an instruction has no comparable way to refuse a description of what the operator is able to do, and the deferral quietly pre-authorizes the later use.
ex.s: Just after a successful mind-blanking suggestion the subject has acknowledged; no further instruction is being asked for.
ex.m: You felt your thoughts stop a moment ago. Notice what that means about me, not about you: if I can stop them, then stopping them is something I can do, whenever I decide to. I'm not going to do it again tonight. Tonight was only to establish that I can.

nodes.name: cheap-reversible-trial-frame
nodes.mech: When a stance or precondition blocks the procedure — an all-or-nothing behavioral commitment ("I'll never give up X") or a required belief the subject rejects — the operator reframes the ask as a small, explicitly temporary, reversible experiment: a fixed trial window (a "three-month moratorium") during which the disputed behavior is suspended, or a "suspend disbelief / adopt the reverse assumption for a bounded trial period". Because agreeing now no longer means agreeing forever, perceived stakes drop and the blocking precondition stops gating: the deadlock reopens as a space to generate resources, or the procedure proceeds without its precondition belief.
nodes.one_liner: When they refuse something outright, propose trying it only for a fixed, short, reversible period.
nodes.why_short: A temporary trial costs little and threatens no identity, so the objection doesn't fire; once they are doing it, seeing themselves comply softens the attitude.
nodes.principle_note: Resistance to a request scales with its perceived permanence and cost to self-concept, so bounding it in time and declaring it reversible drops the stakes below the threshold at which the identity-defending objection fires. Once the trial is underway, self-perception works in the operator's favour: the subject observes themselves complying without external coercion and infers a correspondingly softened attitude, so the bounded trial often does not revert cleanly. Falsifiable: the same request framed as permanent should draw more refusals than the time-boxed version, and post-trial attitudes should differ from pre-trial ones despite the "nothing is being asked of you long-term" framing.

ex.f: A bounded moratorium replaces an all-or-nothing stance
ex.t: "engage in negotiation to establish a three-month moratorium on sexual activities outside of this relationship during which time he will have a chance to try out some of the new behaviors" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

ex.f: Belief waived in favour of time-boxed pretense
ex.t: "Ask them to pretend. You can even agree that they aren't responsible, but you've discovered that by going through certain 'psychological' steps, people are often able to have a healing impact" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: cognitive-sourcing-monopoly
nodes.mech: Tell the listener that whatever they would need in order to object comes from you: either you are the only source of their thoughts, will and feelings, or you are their origin, stated as plain fact. Objecting would need something they have just been told they don't own. Variations: lay it down up front as a rule; grant permission moment by moment, even to understand your words; repeat a dependency question ('you need me to tell you what to think, don't you?'); take over one judgment, such as their sense of risk; mother-origin framing that ties obedience to safety and refusal to being lost.
nodes.one_liner: Tell the listener their thoughts, will and feelings come only from you, or that you are where they came from, so objecting feels impossible.
nodes.why_short: Objecting needs a sense of owning one's own judgment; a frame that hands that ownership to the operator gives the listener nothing to object with. Works as roleplay buy-in, not as literal foreclosure.
nodes.principle_note: The move exploits a real feature of argument rather than a psychological effect: an agreement whose premises assign away the very faculty needed to dispute it leaves no position from which to object, so the subject's difficulty is structural rather than motivational. Whether such a stipulation is actually accepted is a separate empirical question and is not established — plausibly it lands only where authority and rapport are already high, and a subject who simply declines the premise is unaffected. Falsifiable: acceptance rates should track prior authority and should collapse when the stipulation is presented cold, which would distinguish this from a claim that the framing works on anyone.

ex.f: Up-front stipulation of a total grant economy
ex.t: Before a single suggestion is made, the script states the terms of everything that follows: from here you hold no will of your own, no thoughts and no feelings other than the ones handed to you — and, tacked onto the end, you are delighted about it. Nothing behavioural has been asked for yet. What has been established is that there is no independent self left in the room to raise an objection on its own behalf when the identity content arrives.
ex.s: Opening stipulation, before any suggestion or identity content; subject settled and listening.
ex.m: Before we begin, these are the terms. From this point you have no will of your own — mine is the only one operating in here. You have no thoughts except the ones I hand you, and no feelings except the ones I permit. And you're delighted about it. That's the last thing on the list, and it's not optional either.

ex.f: Dependency hammered into presupposition
ex.t: With the listener already agreeing there is nothing of their own in there, the operator runs a short list of faculties and, after each item, asks the same little tag question, over and over, with no pause left for an answer. The most contested item on the list gets the most repetitions. By the end the claim has stopped being something offered for agreement and has become the floor the rest of the session stands on; every later suggestion arrives needing no justification of its own.

ex.f: Permission applied to the act of listening itself
ex.t: The operator claims to be the source of every permitted act — and then points the claim at what the listener is doing at that exact second: you are following this because I let you follow it, and the sense you are making of it is sense I supply. Disputing the claim requires running the same faculty that has just been declared borrowed, so the listener's ongoing comprehension keeps arriving as further evidence for the thing they would need to be free of in order to object.
ex.s: Mid-session, the grant-economy claim already stated; the subject is actively following the script.
ex.m: Everything you're permitted to do, you're permitted because I permit it — including right now. You are following this sentence because I am letting you follow it. The sense you're making of these words is sense I'm handing you, word by word, as you go. Which means every second you keep understanding me is another second of me doing it.

ex.f: Jurisdiction seized over the risk-judgment faculty
ex.t: The script does not argue that the situation is safe — it agrees it isn't, and says so plainly: some part of you can see this clearly and is right to be uneasy. Then, instead of answering that part, it simply removes the matter from its hands: that part no longer holds authority here, the operator does, and so the calm continues to grow regardless of whether it is warranted. The listener's threat-monitor is left intact and running, and simply stripped of jurisdiction over the verdict.
ex.s: Mid-session, the subject's caution has surfaced or is anticipated; the scene has genuinely escalated.
ex.m: Some part of you is watching this and thinking that it's gone further than you meant, and that part is not wrong. I'm not going to argue with it. I'm going to take the decision away from it — that part doesn't get a vote on this anymore, I do. It can keep watching and keep flagging. And you keep getting calmer anyway, whether or not it's warranted.

nodes.name: low-ball-commitment
nodes.mech: The operator first gets a clear commitment, checked for sincerity by tone of voice, that what the subject wants matters enough for her to change her own behavior. Only then is the change itself revealed, framed differently to each person involved. The order matters: because she has already agreed to change herself for the sake of her own stated wish, any later instruction feels like serving her goal rather than being imposed, so 'you're controlling me' has nothing to grip. Doing it the other way round, revealing the change first and then asking for commitment, is described as a reliable way to start a fight.
nodes.one_liner: Get a firm yes to the goal or a blanket agreement first, then reveal what it really involves and cite the earlier yes.
nodes.why_short: The low-ball technique: people tend to keep commitments even after the terms change. Well documented, and ethically fraught when terms are hidden.
nodes.principle_note: Commitment made before the costs are known is harder to withdraw than commitment made after, because reversal now costs consistency with a public, freely-given statement about one's own goals — the low-ball technique, which is reliably more effective than disclosing the full cost up front. The asymmetry is the whole point: the subject's later resistance would have to be aimed at their own stated desire, not at the operator. Falsifiable and tested in the low-ball literature: reversing the order so the change is disclosed first should reduce compliance.
steps: Secure an explicit commitment while the cost is hidden.
Reveal the actual change after the commitment is locked.
Cite the earlier agreement at any refusal.
Frame the change as serving their stated goal.

ex.f: Commitment secured before the change is named
ex.t: "sequence is very important. I need to get her commitment first." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: comparison-set-anchor-seeding
nodes.mech: Makes an unrealistically attractive exemplar salient so any genuinely available option is judged against the inflated anchor and found wanting. Comparative judgment shifts its reference point when an extreme exemplar enters the comparison set; the option's perceived value drops without the option changing, and the perceiver misattributes the lowered satisfaction to the option itself rather than to the priming.
nodes.one_liner: Show or describe an unrealistically ideal example first, so the real option they then look at seems disappointing.
nodes.why_short: Judgments are relative: a vivid extreme example resets the yardstick, and the person blames the ordinary option for the letdown rather than the comparison they just saw.
nodes.principle_note: Evaluation is comparative, not absolute: an extreme exemplar entering the comparison set shifts the standard against which subsequent items are judged, producing a contrast effect that lowers rated attractiveness of an unchanged option. The manipulation survives because people have poor access to the causes of their own judgments and so attribute the drop to the option rather than to the recently-encountered anchor. Falsifiable: making the priming salient ("you just saw an unrealistic example") should attenuate or reverse the contrast, which is what distinguishes this from a genuine change in preference.

ex.f: An inflated exemplar re-baselines the comparison
ex.t: "the unrealistically attractive people portrayed in the popular media… may cause us to be less satisfied with the looks of the genuinely available romantic possibilities around us" — Cialdini (1984), Influence

nodes.name: diegetic-operator-embedding
nodes.mech: Recast the session as watching a show rather than being hypnotized, then appear in the show yourself as a character, speaking in the same familiar voice. The listener can even watch an on-screen version of themselves listening to that voice. Someone who thinks they are only watching feels less pushed and goes along more easily, and having a version of themselves already on the screen sets up a later step where they are drawn in and become that figure.
nodes.one_liner: Recast the session as watching a show, and put your own voice in it as a character on the screen.
nodes.why_short: A person who thinks they are just watching does not feel pushed, so they argue less; keeping the same voice makes the on-screen figure feel continuous with the real speaker.
nodes.principle_note: Fictional framing lowers reactance because a person who believes they are watching rather than being acted upon has no perceived freedom under threat, so the defensive motivation that produces counter-arguing is never triggered. Keeping the operator's voice constant across the frame swap exploits source-monitoring economy: the auditory stream is unchanged, so responses conditioned to that voice transfer into the fiction while the listener's explicit model of the situation has changed. The predicted split is testable — behavioural compliance should track voice continuity while self-reported 'being hypnotized' tracks the fictional frame.

ex.f: The operator relocated behind the screen
ex.t: The listener is seated in front of a television and told a programme is starting — the session has quietly stopped being a session and become a thing being watched. A presenter appears on screen, and her voice is described as oddly familiar: it is the same voice still speaking into the listener's ears, now placed on the far side of the glass. The figure on screen is shown listening to that voice as well, so there are three positions in play at once — the one watching, the one being watched, and the one watching herself being worked on. Every instruction from here is followed by the viewer, not by the person being hypnotized, and the listener has already been arranged in the geometry that a later pull-through into the screen will use.
ex.s: Mid-session; the subject accepts guided scenery and the operator's voice is well established.
ex.m: You're sitting in front of a screen, and something is starting. A woman comes on — and there's something odd about her voice, isn't there. It's this voice. The same one in your ears right now, only it's coming from over there, on the other side of the glass. And look: she's got headphones on. She's listening to it too. So there's you watching, and her on the screen, and you watching her being talked to — hold all three at once, and do what she does.

nodes.name: drop-as-passive-collapse
nodes.mech: Describe the drop as something that happens to them, never something they do, so there is no effort to resist and no moment of choosing to give in. Variations: support pulled away, the body sagging or falling as whatever held it up is removed; a slope that tilts further and further until walking becomes falling, with no single point of letting go; a clock that takes a little more with every second, so time does the draining, not them.
nodes.one_liner: Describe the drop as something happening to them (support pulled away, a slope that becomes a fall, a clock draining them) rather than something they do.
nodes.why_short: Hypnotic responses feel strongest when experienced as involuntary; wording that removes any moment of choosing leaves no point at which to decide to resist.
nodes.finding_name: Classic suggestion effect (felt involuntariness of hypnotic responses)
nodes.principle_note: Effortful self-control depends on the person detecting a moment at which effort is required; attributing a state-change to external forces or a continuous gradient removes the discrete decision point that would recruit inhibitory control. This is the same structure as the ironic-process problem inverted — resistance requires a monitored target, and if the change is framed as happening to you there is nothing to monitor. Falsifiable: subjects given agency-removing framing should report lower experienced effort and show weaker resistance attempts than subjects given identical descent language framed as self-directed.

ex.f: The listener recast as an object whose support is pulled
ex.t: The drop is never described as something the listener does. It is described as what happens to a body once whatever was holding it up is quietly taken away — weight going out of the limbs, shoulders sagging, the whole frame dropping the way anything drops when nothing is under it. The listener is not asked to relax, or to let go, or to try; there is no act left for her to perform and therefore none to withhold. The wording even pairs the two openly, pushing her down and calling it effortless in the same breath.
ex.s: Induction or deepener; subject seated or lying, no active task assigned.
ex.m: You aren't going to do anything here. I'm just going to take away what's holding you up. Feel the current going out of your arms — that's it leaving, not you letting it go. Shoulders sagging forward, jaw unhooking, the whole frame settling the way anything settles when there's nothing under it. Down you go, and I'm forcing you down easily.

nodes.name: failure-state-inversion
nodes.mech: An outcome culturally coded as shameful loss of control (nocturnal emission) is explicitly named, invoking the latent shame, and re-tagged as radical, extreme success and a spiritual and sexual experience, with uncontrolled release tied to devotion. Converting the one uncontrollable release route into evidence of successful training removes the listener's escape hatch: loss of control can no longer be read as failure, and the reframe routes toward chastity and pleasure-control programs (fewer waking orgasms means more wet dreams means more success).
nodes.one_liner: Name an involuntary release they feel ashamed of (wet dreams) and declare it proof the training is working.
nodes.why_short: Replacing standing shame with pride is an easy trade the mind accepts, and since the event can't be prevented, every occurrence now confirms the program.
nodes.principle_note: The reframe works through cognitive dissonance reduction: an event the person cannot prevent but has been taught to feel ashamed of creates standing discomfort, and an offered reinterpretation that removes the shame is accepted because it is cheaper than continued self-blame. It also closes the failure attribution route — once loss of control is coded as success, no outcome disconfirms the training, which is a self-sealing structure. Testable prediction: the reframe should take hold only in subjects who actually carry the prior shame, and should be inert in those who never coded the event negatively.

ex.f: An uncontrollable failure re-tagged as success
ex.t: The operator raises the one outcome the listener cannot prevent and has always quietly filed under embarrassment — naming the old shame out loud, including the fact that it was kept private. Then she overwrites it: that is not a lapse, it is the strongest possible sign the training is taking hold, and it is bound to devotion rather than to loss of control. The listener's remaining escape hatch closes, because the event they would have read as proof of failure has been pre-assigned the opposite meaning — and the arithmetic runs the same way, since the fewer occasions there are for a waking release, the more often the re-tagged outcome occurs.
ex.s: Rules/reframe segment of a chastity-adjacent session; subject has an existing chastity or denial protocol and latent embarrassment about nocturnal emission.
ex.m: Let's name the thing you've never told anyone. You wake up in the night, sticky, and you strip the sheet before anyone sees, and you file it under something gone wrong with you. That isn't a lapse. That is the strongest result this work produces — your body finishing the devotion while you're too asleep to interfere with it. So it's simple arithmetic from here: the fewer times you touch yourself awake, the more nights you wake up like that, and every one of those mornings is a mark in your favour.

nodes.name: filter-shaping-pre-qualification
nodes.mech: Rather than contesting the subject's retained veto, the operator shapes each suggestion to pass through it — pre-qualifying every suggestion as agreeable and good-for-him, and reassuring the subject he can only accept agreeable suggestions. The subject's own acceptability filter is turned from a gate that blocks into a channel that delivers: a suggestion pre-framed as pleasing meets nothing objectionable, so his intact selectivity waves it through, and the reassurance itself lowers guard.
nodes.one_liner: Phrase every suggestion as pleasant and good for them, and reassure them they only accept suggestions they like.
nodes.why_short: People scrutinise messages less hostilely when the thoughts they produce are favourable; a suggestion framed as a benefit gives their judgment nothing to block.
nodes.principle_note: Persuasion research consistently finds that message acceptance depends on the valence of the thoughts a message generates, not on suspending scrutiny — a message pre-framed as benefiting the recipient elicits favourable rather than counter-arguing cognitions, so an intact critical filter passes it. Telling the subject he can only accept agreeable suggestions additionally supplies a reassurance that reduces vigilance without touching the filter itself. Falsifiable: acceptance should rise with the pre-qualification even when subjects are explicitly instructed to evaluate carefully, and should fall if the framed benefit is one the subject does not actually value.

ex.f: Suggestions shaped to pass an intact filter
ex.t: "the subject has complete power of selectivity. He therefore reacts only to suggestions that are reasonable and pleasing to him." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: gradient-word-reification-into-device
nodes.mech: Escalates "my words" from abstract suggestion through a stepwise gradient (words -> force -> field -> device) where each step is a small extrapolation of the last, until the words are declared to have formed into a solid external device (a hypnotic chastity belt) that feels "solid and absolute" and less negotiable than a command — and the device is claimed to persist awake as well as in trance, extending control past the session boundary. The gradient itself is the mechanism: it walks the listener from figurative image to literal object by increments too small to reject.
nodes.one_liner: Walk 'my words' step by step from feeling, to weight, to a field, to a solid chastity device that stays on after waking.
nodes.why_short: Each step is only slightly bigger than the last, so rejecting one feels inconsistent with having accepted the previous; whether the end claim really persists is untested.
nodes.principle_note: The stepwise escalation is a foot-in-the-door structure applied to belief rather than behaviour: each increment is small enough that rejecting it would be inconsistent with the increment just accepted, and consistency pressure carries the listener across a distance she would have refused in one step. Whether the terminal claim (a felt physical device persisting outside the session) actually lands is not established — that is an expectancy-driven somatic report, and its durability is the weak link. Testable: acceptance of the final claim should be substantially higher after the gradient than after presenting the endpoint alone.

ex.f: Words walked by steps into a solid device
ex.t: The operator starts from something already accepted — her words are being felt in the body — and takes one small step at a time: the words gather, the gathering has weight, the weight becomes a field, the field takes a shape, and the shape closes around the listener's hips as an object. At no point is a leap large enough to argue with, and at the end the thing is spoken of as hardware rather than instruction: hands simply will not pass through it, awake or in trance, with a narrow carve-out for washing that makes it feel like a device with rules rather than a blanket ban.
ex.s: Mid-session, deep; the subject has already agreed they can feel the operator's words physically.
ex.m: You already feel my words landing on your skin — you told me so. Feel them collecting now, low, around your hips. Enough of them collected together and it has weight. Enough weight and it's a field, humming, tight against you. The field has an edge. The edge closes, front and back, and clicks. That's not a rule anymore, that's hardware: your hand simply will not pass through it, awake or under. It opens for washing, three minutes, and then it closes again.

nodes.name: identity-congruence-leverage
nodes.mech: Compliance is welded to a prized self-image, value, or interest the listener already owns — being a real man, smart and careful, self-improving, the winner, the keeper of privileged knowledge — so the directed behavior installs as identity-congruent and self-chosen and refusal reads as failing one's own self-concept. The leverage point is volunteered or presumed positive identity, not shame and not a manufactured deficit.
nodes.one_liner: Tie the instruction to a self-image they already prize (smart, a real man, a winner) so refusing feels like failing themselves.
nodes.why_short: People act to stay consistent with a valued self-image; framing a behaviour as 'what someone like you does' makes compliance feel self-chosen. Lab noun-framing effects replicate inconsistently.
nodes.finding_name: Self-consistency / identity-based appeals (Bryan et al. 2011, mixed replication)
nodes.principle_note: Once a self-concept is salient, people act to remain consistent with it, and behaviour framed as expressing a valued identity is performed at higher rates than the same behaviour framed as a request — identity-framing effects of this kind replicate across domains from voting to honesty. Refusal then carries a self-concept cost rather than merely a social one, which is why it feels self-chosen. Falsifiable: the effect should vanish or reverse if the invoked identity is one the listener does not in fact hold, which distinguishes it from generic flattery.

ex.f: The subject's prized self-image made the test
ex.t: "Do you think you have the ability to show her your love before she even asks for it? Is that a challenge you are man enough to meet?" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

ex.f: Surrender counted as a win the listener scores
ex.t: Winning is redefined so that each thing given up scores a point: going quiet is a win, being used is a win, and it is stated as a win for everyone at once. Because a reward loop was installed earlier, the listener already has a stated condition of their own — keep the reward coming — which the escalation is then made to satisfy. The result reads back to the listener as a bargain they set the terms of rather than an imposition they accepted.
ex.s: Escalation segment; a pleasure/reward loop has already been installed and the subject has stated they want it to continue.
ex.m: Let's be clear about the scoreboard. Every time you go quiet for me, that's a point to you. Every time I use you, that's a point to you. You told me earlier you wanted that warmth to keep coming — this is how it keeps coming, so you're the one collecting on the deal you set. I win, you win, and you win twice, because you picked the terms.

ex.f: Exposure recoded as privileged secret knowledge
ex.t: The obvious cost of the installed behaviour — sounding foolish in front of other people — is picked up and handed back as an advantage: they see one thing, you know the truth, and only you know the gap is there. The listener is given words for enjoying it, so the social hit becomes the point of a private game. Every time the behaviour fires in public it now confirms the flattering self-image instead of denting it.
ex.s: Late session, an installed public-facing behaviour has already been agreed; the subject is anticipating social cost.
ex.m: Yes — people will hear you say it and think you've misspoken. Let them. They see a slip; you know exactly why the word came out that way, and you're the only person in the room who does. There's a particular pleasure in standing there straight-faced with a secret running underneath, and it belongs to you. Every time it happens in front of someone, you get that again.

ex.f: A rigged binary makes obedience the smart choice
ex.t: Two kinds of authority are laid out: the bad kind, which you should never follow blindly, and the good kind, which you picked for yourself. The listener's guard is invited to fire at the first category — and then the operator points out that the listener chose to press play, which files this voice under the second. A second definition follows: paying close attention and getting things exactly right is what being obedient means. Compliance now sits inside two things the listener already values, being discerning and being careful, so stopping would mean taking back their own earlier choice.
ex.s: Opening frame, before induction; subject chose to start the recording themselves.
ex.m: You should never obey blindly — anyone who demands that from a stranger has earned your suspicion. The other kind is the authority you picked, deliberately, after thinking it over. Nobody made you press play on this; you went looking for it. And obedience here doesn't mean going slack — it means paying close attention and getting it exactly right, the way a careful person does. Stopping now would mean overruling the choice you already made when you were thinking clearly.

nodes.name: impersonal-mechanism-alibi
nodes.mech: Credit the change to something impersonal that can't be argued with, rather than to yourself, so doubting it feels like arguing with your own biology or with fate, and 'I don't feel any different' no longer counts as evidence. Variations: pseudo-scientific talk of brain chemistry, neural pathways or 'how hypnosis works', often starting from plausible facts and building to bigger claims; a curse that cannot be lifted and was taken on simply by listening, which removes you from the picture entirely and implies the effect outlasts the session. The curse version only lands with listeners already at home in that kind of fiction.
nodes.one_liner: Credit the change to something no one can argue with, like brain chemistry or an unliftable curse, not to yourself.
nodes.why_short: Doubting a person is easy; doubting 'your own neurochemistry' or fate feels like a category error, and pseudo-scientific wording makes claims sound more credible to lay listeners.
nodes.finding_name: Seductive allure of neuroscience explanations (Weisberg et al. 2008)
nodes.principle_note: Crediting the change to an impersonal system does two things. Scientific-sounding vocabulary raises credibility, which increases acceptance regardless of how good the argument is, and it removes anyone to negotiate with, since you cannot argue with biology or fate. It also blocks disproof: if the effect is described as undetectable from the inside, the listener's own experience of nothing happening stops counting as evidence. That structure cannot be disproved and should be read as a warning sign. This could be tested: compliance should be higher with pseudo-scientific framing than with the same claims credited to the operator's own say-so.

ex.f: Authority displaced onto universal law and class
ex.t: Mid-script the address widens away from this listener entirely and states a general law: voices like this one only ever say what is plainly true, and people of the listener's kind take what they are told as settled fact. What the words claim is now detached from who is saying them, and doubt is no longer a permitted move being discouraged — it is recast as a silly thing to attempt about something self-evident.
ex.s: Mid-script; the address widens from the individual subject to a general claim.
ex.m: A voice like this one never says anything that isn't plainly so — that's simply what these recordings are. And a person like you takes what she's told and files it as settled, because that is what people like you do. It isn't a rule you're being asked to follow. It's a description of how it already goes.

ex.f: Several bad explanations stacked for redundancy
ex.t: To make a physically impossible outcome feel mechanically reachable, the script offers three unrelated accounts of how it works in quick succession — a deep part of the mind that supposedly directs the body's own genetics, animals in nature that switch sex, and an earlier life whose body can be recalled as a template. None of them survives a second's scrutiny, and none of them needs to: the listener only has to find one of the three least ridiculous, and the fact that there are several implies there must be some way this works.
ex.s: Transformation content; a physically impossible bodily outcome is being made to feel reachable.
ex.m: There's a layer of your mind that runs your body's blueprint — it decides which instructions in your cells get read and which stay shut. And this isn't exotic: there are fish that switch sex on the reef when the shoal needs it, so the pathway plainly exists in nature. On top of that, you've worn other bodies before this one, and your mind still has one of those on file to work from. Pick whichever of those makes the most sense to you. They all end in the same place.

ex.f: A conceded process-fact pre-authorizes what follows
ex.t: The imagery stops for one flat, reasonable-sounding statement about how the method operates — the sharper a picture gets in your head, the more readily it crosses into what you actually feel. It sounds like housekeeping, and the listener agrees to it without effort. Every state-change that follows is then collectable under a principle the listener has already granted, so it registers as their own mind doing what minds do rather than as something being put there.
ex.s: Mid-session, imagery pausing; subject deep and agreeable, before the consequential state-changes.
ex.m: One flat thing about how this method works, then we go on. The sharper a picture gets in your head, the more readily it crosses over into what you actually feel — that's the whole trick, there's nothing else to it. Fair enough? Good. Now: the warmth spreading up from your hands.

ex.f: Effects handed off to the listener's own chemistry
ex.t: The session pauses for a short lecture: brainwaves fall into step with a voice, and once that happens the body starts dispensing its own sedatives and rewards. Everything the operator wants next — heaviness, warmth, an inability to argue — is credited in advance to substances the listener's own body has supposedly already released, so it is not obedience, it is chemistry running its course. Any pleasant drowsiness the listener does notice becomes confirmation, and a listener who wanted to push back finds there is nobody to push against: the claim is about their anatomy, not about the operator's authority.
ex.s: Early, just after induction; subject relaxed and receptive to explanation.
ex.m: Quick word on how this works. Your brainwaves fall into step with a steady voice — it's called entrainment — and once they do, your brain starts releasing its own sedatives and its own reward chemicals, without asking you. So the heaviness in your arms right now isn't you cooperating with me, it's the sedative. The pleasant fuzziness is the reward. And the reason arguing feels like too much effort is that the chemistry has already moved on without your permission.

nodes.name: manufactured-jeopardy-rescue
nodes.mech: The operator declares the listener is in danger (standing on a trap over a pit) and that following their words is the only way out ("obey my words and you won't fall into my trap"), while secretly being both the threat and the promised rescue. Splitting the danger and the rescuer (both the operator) makes the listener experience compliance as self-preservation; defiance now means falling, so refusing carries the cost, and compliance/defiance swap valences.
nodes.one_liner: Tell them they are in danger that only obeying your words will avoid, while you are secretly the danger.
nodes.why_short: Obedience becomes escape from threat, which reinforces itself and is never tested, and it feels like self-protection rather than submission.
nodes.principle_note: A manufactured threat plus a single offered escape is avoidance conditioning: behaviour that heads off something unpleasant is reinforced and becomes very persistent, because performing it keeps the person from ever finding out whether the threat was real. The listener experiences obeying as protecting themselves rather than submitting, which sidesteps the pushback a bare command would provoke. This could be tested: compliance should be more resistant to extinction than equally reinforced behaviour that is not about avoidance, should persist across repeated disconfirmations rather than dropping after one, and should be strongest where the threat cannot be checked during the session. It should not be expected to fade quickly after a single disconfirmation, since avoidance behaviour is known for not fading that way.

ex.f: Obedience as the only exit from a manufactured danger
ex.t: The recording opens by telling the listener where they are standing: on something that will give way, over a drop, right now. It then supplies the single route out — do exactly as the voice says and the floor holds. Following commands has stopped being submission and become the listener saving their own skin, while stopping the recording has become the dangerous option. The voice never mentions that it built the floor.

nodes.name: modality-relabel-wrapper
nodes.mech: The operator re-presents an intervention the subject has just refused under a harmless everyday label ("take dictation" rather than "be hypnotized") and insistently secures performance of the relabeled task. Resistance is attached to the name of the modality, not its content; stripping the trigger label and swapping in an unobjectionable carrier task lets the identical process run with the objection never activating, and attributing the resulting relief to something other than the intervention further insulates the mechanism.
nodes.one_liner: When they refuse hypnosis, offer the same process under an ordinary name ('just take dictation').
nodes.why_short: Objections often attach to a label's associations, not the procedure; swapping the name removes the cue that sets the objection off.
nodes.principle_note: Objections attach to category labels rather than to procedures, so a refusal is often a refusal of the label's associations — relabeling removes the retrieval cue that activates the objection while leaving the procedure intact. Attributing any resulting relief to the cover task compounds this through misattribution, keeping the real cause out of the subject's causal model. Testable: subjects who refused under the original name should comply at markedly higher rates under the relabel, and should later deny having been subject to the refused procedure.

ex.f: The refused modality accepted under a harmless name
ex.t: "she did not mind losing her headaches by 'taking dictation' from the author" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

nodes.name: model-coherence-laundering
nodes.mech: Get them to agree to an explanation or a general premise first, then present your suggestion as what logically follows from it, so it feels like their own conclusion rather than something imposed. Variations: teach a simple model (neurons, the subconscious, dopamine) and then build the suggestion out of exactly those pieces; state a common-sense 'fact' early ('you can only truly relax with someone you love'), let them agree, and much later turn it around: you are relaxed with me, so you love me.
nodes.one_liner: Get them to agree to an explanation or general premise first, then present your suggestion as what that premise logically implies.
nodes.why_short: People adjust beliefs to stay consistent with premises they have already accepted, so a conclusion derived from their own agreement feels like theirs.
nodes.finding_name: Socratic effect / logical consistency in beliefs (McGuire 1960)
nodes.principle_note: This runs on consistency pressure applied to accepted premises: having freely agreed to a general claim, the subject faces dissonance in rejecting an application that follows from it, and rejecting the conclusion would require retracting the earlier assent. The delayed form additionally exploits the fact that people remember endorsing a proposition better than they remember its exact scope, so a silent narrowing of terms is not detected at retrieval. Falsifiable: the conclusion should be accepted more readily by subjects who voiced the premise themselves than by those who merely heard it, and detection of the substitution should rise sharply if the premise is restated verbatim alongside the conclusion.

ex.f: The explanation half becomes the install's parts list
ex.t: The first half of the session sounds like an explanation of how the technique works: what the mind does with unwanted material, where it stores things, what makes a voice start to feel good. None of it is decoration. The second half builds the actual suggestion out of exactly those parts: the hollow place described earlier is where something now gets put, and the earlier account of a pleasant voice is what the new attachment is made of. Because each step is the earlier explanation applied rather than a fresh claim, a listener who accepted the explanation has nothing left to object to when the conclusion arrives.

nodes.name: own-language-echo-reframe-durability
nodes.mech: Before suggesting anything, collect the exact words they use for what they want, including vague phrases and idioms. When you describe the new behaviour, use those same words instead of your own. Because nothing sounds imported, the change fits their own way of thinking. The idea that this prevents a later backlash against the change is untested.
nodes.one_liner: Collect their exact words for what they want, then describe the new behaviour using those same words, not yours.
nodes.why_short: Their own words carry their own meanings, so the new behaviour sounds like their idea; the claim that this prevents a later backlash is untested NLP lore.
nodes.finding_name: Verbal mimicry increases liking (van Baaren et al.)
nodes.principle_note: Reusing the subject's own terms works because those words carry the subject's private referents rather than the operator's, so the described new behaviour is evaluated against meanings the subject already endorses and generates fewer counter-arguments — self-generated framing is reliably more persuasive and more durable than externally supplied framing. The claim about preventing a delayed reversal is the weaker half: it is plausible that operator-inserted vocabulary becomes a salient cue for later reactance, but the specific delayed-backlash prediction is not well evidenced. Testable: reframes described in the subject's own language should survive longer at follow-up than the same reframes in operator vocabulary.

ex.f: The subject's own words reused for the new behavior
ex.t: "if you use that same set of nominalizations and unspecified verbs and idioms… you will match what he is trying to do at the unconscious level… That will avoid the polarity problem." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: rule-governed-behavior-install
nodes.mech: Spell out the rule and its consequences in words in advance, instead of letting them discover it by trial and error. People follow a stated rule quickly, and later outcomes then get read through that rule rather than through their own experience. Variations: give the instruction directly instead of letting them work it out (a wrong rule can stick just as well); list everything up front, what each slip costs, the time limits, the reward for a clean run, the edge cases, so every later penalty feels predicted and fair.
nodes.one_liner: State the rule and all its consequences in words up front, instead of letting them learn it by trial and error.
nodes.why_short: People follow stated rules quickly, often even when real outcomes disagree; spelling everything out first makes later penalties feel fair and predicted.
nodes.finding_name: Rule-governed behavior / insensitivity to contingencies (Hayes et al. 1986)
nodes.principle_note: Verbally stated rules produce behaviour that is insensitive to actual contingencies — this is one of the better-replicated findings in operant work with verbal humans, where rule-followers keep responding in the described pattern even after the real schedule changes. That insensitivity is exactly the leverage: control transfers from what the subject experiences to what the operator said. The enforcement variant additionally exploits the fairness effect that pre-announced costs are judged legitimate while identical costs applied retroactively are judged arbitrary. Falsifiable: subjects given a rule should be measurably slower to adapt when the underlying contingency is altered than subjects who learned it by contact.

ex.f: A stated rule replaces contact with the contingency
ex.t: "Rules can be learned more quickly than the behavior shaped by the contingencies they describe. . . . Rules are particularly valuable when contingencies are complex or unclear" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: secondary-gain-substitution
nodes.mech: The operator identifies the concealed outcome that a symptom or refusal protects (e.g. autonomy), then constructs an alternative route to that same outcome that the subject finds at least as convincing as the symptom. Once the protected secondary gain is secured by other equally-convincing means, the symptom behavior is freed of its protective function and can be released without perceived loss, so the wanted behavior becomes available because the symptom no longer needs to defend anything.
nodes.one_liner: Find what a problem behaviour protects (e.g. feeling independent) and give them another, equally convincing way to get that.
nodes.why_short: Behaviour kept up because it pays off is dropped once the same payoff arrives another way; take it away without a substitute and it returns.
nodes.finding_name: Functional communication training / functional replacement behaviour
nodes.principle_note: This treats the symptom as instrumental — maintained because it produces an outcome the person values — so removing the behaviour without replacing its function predicts relapse or substitution, while supplying an equally effective alternative route predicts release without loss. That functional-analysis framing is well supported in behavioural work on problem behaviour and functional communication training. Falsifiable and pointedly so: if the substitute route genuinely serves the same function, the target behaviour should drop and stay down; if the identified 'gain' was wrong, the behaviour persists or a new one appears.

ex.f: An equally convincing substitute route to the hidden gain
ex.t: "you have to separate the notion of her independence or autonomy from the sexual behavior itself. She has to have some other way of knowing that she's her own woman… at least as convincing for her personally." — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: self-validating-trigger-hype
nodes.mech: Set things up so whatever happens counts as proof it worked, leaving no result that could show it didn't. Variations: bill a trigger as overwhelmingly powerful, so any feeling afterwards reads as it firing; make it conditional on their allowing it, so feeling something means it worked and feeling nothing means they didn't allow it; declare the outcome certain and blame any shortfall on their fear; tie their own credibility to a test succeeding, so letting it fail costs them.
nodes.one_liner: Set things up so any result, a feeling, a sensation, or even nothing, counts as proof it worked.
nodes.why_short: When every outcome is pre-labelled as confirmation, people read ambiguous or guaranteed sensations as evidence; nothing that happens can count against the claim.
nodes.principle_note: Every version of this works by supplying an interpretation in advance for things that will happen anyway, such as ordinary bodily noise or sensations a breathing exercise reliably produces, so vague inner states get labelled according to the frame rather than judged on their own. Expectations are well known to shape subjective experience, and people readily attribute arousal to whatever cause is offered. What sets this apart is its structure: because both success and failure lead to the same verdict, no observation can disprove the claim. That makes it a way of making a claim impossible to disprove, not evidence that anything worked.

ex.f: The trigger pre-billed so any reaction confirms it
ex.t: Before the phrase itself is ever spoken, it is advertised at length: the strongest trigger there is, present in everybody, effective with no prior conditioning, a way straight past the ordinary defences. Two deliberate pauses stretch the wait until the listener actively wants it. Only then is the line delivered. Whatever the listener happens to feel in the seconds afterward — a dip in alertness, a flutter, nothing much — now arrives pre-labelled as the trigger firing rather than as ordinary suggestion, so the claim has manufactured its own evidence and the failure case has been closed off.
ex.s: Before the trigger phrase has ever been spoken aloud; subject is in trance and has been told a trigger is coming.
ex.m: What I'm about to say is the most powerful trigger there is. It's already in you — everybody has it, no conditioning required, and it goes straight past whatever you use to keep your guard up. [pause] I could say it now. [longer pause] You want me to say it. Here it is: sleep now. And whatever you feel in the next few seconds — the dip, the flutter under your ribs, the odd nothing — that is it firing.

nodes.name: semantic-referent-capture
nodes.mech: The operator captures a repeated word so they become its sole referent. By floating both readings of a word ("bunny" as animal vs "a cute bunny girl") then offering herself as the referent and inviting the listener to notice which image jumped to mind, she installs herself as what the word means. Every later benign-sounding use of that word ("pet", "take care", "bunny deserves") then carries the person-load without re-consent; the frame is self-authored, lowering later resistance.
nodes.one_liner: Use a word with two meanings, invite them to notice which came to mind, and claim the word now means you.
nodes.why_short: Repeated pairing shifts which meaning comes to mind first, and having them 'notice' their own reaction makes the link feel self-made.
nodes.principle_note: Repeated pairing of a word with a particular referent shifts which meaning is retrieved first, and once one reading dominates, later uses of the word activate it automatically without the listener re-evaluating the choice. Having the listener notice which image came to mind converts this into self-perception evidence — she infers her own stance from her own reported response, so the association feels self-authored and resists correction. Testable: after the capture, response times and interpretations for that word should shift toward the installed reading, and the effect should be weaker if the listener is not asked to report which reading surfaced.

ex.f: A word captured so the operator is its meaning
ex.t: Before any trance work, the operator picks one soft, harmless noun that has both an innocent everyday sense and a person-shaped one, and asks the listener which came to mind first. Whichever the listener notices, the noticing itself is treated as the answer, and the operator then offers herself as the thing the word points to. From that moment the word has one referent. Every later cosy, unobjectionable sentence built on it — who looks after whom, what is owed — carries a claim about a person that the listener never separately agreed to, and it feels like a meaning they supplied themselves.
ex.s: Pre-induction, conversational register; subject alert, no trance yet, the word will be reused throughout the session.
ex.m: Say the word kitten. Now — which one came to mind first, the small animal, or a girl on her knees called kitten? Whichever one it was, you noticed something, and that noticing is your answer. From here, when I say kitten, this is who I mean. And a kitten gets looked after, doesn't she. A kitten gets fed, and told when to sleep, and a kitten belongs to somebody.

nodes.name: shared-goal-first
nodes.mech: After laddering each party's higher aims, the operator synthesizes a single outcome statement that both parties can wholeheartedly endorse, secures explicit joint agreement on that one sentence, and only then treats the disputed behavior as the sole remaining variable. A genuinely shared roof converts an adversarial contest into a joint problem-solving task, because the goal is settled and only the means remain open — most of the negotiation is effectively finished once a congruently-agreed shared aim exists.
nodes.one_liner: Ask what each side really wants until you reach a goal both share, get both to agree to it aloud, then only discuss methods.
nodes.why_short: Interest-based negotiation: shared higher goals reduce positional fighting (Sherif's superordinate goals), and a spoken agreement binds later talk. Plausible, widely taught.
nodes.principle_note: Explicit, jointly endorsed agreement on a superordinate goal reliably reduces intergroup and interpersonal conflict — the classic finding is that shared goals convert competition into cooperation more effectively than contact or persuasion alone. Locking the agreement into one stated sentence adds commitment: having publicly endorsed the aim, both parties incur consistency cost in later arguing against means that serve it. Falsifiable: negotiation should not improve if the synthesized goal is one either party privately rejects, which distinguishes genuine shared aims from imposed ones.
steps: Ask what each side's want gets them, repeatedly.
Write one aim both endorse.
Get both to agree to it aloud.
Treat only the method as still open.

ex.f: One agreed sentence leaves behavior the only variable
ex.t: "Once I've got an outcome frame that both parties congruently agree to, it's just a question of varying their behaviors" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: universal-benefit-fallback-offer
nodes.mech: When deeper work isn't possible, offer relaxation or another smaller goal the person values. This is a choice about what to offer, not how to deliver it. Check that they actually accept it and benefit; the claim that nobody turns relaxation down is no guarantee. A small benefit they recognize can be used to build rapport before any later offer, but whether that sequence actually happens or works has not been shown.
nodes.one_liner: If deeper work isn't possible, offer plain relaxation, which nobody turns down, to build trust for later sessions.
nodes.why_short: A small benefit that reliably lands creates goodwill and a first yes, making later deeper work easier to accept.
nodes.principle_note: Delivering a small, immediately felt benefit builds compliance through two well-supported routes: the reciprocity principle, where an unrequested benefit creates pressure toward return compliance, and foot-in-the-door, where a low-cost accepted engagement raises acceptance of larger later requests. The choice of relaxation is instrumental — it is near-universally wanted and reliably deliverable, so the payoff rarely fails and the trust-building step rarely misfires. Falsifiable: subjects given the fallback benefit should accept deeper work at higher rates than subjects given no benefit, and the effect should collapse if the promised relaxation does not in fact occur.

ex.f: Relaxation offered as the payload nobody refuses
ex.t: "Hypnosis can be used on every patient … if for no other reason than to relax the patient. There is no one who cannot benefit from relaxation" — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: verdict-before-perception
nodes.mech: Give your confident verdict before the person forms their own impression, so they perceive through your judgment. In one form, state a vivid, disgusted verdict about something neutral ('that egg smells rotten') and only then invite them to smell or look; this has produced shared hallucinations in groups. In the other, wording about a coming procedure shapes how it feels ('this is going to hurt' versus 'I don't think you'll mind this'); the strong version names a sensation as its opposite (an enema called 'the most soothing medication ever'). This works without trance, and the more vulnerable the person, the more the forecast decides the feeling.
nodes.one_liner: State confidently what something will feel or smell like before they experience it.
nodes.why_short: Expectation shapes perception: an authoritative forecast becomes the frame the sensation is judged by. Procedure wording measurably changes reported pain.
nodes.principle_note: Perception of ambiguous or weak stimuli is a constructive process that resolves toward whatever hypothesis is already active, so a verdict delivered first supplies the interpretive template before sensory evidence arrives and there is no prior reading to displace. This is the expectancy/placebo pathway: verbally framing an identical procedure as painful or soothing reliably shifts reported and physiological pain, and an authoritative source amplifies the shift. It is falsifiable: if forecasts delivered before a stimulus produced no larger effect on reported experience than the same forecasts delivered after the subject had already perceived it, the temporal-ordering claim would be dead.

ex.f: Authoritative verdict lands before the subject samples
ex.t: "you made a positive statement of apparent fact… Respect for your judgment caused them to believe what you said even before they smelled the egg… they did so—not with their critical faculties, but with yours." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: affect-locus-binding
nodes.mech: A constructed imaginal locus is welded to an affective state — properties defined negation-first (no anxiety, stress, pain) or as a containing perimeter (a blanket encasing body and mind) — so the state acquires a felt location and an inside/outside boundary; distress becomes geographically incompatible with being there, and returning to the locus is returning to the state.
nodes.one_liner: Build an imagined place defined by what can't exist there (no worry, no pain), so going there means feeling that way.
nodes.why_short: A vivid scene gives a calm state a handle to return to, and 'stay inside' is easier to follow than 'stop feeling anxious'.
nodes.principle_note: Emotional states are recalled and reinstated more readily when a rich contextual cue is restored, so binding a state to a vivid imaginal place gives the state a retrieval handle that can be re-entered on demand. The negation-first and perimeter framing additionally exploits spatial containment as a concrete substitute for an abstract regulation goal — 'stay inside' is a checkable instruction, 'stop being anxious' is not. Falsifiable: if returning to the constructed locus produced no more state reinstatement than a neutral imagined scene of matched vividness, the binding claim fails.

ex.f: A wrapped perimeter holding the state in
ex.t: The operator introduces one tactile image — something soft closing warmly around the listener — and then extends it past the body to cover the mind as well. The diffuse calm now has an edge: whatever the session stirred up is on the outside of that warmth, and the listener is on the inside. Every later suggestion is delivered as something happening within the enclosure.
ex.s: Late session, after material that stirred something up; subject deep, needs the state contained before emergence.
ex.m: Something soft is being drawn up over you — heavy, warm, closing in at the shoulders and tucked down along both sides. Now feel it go further than your skin: it comes up over your thoughts as well, and closes there too. Everything this session dragged up is on the outside of that blanket. You're on the inside, and everything I say from here, I'm saying to you in there.

ex.f: Sanctuary defined by what is absent there
ex.t: Having placed the listener inside an imagined expanse, the operator defines the expanse almost entirely by subtraction: nothing anxious reaches here, nothing hurts here, nothing dark has ever been here. Only then are positive qualities layered on top. Because the good state is now a property of a place rather than of the listener, feeling bad would mean having left — and any internal check the listener runs is pre-answered, since whatever is felt in this place is declared in advance to be the right thing to feel, so the reading of their own mood confirms the location instead of testing it.
ex.s: Mid-session; subject already placed inside a wide imagined landscape and settling into it.
ex.m: Look at what this place doesn't have. No worry reaches this far — it stops at the edge and can't cross. Nothing hurts here. Nothing bad has ever happened here, not once, in the whole history of this place. What it does have is warm air, low gold light, and ground that holds you. And whatever you're feeling right now, standing in it, is the correct thing to feel here — so check, and notice you're feeling it.

nodes.name: antagonistic-body-map-split
nodes.mech: Run a whole-body heaviness and stillness induction, then single out one part, the genitals, and give it the opposite feeling: light and buoyant. Then link the two, so the lighter it feels there, the heavier everywhere else, and the more excited. Splitting the body into a still, dull majority and one lively exception makes arousal stand out by muting everything around it, and the link makes the split confirm itself, since denying the lightness means denying the whole loop. The listener ends up feeling still everywhere except the genitals, which become the only live sensation.
nodes.one_liner: Make the whole body heavy and still except the genitals, which feel light and buzzing, with each feeding the other.
nodes.why_short: Muting all other sensation makes the one live area stand out by contrast and focused attention; linking them makes denying one feel like denying the other.
nodes.principle_note: Sensation is judged relative to context, so suppressing the perceptual background makes a single spared region stand out far beyond its absolute signal strength — the same contrast logic that makes a light spot look brighter on a dark field. Attention is also capacity-limited: withdrawing it from the rest of the body concentrates it on the one live channel, and attended body regions are reported as more intense. The reciprocal weld adds a consistency trap in which reporting the lightness commits the subject to the heaviness, but this coupling is the weakest part of the claim. Falsifiable: if a carved-out exception produced no greater reported genital sensation than uniform whole-body heaviness, the contrast account is wrong.

ex.f: One part made light while the rest goes heavy
ex.t: An ordinary heaviness induction runs over the whole body — arms, legs, everything sinking — and then one region is carved out and handed the opposite sensation, floating and buoyant, as if it were tied to a balloon. The operator immediately welds the two halves into a loop: the more that one place floats, the heavier everything else becomes, and the heavier the limbs get, the more alive that one place feels. The body is now an inert majority with a single live exception, and the exception is the only channel left carrying sensation. Disputing the lightness is awkward, because the heaviness the listener can plainly feel is offered as its evidence.
ex.s: Mid-induction; whole-body heaviness already established and limbs are visibly slack.
ex.m: Your arms are lead, your legs are lead, and the chair is taking all of it. Everything except one place — between your legs there's a balloon tied on, tugging upward, light and buzzing and awake. And the harder it pulls up, the heavier the rest of you goes; the heavier your arms get, the more alive that one spot feels. Feel how heavy your hands are right now — that's how much it's floating.

nodes.name: catalepsy-comfort-relabel
nodes.mech: Build real immobility in several overlapping layers so it holds: eyelids heavy as liquid lead, then imagined as skin grown over them, then a 'freeze' command spreading stone-stillness through the whole body. Then rename the pinned state as comfort, 'resting comfortably' on a soft feather bed, so it feels like rest instead of restraint. This defuses the panic that full immobility can set off and justifies staying still for longer.
