A closing question, 'did you ever really want to escape?', recasts the stillness as the listener's own preference. The comfort label sits on top of a real restraint; it doesn't remove it.
nodes.one_liner: Lock the eyes and body still, describe it as resting comfortably in bed, then ask if they ever really wanted to escape.
nodes.why_short: The relabel turns restraint into comfort, and the leading question rewrites the earlier wish. Untested.
nodes.principle_note: The same bodily state can be experienced very differently depending on the label available for it, and appraisal — not the sensation alone — largely determines whether restriction is felt as threat or as rest. Pre-supplying the benign label forecloses the threat appraisal that would otherwise recruit panic, and the retroactive 'did you ever want to escape?' exploits the tendency to infer one's own prior attitude from one's observed non-resistance rather than from memory. Falsifiable: if subjects given the comfort relabel reported the same rate of distress under equivalent catalepsy as subjects given no label, the appraisal account fails.
steps: Close the eyes.
Lock the eyelids, then extend the freeze to the whole body.
Relabel the stillness as comfortable rest.
Ask: did you ever really want to escape?

ex.f: Real catalepsy relabelled as lying down to rest
ex.t: The eyelids are pinned twice over — first weighted as though something dense had settled behind them, then sealed as though they had been fastened shut — and a single command word extends the same stillness to the whole body. Only once the immobility is genuinely built does the operator rename it: the listener is not held, they are simply settled somewhere comfortable with no reason to get up. The restraint stays exactly where it was; what changes is what it is called, which is what keeps it from turning into alarm. A closing rhetorical question then hands the whole thing to the listener retroactively, implying no wish to move was ever present — so the pinning reads as their own preference rather than the operator's work.
ex.s: Eyes already closed and stationary; enough compliance established to hold a body command.
ex.m: There is liquid lead sitting behind your eyelids, and over the top of it the skin has grown across the seam — they don't open, there's nothing there to open. Freeze. That same stone runs out through your shoulders, your hips, your feet. And notice what it actually feels like: you're lying on a feather bed, sunk in, warm, the way you'd be at the end of a long day with nowhere to be. Nobody is holding you down. You're just resting. Did you ever really want to get up?

nodes.name: contingency-sign-verification
nodes.mech: While training, check whether a punishment is actually reducing the behaviour. For some people the 'penalty' is rewarding, and the behaviour climbs instead. If the counts go the wrong way, drop it and switch to a different consequence, such as a time-out or rewarding an alternative behaviour, which should be ready in advance. A consequence is judged by what it does, not by what it is meant to be.
nodes.one_liner: Watch whether a punishment is actually increasing the behaviour; if so, stop it and switch to a different consequence.
nodes.why_short: A consequence is defined by its effect: some people find a 'penalty' rewarding, so the only test is whether the behaviour goes up or down.
nodes.finding_name: Response cost / functional definition of punishment (ABA)
nodes.principle_note: Reinforcement and punishment are defined by their effect on behaviour rate, not by the operator's intent or the aversiveness of the event — attention delivered as a reprimand functions as reinforcement whenever attention is the maintaining consequence. Rate data is therefore the only valid test of a contingency's sign, and this move exists because the operator's intuition about aversiveness is a known-unreliable predictor. Falsifiable and routinely falsified in practice: procedures intended as punishers are observed increasing target behaviour.

ex.f: Checking whether the penalty is reinforcing instead
ex.t: "One occurs when the repeated imposition of response cost serves to reinforce, and not punish, the undesirable behavior. When this situation arises, the practitioner should stop using response cost and switch" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: convergent-multichannel-encoding
nodes.mech: Build one sentence so that several hidden routes carry the same message at once: a double meaning, a phrase buried inside a longer one, an implied reading, a word marked out by tone. The listener follows the obvious meaning while every hidden route points the same way, so the message still gets through if one route is missed or rejected. Whether the hidden routes are really absorbed separately is untested.
nodes.one_liner: Hide the same message in several ways at once in one sentence (double meanings, implied readings, buried phrases).
nodes.why_short: Several weak routes to one idea may beat any single one; the claim that each covert channel is separately absorbed is untested NLP theory.
nodes.principle_note: Evidence from multiple independent channels combines toward a stronger posterior than any one channel, and covert channels each carry a low per-channel rejection probability, so redundancy raises the odds that at least one delivery lands unchallenged. Attention is also capacity-limited: monitoring the tracked surface consumes the resources that would be needed to scrutinise the secondary readings, and unchallenged claims are more likely to be accepted. Falsifiable: if the number of co-referring covert channels made no difference to uptake compared to a single covert delivery, the redundancy claim is wrong. Note the honest caveat — the individual covert linguistic forms named here come from a tradition whose effects have replicated poorly.

ex.f: One message carried by every covert channel at once
ex.t: "the Deep Structure meanings … activated … by transderivational search, ambiguity, lesser included structure, derived meanings, analogical marking, and causal modeling statements interact, i.e., all give the same suggestion" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

nodes.name: cross-file-handoff-receptor
nodes.mech: Install a trigger in this recording but never fire it here. Tie it to something that will happen in another recording or a live session, such as a countdown there that 'makes it all real'. The listener leaves primed but not yet set off: this recording is only the first half of a chain, and the payoff is delivered elsewhere.
nodes.one_liner: Install a trigger in this recording but don't fire it; tell them it will go off in another recording or live.
nodes.why_short: A cue-response link can be set up without being used, and an expected but unfinished payoff keeps people anticipating and coming back.
nodes.principle_note: A cue-response association can be established without ever being elicited, so priming and consolidation can occur in one session while retrieval waits for the specified cue — this is ordinary latent learning plus stimulus control. Deferring the payoff also exploits anticipation: an unresolved expected event holds attention and increases the chance of returning for the completion. Falsifiable: if a receptor installed and never fired produced no elevated response to the cue in a later session compared to no prior installation, the handoff does nothing.

ex.f: Trigger installed here, fired in another recording
ex.t: Near the close the operator gives notice that a backwards count will arrive at some later point, not during this recording, and says what it will do once heard: everything laid down so far will switch on and settle into place. The count is then never given. The listener wakes carrying a cue that has not yet done anything; its effect waits for whichever recording or live session supplies the count. A passing remark that the thinking part may not remember this covers the confusion it creates in the meantime.
ex.s: Last minute of the file, deepening finished, no trigger has been fired in this session.
ex.m: Before I bring you up, one thing to leave with you. At some point that isn't now — another recording, or my voice live — you'll hear me count backwards from five. When you hear that count, everything I've laid down in you today switches on and clicks into place all at once. I'm not going to count today. The thinking part of you probably won't hold onto this, and that's fine, because the part that needs it will.

nodes.name: cross-modal-channel-bridge
nodes.mech: Brings a not-yet-active perceptual channel online by bridging it onto an already-vivid one across a shared feature (rhythm, movement): the vivid channel supplies the energy and the shared feature acts as a carry-over rail so the new channel activates riding the old rather than being summoned head-on (head-on summoning drains the state). A companion move seizes an involuntary single-channel slip the subject spontaneously emits, amplifies it, then layers additional channels onto that self-authored anchor until it becomes a full multimodal enactment the subject owns — because the build starts from the subject's own production and each element is confirmed before the next, it meets little resistance.
nodes.one_liner: Bring in a new imagined sense by riding a feeling they already have (a rhythm felt becomes a rhythm heard).
nodes.why_short: Building on an image already active is easier than creating one from scratch, and a shared feature like rhythm gives an easy bridge.
nodes.principle_note: Imagery in one modality recruits partly overlapping representational machinery, so a shared amodal feature such as rhythm or motion provides an existing active representation the new channel can be built on rather than constructed from nothing — cheaper in working-memory terms than head-on generation. Building from the subject's own spontaneous production adds self-generation: material a person produces themselves is better retained and less resisted than material supplied to them. Falsifiable: if bridging via a shared feature produced no faster or more vivid cross-modal imagery than direct instruction, the rail account fails.

ex.f: Riding a shared feature into a new sense
ex.t: "'attach' an auditory hallucination to this hallucinated body sensation. The measure proved most successful" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: Growing an involuntary slip into full enactment
ex.t: "to see her father's mouth moving … then … the remainder of her father's face" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

nodes.name: defusion-observer-stance
nodes.mech: Have them picture each thought that comes up sitting on a leaf floating down a slow stream, and watch it drift away, without trying to change, push away or clear any thought, or to control the stream. When they notice they've got caught up in one, they simply return to watching. The aim is to see thoughts as passing events rather than facts or orders, not to empty the mind; trying to control them undoes it.
nodes.one_liner: Have them place each thought on a leaf floating downstream, watching without trying to change or remove it.
nodes.why_short: Watching thoughts as passing events, without fighting them, reduces how believable and upsetting they feel; trying to suppress them backfires.
nodes.principle_note: Distress from a thought is driven less by its content than by whether it is treated as a literal report about the world; changing the relationship to the thought rather than its frequency reliably reduces its behavioural impact, and this is one of the better-supported components of acceptance-based therapy. The explicit non-control instruction matters because deliberate suppression produces rebound — trying not to think something increases its later frequency — so any 'clear your mind' variant would undo the effect. Falsifiable: if adding a control instruction produced equal or better outcomes than the non-control version, the mechanism is misdescribed.

ex.f: Thoughts placed on leaves, stream left uncontrolled
ex.t: "don't try to change what shows up on the leaves in any way. If ... you find that you are in the stream or on a leaf, just stop and notice that this happened." — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: derived-relations-installation
nodes.mech: With a learner who already handles language, teach a few connections and let many untaught ones appear on their own. Teach that A goes with B and B goes with C, and they will usually also link B back to A and A to C untaught. Check the new links by testing them with no reward. Variations: teach some cells of a grid of combinations and test the rest; add one new item to an existing group so it joins the whole group; give one word a good or bad meaning so everything grouped with it takes it on; build perspective-taking from simple 'I/you, here/there' swaps to double swaps.
nodes.one_liner: Teach a few links (A goes with B, B with C) and let the untaught links (A with C) appear on their own.
nodes.why_short: People spontaneously infer reversed and chained relations from trained ones, so a small taught set yields a large untaught repertoire.
nodes.principle_note: Verbally capable humans respond to relations among stimuli in ways that were never directly reinforced — teach A=B and B=C and the untrained A=C and its reverses emerge — which is why a small trained core multiplies into a much larger repertoire. The extinction probe is what makes this a real claim rather than a story: emergent responses appear on the first novel presentation with no consequences delivered, so they cannot be attributed to reinforcement of that response. Falsifiable and bounded — the effect depends on relational/naming prerequisites and largely fails in learners lacking them, which is itself the standard test of the account.

ex.f: Probes ordered least to most demanding
ex.t: "probe types are introduced sequentially, beginning with symmetry, followed by transitivity… and then combined tests… each probe type is introduced immediately following the minimal training necessary to provide the prerequisites" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

ex.f: Simply telling the learner the base relations
ex.t: "baseline relations can be established, and derived relations promoted, by simply telling the learner about the required overlapping conditional discriminations" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: descriptive-functional-assessment
nodes.mech: Watch the behaviour in its normal setting without changing anything, and each time it happens, note what came just before and what came just after, one line per occurrence. Over many instances a pattern suggests what sets it off and what keeps it going. This needs the behaviour to happen often enough to watch, with consequences you can actually see. Because nothing was tested, it is a correlation and a starting hypothesis, not proof. Variations: real-time before/behaviour/after logging; checking what people report against what you see, timing observation to when it usually happens.
nodes.one_liner: Watch the behaviour in its normal setting and log what happens just before and just after, every time.
nodes.why_short: Patterns in what precedes and follows a behaviour suggest what keeps it going, but observation alone shows correlation, not cause.
nodes.principle_note: Behaviour is largely under the control of its immediate antecedents and consequences, so systematically logging what precedes and follows each instance surfaces regularities that self-report cannot, because people have poor introspective access to the contingencies actually maintaining their own behaviour. The method is deliberately honest about its own limit: observed co-occurrence without manipulation cannot rule out a third variable, which is exactly why the output is labelled a hypothesis. Falsifiable: a descriptive hypothesis can be, and frequently is, disconfirmed by a subsequent experimental functional analysis — moderate agreement rates between the two methods are the known constraint on this technique.

ex.f: Logging antecedent and consequence in the natural routine
ex.t: "running away from tasks and materials occurs most frequently when difficult tasks are presented and that the most common consequence … is a teacher chasing after him and returning him" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: enacted-identity-assembly
nodes.mech: The new identity is built piece by piece from a long series of narrated actions: dressing (panties, bra, stockings, heels, dress, nails, wig, makeup), or movement that leads to clothing changes (twirling, then a skirt, then a dress, then shoes). Each is described as happening automatically, or as a side effect of a suggested movement, before they can think it over. Built from dozens of small accepted acts rather than one 'you are X' claim, the identity is acted out long before it is named. Pleasure is paired with each item as it touches the body, and lines like 'you don't really mind' head off objection.
nodes.one_liner: Narrate them dressing piece by piece as if their hands move by themselves, with pleasure at each step, before naming the new identity.
nodes.why_short: People infer who they are from what they see themselves do; many small pleasant acts build the identity before any label can be argued with.
nodes.principle_note: People infer their own attitudes and identity from observing their own behaviour, especially when no strong external justification for it is salient — so a long chain of performed acts builds an identity attribution more durably than an asserted label, which invites counter-argument. Each accepted micro-act is also a small commitment that raises the cost of refusing the next slightly larger one, the standard foot-in-the-door escalation, while pairing each act with pleasure conditions positive valence onto the associated objects. Falsifiable: if a single 'you are X' assertion produced identity uptake equal to the enacted sequence, the self-perception account is wrong. The automaticity narration is the weak point — its claimed effect on deliberation is not established.

ex.f: Motion supplied first, the change rides on it
ex.t: A light, playful feeling is grown until it spills into movement, and the listener is turning in place out in the open. Each change of clothing then arrives as something noticed mid-movement rather than announced: what is around the legs is not what was there a moment ago, then it is a different garment altogether, then the footwear has changed to match. Nothing is asserted about the listener; the change is presented as a discovered side-effect of the motion they are already making, with a shrug pre-attached — and none of it seems worth stopping for.
ex.s: Playful/light affect already growing; listener is imagining themselves standing in an open space.
ex.m: That lightness gets so big it has to go somewhere, so you spin — arms out, turning in place in the middle of the room. And spinning, you notice the air moving against your thighs, which is odd, because there wasn't a hem there before. Spin again: now it's longer, sweeping wide at the knee, definitely a dress. Spin again and the shoes have changed under you, and they're the right ones for it. You don't really mind. It's not worth stopping for.

ex.f: Identity assembled from automatic dressing acts
ex.t: The operator narrates a long getting-ready sequence in which the listener's hands are already moving, working through one item after another in the order a real routine would take them, each described as being put on before the listener has decided to put it on. Every point of contact with the material is paired with a rising wave of warmth and delight, so the objects themselves accumulate positive charge. No claim about who the listener is has yet been made; by the time one arrives, the listener has performed the role a few dozen times and enjoyed each step of it.
ex.s: Trance established; listener responsive to motor suggestions and no identity claim has been made yet.
ex.m: Your hands are already moving — the panties first, up over the hips, and feel that little rush of warmth as the fabric settles. Now the bra, the clasp, the strap adjusted with a thumb, and the warmth climbs. Stockings next, one, then the other, rolled up the leg slowly because your hands want to do it slowly, and that's delight now, right through the chest. The dress over the head. The heels. You didn't decide on any of it, and every single piece felt good going on.

nodes.name: felt-substance-state-binding
nodes.mech: Introduce one physical material the listener can feel, such as latex, webbing, or something rising up the body, and give it a job: holding thoughts in, keeping them confined, or standing for trance depth. Tighten it, thicken it or raise it to take them deeper, without ever talking about depth itself. Because the same material keeps coming back, each mention reconfirms the state, and a material climbing the body gives a one-way gauge they can feel for certain.
nodes.one_liner: Introduce a felt material (latex, webbing) whose job is holding the trance, and tighten or raise it to go deeper.
nodes.why_short: Trance depth can't be felt directly, but tightness or height can; giving the listener a felt gauge makes depth checkable and adjustable.
nodes.principle_note: Abstract internal variables like 'trance depth' have no perceptual referent and so cannot be checked, whereas a tactile quality has an unambiguous felt magnitude — substituting the concrete for the abstract gives the subject something they can actually verify, and verification of the proxy is then taken as verification of the state. The monotonic spatial version exploits the same thing dial-and-thermometer imagery does: a one-directional scale removes the ambiguity that would otherwise prompt a 'is this working?' check. Falsifiable: if a named-but-unfelt state variable produced equal reported depth to the substance-welded version, the concreteness account fails.

ex.f: Coverage height standing in for trance depth
ex.t: The same clinging material is narrated climbing the body in stages, from the feet upward, and each stage is announced together with a step down in depth. The question of whether the listener has gone deeper now has a physical answer they can check by feel: the material covers more than it did. And it only ever rises.
ex.s: The clinging material has already been introduced earlier in the session; the operator wants a way for the listener to check their depth by feel.
ex.m: It's pooling at your feet now, rising — over the ankles, and that's one, down one step. Feel it climbing your calves, sealing the backs of your knees — two, deeper. Up over your thighs, your hips, cool and tight against everything it covers — three. If you're wondering how deep you are, just feel how far up it's got. And it only goes up.

ex.f: A felt substance given the job of holding thoughts
ex.t: One material is introduced and given a job: it arrives while still fluid, sets across the surface of the mind, and from then on its function is that nothing gets out. The listener is only ever asked to track physical qualities — weight, tackiness, how snugly it fits — and the mental state comes along for free, because the operator welded it there at the start. Fit then becomes a dial: another layer, a little closer, and thinking is that much more enclosed, without confinement ever being named.
ex.s: Early-to-mid trance; listener tracking physical sensation, no state name introduced yet.
ex.m: It goes on warm and wet, pouring over the top of your head, and it's setting — tacky first, then firm, a skin across everything. Its whole job is that nothing gets out. Feel the weight of it above your ears. Feel how it grips your temples. Here's another coat — thicker, tighter, closer to you than the last one — and feel that fit. Nothing gets out.

nodes.name: imagined-to-enacted-collapse
nodes.mech: Before each action, describe a bolder imagined version of it, then let the wording slide from 'you imagine yourself...' to 'you walk over...' to 'you're doing this for real' within the same paragraph, without marking the change, even while the scene is still called a dream. Over time imagining becomes rehearsal for doing, and the pleasure given for imagining carries over into the act.
nodes.one_liner: Describe a bolder imagined act, then slide the tense from 'you imagine' to 'you are doing it' without flagging the switch.
nodes.why_short: Whether something felt imagined or real is judged from its vividness; detailed, continuous imagery with no boundary marker is easy to misclassify as done.
nodes.principle_note: Memory for the source and reality-status of an experience is a reconstructive judgment made from qualities like vividness and perceptual detail, not a tag stored at encoding — so imagined content that is highly detailed and continuous with enacted content is systematically prone to being misclassified as real. Repeatedly imagining an act also raises confidence that it occurred, the imagination-inflation effect, and the unflagged tense slide removes the boundary marker the source-monitoring judgment would otherwise use. Falsifiable: if content delivered with explicit reality-status flags at each transition were misattributed as often as the unflagged slide, the source-monitoring account is wrong.

ex.f: Tense slides from imagined to actually doing it
ex.t: Every act in the sequence is first rehearsed in a bolder version and then performed in a milder one, so imagining has become the ordinary first half of doing. Then, without any marker, the grammar shifts inside a single paragraph: the listener is picturing themselves doing the thing, and two sentences later the verbs have moved into the present and the operator notes that this one is no longer rehearsal. The frame around all of it is still openly a daydream, which is what lets the reclassification pass unchallenged — and the pleasure already paid out for the imagined version transfers intact to the enacted one.
ex.s: Mid-fantasy, dream frame explicit; several imagine-then-do cycles already run and accepted.
ex.m: So you imagine standing up in the middle of that room and saying it to every single one of them. That's the bold version. In the softer one, you just imagine leaning over to the one person and saying it quietly. You're picturing yourself doing that. Picturing your hand on the back of their chair. You lean over. You say it — out loud, and this one isn't the imagining anymore, this one you're actually doing. It's still just a daydream. Keep going.

nodes.name: listener-kept-dissociation-container
nodes.mech: The listener puts their identity, obligations or resistance into a container they make or keep themselves, rather than one the operator provides. Examples: a locked suitcase handed to a porter that 'only you' can open, which parks real-world worries outside the session as a gentle consent gesture; or the strongest possible box, built by the listener so their own mind can't later wave it away. The key ingredient is that the listener makes or keeps it: an object they build is said to be stronger and harder to undo than one merely described, and a container they keep sets anxiety aside without giving it up.
nodes.one_liner: Have them pack their worries or obligations into a container they build and lock themselves, keeping the key.
nodes.why_short: Things people create themselves are remembered and trusted more, and setting worries aside with a way back feels safe rather than like giving them up.
nodes.principle_note: Self-generated material is retained better and defended more readily than material supplied by someone else, so a container the listener builds is harder for them to later dismiss as the operator's invention — the objection 'that was just his suggestion' has no target. Retaining the key also preserves perceived control, and perceived control over an aversive event reliably reduces distress even when it is never exercised, which is what makes the bracketing tolerable rather than threatening. Falsifiable: if operator-supplied and listener-built containers produced equal durability and equal distress reduction, both halves of the account fail.

ex.f: Baggage locked by the listener, key kept
ex.t: Before the session's real work begins, the listener is told to gather everything they are responsible for out in the world into a single container, close it, and secure it with fastenings of their own — the operator is explicit that nobody else can open it, including the operator. It is then handed to a figure who will keep it until the end. The part of the listener that carries obligations is now parked outside the session, so control can be released inside it without any of that surfacing as anxiety.
ex.s: Opening of the session, before induction; listener still alert enough to follow a construction instruction.
ex.m: Before we start: gather everything you're responsible for out there — the messages, the deadlines, the person who needs something from you — and put all of it in a case at your feet. Close it. Put your own locks on it, whatever fastening you like, and understand that nobody else can open this, not your family, not me. Now hand it to the porter waiting by the door. He holds it until the end and gives it back on the way out. It's not gone. It's just not yours for the next half hour.

ex.f: Listener builds the box, operator holds the key
ex.t: Rather than describing a container, the operator refuses to and explains why: a container the operator describes can be argued with, but one the listener is asked to build as strong as they can imagine cannot be talked down by the mind that just made it that strong. The listener builds it. Only then is a lid added — and a lock that opens to the operator's key alone.
ex.s: Trance established; the target material (resistance, a refusal, an obligation) has been named and is about to be contained.
ex.m: I'm not going to describe the box to you, and here's why: anything I describe, some part of you can argue with. So you build it. Make it as strong as you can imagine — thickness, material, whatever your mind says is unbreakable, because you're the one who set that standard and you can't talk down your own work. Have you got it? Good. Now put the resistance in and I'll add the lid. And there's a lock on it, and the only key that turns it is mine.

nodes.name: meta-outcome-laddering
nodes.mech: The operator repeatedly asks each party what their stated want actually accomplishes for them — the aim behind the aim — climbing from a concrete, non-negotiable demand up toward an abstract higher-order value, often four or five iterations deep. Each ascent trades a fixed behavior for a superordinate aim the other side has no reason to reject, dissolving attachment to the specific act; if no genuine higher aim surfaces, the party invents one that is still workable. A zero-sum fight over behaviors is thereby converted into a positive-sum search over compatible goals.
nodes.one_liner: Keep asking 'what does that do for you?' until a fixed demand becomes a broader aim the other side can accept.
nodes.why_short: Fights over positions loosen once underlying interests surface, because different interests can usually be traded off against each other.
nodes.principle_note: Distributive conflict over incompatible positions becomes integrative once the underlying interests are surfaced, because parties usually hold different priorities across dimensions and so can trade — this is the core, well-replicated finding of the interests-versus-positions negotiation literature. Repeated laddering also moves the demand up a means-ends hierarchy toward abstract values, and abstract framings are less tied to a single behavioural instantiation, so attachment to the specific act loosens. Falsifiable: if laddering produced no more integrative agreements than direct positional bargaining across matched disputes, the mechanism is wrong.

ex.f: Asking what the want itself accomplishes
ex.t: "What does letting him know that you are angry do for you?" … "I get the outcome of the outcome, or the intent of the intent. I may have to ask this question four or five times" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: named-safety-belief-purge
nodes.mech: Find the listener's own inner safety check, a belief like 'I can always wake myself up', a warning feeling, or doubt, and switch it off or turn it against itself. This disables a real safety mechanism. Variations: name the belief as a small, once-useful thing, call it the obstacle, and have them release it on an exhale; relabel doubt or hesitation as fear, ego, or proof they need this more; make their subconscious the judge ('as long as your subconscious accepts, you can nod'), so if nothing happens it is blamed on their own resistance.
nodes.one_liner: Name their 'I can always wake up' belief or inner warning, call it an obstacle or fear, and have them release it.
nodes.why_short: A belief named and framed as a hindrance is easier to drop on request; this erodes the listener's refusal channel and is a safety risk.
nodes.principle_note: Refusal in an ongoing interaction depends on having an available account for saying no; all three operations work by removing that account rather than by removing the capacity. (a) Naming a protective belief as a discrete removable object exploits the fact that a metacognitive belief once made explicit becomes arguable, and the paired bodily release supplies a felt 'it happened' event that the subject then reads back as evidence the change occurred. (b) Pre-labelling the warning signal as pathology is a standard attributional pre-emption: once doubt is defined as symptom, the subject's own alarm no longer carries evidential weight for them. (c) Routing consent through an inaccessible 'subconscious' makes the frame unfalsifiable to the subject — compliance proves consent, refusal proves internal conflict — which is precisely the structure a real consent check must not have. Falsifiable at the level of the whole move: if subjects given these framings refused unwanted suggestions at the same rate as controls, it does nothing. The specific claim that any of this disables a genuine faculty is not established; what is well evidenced is that pre-supplied interpretations reduce the rate at which people voice objection.

ex.f: The 'I can always wake up' belief named and purged
ex.t: The operator quotes the listener's own reassurance back to them word for word — the quiet certainty that none of this can reach anything they don't already want, that they could surface any time they chose — and gives it a name: a small protective device, installed long ago, which did its job well and is now the only thing standing between them and going properly under. Getting rid of it is then made physical rather than argued: draw in a breath, gather every bit of tension in the body, hold it and let it be called the last of the resistance, then let the breath out and feel it drain away. What was a belief has been turned into an object, and the object has been discarded in a way the body can confirm.
ex.s: Deep trance, listener responsive; a prior reassurance about being able to wake at will has been given or is assumed.
ex.m: There's a little thought you keep near the front — that none of this can touch anything you don't already want, that you could come up any second you decided to. That's a small safety device somebody fitted a long time ago. It did its job. It's also the only thing left between you and going properly under. So take a breath in — all the way — and gather every bit of tension you're holding, jaw, shoulders, fists, squeeze it all into that one belief. Hold it. That's the last of your resistance in your hands. Now let it go, all at once, and feel it leave.

nodes.name: narrated-motion-entrainment
nodes.mech: The listener's mandated physical movement mirrors the operator's narrated movement, collapsing watching/being-watched and moving/being-moved into one channel so proprioceptive output and visual fantasy reinforce each other; the deepener simultaneously does the eroticization work.
nodes.one_liner: Narrate your own slow movement and have the listener copy it in time, each repetition counting as a step deeper.
nodes.why_short: Moving along with an imagined scene removes the mismatch that marks it as merely pictured, and acted-out imagery feels more vivid.
nodes.principle_note: Imagery that is congruent with concurrent motor output is easier to sustain than imagery that competes with it — self-generated movement supplies proprioceptive feedback matching the narrated scene, removing the mismatch signal that normally marks an image as merely imagined. Enacted imagery is also better remembered and rated more vivid than passively visualized imagery (the enactment effect), so the fantasy accrues the phenomenal weight of something done rather than pictured. Falsifiable: if listeners instructed to move in the narrated pattern report no higher vividness or absorption than listeners told to stay still while hearing identical narration, the account fails.

ex.f: Listener's body mirrors the narrated body
ex.t: The operator narrates a slow deliberate motion of her own body — the lift, the pause, the settling — and has the listener carry out the same motion in time with the words. Each completed cycle is declared another step down, the count of repetitions standing in for a depth gauge. Because the listener is both watching the described body and producing the movement themselves, the felt position of their own limbs keeps ratifying the imagined one, and the same repetition that deepens is the repetition that arouses.
ex.s: Listener physically able to move and has agreed to follow motion instructions; trance light to medium.
ex.m: I'm lifting my hand off my thigh — slowly, up to my collarbone, hold — and settling it back down. You do it with me, same speed, in time with my voice. Up. Hold. Down. That's one, and one is a step lower. Up. Hold. Down. Two. Your arm knows exactly where mine is, because it's in the same place. Ten of these and you'll be as far down as I want you.

nodes.name: phantom-body-ontological-reversal
nodes.mech: Split the listener into a waking body and an imagined body, say that trance removes the difference between real and imagined, then declare the imagined body is the real one while the waking body drifts far away. The imagined body feels whatever you describe, and the listener stops checking those sensations against what they physically feel. How far away the waking body is can be turned up for both depth and arousal. Untested.
nodes.one_liner: Split them into a waking body and an imagined body, then declare the imagined one is the real one.
nodes.why_short: The instruction may loosen the listener's criterion for 'real', so scripted sensations get reported as felt; untested.
nodes.principle_note: People judge whether something was perceived or imagined using cues such as how vivid it is and how much effort it took to form. This technique gives a verbal instruction that shifts the threshold for that judgment rather than changing the cues themselves. That predicts a shift in threshold, not better discrimination: people given the reversal should mistake imagined content for perceived content more often, without getting any better at telling the two apart, and should report the same bodily experience as anyone else whenever they are prompted to check again. If the reversal improved discrimination, or if its effect survived an explicit prompt to re-check, the account fails.

ex.f: The imagined body declared the real one
ex.t: The operator separates the listener into two bodies — the one in the chair and the one in the mind — states that trance erases any difference between what is actual and what is pictured, and then makes the swap explicit: from here on, the pictured one is the true body. Attention is directed to the other body drifting away into the distance. Since sensation now belongs to whichever body the operator is narrating, whatever gets narrated arrives as genuine feeling, and no physical body is being consulted that could contradict it. How far off the discarded body has drifted is then tied to how strongly the sensation registers, so a single instruction deepens and arouses at once.
ex.s: Trance established; listener has already accepted an imagined scene or imagined body.
ex.m: There are two of you now: the one sitting in that chair, and the one in your mind, standing here in front of me. In trance the line between what's real and what's pictured doesn't hold — so let's be plain about it. The one in your mind is the real one. That's the body you're in. The one in the chair is somewhere behind you and getting further away, a hundred feet back now, a room you left. So when I put my hand on this body's throat, that's a hand on your throat. And the further that other one drifts, the more of this you feel.

nodes.name: predicate-generalization
nodes.mech: The operator reduces a predicate toward its least-specified form (active verbs to "do", stative to "be"), generalizes within a sensory channel (speak-talk-intone-whine-cry-plead), or picks verbs whose deep structure smuggles an unstated element (slap/handle/grasp all carry "hand"). Broadening the predicate raises the chance the wording matches the listener's real internal state across more subjects (wider pacing), while unstated content rides in covertly inside the chosen verb without ever being asserted — most relevant in story/metaphor construction.
nodes.one_liner: Use vague verbs ('do', 'feel', 'be') so the line fits whatever the listener is experiencing.
nodes.why_short: Vague statements fit almost anyone and listeners fill gaps from their own experience; the claim that verbs smuggle hidden content is weak.
nodes.principle_note: Underspecified predicates work because the listener fills the gap from their own current state, and self-generated content is both more personally accurate and more persuasive than content supplied by someone else (the self-generation effect). Broad verbs therefore raise hit-rate the same way a Barnum statement does — the wording is true of almost anyone because it asserts almost nothing. The claimed second effect, that verbs with incorporated elements smuggle unasserted content past evaluation, is far weaker evidence: presupposition does reduce scrutiny of embedded content in comprehension studies, but the specific lexical-generalization recipe is a craft heuristic, not a tested one. Falsifiable on the first claim: if generalized predicates produced no higher rate of "that describes me" endorsement than specific ones, the account fails.

ex.f: Stripping the verb to fit any listener
ex.t: "the hypnotist might generalize a predicate to its maximally unspecified form: do for active verbs / be for stative verbs" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

nodes.name: proxy-desire-offloading
nodes.mech: The listener is asked to picture a woman who has been given conditioned compulsions as her backstory. His own wanting is handed to her: she is the one aching, she is the one who needs release. His own act then reads as granting her that release, a kindness to her rather than something he does for himself, which takes the edge off embarrassment while arousal keeps climbing. Because the story says she is the hypnotized one, he can watch the conditioning happen 'to her' without noticing it is aimed at him.
nodes.one_liner: Give the listener's desire to an imagined woman who 'needs' release, so his own climax feels like a generous favour to her.
nodes.why_short: Describing an act as being for someone else makes it feel less about you, which can lower embarrassment and let arousal run with less self-judgement.
nodes.principle_note: Shame tracks threat to self-concept, so re-describing an act as directed at another party lowers its self-relevance and its shame cost. Moral licensing and self-affirmation are the wrong citations here — licensing concerns prior good acts purchasing later transgression, which is not the structure of proxy attribution; the relevant literature is self-distancing and third-person construal, where shifting to a non-self perspective reliably reduces reported affective intensity. Falsifiable: proxy-framed content should yield lower reported shame and higher completion than identical directly-framed content; equal shame ratings refute it.

ex.f: A proxy given the listener's own wanting
ex.t: The imagined partner is handed a backstory in which she has been conditioned: her own release is possible only through someone else's, so her need is urgent and entirely aimed outward. Her eagerness, not the listener's, is narrated as the engine of the scene. The listener's finish is therefore not something they were chasing but something they are giving — refusing it would be withholding — and because the conditioning in the story belongs to her, the listener spends the session watching hypnosis being done rather than noticing it being done to them.
ex.s: Mid-session fantasy, partner figure already introduced; listener aroused and following the scene.
ex.m: Here's what was done to her before you met her: she was conditioned so she can't finish at all except through someone else's. That's why she's like this — the wanting isn't even aimed at herself, it's aimed at you. She's been holding it for days. She's not asking you to enjoy this, she's asking you to end it for her. Nothing happens for her until you let go. So don't hold it back from her.

nodes.name: recall-state-reinstatement
nodes.mech: The subject is walked back into a real experience from their own past in rich detail (where they were, what they saw, heard, smelled, tasted) until the feeling and the body's response come back now. The operator watches for the visible shift and repeats back the details that produced it. Variations: offer a quick string of familiar remembered scenes (sinking into a bath, dragging tired legs into bed) so heaviness arrives by memory rather than by command; use short on-demand mini-trances to bring back one remembered item at a time.
nodes.one_liner: Have the subject recall a real past experience in rich sensory detail until the feeling physically comes back now.
nodes.why_short: Recalling an event re-activates much of the sensory and bodily pattern it had; the more cues across senses, the fuller the return.
nodes.principle_note: Remembering a personal experience is partly a reconstruction: recalling an episode reactivates the sensory and physical pattern from the original moment, and the more cues are supplied across the senses, the more completely that pattern returns. This is the context-reinstatement principle used in the cognitive interview, and it is one of the better-replicated effects in this area: detailed multi-sensory questioning measurably increases how much is recalled and produces observable bodily changes. It also explains why drawing on real memories works without the listener needing to accept anything: the material is already theirs, so there is nothing to resist. This could be tested: if detailed multi-sensory questioning produced no more physical reinstatement than a bare instruction to remember, the account fails.

ex.f: Short trances aimed at one catalogued item
ex.t: "The many items were systematically discussed for their meanings and brief trances were induced to vivify various items." — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: A buffet of remembered tiredness, nothing commanded
ex.t: No instruction to feel heavy is ever issued. Instead the operator runs through a handful of ordinary worn-out moments — the last mile of a long drive with the eyes going, standing up from a chair you had sunk too far into, the arm that has gone dead under someone dozing on it — and lets the listener take whichever one is already theirs. The recalled weight is then simply talked about as though it were present, and there was never a command available to refuse.
ex.s: Early induction; no heaviness command has been issued and none will be.
ex.m: You know the last twenty minutes of a long drive, when your eyes keep going soft at the edges and you're blinking to hold the road. Or standing up out of a chair you'd sunk way too far into. Or waking with someone asleep on your arm and the arm's gone completely dead, all pins and weight. One of those is yours — you already know which. And that weight in the arm, in the eyes, the way the legs don't want to take the stairs. It's a good weight. Nothing to do about it.

ex.f: Interrogating a memory until the body follows
ex.t: "What do you feel like just as you are about to take the first drink? ... You can smell it now. And what exactly did it taste like?" — Bandler & Grinder (1982), Reframing

nodes.name: self-perpetuating-depth-bootstrap
nodes.mech: Instead of the operator delivering each step deeper, the deepening is set up to keep running on its own. Variations: install a circular belief the listener carries ('going deep teaches you to go deeper', 'imagining a deeper state makes it deeper'), which keeps working even after the operator stops talking; tie depth to something that keeps happening anyway (each breath, each word, each moment of listening) so the listener cannot avoid going deeper except by leaving.
nodes.one_liner: Tell the listener their trance deepens by itself, either because going deeper teaches them to go deeper, or with every breath or word.
nodes.why_short: Once a person expects deepening to keep happening, they read any change as more depth; nothing they notice can count against the claim.
nodes.principle_note: Deepening claims of this shape are unfalsifiable by construction, and that is precisely the source of their power rather than an objection to it: because any degree of experience counts as confirming evidence, the listener finds no observation that would contradict the rule and so keeps applying it. The time-yoked form additionally removes the failure branch — an event guaranteed to occur cannot be missed, so the listener never accumulates a disconfirming instance, which is the same structure that maintains superstitious conditioning under non-contingent reinforcement. Response expectancy supplies the actual effect: subjects who expect progressive deepening report progressive deepening. Falsifiable at the level of the whole technique even though its internal claim is not: if subjects given a self-running rule showed no greater depth report at the unsupervised tail than subjects given a single static depth statement, the account fails.

ex.f: A circular rule left running after the operator goes
ex.t: The operator states, flatly and as fact, that there is no bottom to this — and that being deep is itself what teaches a person to go deeper, because picturing a deeper state is what produces one. The circle is the point: whatever depth the listener has reached becomes the licence for the next one. Nothing further has to be said, which is convenient, since the operator is about to stop speaking and leave the listener there.
ex.s: Tail of the session; deepening done and the operator is about to fall silent or end the file.
ex.m: Here's how this works, and it's just a fact about you: being in a deep trance is what teaches a mind to go deeper. Picturing yourself further down is what puts you further down. So every level you reach is what makes the next one possible, and there's no bottom to it — no floor, no last step. I'm going to stop talking now. You'll keep going.

nodes.name: somatic-carrier-sweep
nodes.mech: The operator names one feeling (warmth, tingling, arousal) and describes it travelling through the body while the listener follows it with attention, then says what it brings wherever it arrives. Variations: send arousal rising from the genitals up into the head so the mind feels 'filled' and ready for what comes next; sweep sunlight-warmth through the whole body and split it at the groin, so everything else turns sleepy while that one spot turns hot, two opposite states sitting side by side because they came from one source.
nodes.one_liner: Describe one sensation, like warmth or arousal, travelling through the body, steering where it lands and what it brings.
nodes.why_short: Paying attention to a body area makes sensations there feel stronger; a moving description drags attention, and felt sensation follows.
nodes.principle_note: Attending to a body region measurably amplifies sensation there and attenuates it elsewhere, so narrated sensation moving through the body is a moving attentional spotlight and felt sensation tracks it. Falsifiable: region-specific changes in reported sensation should follow the narrated location, with no such gradient when identical sensation is described globally. The bifurcation claim — that a shared metaphoric source suppresses conflict detection between contradictory states — should be dropped or tested separately; as written no observation could contradict it, since any unnoticed contradiction confirms it and any noticed one is attributed to a failed frame.

ex.f: Arousal routed upward and delivered to the head
ex.t: The operator gives the arousal a direction and narrates it travelling: starting low, rising through the waist, the chest, the throat, and finally arriving in the head, where it closes over the brain. The listener follows the motion with their attention, so a diffuse feeling becomes a located process with a destination. The point is the destination — the sensation has been delivered to the thinking part, which is what the next suggestion will operate on.
ex.s: Arousal already present and located; the next suggestion will target cognition.
ex.m: Find where it's strongest — right there, low, between your hips. Now it's moving. Up through the belly, warm, into the chest, feel it pass the ribs. Up the throat, over the jaw. And into your head, where it spreads out and closes over your brain like warm oil. Your thinking is inside it now. Everything I say from here goes through that.

ex.f: One warmth split into sleepy and aroused
ex.t: A single warmth — sunlight, entering at the face — is walked down through the body a region at a time. Partway through, without any announcement that something has changed, the same warmth is described as doing two different jobs: heavy and drowsy everywhere it has already passed, and hot and urgent at one point. Because both readings are attributed to one source the listener has been tracking all along, the two states do not compete; a later word for the combined feeling gives the listener a label for something that should not be possible, and they take it.
ex.s: Body scan in progress from the head down; listener tracking a single warmth source.
ex.m: Sunlight on your face, warm on the cheekbones, and it's soaking downward — through the jaw, the neck, the shoulders, and everywhere it's already been is heavy and slow and sleepy. Down through the chest, the belly, heavier still. And where it reaches your cock it doesn't go heavy, it goes hot, and tight, and urgent — same sunlight, doing both. Sleepy everywhere, aching in one place. That's what we're calling drunk, and you're drunk now.

nodes.name: somatic-effect-portability
nodes.mech: Relocates an already-installed somatic effect (an anesthesia, a felt sensation) from one body region to another purely by declaring the transfer — no fresh elicitation at the destination — optionally tying the jump to a confirming motor act (touch, dwell, countdown) or a discrete cue (finger snap). Because the subject already took the original effect at face value, the declared relocation is accepted on the same credit, and each successful move makes the next assertion more plausible (often reported stronger, each move also an amplification cycle). The operator's speech partitions and re-deploys the body's felt state on command.
nodes.one_liner: Once a suggested feeling (like numbness) has taken in one spot, simply declare it moves to another spot.
nodes.why_short: The subject already accepted the effect once; rejecting the move would mean doubting their own experience, so accepting is easier.
nodes.principle_note: Once a subject has accepted a suggested effect, the cost of rejecting the next related suggestion rises — reversing means retroactively discrediting their own prior experience, which carries self-concept cost, so accepting the transfer is cheaper than denying the original. This is the consistency principle operating as an escalating commitment ladder, reinforced by response expectancy: the demonstrated success of the first effect raises expectancy for the second, and expectancy is among the strongest single predictors of suggestion response. The confirming motor act adds a self-perception cue — the subject observes themselves complying and infers the effect took. Falsifiable: it predicts relocation success is conditional on the original effect having been reported as successful; subjects whose first effect failed should show no better than baseline response to the declared transfer.

ex.f: Declaring an anesthesia into a new site
ex.t: "In about three seconds, that anesthesia will transfer to the other hand" — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

ex.f: Cue-anchored jump to a new body region
ex.t: "I'm going to transfer the anesthesia from this hand to that leg. … I'll snap my fingers and the anesthesia will jump down to your toes." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: temporal-lag-function-discriminator
nodes.mech: Uses latency between a social event and a target behavior, together with changes in attention or competing stimulation, to refine candidate explanations for naturally observed behavior. Record the timing relative to the event and relevant context rather than only whether the behavior occurred. The stored vignette asks the reader to formulate a working hypothesis about delayed onset and worsening after a setting change. Those observations are clues, not a universal immediate-versus-delayed diagnostic rule; compare alternative explanations and corroborating observations rather than treating delay alone as proof of social or automatic maintenance.
nodes.one_liner: Measure how long after a social event a behaviour appears, to guess whether attention or something internal keeps it going.
nodes.why_short: Behaviour kept going by social consequences should track attention; behaviour kept going by its own sensations should not.
nodes.principle_note: Different possible maintaining conditions motivate different timing and context predictions, making latency useful in hypothesis formation. The linked textbook exercise asks for a working hypothesis and rationale; it does not supply a validated latency cutoff or an experimentally confirmed answer. Descriptive timing patterns and experimentally tested functional relations must remain distinct. The specific immediate-versus-delayed diagnostic claim in the previous record is not established by the reviewed passage. A test of that claim would require independently established functions and comparisons across cases, not merely the vignette's chronology.

ex.f: Lag after a social event as the datum
ex.t: "About 4 minutes after the staff member leaves, however, the clothes start coming off" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: subject-material-utilization
nodes.mech: Never dispute what the subject presents; accept it and steer it toward the goal, so resistance has nothing to push against. Variations: split a feared mix of symptoms and use the workable part as an induction step; give soft suggestions beneath a protest without arguing; use the subject's own beliefs as leverage they can't refuse; remove the object of a fixed fear, then let them experience that it's gone. When words and body disagree, always side with the signal outside awareness. When a part of the person stonewalls, ask questions one step to the side until surprising material surfaces.
nodes.one_liner: Never argue with what the subject brings; accept their symptom, boast or protest and steer it toward the goal.
nodes.why_short: Contradiction gives people something to defend and strengthens their position; accepted material leaves nothing to push against.
nodes.principle_note: Contesting a stated position reliably strengthens it — direct contradiction triggers reactance and gives the person something to defend, and defending a position increases commitment to it via the consistency principle. Accepting the offered material and re-aiming it removes the target for that defence, so the effort that would have gone into counter-argument has nothing to oppose. The nonverbal-precedence rule is a weaker component: the claim that the channel outside awareness is more truthful is a craft heuristic, and the actual research on nonverbal-verbal incongruence supports only that nonverbal cues carry independent information, not that they are systematically more valid. The sideways-questioning component rests on the better-supported point that indirect questions bypass the rehearsed defences attached to the direct one. Falsifiable: it predicts that accepting and redirecting a stated objection yields more subsequent movement than contradicting it; equal outcomes would refute the core.

ex.f: Accept the boast, then narrow its scope
ex.t: "Certainly you remember. You are here in the office. Naturally here in the office you can remember everything…" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: Reprice refusal as choosing the hard route
ex.t: "Too bad. You don't want treatment the easy way. You'll have to have it the hard way." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

ex.f: Partition the symptom, re-command the residue
ex.t: "It would really be enough just to get stiff without crying… 'No, you will first get stiff… Just get more and more stiff…'" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

ex.f: Suggestions run beneath an unargued protest
ex.t: "This demand was met by employing softly spoken suggestions of slow, progressive relaxation, fatigue, and sleep… the patient sat on the edge of his chair, gesticulated, and bitterly denounced the entire procedure as stupid" — Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. I

nodes.name: thought-string-reused-as-restraint
nodes.mech: The operator mimes pulling the listener's thoughts out of their forehead as a long string, keeps hold of it, then uses that same string first as a gag and then as a rope tying the listener to the operator's words. Reusing one imagined object keeps the scene easy to follow. Any trouble thinking during it is called proof that the thoughts really are gone, not a sign the trance failed. Variations: invite the listener to 'try to talk', where clear speech proves the operator now holds the thoughts and garbled speech proves they are lost.
nodes.one_liner: Pretend to pull the listener's thoughts out as a string, then use that same string as a gag and a rope.
nodes.why_short: One concrete object reused across a scene is easy to keep track of, so the fantasy stays vivid without effort.
nodes.principle_note: Abstract states are hard to hold in working memory; a single concrete object with a stable identity is cheap to track, so reusing one externalized object across three functions keeps the whole fiction within capacity where three separate metaphors would not be. The self-confirming loop is the more consequential part: by pre-assigning both possible outcomes to success, the technique makes cognitive difficulty count as evidence of working and its absence count as evidence too, which is the classic structure of an unfalsifiable claim — and unfalsifiable claims resist disconfirmation precisely because no experience registers as counter-evidence. Falsifiable at the technique level: it predicts that a persistent reused object sustains the effect longer than three separate one-shot objects delivering the same content.

ex.f: The same cord reused as gag and restraint
ex.t: One object does three jobs and never leaves the scene. Having drawn the cord out, the operator dangles it just out of reach — you can have this back, if you can talk me into it — then, before an answer arrives, draws it across the listener's mouth and ties it off behind their head. The thing the listener would have used to object is now the thing keeping them quiet, and the remaining length goes around the body.
ex.s: The cord is already drawn out and in the operator's possession; listener still trying to speak.
ex.m: I'm holding it right here — see it? You can have it back if you can talk me into it. Go on. No, too slow. Open your mouth. There — the cord goes across your tongue, back behind your teeth, and I'm knotting it at the back of your head. The thing you'd have used to object with is what's keeping you quiet now. And there's plenty of it left over, so arms down, and I'll wrap the rest around you.

ex.f: Thoughts drawn out as a cord, then knotted
ex.t: The operator describes a thin cord poking out above the listener's brow, gives it a slow pull, and narrates the whole line of thinking coming out with it, coiling loose in her hands. Then she invites them to speak: go on, argue for it back. Whatever comes out is read as proof — clear words mean she is holding nothing, which is impossible, so it must be mush, and mush is exactly what she said would happen. With the argument settled she loops the cord twice around the listener's wrists and knots it to the next thing she says, so the only thing still holding them upright is her voice.
ex.s: Trance established; listener has been told their thoughts are a physical thing and is not resisting the frame.
ex.m: There's a thread poking out just above your eyebrow. I've got it between two fingers — and I'm pulling, slow, and your whole train of thinking is coming out with it, yard after yard of it, coiling in my palm. Go on then: argue for it back. Make your case. Anything clear you say means I'm holding nothing, and I'm plainly holding it, so it's going to come out as mush — which is exactly what I told you would happen. Wrists together. Two loops, and a knot, and the other end is tied to my voice. That's the only thing keeping you upright now.

nodes.name: wish-routing-acceptance-preload
nodes.mech: The operator selects a suggestion the subject already actively craves and phrases it as the exact words the subject is anxious to hear, often echoing a wish held below conscious awareness. Because the message names something the subject already wants, acceptance is pre-loaded and the subject meets the suggestion halfway; resistance never engages because nothing in the message is opposed to them, and the subject supplies the conviction themselves. It fails wherever the underlying want is simply absent — the deciding tell.
nodes.one_liner: Phrase the suggestion as exactly what the subject already wants to hear.
nodes.why_short: People scrutinise welcome claims far less than unwelcome ones, so a wanted suggestion is accepted with little checking.
nodes.principle_note: Motivated reasoning is the mechanism: people apply markedly less scrutiny to propositions they want to be true, demanding "can I believe this?" rather than "must I believe this?", so a suggestion naming a pre-existing desire passes evaluation cheaply. Because the subject supplies the motivational content themselves, there is also no external position to resist, so reactance never engages. The technique's own stated failure condition is what makes it falsifiable and unusually honest — it predicts near-zero effect where the underlying want is absent, which is directly testable by pre-screening desire and comparing response rates.

ex.f: Say the words the subject already craves
ex.t: "Let the patient hear those words which he is anxious to hear… I was really echoing what you have been thinking below the level of conscious awareness." — Elman (1964), Hypnotherapy

nodes.name: arousal-substrate-induction
nodes.mech: The induction runs on rising arousal or need instead of relaxation. Rather than settling the listener down, it keeps turning desire up and treats each rise as going deeper: you sink further because you want more. The usual trance signs still show up (narrowed attention, less sense of choice, easier acceptance) but the listener feels aroused or needy rather than hypnotized. There is no breathing work, countdown or relaxation imagery; pauses and holds are framed as making the want stronger, and the only count is the one that wakes them.
nodes.one_liner: Build the induction on rising arousal or need instead of relaxation: you go deeper because you want more.
nodes.why_short: Strong arousal narrows attention as relaxation does, so focused absorption can come from excitement rather than calm.
nodes.principle_note: This works because the trance correlates it targets — narrowed attention, reduced self-monitoring, diminished sense of agency — are consequences of attentional absorption, not of low physiological arousal, and high arousal narrows attention just as effectively as relaxation does (arousal-induced attentional narrowing is one of the more robust findings in the area). Relaxation is therefore one route to absorption rather than a requirement, which is why removing every relaxational cue does not remove the effect. Elevated arousal may additionally be misattributed to the scenario rather than to the induction, sustaining the frame. Falsifiable: it predicts arousal-substrate inductions produce comparable absorption and suggestibility scores to relaxation inductions in the same subjects; a reliable deficit would refute it.

ex.f: Escalating need substituted for relaxation
ex.t: The variant runs on a deficit rather than a charge: the speaker claims to live on wanting, and says she is turning the listener's wanting up because it feeds her. There is no invitation to close the eyes and no descent imagery; the pivot arrives when she announces the dial is hers now, and the listener finds their attention has already narrowed to the one thing they are not being given. The supernatural framing does the load-bearing work — it lets a rising, restless, unsatisfied state be read as being taken over, which is the trance report the file is actually after.
ex.s: Arousal-substrate session, deficit variant; listener has been kept short of any release and eyes may be open.
ex.m: I don't eat food. I live on what you're feeling right now, and the hungrier you are the better I'm fed — so I'm turning you up. Not because you asked. Because I'm hungry. There's a dial for how much you want, and as of this moment it's mine, not yours, and I'm turning it. Notice that everything else in the room has gone quiet and there's only the one thing you're not getting. That's me in there. That's what being taken over feels like.

ex.f: Arousal escalation used as the depth vector
ex.t: Nothing in the recording asks the listener to breathe out, settle, soften, or descend; there is no staircase, no beach, no counting down at all. The line is simply that the ache keeps climbing, and every depth marker is bolted to that climb — you are further under because you want it more, not because you are more relaxed. Twice the operator freezes the body mid-reach, and even the freeze is sold as pressure that has nowhere to go. The only count in the whole file is the one at the end that lets the listener out.
ex.s: Opening of a session run entirely on arousal; no relaxation cue has been or will be used.
ex.m: I'm not going to ask you to breathe out, or settle, or count down anything. There's no staircase here. The only thing happening is that the ache gets worse — and that's the measure. You're not deeper because you're relaxed, you're deeper because you want it more than you did a minute ago. Reach for it. Now stop. Hold there, hand where it is, don't move — feel all that pressure with nowhere to go? That's another level down.

nodes.name: authority-role-inversion
nodes.mech: The operator offers to be the contractee — the higher-power party performs a task while the lower-power target controls and delivers the reward — explicitly conceding the suspected unfairness. The target gets direct evidence that contracts are honored and that they hold real power, dissolving an "I always get the short end" prior through a demonstrated reversal of the power asymmetry; a power-imbalance objection is converted into trust by enacted role reversal.
nodes.one_liner: Offer that the first deal is one where you do the work and the suspicious person controls the reward.
nodes.why_short: A costly demonstration that you keep bargains updates distrust faster than promises do.
nodes.principle_note: Trust is updated by demonstrated behaviour far more than by assertion, and a costly, disconfirming demonstration updates a prior faster than a cheap one — this is the standard logic of belief revision under evidence, and the operator taking the disadvantaged role makes the demonstration costly. Conceding the unfairness first adds a separate lever: acknowledging a legitimate objection before the target raises it reduces the perception of manipulative intent and increases persuasion, a well-supported two-sided-message effect. Falsifiable: it predicts a larger shift in the target's fairness expectations after an enacted reversal than after a verbal promise of fair dealing; equal shifts would refute it.

ex.f: Operator signs the first contract as the performer
ex.t: "let's make the first contract be for my (our) behavior and you control the reward... the nonsigner may learn that contracts can work" — Cooper, Heron & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis, 3rd ed.

nodes.name: autonomic-process-hijack
nodes.mech: Breathing is recast as a dose: the operator is revealed to be a gas, so every breath takes more of her in, sometimes marked by a hand-over-mouth image on key lines. Since no one can stop breathing, getting out by 'stopping' is framed as impossible. Numbness, fading body sense and being unable to move are announced ahead of time as harmless side effects not to dwell on, so when they appear they confirm the story instead of alarming the listener. The script openly invites any fantasies about hypnotic drugs the listener already has.
nodes.one_liner: Frame breathing as taking in the operator's 'gas', and label numbness and heaviness in advance as expected side effects.
nodes.why_short: Stillness naturally brings numbness and heaviness; calling them expected in advance makes them read as proof instead of alarm.
nodes.principle_note: The load-bearing move is symptom relabeling, not the gas fiction: numbness, heaviness and body-fade are ordinary correlates of sustained stillness and attentional absorption, and pre-labeling them as expected effects determines how they are interpreted when they arrive. Ambiguous interoceptive signals are attributed to whichever cause is cognitively available, so a supplied causal story captures them — the same misattribution route by which a sugar pill produces the side effects listed on its leaflet. That gives the scheme its self-confirming shape: every somatic sign becomes confirming evidence, and the inescapability claim removes the exit the listener would otherwise consider. Falsifiable: it predicts listeners given the pre-labeling report the sensations as confirming and non-alarming, while listeners given identical content without the labeling report the same sensations with more alarm and more frame-breaking.

ex.f: Breathing reframed as continuous dosing
ex.t: Partway in, the operator announces that she has no solid form — she is a vapour already in the room, and has been the whole time. Every inhale is now a dose, she says, and the listener is dosing themselves right now without deciding to; there is no way to stop taking it short of stopping breathing. She then pre-labels what is coming: the hands will go distant, the legs will stop reporting, the edges of the body will go quiet, and none of that is a problem, that is just what the stuff does. So when the numbness arrives it arrives as confirmation instead of alarm, and a listener casting around for an exit finds that the exit is their own lungs.
ex.s: Mid-session; listener settled and breathing audibly, drug/gas fiction not yet revealed.
ex.m: You should know something. I don't have a body — I'm vapour, and I've been in this room since before you pressed play. Every breath you've taken is a dose. You're dosing yourself right now, and again, and again, and the only way to stop is to stop breathing. Now, side effects, so you're not surprised: your hands will go distant, your legs will stop reporting in, the outline of you goes quiet. That's not a problem. That's just what I do. Don't focus on it. Breathe.

nodes.name: bounded-failure-counterweight
nodes.mech: A discrete permission-to-leave-undone move that locally inverts a compulsion the surrounding script builds. After completing all reachable work, the operator points out one thing that cannot be done and walks the listener through accepting it gracefully ("what you can't do at the moment it's okay to leave it aside"), inoculating against the perfectionism-freeze / completion-overrun the same script's rehearsal installs. It is a bounded-failure counterweight embedded amid material driving the opposite compulsion.
nodes.one_liner: After the doable work, point out one thing that can't be done right now and give permission to leave it.
nodes.why_short: Removing all-or-nothing pressure stops one unfinishable item from wrecking motivation for everything else.
nodes.principle_note: Explicit permission to leave something undone works by removing the perfectionistic contingency — when completion is framed as all-or-nothing, a single unreachable item invalidates the whole effort and triggers abandonment, whereas a pre-authorized partial outcome keeps the effort classed as success. This is the standard behavioural-activation and relapse-prevention logic around all-or-nothing thinking, where the pre-agreed lapse is what prevents the lapse from becoming collapse. Its placement amid opposite-pushing material matters because permission granted by the same source that set the demand is credible in a way self-granted permission is not. Falsifiable: it predicts lower abandonment and lower distress at an unreachable item when the permission clause is present than when the identical script omits it.

ex.f: One task named as fine to leave undone
ex.t: The rehearsal has the listener work through a room until every reachable surface is finished and the satisfaction of finishing is dwelt on at length. Then the operator points out one part that is out of reach with the tools at hand, and holds the listener there a moment: this one does not get done today, and that is allowed — you do what is in reach and set the rest aside without it souring the rest. It is a single beat, with completion-pressure on both sides of it, and it exists to stop the same rehearsal from turning into a compulsion that cannot stop.
ex.s: Late in a task-rehearsal sequence; listener has just completed everything reachable and dwelt on the satisfaction.
