ex.m: For the next twenty minutes I am not going to correct you at all. Not once, no matter what your hands do. Sit exactly as you are, keep your hands loose in your lap, and let them go wherever they want to go — I'm going to sit here and count, and neither of us is going to say a word about it.

nodes.name: graded-induction-suppression-spread
nodes.mech: When a set of triggers has been trained along a series (positions in a row, points on a scale, a run of tones), weakening one also weakens its neighbours, more the closer they are. The nearest drops to almost nothing, the next to about half, and the far end is untouched. So choose which trigger to weaken by the stretch you want flattened: weaken one at the end to flatten that side, or one in the middle to dip the middle and leave both ends.
nodes.one_liner: If you weaken one trigger in a graded series, its nearest neighbours weaken too, and the far ones are untouched.
nodes.why_short: Conditioning spreads to similar stimuli in proportion to how similar they are, and suppression spreads the same way. Well documented in animal learning.
nodes.principle_note: Conditioning attaches not to a point stimulus but to a region of a stimulus dimension, so changes made at one value transfer to nearby values in proportion to their similarity — the same generalization that spreads acquisition also spreads suppression, giving a falloff curve rather than a clean edge. This predicts an ordering constraint the operator can exploit: the shape of the resulting profile depends on where in the series the suppressed anchor sits. Falsifiable: suppress a mid-series anchor and measure the immediate neighbours; if they hold their pre-suppression strength, or if all members drop equally regardless of distance, the gradient claim is wrong and the effect is either absent or an undifferentiated web. Note the specific ratios (nearest to near-zero, second to about half) are a reported profile from one ordered series, not a constant to be assumed across dimensions.

ex.f: Mid-series anchor suppressed to scoop a symmetric well
ex.t: Suppression at the mid-series locus spreads outward by perceptual distance rather than by any stated rule, so anchors two and four come back weak and anchors one and five test near full strength — a gradient, not a boundary. The operator confirms by walking the row afterward and observing a symmetric dip centred on the treated spot, with no instruction ever given about the neighbours.
ex.s: Five touch anchors have been conditioned in order along the subject's forearm, wrist to elbow, and each reliably produces its own response; the operator wants the middle band flat and both ends intact.
ex.m: The third spot — the one halfway up — I'm pressing now, and it does nothing. Nothing at all, no matter how long I hold it. Feel it go flat under my thumb. Just that one.

ex.f: End-of-series anchor suppressed to flatten a one-sided tail
ex.t: Because the suppressed locus sits at the end of the dimension, the falloff runs in only one direction: position four drops substantially, three a little, and one and two are untouched. The operator observes an asymmetric tail rather than the symmetric well produced by a mid-series choice, which is the whole reason anchor selection is the move.
ex.s: Same conditioned row of five, but the operator wants the top of the series dulled while the lower positions keep working at full strength.
ex.m: The last one, up at the elbow — press it yourself. It's dead. Empty. Press it again and feel how there's nothing there to find.

nodes.name: ratio-cost-collapse-threshold
nodes.mech: Ask for too much effort per reward and the behavior stops, even though the reward is still paid every time the requirement is met. Nothing is taken away; the task just is not worth doing anymore. It can happen by raising the demand, or by letting the reward lose its appeal while the demand stays put. The result is someone who stops working beside a reward they still want and could still get.
nodes.one_liner: Demand too much effort per reward and the behaviour stops, even though you always pay out as promised.
nodes.why_short: Behaviour depends on how much reward each unit of effort buys. Raising the requirement too fast causes 'ratio strain', a well known operant finding.
nodes.principle_note: Whether a behaviour keeps going depends on the return per unit of effort, not just on whether a reward arrives. A deal can be honoured perfectly and still fail once the effort costs more than the reward is worth (ratio strain; the breaking point on ratio schedules). Because the collapse is about the exchange rate, you can cause it from either side, by raising the demand or cheapening the reward, and you reverse it by restoring the ratio. Testable: after a collapse, drop the demand back below the threshold with the same reward; if responding does not recover promptly, something lasting was damaged and this is closer to extinction. Or keep the demand and raise the reward; if responding does not resume, the collapse was not about relative return. A caution: someone stopping beside an available reward can also mean they are satiated, or that the task has become linked with something unpleasant, and those need different fixes.

ex.f: Requirement raised past the effort/return boundary with the payoff honoured
ex.t: The contingency stays intact and honoured, so nothing is being extinguished — the behaviour dies purely because a run no longer repays the effort it costs. The tell the operator watches for is a subject who stalls beside a reward they visibly still want and could still obtain, and who resumes promptly when the requirement is dropped back to twenty; a slow or absent recovery would mean extinction instead.
ex.s: A subject has been reliably earning a specific reward by repeating a phrase; the operator now walks the requirement up while paying out every single time it is met.
ex.m: Twenty repetitions earns it. Good — that's yours. Now it's sixty. Good. Now it's two hundred, and yes, you will get it at two hundred, exactly as before, every time, I'm not going to stop paying.

nodes.name: decoy-target-affect-split
nodes.mech: One affective response is split across two targets: a conspicuous, ridiculous stand-in absorbs the sanctioned surface reaction (the audience laughs AT the buffoon), while the sharper unsanctioned charge — contempt, indignation, distrust — is silently re-aimed at the institution, doctrine, or person standing behind the decoy. Because the audience believes it is only enjoying the harmless figure, no defense is mounted for the real target, and the critique is absorbed without ever having been argued. The move requires a visible stand-in genuinely attached to the real target, so that discrediting the front contaminates the back by association rather than by assertion.
nodes.one_liner: Offer a ridiculous stand-in to laugh at, so the audience's contempt quietly sticks to the real person or institution behind it.
nodes.why_short: Feelings toward one thing rub off on things closely linked to it, and people often forget where an attitude came from. Since nothing was argued, nobody pushes back.
nodes.principle_note: Attitude toward a target moves when something reliably associated with it is devalued, and evaluations acquired that way are not tagged with their source — so the audience ends up holding the verdict without holding a memory of being argued into it, which is why it survives arguments it never engaged. Falsifiable: if a listener's rated attitude toward the real target is unchanged after a decoy pass but shifts under direct criticism, the transfer is not occurring; likewise if listeners can accurately report that the decoy segment changed their view of the institution, the undefended-because-unnoticed part of the account fails. Weakening the decoy's real association with the target should weaken the effect; if the effect persists with an arbitrary decoy, the mechanism is something other than associative transfer.

ex.f: Ridiculous stand-in absorbs the laugh while contempt travels to the institution behind it
ex.t: The audience's declared reaction is fully occupied by the harmless figure, so no defence is mounted for the body standing behind him, and the sharper charge — contempt, distrust — arrives at the institution without ever having been argued. The operator observes the subject laughing along and, later, treating the source itself with a flatness they never chose or defended.
ex.s: Mid-session framing passage, addressing a body of outside advice the subject has been consulting; a specific pompous public figure who fronts that advice has already been established as a running joke.
ex.m: Picture him again — the diplomas on the wall behind him, the little laser pointer, the way he says "studies show" and then adjusts his tie. Go ahead and laugh, he's ridiculous. And every single word he reads out was written for him upstairs, by people who chose him for it.

nodes.name: compulsory-shared-transgression
nodes.mech: An act the group would individually refuse is made executable by requiring that every member perform it, at the same time and without exemption. Because no one acted alone, no one holds an identifiable share of the culpability — the responsibility that would have blocked any single actor is spread until each person's portion falls under their own threshold for refusing. The universality is not incidental decoration: exemptions destroy it, since one abstainer restores a locus of comparison and re-individuates everyone else. Its second effect is durable: having all done it, the group now has a common disqualification from denouncing it, which binds membership past the moment.
nodes.one_liner: Make everyone in the group do the forbidden act together, at once, with no one exempt.
nodes.why_short: Responsibility feels split across co-actors, so each person's share falls below what would stop them. Shared guilt afterwards binds the group.
nodes.principle_note: Willingness to do something one judges wrong rises as the number of co-actors rises, because the anticipated blame each person expects to carry falls with the count — the deterrent being defeated is anticipated accountability, not the moral judgment itself, which typically survives intact. Falsifiable: vary group size and the presence of a single exempted abstainer while holding the act and the instruction constant. If participation rate is flat across group sizes, or if it is unaffected by the presence of an abstainer, diffusion is not the operative variable. It also fails if participants who complied report no lower self-attributed responsibility than solo compliers — the mechanism predicts the accounting shifts, not merely the behavior.

ex.f: Simultaneous universal execution with no exemptions
ex.t: Simultaneity and universality mean no member can locate an identifiable share of the culpability, so each person's portion drops below their own refusal threshold and the act becomes executable. The operator watches for hesitation resolving at the count, and should note the durable second effect: having all done it, the group now shares a disqualification from denouncing it, and one permitted abstainer would have restored the locus of comparison that makes refusal possible again.
ex.s: A group session where every member is present and the operator is entirely visible as the one giving the instruction; the act in question is one no individual would perform if singled out.
ex.m: On three, all of you at once — every hand, no one sitting this out, no exceptions and no one watching from the side. If you are in this room you are doing it. One. Two. Three.

nodes.name: outward-reproach-inversion-rule
nodes.mech: The operator installs a standing interpretive rule rather than a one-off reading: every complaint the subject makes about someone else is returned as a statement about the subject. The direction of the accusation is inverted mechanically, without regard to whether the outward charge was accurate, on the stipulated premise that a reproach aimed outward is the audible half of one aimed inward. Because the rule is general, it applies before any particular grievance is examined, so the subject's whole channel for external criticism becomes a channel for producing self-directed material — and complaining about the rule is itself a complaint, and gets the same treatment.
nodes.one_liner: Set a rule: any complaint about someone else is really about you, including complaints about the rule.
nodes.why_short: A blanket rule applied before any complaint is examined can't be checked case by case, and because it applies to objections too, it can never be shown wrong.
nodes.principle_note: A blanket rule applied before any complaint is examined removes the case-by-case check that would let some complaints stand. Its reach comes from being general, not from being right in any particular case, and the fact that it also applies to objections about the rule is what makes it hard to get out of, not any evidence in its favour. Testable: apply the rule to complaints where the outward charge can be independently checked and some are true. If the person accepts the inversion as readily for true complaints as for uncheckable ones, uptake is driven by the rule's form rather than its accuracy. If instead people reliably reject the inversion when a complaint is verifiably true, the rule is not as sweeping as claimed.

ex.f: Standing content-neutral inversion, self-applying to objections
ex.t: Because the inversion is applied before the outward charge is examined and without regard to its accuracy, the subject's entire channel for external criticism is repurposed into a generator of self-directed material rather than closed off. The operator observes complaints continuing to arrive — that is the point, the rule yields content rather than silence — and observes objections to the rule feeding themselves back into it.
ex.s: Early in an arrangement, installed as a rule before any particular grievance has been raised, so it is in force whenever the subject next complains about anyone.
ex.m: Here is how we handle complaints from now on. Anything you say about someone else, you are saying about yourself — I will hear it that way every time, before I've even considered whether they did it. If she's cold, you're cold. And if you tell me this rule is unfair, then what you've just told me is that you are unfair.

nodes.name: protective-drive-moralized-as-fault
nodes.mech: A pre-existing protective or attachment drive — a parent's pull toward a child, loyalty to a partner, the reflex to shield someone — is recoded as a moral failing: attachment is possessiveness, protectiveness is lack of faith, the ordinary impulse is named as the sin. The subject then generates guilt at exactly the moments they behave normally, and the drive begins suppressing itself without further operator input, because every expression of it now arrives pre-labeled as evidence of the fault. This disables a defense from the inside rather than arguing against it: the operator never has to prohibit the behavior, only to supply the label the subject applies to their own impulse.
nodes.one_liner: Relabel a normal protective urge, like checking on a child or partner, as a moral failing.
nodes.why_short: Once a feeling is labelled shameful, the person polices it themselves, so each normal impulse now brings guilt and the urge fades without outside pressure.
nodes.principle_note: A drive that is under moral surveillance is regulated by the person holding it, so labeling it converts an external prohibition into self-enforcement — which is why the suppression continues in the operator's absence and why it targets frequency of expression rather than the drive's strength. Falsifiable: the account predicts guilt reports rise specifically at moments of ordinary expression, not diffusely, and that the underlying drive persists while its expression drops. If measurement shows the drive itself weakening in parallel — or shows guilt distributed evenly rather than time-locked to expressions — the self-suppression story is wrong. It is also falsified if removing the label restores expression only slowly or not at all, since a label-driven mechanism should be more reversible than an extinguished drive.

ex.f: Pre-existing protective drive relabelled as the fault itself
ex.t: No behaviour is prohibited and no remedy is offered — only the label — so the drive begins suppressing itself the moment it next arises, because every ordinary expression now arrives pre-tagged as evidence of a fault the subject supplies themselves. The operator observes guilt appearing at exactly the moments of normal behaviour, and the checking rate declining with no further input.
ex.s: Out of session or in conversation, addressing a drive the subject already held with positive standing — here, the reflex to check on and shield a family member — with nothing yet installed for them to fall short of.
ex.m: That pull you feel to call and check she's alright — sit with what it actually is. It isn't care. It's you needing to be needed. Every time you reach for the phone, that's the wanting-to-own showing itself, and you'll feel it again in about an hour.

nodes.name: external-tie-severance
nodes.mech: Family, employment, and friendships outside the group are dismantled under sustained pressure — moves, schedule capture, prescribed cutoffs, relabeling outsiders as hostile — until the group is the only source of belonging, income, and information. Two things go at once: the triangulation channel, since no one remains who could compare the group's claims against an outside account, and the exit route, since leaving now costs everything rather than costing membership. Neither is a claim made to the subject; both are structural facts about their life, which is why the effect does not depend on the subject believing anything in particular.
nodes.one_liner: Gradually cut their outside family, job and friends until the group is their only source of belonging, money and information.
nodes.why_short: People correct beliefs by checking with others, and leaving is cheap when you have a life outside. Remove both and doubt has nowhere to go and exit costs everything.
nodes.principle_note: Belief correction depends on access to independent sources, and the cost of leaving a group is set by what one has outside it — so cutting external ties raises exit cost and removes correction at the same time without any persuasion being attempted. Falsifiable: the account predicts that restoring a single outside contact should produce measurable belief revision and raise departure rates even with all in-group content unchanged. If reconnecting former members to outside ties reliably produces no revision, the correction-access half is wrong. It further predicts that members with intact outside employment or kin leave at higher rates than matched severed members; equal rates would show that severance is a correlate of commitment rather than a cause of retention.

ex.f: Removing the material means of consulting an outside reference
ex.t: Nothing has been asserted about the outside world and nothing relabeled — the subject can go on believing their family is entirely reasonable and still have no income, no transport, and no independently held line with which to reach them. The operator observes the erosion downstream: perception-checking stops not because it was defeated but because there is no longer a position from which to attempt it, and the group's account becomes the only reachable one.
ex.s: Months into a live arrangement, out of session, where the subject has already moved into shared housing and the operator now closes the remaining independent channels; no claim is being made about anyone's trustworthiness.
ex.m: Give notice at work on Monday — we'll cover you, so you won't need the income. The car goes back this week; I'll drive you where you need to go. And the phone plan comes off your name onto the house account, so you don't have to think about the bill again.

ex.f: Schedule capture and relocation, with no cutoff ever announced
ex.t: Nothing is ever framed as a demand to drop anyone: the group's calendar simply expands until no unclaimed evening remains, and a relocation puts distance in the way of the rest. The ties end by attrition, so there is no moment the subject can point to as the one they should have refused, and no instruction to disobey. The structural tells are the ones to read — whether an outside account could still be reached to check a claim, and what leaving would now cost. Both answers change long before anyone notices a decision was made.
ex.s: Out of session; a debrief or orientation frame where a recruiter describes how membership works, with the subject already attending regularly.
ex.m: Nobody here is going to ask you to give anyone up — that's not how we do things. What I'd suggest is you come to the Tuesday study as well as Sunday, and Thursday service prep, and we do Saturday work parties most weeks. And there's a room opening up in the house on the north side, forty minutes closer, cheaper than what you're paying. Take it and you'd have your evenings back. See how it looks in six months.

nodes.name: pre-pairing-exposure-immunization
nodes.mech: Repeated unpaired exposure to a cue before it is paired with an outcome can reduce subsequent evaluative conditioning relative to a cue without that exposure history. The relevant operation is pre-exposure before acquisition, not weakening an already established cue association. The cited meta-analysis distinguishes cue-only trials before, during, and after pairing: before and after trials were associated with reduced evaluative-conditioning magnitude, while intermixed trials during acquisition showed a different pattern. Two possible writing applications remain hypotheses: participant-side familiarization with a prospective cue, and author-side reserving a cue until its meaningful introduction. Neither application establishes durable immunity, a fixed maximum installable response, or a prescribed exposure count.
nodes.one_liner: Before trying to charge a cue, expose it repeatedly with nothing happening, or do this yourself to blunt a cue someone might use on you.
nodes.why_short: A stimulus first experienced as meaningless is slower and harder to condition later. Replicated widely across species.
nodes.principle_note: A review of evaluative-conditioning studies (learning to like or dislike something through pairing) found that showing a cue on its own, with nothing happening, weakens later conditioning when it comes before the pairing (latent inhibition) and weakens existing conditioning when it comes after (extinction). Exposures mixed in during the pairing are a separate case. So timing matters and should be kept clear. The evidence does not show that exposure after pairing does nothing, that early exposure guarantees a lower ceiling, or that repeating a cue a hundred times a day protects someone against its use in scripts. Ideas such as the cue being learned as irrelevant may explain the pre-exposure effect, but they are explanations, not direct evidence for these uses. Whether any protection lasts over time or carries into other settings has not been tested.

ex.f: Subject-side immunization: pre-spending a cue's conditionability
ex.t: This illustrates the temporal difference between prior unpaired exposure and later pairing. The cited review supports a pre-exposure effect on evaluative-conditioning magnitude in its evidence base, but does not supply this human script scenario, a fixed daily dose, or proof that the word can never acquire a strong response. A source-grounded comparison would retain the exposure history and avoid inventing a measured flattened asymptote.
ex.s: A hypothetical familiarization example before a particular cue-outcome association has been introduced; no protection or conditioning ceiling is assumed.
ex.m: The character repeatedly encounters the same word in ordinary, unpaired contexts before it acquires a special role in the story. Treat the possible effect of that history as a question, not as an instruction promising immunity.

ex.f: Operator-side sequencing constraint: never spend a cue on ambient use
ex.t: The author-side variant preserves the useful sequencing question: has this cue already appeared without its intended association? It does not claim that all earlier ordinary usage spends a fixed store of conditionability or that later cue-only exposure is inert. The cited review explicitly treats post-pairing CS-only trials as capable of reducing evaluative conditioning.
ex.s: At the writing stage, an author compares a cue used incidentally in the opening with a cue first introduced at its meaningful moment.
ex.m: Mark the cue's first appearance and any earlier unpaired uses. If reserving it for the meaningful passage, record that as a design choice and a hypothesis about exposure history, not as a guarantee of a stronger install.

nodes.name: external-role-entry-lock
nodes.mech: Two pressures are set before the person hears what the program is really about, and neither comes from the session itself. First, the real content is held back at invitation; what is described is a harmless cover, such as a training day or workshop, that nobody would refuse. Second, the invitation comes through someone with real power over the person (an employer, supervisor, licensing body or landlord), so attending becomes a condition of something they depend on. Once the real content appears, walking out means risking their job. Requests to leave are refused or put off, so their staying, later cited as consent, was never free.
nodes.one_liner: Invite people to a program under a harmless label through their boss or licensing body, so leaving once the real content appears costs their job.
nodes.why_short: Uses an existing power structure so the cost of leaving is high. A known high-control group recruitment pattern; described here so it can be recognised.
nodes.principle_note: Two separate effects compound. Sunk-cost and effort-justification research shows that people who cannot leave a situation without material loss tend to resolve the dissonance by revising their evaluation of the situation upward rather than by absorbing the loss — attitude follows the constrained behaviour. Separately, the compliance literature on legitimate authority shows that requests routed through an established role relationship draw far higher compliance than identical requests from a stranger, because the role, not the request's content, is what is being evaluated. Falsifiable: run the identical program with identical nondisclosure but voluntary attendance and no employment link. If uptake, stated endorsement, and refusal-to-leave rates are the same, then the structural cost is decorative and the nondisclosure alone is carrying the effect. It would also be contradicted if subjects with genuinely portable skills and easy re-employment showed the same retention as those with high exit cost — the mechanism predicts retention should track the actual cost of leaving, not merely its assertion.
steps: Disclose only a harmless cover when inviting.
Make attendance a condition of employment or licence.

ex.f: Benign cover at invitation plus third-party role power holding the exit cost
ex.t: The harmless cover is not something anyone would turn down, and the cost of leaving is held by the employer rather than the operator. When the person later asks to leave, the request runs into a real cost, not just awkwardness, so their staying, which may later be cited as consent, was never a free choice.
ex.s: The invitation, made outside any session and before any of the real content exists. The person's supervisor, not the operator, makes the approach.
ex.m: Attendance is expected for everyone on your team — it's a two-day communication workshop, and I've already put you on the list. HR is tracking who completes it, so let me know if there's a genuine conflict and we'll find you another date.

nodes.name: credentialed-intermediary-duty-inversion
nodes.mech: A third party whose professional role carries a presumed duty of confidentiality and independent loyalty to the subject — clinician, counselor, sponsor, chaplain — is recruited and their role duty inverted while the professional surface is left intact. The channel then runs both ways: contents the subject discloses under the confidentiality presumption are reported upward, and directives from the centre come back down wearing clinical authority ('as your therapist, I'd advise'). The same figure gatekeeps outside care, so second opinions are pre-screened, and doubters routed to them for help are retained rather than released. What makes it work is that the subject's own disclosure is the instrument: the more candidly they use the channel, the better the surveillance and the more precisely targeted the returning directives.
nodes.one_liner: Recruit their therapist or counsellor so private disclosures get reported to the group and the group's orders come back as professional advice.
nodes.why_short: People confide more when they believe a channel is private, and trust advice wearing professional credentials. Turning that role against them abuses both.
nodes.principle_note: Disclosure behaviour is governed by expectations about how information will travel, not by the information's content — the privacy literature shows candour rises sharply when a channel is believed confidential and collapses when the belief is broken. Inverting the duty while preserving the surface keeps the subject's disclosure calibrated to a channel that no longer exists, which is why the yield is higher than any direct interrogation would produce. On the return leg, source-credibility research gives the second half: identical advice attributed to a credentialed source is accepted at higher rates and subjected to less counter-argument, so a directive laundered through clinical framing meets less scrutiny than the same directive from the centre. Falsifiable: if subjects told plainly that session contents are shared upward went on disclosing at the same rate and accepted the returning directives equally, the confidentiality presumption would not be load-bearing and the mechanism would reduce to ordinary advice-following. Also contradicted if uptake of the relayed directives were no higher than uptake of the same directives delivered unlaundered by the centre.

ex.f: Directive returning downward wearing the clinical credential
ex.t: The directive arrives wearing a genuine credential, so refusing it means refusing professional advice rather than the operator. Referral is routed through the same figure, so second opinions are pre-screened; the operator observes whether the subject stops seeking outside input independently.
ex.s: Weeks in; the subject has been seeing a counselor the operator recruited, and has just been told to raise a specific doubt with her in session.
ex.m: Bring it to her on Thursday — all of it, the way it actually sits in your head, not the tidy version. She'll tell you straight, and whatever she says, that's the answer; I'm not going to argue with someone who's actually qualified. And if she thinks a second opinion would help, she'll be the one to point you at the right person — she knows who's good.

ex.f: Upward leg: the disclosure presumption harvested and cashed back
ex.t: The subject's own honesty becomes the tool: the more openly they use the confidential setting, the sharper the instructions that come back. A sign the arrangement is holding: the subject keeps confiding even after learning that what they say is being passed on, because the framing has recast the breach as coordinated care.
ex.s: The next session with the operator, after the subject's counseling appointment; the operator already holds the contents of that hour.
ex.m: You told her about the thing with your sister — the Tuesday you didn't call back. I'm not going to pretend I don't know; she and I talk, because we're both on your side of this. So let's use it: she thinks the pattern there is the same pattern you're running with me, and she's right, and she'd like you to start with me the way you started with her.

nodes.name: element-decode-against-held-key
nodes.mech: The operator holds a key in advance — a theory of what the subject wants, fears, or is — and treats the subject's productions as ciphertext to be decoded element by element against it. Arbitrary detail is not dismissed as arbitrary; each fragment is assigned a mapping, and the accumulated mappings are then presented back as a reading of what the material was really about. Because the material is unstructured and the key is flexible enough to absorb any element, the decode always succeeds, and its success is presented to the subject as evidence that the key is correct. The subject supplied the content, so the reading arrives as a discovery about themself rather than a claim from the operator, and disputing it requires disputing their own material.
nodes.one_liner: Go in with a theory of who they are, decode every detail of their dream or story against it, then present the fit as proof.
nodes.why_short: A flexible key can explain any detail, so the decode always appears to work. People find readings built from their own material very convincing.
nodes.principle_note: The engine is the Barnum/Forer effect combined with confirmation bias in an unconstrained mapping space. When a key can be applied flexibly to material with no independent structure, the number of available mappings grows fast enough that a fit is always findable, and the finding of it carries no evidential weight — but subjective accuracy ratings for such readings are consistently high, and high specifically when the recipient supplied the raw material, because they can verify the elements are genuinely theirs even though the mapping is not. This is why decode readings feel more probative than generic ones. Falsifiable and this has actually been done: give the subject a decode generated against a key drawn for a different person, or against no key at all, and collect accuracy ratings. If the mismatched decode rates as accurate as the matched one, the key is contributing nothing and the apparent confirmation is entirely recipient-side fitting. It is also contradicted if decodes made blind to biographical information were rated as accurate as decodes made with it — the mechanism requires that the pre-held key, not the procedure's form, be doing the work.

ex.f: Per-element decode of volunteered imagery against a pre-held key
ex.t: The key absorbs any element, so the decode always closes, and its closure is cashed back as proof the key was right. Because the raw material was subject-supplied, disputing the reading means disputing their own account; the operator watches for the shift from puzzlement to recognition, then for the subject volunteering new details already pre-fitted to the key.
ex.s: Mid-session; the operator has already privately decided the subject is organised around wanting permission to stop being responsible, and has just had them describe a daydream in detail.
ex.m: Listen to what you actually gave me. The door was unlocked — that's not scenery, that's you telling me nobody was making you. The bag you left in the hallway is the part of you that carries things for other people. The rain outside meant it was safe to stay in. Three separate pieces, all pointing the same direction, and you're the one who put them there — so tell me I'm wrong about what you want.

nodes.name: retrospective-influence-disclosure
nodes.mech: After a frame is already installed and running, the subject is given the two things that were withheld while it was being installed: the facts that were kept from them at the point of entry, and a plain naming of the influence steps that were used on them, in the order they were used. The combination lets the subject re-read their own conversion as an engineered sequence rather than a discovery, which is what re-opens the stay-or-leave decision as genuinely theirs. It is restorative rather than persuasive — it does not argue for leaving, and a subject who stays after it has run has made a choice the pre-disclosure subject could not have made. The operator's license narrows when it runs: nothing about the frame is left available to be cashed later.
nodes.one_liner: Afterwards, tell them what you held back at the start and walk through the influence steps you used, in order.
nodes.why_short: Debriefing studies show that explaining how a belief was produced, not just correcting it, reduces how much of it sticks. That gives the person back a real choice.
nodes.principle_note: The direct evidence comes from debriefing research. A debriefing that both supplies the withheld facts and explains the procedure that produced the belief reliably reduces lingering belief, whereas a bare factual correction often does not: people keep a belief after being told its basis was false, but less so once shown how it was manufactured (belief perseverance; process debriefing). That is why both halves are needed. Two limits: this research uses short laboratory manipulations, so applying it to a belief held for years and reinforced socially is an inference, and effects are likely smaller and slower where relationships and identity are involved. Testable: compare giving the facts alone with facts plus walking through the steps; if belief and commitment shift the same, naming the steps adds nothing. And if disclosure reliably pushed people one way, such as toward leaving, rather than simply reopening the decision, it would be persuasion in disguise rather than a genuine return of choice.

ex.f: Withheld facts plus a named step-by-step of the influence used
ex.t: Supplying the withheld facts alongside the named sequence lets the subject re-read their conversion as engineered rather than discovered, which reopens the stay-or-leave decision as genuinely theirs. Nothing is collected — the operator's later leverage is spent, not banked — and the tell of a correct run is that the subject can now argue against the frame using the operator's own inventory.
ex.s: The frame is installed and running; the operator initiates the disclosure unprompted, out of trance, with nothing pending and nothing being asked for.
ex.m: Two things I kept from you when you came in, and you should have had both: I already knew the answer to the question I opened with, and the people you met on the second night were there because I asked them to be. And here's the order I did it in — I matched your breathing, I put you next to someone who agreed before you spoke, I named your doubt before you could, and I made leaving expensive by giving you something you'd have to hand back. That's all of it. None of that is an argument to stay and none of it is an argument to go; you decide now with what you should have had then.

nodes.name: venue-as-screening-filter
nodes.mech: Rather than screening people, the operator screens locations, then lets the location do the screening: a physical choke-point through which a desired population must pass in an already-qualified state — arriving alone, in transit, newly displaced, at a loose hour — is selected, and the operator simply waits there. Because everyone at that spot already meets the criteria the operator would otherwise have to test for, no qualifying questions are asked and no selection is visible. First contact can then be minimal and warm, and it reads as spontaneous kindness from a stranger rather than as solicitation, because from inside the encounter there is no evidence that the encounter was arranged. The move happens entirely before any contact exists, which is what makes it invisible to the person being selected and unavailable to any consent process running downstream of contact.
nodes.one_liner: Choose a place where the people you want pass through already alone or vulnerable, wait there, and open with small kindness.
nodes.why_short: The location does the screening, so no selecting is visible. The target can't see who didn't pass through, so the meeting feels like chance.
nodes.principle_note: Selection effects are invisible from inside a sample: a person who encounters an operator at a location cannot observe the counterfactual population that did not pass through it, so a heavily filtered encounter is indistinguishable from a chance one on the evidence available to the participant. Base-rate reasoning about how likely this kind of meeting was requires knowing the denominator, and the venue conceals it. Falsifiable: compare uptake from the same approach script delivered at a selected choke-point versus at a matched-traffic control location; if uptake is equal, the venue is contributing nothing and the effect belongs to the script. Also testable independently: if people approached at choke-points do not rate the encounter as more spontaneous than those approached elsewhere, the reads-as-kindness half of the claim fails even if the yield half holds. This is recorded as a mechanism operating on non-consenting targets and is listed for recognition and defence; the consent and bounding flags mark that it has no legitimate deployment against someone who has not agreed to be approached.

ex.f: Choke-point selection, then minimal warm first contact
ex.t: Everyone standing there at that hour is already alone, in transit and unmoored, so no qualifying question is asked and no selection is visible. From inside the encounter there is no evidence it was arranged, so it reads as spontaneous kindness; the operator observes only base rates — how often the offer is taken at that spot — because the selection work finished before anyone spoke.
ex.s: No subject exists yet. The operator has chosen a location whose traffic is already qualified — the last bus platform, the hostel kitchen at 2am, the hospital smoking area — and has simply been present there for an hour.
ex.m: There's another one at ten past, if that was yours that just went. I've got a spare coffee going cold here — take it, I'm not going to drink two.

nodes.name: spontaneous-charge-redirection
nodes.mech: A strong relational charge forms between subject and operator that the operator did not build and did not ask for — intensified attachment, hostility, idealization, or a mixture — and instead of managing it as an obstacle or letting it distort the work, the operator captures it and points it at the task. The charge becomes the engine: the subject's investment in the operator is redirected into investment in doing the work, so the very intensity that was derailing sessions is what now sustains them. The defining fork is capture versus manufacture — the operator did not create this charge and could not have, which is why the move is only available reactively and why misreading a manufactured attachment as a spontaneous one is the main failure. Because the charge is bidirectional, the operator's own investment is part of what has to be named and handled rather than assumed neutral.
nodes.one_liner: When the subject develops a strong unasked-for feeling toward you, name it and point that energy into doing the work.
nodes.why_short: Strong investment in a person can be channelled into effort on tasks linked to them. This comes from clinical writing on transference and hasn't been tested directly.
nodes.principle_note: Motivation can transfer between goals that feel linked, so an existing strong attachment can be recruited to sustain effort on work the person would not otherwise keep up; the feeling supplies drive that instruction alone does not. That same link is why it is high-risk: the work now depends on the relationship, and effort is likely to collapse if the relationship does. Testable: if people whose feeling was openly redirected into the work engage no better than matched people whose feeling was simply acknowledged and set aside, the redirection adds nothing beyond ordinary rapport. More importantly, if they keep going just as well after the relationship ends, the work was never running on the attachment and the dependency worry is unfounded. Consent and limits matter, because steering an attachment the person did not choose to form, without saying so, turns an unasked-for bond into leverage. The related clinical idea of working with transference is not independently established.

ex.f: Unbidden intensity named, then pointed at the task
ex.t: The charge stops being an obstacle and becomes the engine, so the intensity that was derailing sessions is what now sustains them. The operator must first verify the charge is unbidden — the check is that nothing in their own conduct engineered stake or debt — since misreading a manufactured attachment as spontaneous is the named failure; the operator's own investment gets named rather than assumed neutral.
ex.s: Several sessions in; a strong attachment the operator did not build has formed and is derailing sessions — the subject is preoccupied with the operator's approval rather than with the material.
ex.m: Something has got very strong between us, and I didn't build it and neither of us asked for it. I'm not going to pretend it isn't there, and I'm not going to let it eat the hour. So we're going to spend it: all of that wanting-me-to-be-pleased goes into the thing you've been walking around for three weeks. Do that piece now, out loud — and yes, do it for me, because that's what currently has fuel in it.

nodes.name: friction-as-artifact-filter
nodes.mech: The operator deliberately arouses resistance around a piece of material before accepting it, on the reasoning that material which survives active friction is less likely to be an artifact of the operator's own influence. Rather than smoothing the path so the subject agrees easily, the operator pushes back, invites contradiction, states the opposing case, or withholds the confirmation the subject is angling for, and only credits what still stands afterward. The move constrains the operator rather than the subject: it deliberately raises the cost of getting a yes, and it makes an easy yes a warning sign rather than a success. Its practical form is a rule about what counts as evidence in the operator's own notes — agreement obtained without friction is provisionally discounted, and material the subject maintained against pressure is weighted up.
nodes.one_liner: Push back and argue the other side before accepting their agreement, and treat an easy yes as suspect.
nodes.why_short: Going along and truly agreeing look the same when agreeing is easy. Making a yes cost something tells the two apart and cuts down on answers just meant to please you.
nodes.principle_note: Compliance and genuine endorsement produce the same surface response under low-friction conditions, so an easy yes carries almost no information about which one occurred; adding a cost to agreeing separates them, because a subject merely going along has little reason to pay it. The filter works by raising the response threshold until demand characteristics stop being sufficient to clear it. Falsifiable and directly checkable: compare material accepted under friction with material accepted smoothly on any independent criterion — later stability, corroboration from outside the session, whether it survives a change of operator. If the friction-filtered material fares no better, the filter is costing sessions and buying nothing. There is also a real failure mode worth stating: friction selects for stubbornness as well as for accuracy, so a subject who simply digs in under pressure will pass this filter while a compliant but correct subject fails it, which means the filter reduces one artifact class at the price of introducing another.

ex.f: Counter-case stated before the yes is accepted
ex.t: Raising the cost of a yes means only material that survives friction gets credited, and an easy yes becomes a warning sign rather than a result. The operator observes the difference between a subject who holds the claim under pressure and adds detail, versus one who folds or softens — the latter marks probable operator artifact and is discounted in the notes.
ex.s: The subject has just produced a piece of material the operator would like to credit — a memory, a preference, a stated want — and is visibly angling for confirmation.
ex.m: Before I take that: I think you might be handing it to me because I've been leaning on it for twenty minutes and you can hear which answer I want. So here's the opposite case — that it never mattered to you and you've assembled it just now out of what I've been implying. Argue me out of it. If you can't be bothered to argue, I'm writing it down as mine, not yours.

nodes.name: out-of-band-corroboration-confrontation
nodes.mech: The operator steps outside the conversation and gets an account of the disputed events from an independent person with no stake in how the subject comes across, then returns and lays out where the two accounts differ. Because the operator now holds a version the subject did not write and cannot revise, the usual ways of smoothing things over (vagueness, qualifying, gradual restating) stop working. This usually forces a clear retraction, which is informative in itself: the point defended hardest tends to be where something was being hidden. The outside source does the work, not the tone of the confrontation, which can stay gentle.
nodes.one_liner: Check their story with an independent outside person, then confront them with the differences.
nodes.why_short: A story only they can check is easy to keep up. An independent account they can't change ends that control, so vagueness and rewording stop working.
nodes.principle_note: An account defended in private is cheap to maintain because the only auditor is the person maintaining it; introducing a record the subject neither produced nor can revise removes that monopoly, and the cost of continuing to defend rises sharply once a second source is in the room. The retraction is informative for a separate reason: effortful defense is not distributed randomly across a narrative, so the locations where it concentrates carry information about what the subject is protecting. Falsifiable: if subjects retracted at the same rate and at the same points when confronted with a discrepancy the operator merely asserted (no actual third party consulted) as when a real independent account was produced, then the out-of-band sourcing is decorative and the effect is ordinary confrontation pressure. Equally, if the retraction points were uncorrelated with independently established concealment, the diagnostic claim fails. Note this move also generates false retractions under pressure, so a retraction is evidence about defense intensity, not about truth.

ex.f: Independent account collected outside the session, then the discrepancy laid down
ex.t: Because the operator holds an account the person did not write and cannot revise, vagueness and slow restatement stop working, and a clear retraction usually follows. That retraction is telling, since the point defended hardest is often where something was hidden. The tone can stay gentle; the outside account does the work, not pressure.
ex.s: The subject has given a shifting account of a disputed episode; between sessions the operator has spoken with a third party who was present and has no stake in the subject's self-presentation.
ex.m: I spoke to the person who drove you home that night. Her account and yours don't match on one point: she says you'd already made the call before you got in the car, and you've told me twice it was after. I'm not angry and I'm not building a case — I just can't work from a version I know isn't the one that happened. Which of those is true?

nodes.name: designated-bearer-culpability-transfer
nodes.mech: A group's shared blame is piled onto one person through an acted-out ritual, and that person's acceptance is staged to look like their own free choice. Everyone else leaves feeling lighter without having admitted anything. Because the transfer is performed rather than argued, there is no claim for anyone to dispute, and because the bearer seems to volunteer, nobody, including the bearer, experiences it as something forced on them.
nodes.one_liner: Stage a ritual where one member 'chooses' to take on the group's blame, so everyone else walks away feeling cleared.
nodes.why_short: Pinning blame on one visible person gives everyone else a clean exit; acting it out rather than arguing it leaves nothing to dispute, and the 'volunteer' framing hides that anyone was assigned.
nodes.principle_note: Groups discharge collective liability more readily onto a single identified bearer than by distributing it, because a concentrated attribution gives the remainder a clean exit that a distributed one does not; enactment rather than argument supplies the warrant, since a performed act leaves no premise available to dispute. The self-chosen surface matters independently: a transfer that reads as volunteered does not activate the fairness objections an assignment would, from the group or from the bearer. Falsifiable: run the same re-enactment with the bearer visibly assigned by the group rather than appearing to elect the role; if the group's reported relief and the bearer's uptake are unchanged, the concealed-choice element is decorative and the effect is plain scapegoating. Separately, if participants' sense of their own culpability is unchanged after the ritual — measured before and after — the transfer claim fails outright, whatever the bearer reports.

ex.f: Staged re-enactment with the load taken up as the bearer's own election
ex.t: Blame moves sideways across persons, from the collective onto one member, and the ritual form supplies the warrant — the transfer is enacted, so there is no proposition to contest. The self-chosen surface conceals the reassignment, so no participant experiences having imposed anything; after the move a different person is carrying what the group was carrying, and everyone else leaves lighter with standing intact.
ex.s: A group session closing out a period the whole group is implicated in; one member has been quietly set up all evening as the one who will step forward, and everyone is standing in a ring.
ex.m: One of you is going to take up what the rest of us have been carrying. Nobody will be asked and nobody will be chosen — whoever it is will simply step into the middle when they're ready. When you step in, you carry it for all of us, and the rest of us set it down. Step in when it's yours.

nodes.name: peripheral-first-inhibition-spread
nodes.mech: To get rid of an unwanted reaction, the operator never works on it directly. Instead they start with cues that only faintly resemble the real one and let those fail to produce the reaction, then move step by step to closer and closer cues. The weakening spreads inward, so by the time the original cue is reached, if it ever is, it already sits among similar cues that no longer work. Because the guarded cue is never approached while it is still guarded, the person never has a reason to defend it.
nodes.one_liner: To weaken an unwanted reaction, work only on similar cues far from it, moving gradually closer, and never touch the original directly.
nodes.why_short: Extinction at one point spreads to similar cues; working the neighbours first avoids provoking the defences that tackling the target head-on would raise.
nodes.principle_note: Training a cue to mean that nothing happens does not stay local. The effect spreads to similar cues along a gradient (generalization of conditioned inhibition), so working on neighbouring cues leaves suppression that reaches the untouched target in proportion to how similar it is. Working from far to near lets that effect build up before you approach the defended cue, instead of provoking the protection that direct contact would. The test is sharp and cheap: run the sequence but stop before the target, then check the target. If its response is unchanged, nothing spread and every gain was local. And if starting near the target works just as well as starting far away, the order does not matter and this is just ordinary extinction. Pavlov explained the spread with a physiological theory of 'irradiation' that has since been abandoned; the gradient itself holds up, his explanation does not.

ex.f: Outward-in ladder: distant neighbours worked, the defended cue untouched
ex.t: The neck is never touched while it is still defended, so the subject has no reason to put up the protection that direct work would trigger. Meanwhile the learning that nothing happens builds at the neighbouring spots and spreads inward toward the neck. To check whether it is working, stop short of the neck and test it: if the flinch is unchanged, nothing has spread.
ex.s: The subject flinches hard at one specific cue — a hand at the back of the neck — and has defended it every time it was approached directly. The operator opens at the far end of the same dimension.
ex.m: Today I'm not going anywhere near your neck. Give me your left forearm — two fingers resting there, and nothing happens, and you notice nothing happens. Now the inside of the elbow: same thing, nothing. Now the top of the shoulder. Nothing there either. That's where we stop for today.

nodes.name: specificity-demand-degeneralization
nodes.mech: When the person speaks in vague generalities, the operator treats this as hiding rather than imprecision and will not move on until they give one concrete instance: which time, which person, what exactly was said. A vague worry has no edges, so it cannot be examined or argued with; a single specific example can be checked and has a definite feeling attached. Usually the person gives an example and the diffuse dread turns into something nameable that can be worked on. The point is to keep pressing each time they drift back into generalities, not any single question.
nodes.one_liner: When the subject speaks vaguely, refuse to move on until they give one concrete example: which time, which person, what was said.
nodes.why_short: A vague statement can't be checked or felt; a specific instance has edges, so it can be examined and the diffuse feeling becomes something nameable to work with.
nodes.finding_name: Concreteness training (Watkins); NLP meta-model is the folk version
nodes.principle_note: A vague generality has nothing specific to check and nothing particular to feel, so it can be held indefinitely at little cost. Replacing it with one real instance brings in both, which is why people resist the swap and why it changes what there is to work with. The operator's job is to keep refusing the retreat, because the person will drift back to generalities whenever allowed. Testable: compare steadily demanding instances with sympathetically accepting the general version; if both lead to the same feelings and the same progress afterwards, the specificity does nothing beyond attention or persistence. A serious risk: pressing for an instance may produce an invented one rather than a recalled one. Pressured recall is known to generate confabulation, and if supplied instances match independently checkable events no better than chance, that is what is happening. The approach resembles the NLP 'meta-model' challenge, which is not itself established.

ex.f: Holding out for one instance across successive retreats into abstraction
ex.t: A diffuse formulation has no edges and cannot be examined or contradicted; forcing one instance in its place collapses it into a proposition with a truth value and a specific affect attached. The operator's persistence across each retreat is the technique rather than any single question, and the observable result is the dread resolving into something nameable and workable.
ex.s: The subject is describing a diffuse dread — 'people always end up disappointed in me' — and each attempt to pin it down slides back into a generality.
ex.m: Not people. One person, one time. Which one. — 'A lot of them' isn't a time; give me the day. — Now what did she actually say. Her words, not your summary. Say the sentence.

nodes.name: operator-completed-disclosure
nodes.mech: When the person stalls partway through saying something they cannot bring themselves to say, the operator says the rest of it for them and leaves them only to agree or correct. The hard part, actually naming the thing, is done by the operator, so the person only has to not object, which is much easier than producing the words. The risk is real: a wrong guess that the person accepts out of relief or pressure puts the operator's words into the record, and in the moment there is no reliable way to tell a true accepted completion from a false one.
nodes.one_liner: When the subject freezes mid-confession, finish the sentence for them and let them just agree or correct you.
nodes.why_short: Saying something makes you its author; nodding along to someone else's words is much cheaper, so the block is bypassed. Risk: they may accept a wrong guess.
nodes.principle_note: The barrier at a stall is usually the act of saying rather than the content itself, since uttering a thing makes one its author in a way that assenting to another's utterance does not — so relocating the utterance to the operator removes the specific cost that was blocking while leaving the information transfer intact. Assent is cheaper than production for the same proposition, and that gap is the whole lever. Falsifiable: compare stalls closed by operator completion against stalls met with silent waiting. If disclosure rates are equal, the completion is buying nothing over patience. The contamination claim needs its own and harder test, because it determines whether this move is usable at all: seed deliberately incorrect completions at stall points and measure the acceptance rate. If subjects reliably reject wrong completions, the risk is manageable; if wrong completions are accepted at a substantial rate — which is what the suggestibility of the stall moment predicts — then anything obtained this way is a joint construction and must not be treated as the subject's own report. Until that rate is known, output from this move should be labelled operator-contaminated by default.

ex.f: Operator speaks the stalled remainder; subject left only to assent or correct
ex.t: The threshold drops from producing the words to not objecting to them, which is materially cheaper, and the disclosure enters the record jointly authored. The intrinsic cost is contamination: an accepted true completion and an accepted false one look identical in the moment, so the operator marks it as operator-supplied and re-tests it later from a different angle.
ex.s: The subject is mid-sentence on loaded material of their own, has stopped dead, and is not going to finish it.
ex.m: You wanted him to notice you were gone. That's the end of the sentence — I'll say it so you don't have to. Nod if that's it, or tell me which word I got wrong.

nodes.name: motor-discharge-affect-venting
nodes.mech: Built-up emotion that has had no outlet is let out through the body: shouting, sobbing, crying, shaking, or a permitted noise. The operator does not reinterpret the feeling, argue with it, or tie it to a trigger; they simply give it a physical way out, and the intensity drops as the action runs. Used to bring a flooded, overexcited or stuck person back to a workable level, or to end a heavy scene without leaving them still charged up.
nodes.one_liner: Let built-up emotion out through the body: shout, sob, shake, or make a permitted noise, without reinterpreting it.
nodes.why_short: Physical expression gives arousal somewhere to go and can bring a flooded subject back to a workable level, though venting anger can also amplify it.
nodes.principle_note: Vigorous physical and bodily output is physiologically incompatible with sustaining a peak stress-arousal state at full strength: the activity itself uses up the arousal it expresses. That is why crying, shouting and shaking are, across cultures, the usual end of an emotional episode rather than its middle. Testable: if instructed venting left reported intensity and bodily markers of arousal unchanged, or raised them, compared with sitting still, in the same aroused people, the idea is wrong. It also predicts that venting should work whatever the emotion; if it only ever lowered negative feelings and never calmed over-arousal from positive ones, the claim would be much narrower.

ex.f: Vocal discharge on a counted release after a stalled peak
ex.t: The stored excitation is given a motor channel with a defined start and a defined end, so it is spent rather than contained. The operator watches for the shoulders dropping on the exhale and the breathing rate falling within two or three breaths; if the rigidity persists, the discharge did not run.
ex.s: Late in a heavy scene; the subject is flooded, breathing fast, gone rigid, and has not moved or made a sound in a minute.
ex.m: Don't hold it. On three I want it out of your mouth — as loud as it comes, no words, just the sound. One. Two. Three — out, all of it, keep the sound going until your lungs are empty, and then take one slow breath in.

ex.f: Tremor-permitted shaking through the limbs
ex.t: Removing the clamp converts a suppressed tremor into a running motor discharge, and the intensity decays as the movement spends it. The observable is the tremor tapering unaided and the jaw releasing; nothing is relabelled as depth, so the subject simply comes back into a workable band.
ex.s: Subject has been held at high arousal and is visibly trembling but clamping down on it — jaw set, hands gripping.
ex.m: Let the shaking have your arms. Unclench your hands, let your elbows go loose and let it run all the way down to your fingers — don't steady it, don't make it bigger, just stop stopping it. Stay with it until it slows down on its own.

ex.f: Sanctioned crying to close a scene without stranded charge
ex.t: Explicit permission plus an untimed window lets the secretory channel run to completion, so the residual charge is discharged inside the scene rather than carried out of it. The operator watches for the crying to peak and then self-terminate; a subject who tightens instead has not accepted the permission and needs the offer repeated more plainly.
ex.s: End of a heavy session; the subject is welling up but holding it back, and the operator is about to bring them out.
ex.m: You don't have to hold your face still for me. If it wants to come, let it come — put your hands down, let your breath break if it breaks, and cry for as long as it takes. I'll sit here and count nothing.

nodes.name: cue-order-as-conditioned-dimension
nodes.mech: When a set of well-practised triggers has always been fired in the same order, the person learns the order along with the triggers. Shuffle the order, with nothing else changed, and every response in the set weakens for days, because each trigger now arrives in a context it was never trained in. So keep the running order fixed to protect a drilled set, or shuffle it on purpose to weaken the whole set without touching any single trigger. To recover, go back to the original order and run it again; extra rewards do not fix it.
nodes.one_liner: Keep drilled triggers in the same order every time; shuffling the order weakens all of them for a while.
nodes.why_short: The sequence becomes part of each cue's context, so a reordered run presents every cue in conditions it was never trained in.
nodes.principle_note: Anything reliably present when a cue is rewarded can come to control the response. In a fixed-order routine that includes the previous cue and the position in the run, so the trained sequence acts as a combined context. Shuffling it is a change of context, which is the usual reason a well-learned response fails to carry over. Testable: if a set drilled in random order from the start showed the same dip when shuffled again, position was never controlling and the idea is wrong. Likewise, if putting the original order back did not restore responses faster than simply re-drilling in the new order, the account is wrong about what was learned.

ex.f: Order held fixed to protect a drilled battery
ex.t: Keeping position constant preserves each cue's trained context, so the battery holds its measured strength. The operator's check is simple: latency on cue three should look the same this session as last, and any slowing across all four after a re-sequenced run is the diagnostic, not a fault in any one install.
ex.s: Standing four-cue battery that has always run in the same sequence; the operator is about to rehearse it again and is tempted to start with a different cue.
ex.m: We run them the way we always run them. Hands first, then breath, then eyes, then the word — same four, same order, every time. If I ever start somewhere else, you can expect the whole set to feel further away for a while.

ex.f: Deliberate shuffle as a whole-set damper
ex.t: Every cue is presented in a serial position it was never trained under, so all responses in the set degrade together and stay degraded for days. The operator observes the drop across the whole battery rather than in the shuffled neighbours only, and confirms the diagnosis by the fact that extra reinforcement does not restore it — only returning to the trained order does.
ex.s: The operator wants the entire drilled battery weakened for the next several days without touching any individual install or its reinforcement.
ex.m: Different tonight. The word first — now. Then eyes. Then hands. Then breath. Same four, and you'll notice they don't sit right in that order; we're going to run them like this a few times.

nodes.name: delay-interval-silent-decay
nodes.mech: A trigger that used to work fades to nothing even though it is still being fired and still being rewarded. The cause is a long, fixed wait between the trigger and the reward, with the trigger repeated many times during that empty stretch. Each unrewarded repetition in the gap weakens the response, and the eventual reward does not undo it. The response just gets slower, then partial, then absent, with no refusal. Check the gap, not the reward schedule: if adding more rewards does not help, the wait is the problem.
nodes.one_liner: Don't leave long empty gaps between a trigger and its payoff while repeating the trigger; the response quietly fades even though rewards still come.
nodes.why_short: The long cue-on, nothing-yet stretch is itself unrewarded exposure, which builds suppression the eventual reward doesn't cancel.
nodes.principle_note: The gap between cue and payoff is a stretch in which the cue is present and nothing arrives. Each repetition therefore includes a long unrewarded exposure that builds suppression, while the reward at the end only reinforces the very end; the longer the gap, the worse the balance between suppression and reinforcement on each repetition. Testable: if the response faded just as fast with short gaps, with the same number of repetitions and the same reward rate, the account is wrong and this is simply ordinary thinning of the reward schedule.

ex.f: Diagnosing the gap between cue and payoff
ex.t: Collapsing the cue-to-payoff interval and cutting the repetitions inside it removes the suppressive work the empty gap was doing, which is the only fix — the contingency was already intact, so more reward could not help. The operator watches for latency to shorten over the following sessions; if it does not, the interval was not the driver and the diagnosis was wrong.
ex.s: A previously reliable cue has gone slow then absent over several weeks; the operator has been firing it repeatedly through a long lead-in before the reward arrives, and has already tried adding reinforcement without effect.
ex.m: I've been saying the word from the moment we start and not paying it off until the end — that gap is what's killing it, not you. So from tonight the word comes once, and what it earns arrives inside two seconds. Nothing else changes.

nodes.name: new-install-battery-interference
nodes.mech: Adding one new trigger to an established set temporarily weakens all the existing ones, not just the similar ones. The dip shows up right after the new install, hits responses that were solid the session before, and clears by itself over the next few sessions if the set is simply run again. Nothing went wrong; installing is itself the disturbance. So the set is weaker for a while after every addition: stacking several new installs into one stretch compounds the dip, exactly when the operator is most likely to test the set and wrongly conclude it all failed.
nodes.one_liner: Expect every existing trigger to dip temporarily right after you install a new one; don't install several at once and then test.
nodes.why_short: Triggers drilled together share a context; changing the set changes that context, briefly disturbing all of them.
nodes.principle_note: Triggers drilled together are not independent: they share a setting, a session format and an operator, so changing the set changes the conditions every one of them was trained under. For a while the whole set is being re-learned against a new arrangement, not just the new item. Testable: if the dip hit only triggers that share a sense, position or theme with the new one, this is interference between neighbouring cues rather than a set-wide effect. And if the dip did not clear on its own over repeated runs, it is damage rather than temporary interference, and the advice to wait it out is wrong.

ex.f: Pre-framing the post-install dip before it is misread as failure
ex.t: The dip is transient and self-correcting, so the intervention is scheduling and expectation rather than repair. The operator's observable is that all pre-existing members are slower, not just the ones adjacent to the new install, and that a plain re-run over subsequent sessions restores them without extra reinforcement.
ex.s: Immediately after installing a fifth cue into an established four-cue battery, with a test of the older cues due next session.
ex.m: One thing before we stop. The four you already have are going to feel muddy for a session or two now that there's a fifth — that's the adding, not the losing. Don't chase them, don't drill them harder; we just run all five as usual next time and they come back on their own.

ex.f: Refusing to stack installs into one arc
ex.t: Spacing installs prevents the dips from compounding into a battery-wide failure at exactly the point the operator is most likely to test. The tell that the constraint was ignored is a set-wide drop with no individual cue implicated and no mis-install to find.
ex.s: Planning session; the operator has three new cues ready and is deciding whether to install them all tonight.
ex.m: We're doing one tonight, not three. Three in one sitting and everything you already have goes flat at once — then I test the set, find it soft, and start pulling apart installs that were never broken. One now, the rest a week apart.

nodes.name: dead-sibling-battery-drag
nodes.mech: When one trigger in a regularly run set has gone dead, worn out or been spoiled by a bad experience, keeping it in the routine drags down the triggers fired alongside it. Removing it lifts the rest without any re-drilling. You can tell this apart from general tiredness because a trigger fired on its own is unaffected; only the ones run together with the dead one are weaker. It also works in reverse: a deliberately deadened trigger can be slipped into a set to dampen the whole set.
nodes.one_liner: Drop a dead or spoiled trigger from the routine; keeping it in drags the others down. Conversely, park one in to dampen a set.
nodes.why_short: Speculatively, a cue that predicts nothing lowers the whole run's expected payoff, so readiness for its siblings falls too.
nodes.principle_note: Cues fired in the same run are judged against each other. A cue that reliably predicts no payoff lowers the expected value of the whole run, so the subject's readiness to respond is set by the run as a whole rather than by each cue alone. That is why the effect depends on the cues appearing together, and why removing the dead one, rather than retraining it, is the fix. Testable: if a weakened trigger fired alone, in a session where the dead cue never appeared, showed the same weakness, the problem is not about the cues appearing together and is ordinary general suppression. And if retiring the dead cue did not lift the others over a comparable number of repetitions, the claimed cause is wrong.

ex.f: Retiring the poisoned cue to lift its co-present neighbours
ex.t: Removing the suppressed member stops it re-weighting the cues fired alongside it, so the rest recover without any work being done on them. The confirming observation is specificity: only cues that shared a run with the dead one improve, and a cue that was always fired alone shows no change — which rules out general fatigue or satiation.
ex.s: One cue in a five-cue battery was extinguished or soured months ago but is still being fired alongside the others; the other four have all been sitting below their old strength, while a cue tested in isolation still runs clean.
ex.m: The old snap cue is out of the set — I'm not using it again, and you won't hear it in a run. We keep the other four exactly as they are, no extra drilling, and we run them clean tonight.

ex.f: Parking a dead cue as a deliberate broad-spectrum damper
ex.t: A suppressed cue kept in the running set drags the responses of everything fired with it, damping the whole battery from one insertion. The operator watches for a uniform softening across co-present members that reverses on removal, which distinguishes it from the individual cues having weakened on their own.
ex.s: The operator wants a live battery running at reduced strength without extinguishing any individual member, and has an already-suppressed cue available.
ex.m: We're putting the old snap cue back into the run — right in the middle, between the breath and the word. It doesn't have to do anything. It just travels with the others.

nodes.name: suppressor-strength-matching
nodes.mech: In the reported animal-conditioning arrangement, the relative strength of the stimuli in a combination matters to the quick and complete establishment of a conditioned inhibitor: Pavlov recommends choosing the additional stimulus so that it is not much weaker than the positive component. This is a relation between stimulus strengths in the conditioning arrangement, not a requirement to match rehearsal counts or installation effort between two human commands. The same passage describes a possible developmental continuity: the new stimulus initially produces external inhibition through the investigatory reflex, and this can gradually and almost imperceptibly become permanent conditioned inhibition. Retain both the relative-stimulus-strength observation and that transition as supporting material for thinking about cue competition and acquisition; neither supplies a procedure for building, testing, or maintaining a human stop signal.
nodes.one_liner: Drill a safeword or stop-cue as hard as the response it must interrupt, and re-drill it whenever that response gets stronger.
nodes.why_short: When two learned tendencies collide, the stronger wins; a casually installed off-switch loses silently to a heavily drilled response.
