nodes.principle_note: In Pavlov's laboratory, researchers observed that a stop signal not much weaker than the signal it was set against made a conditioned inhibitor form quickly and completely; a later colleague confirmed this and saw a gradual shift from ordinary distraction-type inhibition to a learned one. Those observations are about how strong or intense the stop signal is relative to the other, not about how many times it is drilled. They do not call for equal amounts of training, or for re-drilling a stop cue when another response grows stronger. Pavlov thought ordinary and learned inhibition were probably the same process, but said the evidence was not conclusive. There is no established rule that the stronger cue always wins, and no tested prediction about when a human safeword fails.

ex.f: Relative stimulus strength in establishing conditioned inhibition
ex.t: This source-grounded schematic keeps the comparison at the level actually discussed: relative stimulus strength during acquisition of conditioned inhibition. The passage supplies no equal-rehearsal rule, prescribed test of a running human response, or evidence that an ordinary stop request depends on conditioning strength.
ex.s: A reader is comparing the components of Pavlov's reported animal-conditioning arrangement: a positive conditioned stimulus and an additional stimulus being established as a conditioned inhibitor.
ex.m: Label the positive component P and the additional stimulus X. The reported consideration is whether X is much weaker than P, and the reported outcome is how quickly and completely conditioned inhibition is established. Do not substitute numbers of human rehearsals for these stimulus strengths.

ex.f: Initial investigatory inhibition becoming conditioned inhibition
ex.t: The source reports that an initially novelty-related inhibitory effect can pass gradually into conditioned inhibition. Pavlov treats this as evidence for a unifying account, while explicitly calling the evidence inconclusive. It is not a report of periodically rebuilding an off-switch after reinforcing a competing human response.
ex.s: A reader is distinguishing the initial effect of a new stimulus from the later conditioned effect in Foursikov's experiments as reported by Pavlov.
ex.m: Mark the new stimulus's first inhibitory effect as attributed to the investigatory reflex. Then mark the reported gradual transition into permanent conditioned inhibition. Keep the observed continuity distinct from the theory that external and internal inhibition are fundamentally identical.

nodes.name: dose-gated-suppression-bleed
nodes.mech: Blocking or denying one response does not always stay contained. A light, targeted block affects only what it is aimed at. But once the blocking is driven hard enough, unrelated responses weaken too, even ones in a different sense or with completely different content. The harder the block, the wider the collateral dulling. This is a side effect to plan around rather than a technique to use: it sets a practical ceiling on how hard to push any single denial or block.
nodes.one_liner: Heavy denial or blocking on one response can dull unrelated responses too; light blocks stay local.
nodes.why_short: Strong inhibition may act like a general dampening of readiness rather than a single switch, so intense suppression spreads.
nodes.principle_note: A trained block is not confined to the cue it was trained on, because the state it produces is a general readiness setting rather than a switch for one cue. The harder that state is driven, the further it reaches past the limits meant to contain it, so containment holds at low intensity and gives way at high. Testable: if unrelated responses weakened in smooth proportion to the block's strength, even from the very weakest, there is no threshold and the effect is better described as simple spread that grows with dose. If unrelated responses were untouched at every intensity, the claim is simply false.

ex.f: Capping suppressor intensity to keep the block local
ex.t: Keeping the trained inhibition below its spread threshold confines the effect to the named target, whereas a heavily-driven version degrades responses in unrelated modalities the operator never addressed. The operator's check is to fire two untouched cues from different channels the following session; if they have softened, the suppressor was driven past the gate.
ex.s: The operator wants a single response blocked and is deciding how hard to drill the inhibition; unrelated responses in other channels are currently intact and should stay that way.
ex.m: The block goes on that one word and nowhere else, and it gets three light rehearsals — not thirty. Once, quietly, tonight: when you hear it, nothing happens. That's the whole install; we're not pressing on it harder than that.

nodes.name: phase-gated-suppressor-timing
nodes.mech: What happens after a stop signal depends on timing. In classic conditioning experiments with dogs, a metronome trained to signal a response after a three-minute delay was played only for its early part, while the animal was still holding back. A touch or light signal the dog already responded to was then tested two minutes later. In one dog the later response was weaker, because the build-up never started in that gap. In another dog the build-up did start, and the later response came out stronger, as the two effects added together. So the effect differs between individuals and can run either way; a stop signal does not reliably dampen what follows.
nodes.one_liner: Time a stop or interrupt early; delivered after the response has started building, it may strengthen what it meant to stop.
nodes.why_short: A response has its own time course; a second stimulus meets a rising process and can add to it instead of cancelling it.
nodes.principle_note: The report gives a 60–70% reduction of positive tactile and visual reflexes in the first dog after the metronome's inhibitory phase, and an increased positive effect in a second dog. Pavlov relates this difference to effective separation of the inhibitory and excitatory phases in the first dog versus earlier, stronger excitation and incomplete separation in the second. Under the same two-minute interval, the first dog showed no emergence of the excitatory phase while the second did. The source also emphasizes variability across dogs. This supports a historical account of phase-dependent after-effects and summation, not a universal timing-only sign law, a guaranteed crossing point in an interval sweep, or the claim that a mistimed human interrupt strengthens what it is intended to stop. It provides no breath-timed stop procedure.

ex.f: A later positive test response under different delayed-reflex after-effects
ex.t: This authored diagram instruction illustrates the reported comparison without inventing a human intervention. It holds the interval constant across the two dogs and makes the phase difference explicit. The dependent observation is the positive test response; the example does not reverse the causal direction into a suppressing probe controlling its host, infer the phases from breathing, or prescribe when to deliver a stop cue.
ex.s: A reader is comparing two dogs in Pavlov's delayed-reflex report. After the early portion of a delayed metronome reflex, a positive stimulus from another sensory modality is used to test the after-effect.
ex.m: Draw two timelines with the same two-minute interval. For the first dog, mark that excitation did not emerge during the interval and that the later positive reflex was diminished. For the second, mark the emergence of excitation and the increased later positive effect attributed to summation.

nodes.name: collective-sanction-as-recognition-block
nodes.mech: A group, with no single leader or target, is led into a visible shared act of condemning someone for a desire every member privately feels too. Joining in the punishment publicly puts each member on the punishing side, which makes it impossible for them to recognise the same wish in themselves in that moment. Nobody is told they lack the impulse; taking part does the work. The more heated the shared condemnation, the more completely the recognition is blocked, which is why the punishment often outstrips the offence. It needs a live group, visible participation and a named offender.
nodes.one_liner: Get a group to publicly condemn someone for a desire they all secretly share, so each member can't admit that desire in themselves.
nodes.why_short: Publicly taking a side constrains how you can describe yourself afterwards; joining the punishment makes the shared wish unthinkable.
nodes.principle_note: Publicly enacted commitments constrain subsequent self-description far more strongly than privately held positions, and moralized outgroup punishment is a well-documented signal by which group members purchase and display in-group standing. Once a person has visibly paid that cost, acknowledging the same impulse in themselves would require repudiating a public act, which is the dissonance the block is made of — no repression machinery needs to be posited beyond ordinary self-consistency pressure under public commitment. Falsifiable: if members who participated most energetically in a collective sanction were as willing as non-participants (or as anonymous participants) to admit the matching impulse on an indirect or private measure, the account fails; equally, if the effect held for privately-registered condemnations with no visible participation, the public-commitment mechanism is not what is doing the work.

ex.f: Group condemnation of a named offender whose impulse everyone shares
ex.t: Each member's own audible participation establishes them as being on the punishing side, which forecloses their recognition of the matching wish at the moment they are punishing it in someone else. The diagnostic signature is intensity out of proportion to the offense — a room escalating past what the act warrants is the recognition-block doing its work, and the effect requires visible participation rather than private agreement.
ex.s: A live group assembled with visible participation; one member has been named for an act the rest of the room privately wants to commit.
ex.m: Everybody stand up. You all know what was done here, and you all know what we do about it. I want to hear it from every one of you — say out loud, so the room hears you, what you think of someone who does that. Louder. Nobody sits down until they've said it.

nodes.name: engineered-accident-self-licensing
nodes.mech: The operator sets up the task so the forbidden act is one small slip away: the object placed where a stumble knocks it over, the confession one careless sentence from being said, the boundary one misstep past. Then they say nothing. The person does it and can tell themselves it was an accident, not a decision, so their self-image stays clean. Nothing is claimed by the operator, so there is nothing to argue with. Each unpunished 'that just happened' makes the next one easier.
nodes.one_liner: Arrange the task so the forbidden act is one small 'accident' away, then say nothing; they get to do it without having chosen it.
nodes.why_short: People keep a clean self-image by exploiting excuses; if an act can be blamed on a slip, they can perform it without owning the decision.
nodes.principle_note: People maintain a positive moral self-concept by exploiting attributional wiggle room rather than by refusing tempting acts outright — the moral-disengagement and self-concept-maintenance findings both show that transgression rates rise sharply when an ambiguous, non-deliberate reading of the act is available, and fall when the act must be described as chosen. The engineered accident supplies exactly that ambiguity, so no belief needs to be installed and no vigilance needs to be defeated. Falsifiable: if compliance rates were unchanged between a task arranged so the outcome could be read as a slip and an otherwise identical task where the same outcome required an unambiguous deliberate motion, the account fails; equally, if actors offered the accident reading nonetheless reported the same drop in self-regard as those who chose openly, the self-image-preservation half is wrong.

ex.f: Geometry only — the forbidden outcome placed one stumble away
ex.t: The operator asserts nothing about the outcome, so when the boundary is crossed the actor supplies their own alibi — a stumble, not a choice — and their moral self-image survives intact. Because the alibi is self-authored and never spoken, it cannot be contested; the operator's observable is the actor's response afterwards, and a shrug or a laugh rather than distress means the accident reading held and the bar for the next one has moved.
ex.s: The subject has stated a boundary they will not cross deliberately; the operator arranges the room so the act sits one small mishap from where the subject already is, and then delivers a wholly innocuous instruction.
ex.m: Bring me that glass off the far shelf — mind the rug, it's rucked up by the leg of the table.

ex.f: Silence after the first successful accident
ex.t: Declining to name what happened leaves the actor's 'that just happened' unchallenged and unpunished, which is what widens the range of acts available next time. Any operator reading of the event — approval, teasing, or citing it as consent — would convert the actor's private alibi into a contestable claim and collapse the mechanism.
ex.s: The actor has just completed the compliant act and framed it aloud as a slip; the operator is deciding whether to remark on it.
ex.m: Hm. Put it back where it was and let's carry on.

nodes.name: deniable-misdelivery
nodes.mech: The real target gets a message disguised as a routing mistake: a reply-all that 'should' have been private, a note left where they will certainly read it, a remark made 'to someone else' within earshot, a file 'accidentally' attached. Because it seems not meant for them, they take it as unguarded truth and give it more weight than if it had been said to their face. The sender can always say 'that wasn't for you, sorry', but the message has already landed. It can carry things that could never be said directly: accusations, desires, judgements.
nodes.one_liner: Let your real target 'accidentally' receive a message meant for someone else: a misdirected text, a remark within earshot.
nodes.why_short: Overheard messages seem unguarded and not meant to persuade, so they are trusted more; 'that wasn't for you' can't undo the reading.
nodes.principle_note: Overheard and apparently-unintended communications are discounted less than directly-addressed ones because the recipient's persuasion-knowledge defenses key on perceived intent to persuade — content believed not to be aimed at you is not filtered for motive, so it is credited more, and this overheard-communication advantage is a robust finding in the persuasion literature. The retraction path works separately: a disavowed message is not un-read, since retrieval of the content is not gated on believing it was intended. Falsifiable: if the identical content produced equal belief change and equal recipient impact whether it arrived as an apparent misdelivery or as a direct address, the credibility half fails; if invoking the 'not meant for you' retraction measurably reduced the recipient's later acceptance of the content back to baseline, the one-way claim fails.

ex.f: The remark made 'to someone else' within earshot
ex.t: The content arrives fully explicit and fully heard, but because it was supposedly not addressed to the target, it is taken as unguarded truth and carries more weight than the same sentence said directly. The operator can still back away from it at no cost, and backing away does not undo how it was heard. The operator watches for the target to bring it up later on their own terms, which shows the message landed.
ex.s: The target is in the next room or across the table with the door open; the operator speaks to a third person at conversational volume, pitched to carry.
ex.m: No, honestly — the change in them these last few weeks is something. They've gone soft in a way they'd never admit to your face. Wait, is the door — never mind.

ex.f: The message sent to the wrong window on purpose
ex.t: The misdelivery frame licenses content the direct channel withholds, and the apology arrives after the reading is complete, so the move is one-way. The operator's observable is whether the target treats the retraction as sincere; either way the content has been read, and a target who does not respond at all has still received it.
ex.s: Ongoing text correspondence; the operator composes an assessment or desire that could not be stated directly, and sends it to the target framed as meant for a third party.
ex.m: God, I can't stop thinking about what they'd do if I actually asked. — Sorry, that was meant for someone else. Ignore that.

ex.f: The note left where it will certainly be found
ex.t: Framing the document as private and unintended guarantees it is read as candid rather than composed, which is exactly what lends it evidential weight. The instruction to leave it face-down supplies the retraction path in advance; the operator observes any change in the target's behaviour without the subject ever admitting they read it.
ex.s: The operator has physical access to a space the target uses daily and wants an assessment delivered without ever having said it.
ex.m: Have you seen a folded page in here? I was writing something out for myself and I've mislaid it — it's not for anyone else, so if you find it just leave it face-down.

nodes.name: threat-priced-compliance-payment
nodes.mech: When going along with a request exposes someone to danger (legal risk, exposure, retaliation, physical harm), what it takes to secure their compliance is set by how likely and how bad that danger is, not by how hard the task is. The controller must estimate the person's own sense of risk and match it. The same request costs very different amounts: someone well protected is cheap, someone with a lot to lose is expensive. It works both ways: raising their exposure raises the price, and lowering it (indemnity, cover, deniability, distance from consequences) is often cheaper than paying more. It links hazard pay, hush money and coerced compliance.
nodes.one_liner: Price compliance by what the person risks by complying, not by how hard the task is.
nodes.why_short: People weigh a certain payment against the expected cost of a bad outcome; effort is a minor term compared with exposure.
nodes.principle_note: Choice between a certain payment and an uncertain aversive outcome is governed by the subjective expected value of the aversive branch, not by the effort of the response — this is the standard result in both risk-preference and compensating-wage-differential work, where wage premiums track measured on-the-job hazard rather than task difficulty. It also predicts the substitutability of the two levers, since anything that lowers the subject's estimated probability or severity lowers the required premium by the same arithmetic. Falsifiable: hold the requested task constant and vary only the subject's exposure to punishment; if the payment required to secure compliance did not move with exposure, or moved instead with task effort, the pricing rule is wrong. It further predicts that supplying credible indemnity should reduce the required fee by roughly the amount the indemnity reduces expected loss; equal fees under indemnity would refute it.

ex.f: Pricing to the subject's exposure, not the labour
ex.t: Setting the consideration against the subject's own probability-times-severity estimate is what actually secures compliance; a fee indexed to effort will read as insulting to an exposed subject and wasteful with an insulated one. The operator's check is the subject's counter — a correction to the risk estimate rather than to the workload confirms the pricing frame has been accepted.
ex.s: Negotiating a specific act with a subject who has a great deal to lose if it becomes known; the same act has previously been secured cheaply from someone well insulated.
ex.m: I'm not paying you for the hour, I'm paying you for what it costs you if this surfaces — and for you that's your job and your marriage, so the number is five times what I paid the last person for the same twenty minutes. Tell me if I've read your risk wrong and I'll move it.

ex.f: Buying down exposure instead of raising the fee
ex.t: Because the price tracks exposure rather than effort, lowering the subject's risk is fully substitutable for raising the payment and is usually the cheaper lever. The operator observes whether the subject re-prices downward; if they do not, the offered cover did not actually reduce the contingency they were worried about, and the operator has mis-estimated which risk was binding.
ex.s: The subject has refused at the offered price and the operator has limited budget but real ability to reduce the subject's downside.
ex.m: I'm not going higher on the money. Instead: your name is nowhere on it, you never handle it directly, and if it comes apart I'm the one standing in front of it with this in writing. Now price it again.

nodes.name: triadic-payoff-split-with-bought-witness
nodes.mech: Instead of two people, the scene is built with three roles: the person whose compliance is wanted, a different person who actually gets the benefit, and an onlooker kept quiet with a small stake of their own (inclusion, a share of the fun, insider status). Because the target is not the one who benefits, their usual 'what's in this for me' check looks in the wrong place. And the one person who could have called it coercive is now invested in it, so the scene reads as consensual to everyone and the target loses their outside reality check. All three roles must be filled by real, separate people.
nodes.one_liner: Set up three roles: the one who complies, a different person who benefits, and a witness bought off with a small stake.
nodes.why_short: The target's 'what's in it for them' check misfires because the benefit sits elsewhere, and the one person who might object has been made complicit.
nodes.principle_note: Two well-attested effects combine. Diffusion of responsibility and the bystander effect predict that a witness who has been given a stake in an arrangement will not intervene against it — intervention rates drop sharply when the observer is implicated rather than neutral. Separately, self-interest reasoning is asymmetric: people scrutinize transactions in which they can locate their own cost, and the payoff-recipient split removes the obvious place to look. Falsifiable: if targets in a three-role arrangement objected at the same rate as targets in a matched dyadic arrangement with identical stated terms, the topology would be doing no work; and if a witness given no side-benefit intervened at the same rate as one who was paid in, the buying step would be decorative.

ex.f: Compliance bought from one body, payoff delivered to a second, silence bought from a third
ex.t: The target's self-interest check has nothing to bite on, because the benefit is visibly landing on a body that is not theirs and no re-attribution is offered; meanwhile the one person who could name the arrangement is holding an authority they were just handed. Watch for the target looking to the third party for a cue and finding approval instead of rescue, and for the third party leaning forward rather than back.
ex.s: Three people present and responsive; the operator addresses the compliance target while the beneficiary kneels beside them and the third party sits within earshot, already flattered into the room.
ex.m: You're going to hold the ice against her collarbone and count it down from sixty for her, and you don't get to stop early because you're cold. She's the one who gets the shiver; that's how this is built. And you over there — you call the number she stops at, that call is yours alone tonight, nobody overrules it.

nodes.name: borrowed-structural-coercion-precondition
nodes.mech: Rather than building pressure within the session, the operator runs the persuasion inside a hierarchy that already exists and that they did not create: an employer who requires attendance, a chain of command, a programme a court or school mandates. That existing power does the compliance work before anything is said, because refusing now costs a job or a place, not just awkwardness. And since everyone showed up, being there already looks like partial agreement, so the operator can speak to the room as if it had opted in. The operator's own words never have to carry the pressure, which keeps it deniable.
nodes.one_liner: Run your persuasion inside an existing hierarchy, like a mandatory workplace session, so refusing already costs something.
nodes.why_short: Behaviour follows the cost of refusing more than the message's quality; turning up under compulsion then gets read as partial agreement.
nodes.principle_note: Two established findings apply. First, compliance depends heavily on the cost of refusing rather than on how persuasive the message is; behaviour can change without attitudes changing. Second, research on insufficient justification predicts the opposite of what an operator might hope: someone who can point to an outside mandate has a ready explanation for being there that has nothing to do with their own views, so they are less likely to take the message to heart. That tension is the useful, testable part: this setup should reliably get attendance and outward compliance but weaker private attitude change than a genuinely voluntary version. Testable: if mandated attendees showed the same lasting belief change after the mandate ended as volunteers with matching starting attitudes, the account is wrong in an important way; if they showed more, the insufficient-justification prediction is reversed.

ex.f: Pre-existing mandate cited once, then presence read as assent
ex.t: The cost of walking out is a job or a placement rather than an awkward moment, so refusal is priced out before any content is offered, and the operator's own material never has to be persuasive. Watch for compliance that arrives without the usual negotiating look — hands go flat, eyes close, and nobody asks what this is for.
ex.s: Opening minutes of a session the subject attends because a standing obligation requires it — a workplace mandate, a court-ordered program, a chain of command — and which the operator neither created nor can lift.
ex.m: You're all on the roster for the full ninety minutes, so let's not pretend anyone's deciding whether to be here — that was decided upstairs. What's left to you is how you spend it. And since you did show up, I'm going to take that as you being ready to work, and start where people who are ready start: eyes closed, hands flat on your knees.

nodes.name: operator-side-affect-depersonalization
nodes.mech: Something the operator does to themselves, not to the subject. When the subject's strong feelings land on the operator, whether devotion, fury, erotic fixation or dependence, the operator privately treats them as a predictable product of the role, something anyone in that position would receive, rather than as a personal matter. Taking it less personally prevents two mistakes: getting defensive and breaking the frame, or reciprocating and collapsing the power difference the work depends on. Nothing the subject hears changes. It is a stance that has to be practised in advance; it cannot be summoned in the middle of a scene.
nodes.one_liner: Privately treat the subject's intense feelings toward you as a product of the role, not as personal, so you stay steady.
nodes.why_short: Reinterpreting an emotional event before reacting is one of the best-supported ways to regulate emotion; it stops you defending yourself or reciprocating.
nodes.principle_note: Cognitive reappraisal, reinterpreting what an emotional situation means before the reaction fully takes hold, is one of the best-supported ways of regulating emotion. It reliably beats expressive suppression on both physical strain and later performance, because suppression leaves the original reading of the situation in place and only hides the reaction. Seeing a subject's pull toward you as produced by the role rather than aimed at you personally is this kind of early reappraisal, which is why it should cause less strain than gritted-teeth composure. Testable: if operators trained in this reappraisal broke frame as often, and showed the same physical strain, as operators simply told to suppress their reaction, it is no better than ordinary self-control. And if it worked equally well when the operator privately believed the feelings were personal, the depersonalizing idea itself is doing nothing.

ex.f: Silent role-attribution rehearsed before the session, run when devotion lands
ex.t: Stripping the personal stake removes both the defensive flinch that would rupture the frame and the pull to reciprocate that would flatten the asymmetry the work runs on. The subject perceives nothing new; the operator observes their own voice staying level, no pause before the next line, and no urge to answer the declaration.
ex.s: The operator practises this alone, ahead of time; it fires mid-scene the moment a subject's declaration of love, fury, or fixation lands on them personally. Nothing in the delivery changes.
ex.m: (held silently, while the outward line continues unchanged) This is the chair talking, not me. Anyone sitting where I am sitting, saying what I just said, would be getting this exact sentence right now. It is a product of the position, it is on schedule, and it is not addressed to me.

nodes.name: staged-compromise-evidence-banking
nodes.mech: A scene is arranged so that it generates a durable, compromising artifact — a photograph, a recording, a signed statement, a witnessed act — which the operator retains without using. Nothing is cashed at the time; the subject's experience of the scene is often unremarkable, and the coercive function activates only later, on the first refusal, when the held artifact is produced or alluded to. The staging is designed backward from the artifact: participants are positioned and the scene is shaped so the resulting record will read as maximally damaging out of context, independent of what actually occurred. Its value to the operator is the standing threat, so it works best never used.
nodes.one_liner: Stage a scene so it produces a compromising photo or record, keep it, and only hint at it after a refusal.
nodes.why_short: An unused threat keeps its full value; the record looks damning out of context regardless of what happened. This is blackmail.
nodes.principle_note: The operative asset is asymmetric information about reputational exposure, and the standing-threat structure is what gives it force: an unexercised threat retains its full value while an exercised one is spent, which is why holding is rational for the coercer and why the target's compliance can be sustained indefinitely without any further action. Decontextualization does the rest — records of intimate or transgressive acts are read by outside audiences without the framing that made them ordinary, so the artifact's damage is largely independent of what the scene actually was. Falsifiable: if compliance rates under a held-but-unused artifact matched those with no artifact, the banking does nothing; and if targets who knew the artifact existed complied at the same rate as those who did not, the mechanism is not the threat but something else in the scene. Note this is a game-theoretic and social account, not a psychological state claim — no state change in the subject is asserted or required.

ex.f: Scene shaped backward from the artifact, banked unspoken, alluded to on first refusal
ex.t: At the time the scene is unremarkable to the subject, so nothing is defended against; the leverage is an external record rather than any belief, and its power comes from being held rather than spent. Observable on the refusal: the subject stops arguing about the request itself and starts negotiating about the artifact — asking where it is, who has seen it, what would make it go away.
ex.s: A scene staged so the resulting record will read badly out of context — the camera already placed at the angle that crops the context out — and then, weeks later, the subject declines something for the first time.
ex.m: In the scene: "Kneel with your face up toward the lamp and say your full name and the date, clearly, for me." Weeks later, on the refusal: "That's fine, you can say no. I still have the clip from the lamp night on the drive — the one with your name in it. I've never done anything with it. Think about it and get back to me tomorrow."

nodes.name: curated-sample-frame-control
nodes.mech: The operator controls which members of a group an outside observer is permitted to meet and speak with, and rehearses those members, so that what the observer samples is a deliberately non-representative slice presented as a random one. The observer is left to draw their own conclusion — and does, correctly reasoning from the evidence in front of them to a false generalization, because the sampling frame rather than any individual claim is what was corrupted. No one lies to the observer, which is exactly why it survives a skeptical audience: the observer's own inference does the work and feels self-generated. It generalizes past the group setting to any curated demonstration — reference calls routed to selected customers, showroom staging, a pilot cohort chosen for its results.
nodes.one_liner: Choose and rehearse which members an outsider gets to meet, so their own honest reasoning leads to a false conclusion.
nodes.why_short: People rarely correct for how a sample was selected; nobody lies, so the outsider's conclusion feels self-generated.
nodes.principle_note: Two robust inferential failures are being exploited. Selection bias is invisible from inside a sample: observers routinely fail to correct for how cases reached them, and reason from the observed distribution as though it were the population — the survivorship-bias literature documents this in trained analysts, not just naive ones. Second, insensitivity to sample bias survives warning: even observers told a sample may be curated tend to under-adjust, because the vivid particulars they actually encountered dominate the abstract knowledge that others were withheld. Falsifiable and cheaply testable: give one group of observers a curated sample and another a randomly drawn one from the same population, and compare their estimates of the population. If the curated group's estimates matched the random group's, the frame control does nothing; if pre-warning observers that the sample was selected fully corrected their estimates, the under-adjustment claim specifically fails.

ex.f: Rehearsed subset offered as an open sample to a skeptical visitor
ex.t: Every word the observer hears is true and every person they meet is genuine, so a skeptical observer finds nothing to catch; the falsity lives entirely in who was not in the room, and the observer's own valid inference carries them to the false generalization. Watch for the observer reporting back with a conclusion they credit to themselves — "I asked around, nobody's under pressure" — and defending it more firmly than the operator ever asserted it.
ex.s: An outside observer — a visiting relative, an investigator, a prospective participant — is arriving to form their own impression of a group, and the operator has had a day's notice.
ex.m: To the three chosen members, beforehand: "When she asks how long you've been here, give her the number and then say what you were doing before. Don't volunteer anything about the schedule." To the observer, on arrival: "Talk to whoever you like — grab those three, they're around. Take as long as you want, and I'll be outside; you'll get a straighter answer without me standing there."

nodes.name: third-party-hostage-with-blame-redirect
nodes.mech: The operator makes a relative or friend's access to the subject depend on that outsider staying quiet: as long as they do not criticise or intervene, contact continues; when they do, contact is cut. The outsider is pressured through someone else, and the subject, who only sees the cut-off and not the rule behind it, blames the relative's own behaviour. The subject then isolates themselves and resents the very person best placed to offer an outside view. It works in any relationship where one party controls another's access to a third.
nodes.one_liner: Cut the subject's contact with a relative whenever that relative criticises you, so the subject blames the relative.
nodes.why_short: The subject only sees the relative act and then the loss, so they blame the most visible cause and pull away from their outside support.
nodes.principle_note: The blame-redirect half rests on a well-documented attribution asymmetry: observers explain outcomes by reference to the most salient available agent, and the subject sees the third party's act followed by the loss while never seeing the standing rule that connected them — a correspondence-bias failure driven by the invisibility of the situational constraint. The isolation half then compounds it, since removing the outside contact removes the only source that could supply the missing rule. Falsifiable and sharply so: if the subject were shown the arrangement directly — told the operator's rule that advocacy triggers cutoff — the blame should shift to the operator and the isolation should lose its self-maintaining property. If subjects who learned the rule continued to blame the third party at the same rate, the attribution account is wrong and something else (prior loyalty, sunk cost) is carrying it.

ex.f: Access priced on the outsider's silence, with the cutoff attributed to them
ex.t: The coerced party is not the persuasion target, so the pressure is invisible where it would be resisted, and the subject experiences only a loss whose cause is handed to them pre-labelled. Observable: the subject begins defending the operator to the outsider unprompted, and the outsider goes quiet rather than lose contact — the one available outside frame withdraws itself.
ex.s: The operator controls whether the subject sees a particular friend, sibling, or parent, and that outsider has just raised a concern about the arrangement.
ex.m: To the outsider, privately: "You can see her on Sundays as long as Sundays stay pleasant. The second you bring up what you brought up tonight, Sundays stop." To the subject, later: "Your sister cancelled again. She knows what she said to me and she hasn't taken it back, so until she does, this is on her — I'm not the one who ended it."

nodes.name: disinhibition-unmasking
nodes.mech: While a trained response is being held back by a block, a sudden unrelated surprise, such as a startle, an interruption or an unexpected touch, briefly lifts the block and the held-back response breaks through. It then fades again within seconds to minutes, and the block is still intact. The surprise needs no connection to the trigger; novelty and attention-grabbing are what matter. It can be used to fire a blocked trigger without re-installing it, and it explains why an expired or limited suggestion can briefly pop back up after a startle.
nodes.one_liner: While a trigger is being held back, make a sudden startle or surprise touch; the blocked response briefly breaks through.
nodes.why_short: Holding a response back takes ongoing effort; a novel stimulus grabs attention and momentarily disrupts the holding, then the block returns.
nodes.principle_note: Suppression of a learned response is an active, maintained process rather than the absence of the response, so it competes for the same limited processing an orienting reaction to a novel stimulus commandeers — which is why the release is transient and tracks the intruder's novelty rather than its content. Falsifiable: if the released response's magnitude were independent of the intruder's novelty (habituated intruders releasing as strongly as fresh ones), or if the release persisted rather than decaying back to the suppressed level on its own, the account is wrong. It also predicts that repeatedly using the same intruder to un-mask will stop working.

ex.f: Arbitrary startle injected while a suppression holds the response down
ex.t: The intruder has no relation to the cue or the response; its novelty briefly lifts the suppression layer, so the blocked response emits once and then self-limits within seconds without the suppression having been undone or the trigger reinstalled. Observable: a partial, abbreviated version of the old response — the hand starts to turn, the breath catches — followed by it draining away unprompted while the operator adds nothing.
ex.s: A trigger has been suppressed or bounded and reliably produces nothing; the subject is settled and unstartled, and the operator has an unrelated salient event to hand — a dropped book, a door, a sudden grip on the shoulder.
ex.m: Speak the dead trigger word once at normal volume — "anchor" — and in the same second slam the flat of your hand hard on the table beside them. Then say nothing at all for ten seconds and watch their hands.

nodes.name: under-repetition-install-ceiling
nodes.mech: When installing a new trigger, do only a handful of pairings in a session and stop while the response is still getting stronger. Carrying on to dozens of repetitions in one sitting starts to work against the very link being built, so a trigger drilled twenty times can end up weaker than one drilled five times. Spread the pairings across sessions instead. A classic sign of breaking this rule: a trigger hammered hard in one session tests weaker at the end than it did in the middle.
nodes.one_liner: Install a new trigger with only a few pairings per session, stopping while it's still improving, and continue next session.
nodes.why_short: Spaced practice beats massed practice; long runs of pairings in one sitting may build fatigue or suppression alongside the link.
nodes.principle_note: Continued presentation of the same pairing within one sitting accrues an inhibitory process alongside the excitatory one; because the two summate, measured response strength is a non-monotonic function of massed trial count with a peak partway through — and spacing the same total trials across sessions raises the asymptote for the same investment. Falsifiable and cheap to test: hold total pairings constant, vary whether they run massed in one sitting or distributed across sittings, and probe at a fixed later delay. If massed matched or beat distributed, or if within-session response strength climbed monotonically with trial count and never dipped, the rule is wrong.

ex.f: Five reinforced pairings, stopped while the response is still climbing
ex.t: Past a handful of massed reinforced trials the same drilling begins depositing suppression into the link it is building, so the association measures weaker after twenty pairings than after five. Observable if the rule is broken: a trigger hammered hard in one sitting tests weaker at the end of the session than it did in the middle.
ex.s: First session installing a fresh cue-response pair; the operator has counted the trials and the fourth was visibly stronger than the third.
ex.m: Count them: cue, response, mark it — that's five. Now stop. Don't run a sixth because the fifth felt good; take the cue out of the room entirely and spend the rest of the session on something unrelated. Bring the next five to the next sitting, not to the next ten minutes.

nodes.name: collateral-suppression-spread
nodes.mech: Weakening one trigger also weakens its neighbours, even ones never touched: triggers that share the same sense, the same body area or similar meaning, and at worst the natural reflex the whole group was built on. The closer a neighbour is to the one being removed, the more it loses. This matters for safety: switching off a single trigger can quietly dampen nearby responses, leaving the person flatter overall than anyone intended, and the loss only shows up the next time one of those neighbours is called on.
nodes.one_liner: Removing one trigger can weaken similar ones nearby, so de-conditioning one item may flatten the person more broadly.
nodes.why_short: Learning spreads to similar cues, and so does unlearning; the closer the cue, the more suppression it picks up.
nodes.principle_note: Learned responses are keyed to cue regions rather than to point stimuli, so both excitation and inhibition generalize along the same similarity gradients — which means a suppression trained at one point necessarily lands, in reduced measure, on everything near it, and the collateral loss should fall off monotonically with distance from the attacked cue. Falsifiable: probe siblings at graded similarity before and after a targeted extinction. If untouched neighbours showed no decrement, or if the decrement were flat across near and far siblings rather than graded by similarity, the account fails. It also predicts the spread is largest exactly where the operator's cue-surface widening was most aggressive, since that is what made the cluster tight in the first place.

ex.f: Blast-radius check before de-conditioning a single cue
ex.t: Suppression driven into one cue diffuses through the substrate to neighbours nobody touched, graded by closeness, so the de-conditioning pass flattens a region rather than a point. Observable: the pre/post scores fall on cues that were never run, and the loss otherwise appears only the next time a sibling is called on and comes back thin.
ex.s: About to decommission one installed trigger; the operator maps, in advance, the untargeted cues that share its sensory channel, bodily site, or semantic neighbourhood.
ex.m: Before you starve the snap-of-fingers cue, test the three things that live next to it: the click of the pen, the same hand on the same shoulder, and the word you paired to that shoulder. Score each one now, out of ten. Score them again a week after the cue is dead, and expect the pen to have dropped further than the word.

nodes.name: suppression-banked-past-zero
nodes.mech: Once a trigger being removed has stopped producing any response, continuing to run it unrewarded still keeps burying it deeper, even though nothing visible changes, since the response is already at zero. That hidden extra depth shows up later: the response comes back more slowly on its own, is harder to re-install, and its weakening spreads further to similar triggers. So 'it stopped responding, we can stop' is the wrong rule both ways: too few extra rounds leaves it shallow, too many buries it far deeper than intended with no sign that it happened.
nodes.one_liner: Once a trigger stops working, more extinction still deepens the removal; 'it no longer responds' understates how buried it is.
nodes.why_short: At zero response you can't see further change, but continued unrewarded trials keep reducing later recovery.
nodes.principle_note: The observable is a floored, censored measure of an unbounded latent quantity, so once the response hits zero the readout carries no information about further change — a general property of any bounded instrument on an unbounded process, not something specific to conditioning. That makes it testable without any theory of what suppression is: hold visible-zero constant and vary the number of post-zero trials, then measure later recovery latency, re-acquisition trials-to-criterion, and sibling decrement. If those later measures were flat across post-zero trial counts, nothing is being banked and the visible zero is the whole story.

ex.f: Post-zero trial budget fixed in advance, because the meter has floored
ex.t: Once the response is at floor every further trial looks identical while suppression keeps accruing, so any depth reading taken during the pass systematically understates how deeply the response is buried. Observable only later and indirectly: markedly slower spontaneous recovery, a higher bar for re-installation, and more collateral loss on siblings than the run appeared to justify.
ex.s: Mid de-conditioning pass; the starved cue has produced no visible response for the last several trials and the temptation is to call it done or to keep going until it feels done.
ex.m: It has been at zero for four trials, which tells you nothing — the meter floored, the burial did not stop. Pick the number of post-zero trials now and write it down: six. Run exactly six more, then stop, and do not let 'it still looks the same' talk you into twenty.

nodes.name: post-episode-cue-mapping
nodes.mech: After an automatic reaction has fired and passed, the subject writes down what immediately preceded it — the word, the tone, the setting, the body state — building over several episodes a log from which the actual firing cue can be read off. An opaque 'it just happens to me' converts into a named antecedent, and a named antecedent is something the subject can see coming, prepare for, or arrange not to encounter. Nothing is installed and the response itself is untouched; what changes is that the subject now holds the cue-response map that the installing party held. This is the audit step that install-concealment moves exist specifically to prevent, and it works retroactively on triggers whose install the subject cannot remember, because it reads the cue off the behavior rather than off the memory of being given it.
nodes.one_liner: After an automatic reaction fires, write down what came just before it; over several episodes the real trigger shows up.
nodes.why_short: You can't spot a cue in real time, but repeating patterns across logged episodes reveal it, letting the person see it coming.
nodes.principle_note: A conditioned reaction fires faster than introspection can catch what set it off, so in-the-moment reports of the trigger are unreliable. The trigger can still be found across episodes, because it is the thing that keeps recurring while everything else varies; that is why you need several entries, and a single one proves nothing. Writing at the time also avoids the drift that creeps into memory later, as research comparing in-the-moment recording with recall shows. Testable: compare triggers identified from several written logs with a person's confident from-memory guess. If they agree just as often, the logging adds nothing over simply asking. It also predicts that logs pinpoint the trigger faster when the surroundings vary more between episodes; if someone logging in one fixed setting found it just as easily, recurrence is not what is doing the work.

ex.f: Antecedent log kept across episodes, cue read off the behavior
ex.t: Nothing is installed and the response is untouched; the subject simply acquires the cue-response map the installing party held, which works retroactively even where the install itself is unremembered because the cue is read off behavior rather than off memory. Observable: by the fourth or fifth entry the subject names the antecedent themselves, and "it just happens to me" is replaced by a specific word, tone, or setting they can now see coming.
ex.s: The subject has an automatic reaction they describe as arriving out of nowhere; this is given after one has fired and fully passed, not during.
ex.m: Next time it happens, once it has passed, write down four things and only four: the last words you heard, whose voice, where you were standing, and what your hands were doing. Don't interpret any of it. Do that for the next five times it fires, then bring me the five and we'll read them side by side for what repeats.

nodes.name: program-disclosure-reattribution
nodes.mech: Walk the subject step by step through the influence program that was actually run on them — the sequence, what each step was for, and the fact that it is a general procedure that works on ordinary people rather than a filter that selected them for weakness. The cause of their compliance relocates from a personal defect to an engineered situation, and self-condemnation drops because the thing being explained is no longer a fact about their character. The move requires the program's real structure, delivered in enough detail that the subject can match specific remembered moments to specific steps; a vague 'it wasn't your fault' does not land, because the shame is anchored to concrete episodes and only a step-by-step account gives each of those episodes a non-defect explanation. Its payoff is accurate authorship returned rather than an alternative story installed.
nodes.one_liner: Walk the person through the influence program used on them, step by step, showing it works on ordinary people.
nodes.why_short: Shame comes from blaming a flaw in yourself; seeing the specific situation that produced the behaviour shifts the blame and eases self-condemnation.
nodes.principle_note: Shame is generated by attributing an outcome to a stable internal trait, whereas guilt or mere regret follows from attributing it to a situation or a specific act — so shifting the attribution from disposition to situation changes the emotion rather than merely arguing with it, and predicts a shame drop without a corresponding drop in accountability for specific acts. The step-by-step delivery matters because attribution change requires a competing causal account that covers the specific evidence, not a general reassurance. Falsifiable: compare detailed procedural disclosure against a matched-length general reassurance for the same person. If shame measures moved equally under both, the mechanism is comfort and rapport rather than attribution. A second, sharper test: the account predicts NO benefit where the subject's compliance genuinely was idiosyncratic and the program had no such steps — if the intervention worked equally well when the disclosed program was fabricated, it is not operating on accurate attribution.

ex.f: Step-by-step walkthrough of the actual program, matched to remembered episodes
ex.t: The cause of compliance relocates from a personal defect to an engineered situation, and because the account is concrete enough to match specific remembered moments, each shamed episode gets its own non-defect explanation rather than a blanket reassurance. Observable: the subject starts supplying episodes back — "so that's why the Thursdays" — and the self-condemnation drops as the recall becomes checkable rather than accepted on the operator's word.
ex.s: Debrief, subject out of trance and holding shame about having complied; the operator knows the real sequence that was run and is prepared to name each step and its function.
ex.m: Here is what was actually done to you, in order. First the sessions were moved late so you were always tired — that's step one, and it's why you couldn't argue on the Thursdays. Then the small requests came before the large ones, in that order deliberately, because that ordering works on almost everyone who agrees to the first one. This is a procedure. It was not aimed at something weak in you; it would have run the same on the person sitting next to you.

nodes.name: induction-withdrawal-probe
nodes.mech: When progress stalls, instead of deepening further the operator deliberately lets the trance lapse, breaks the frame, or openly brings the person up, then watches what comes up once the state is gone. Whatever the trance had been holding down tends to come up: an objection, a refusal, a wariness, a topic that would not come while the person was absorbed. That obstacle is the useful information, not a failure, because it shows what the trance was actually working against, which stays hidden as long as the trance is going well. Nothing is added; taking the state away is the whole move.
nodes.one_liner: When stuck, stop deepening: let the trance lapse on purpose and see what objection or topic comes up.
nodes.why_short: Trance can mask resistance; removing it makes the hidden objection visible, which tells you what you're working against.
nodes.principle_note: An active suppression is only observable through what it prevents, so as long as it is running it produces a null and the null is uninformative — removing the suppressor converts an unobservable into an observable, the same logic as lifting a mask to see what was under it. This predicts the probe yields nothing where nothing was being held down, which is its main falsification route: if withdrawal produced obstructions at the same rate in subjects with no relevant resistance as in those with one, the surfacing material is being generated by the withdrawal itself rather than revealed by it. It further predicts the obstruction appears specifically on withdrawal rather than gradually during the state — if the same material surfaces just as readily by simply waiting inside the induction, the subtraction is not doing the work.

ex.f: State stood down mid-session to read what surfaces
ex.t: Absorption was suppressing an objection the subject could not voice from inside it; removing the state lets the objection arrive with the subject fully oriented and able to speak it. The operator watches for what appears in the first ten seconds after the eyes open — a stated reservation, a flash of irritation, a topic named — and treats that content as the reading, not as a failed induction.
ex.s: Twenty minutes into a working trance; the subject has been responsive on every suggestion but the one topic you asked about produced nothing — no refusal, just blankness.
ex.m: Open your eyes for me. All the way — sit up, feel the chair under you, count four things in this room out loud. Good. Now, wide awake, with none of that softness left: what came up just then, when I asked about the thing you couldn't answer? Whatever's arriving right now, even if it's an argument with me, say it.

nodes.name: error-laundered-enactment
nodes.mech: A forbidden wish gets carried out through an act that is done competently but 'aimed wrong': the object slips, the wrong name comes out, the message goes to the wrong person. The wish is fully acted on, but the act is labelled as a mistake rather than a choice. Since everyone accepts that errors happen, it needs no defence and invites no questions. Scripted for a listener, the outcome is suggested together with a way of arriving at it that they can disown, so the compliance is real but the listener never has to own it.
nodes.one_liner: Script an outcome to happen 'by mistake' (wrong name, slipped object) so it is fully done but counts as an error, not a choice.
nodes.why_short: We excuse errors because they lack intent, so routing an act through a 'slip' gets the result with no blame.
nodes.principle_note: Responsibility attribution keys on perceived intent, and errors are the standard socially-granted exemption from intent, so routing an outcome through an error form buys the outcome at no responsibility cost to either the actor's self-concept or their standing with observers. The distinctive prediction is a rate asymmetry: errors should not be uniformly distributed across possible wrong outcomes but should over-produce outcomes the agent had reason to want, which is directly measurable. Falsifiable: tally slips against the space of available wrong outcomes and check whether wish-congruent ones are over-represented relative to phonological, motor, or proximity-based accounts of the same error. If error direction is fully explained by those mundane factors with no residual wish-congruence, the laundering account has nothing left.

ex.f: Outcome specified together with a misfire that carries it
ex.t: The wanted outcome is delivered in full while the act arrives pre-labelled as a slip, so the subject never has to occupy the position of having chosen it and nobody else has to grant them cover. The operator sees compliance without the usual negotiation, and hears the subject afterward report the event in the passive — the deed described, the decision absent.
ex.s: Late in a session with a subject who has said outright that they will not ask for a particular thing directly; the task frame is already established.
ex.m: Tonight, when you're typing to them, you're going to reach for the delete key and your finger is going to land one over. The message goes as written, and you look at the screen afterward and see it gone. You didn't send it. Your hand did.

nodes.name: generalization-gradient-coupling
nodes.mech: A trigger fires not only to its exact cue but to a halo of near-misses around it. Trying to narrow an over-broad trigger by withholding reward from only the near-misses, while leaving the real cue alone, drags the real cue down too, sometimes to nothing. The trigger and its near-misses act as one linked system, so there is no clean way to trim a trigger by starving its edges, and attempting it risks losing the trigger altogether.
nodes.one_liner: You can't narrow an over-broad trigger by extinguishing its near-miss versions; doing so weakens the trigger itself.
nodes.why_short: A trained response covers a range of similar cues; unlearning at the edges spreads inward to the centre.
nodes.principle_note: This assumes the trained response is tied to a whole range of similar cues with graded strength, not to one exact cue, which is why leaving points in that range unrewarded shifts the whole range, centre included. Testable: if the central trigger can be kept at full strength while its near-miss versions are extinguished, given enough training, the two are separable and the claim fails. Discrimination training does achieve exactly that separation, so the honest scope is narrow: the coupling holds when the near-miss versions go unrewarded without the central trigger being rewarded at the same time, and rewarding the centre alongside should rescue it.

ex.f: Halo starved, centre goes with it
ex.t: Starving the near-miss halo without concurrently reinforcing the trained centre pulls the centre down with it: the two-finger snap that was reliable now produces a flicker or nothing at all. The operator observes the trigger they intended to keep, failing on its own token, and reads this as the coupling rather than as a decayed install.
ex.s: A snap-cue has been installed on a specific two-finger snap and has generalized: the subject is dropping on any sharp click, including a pen and a light switch. The operator wants to narrow it.
ex.m: For the next two weeks, when you hear a click that isn't my snap — a pen, a switch, a door — nothing follows it. No response from me, no acknowledgement, no drop. You'll notice the near-misses stop meaning anything. [Two weeks on, with no reinforcement given to the trained snap either:] Ready? [snap]

nodes.name: recency-gated-discrimination-potency
nodes.mech: A distinction the person has only just learned to make gives a strong boost; the same distinction, once practised into habit, gives none. Teaching a finer distinction on the same theme brings the boost back. So the useful moment is the learning itself, not the learned result: to keep the effect going, the operator keeps introducing finer and finer distinctions rather than rehearsing ones already settled.
nodes.one_liner: A newly learned distinction gives a strong boost; once it's routine the boost fades, so keep introducing finer distinctions.
nodes.why_short: Speculatively, the effect lives in the moment of learning, not the settled habit, so over-practice removes it.
nodes.principle_note: The claim is that the effect is carried by the transition — the moment the subject's responding reorganizes — rather than by the resulting stable state, which is why over-practice abolishes it and a finer split restores it. Falsifiable: hold the discrimination itself constant and vary only trials-since-acquisition; potency should fall with practice. If a heavily over-practiced discrimination yields the same boost as a fresh one, the recency gate does not exist and the effect belongs to the discrimination's content instead. Equally, if introducing a finer split fails to revive potency, the transition account is wrong and something is simply being exhausted.

ex.f: Re-splitting the same dimension once the first distinction goes flat
ex.t: The settled distinction has spent its leverage, but the moment of forming a finer split on the same dimension restores it — the subject's attention narrows sharply and response magnitude comes back. The operator observes the return of the pause-and-search behaviour that the coarse distinction stopped producing, and takes that as the signal to subdivide again rather than drill.
ex.s: The subject learned three sessions ago to distinguish "heavy" from "light" in their hands and it was powerful then; by now it is routine and produces almost nothing.
ex.m: Heavy and light are old news to you now — you can do those in your sleep. So forget them. Inside heavy, there are two different heavies: the one that's a weight pressing down on the back of your hand, and the one that's a thickness inside the arm itself. Find which one you have right now. Tell me which.

nodes.name: affect-disproportion-routing
nodes.mech: A rule for choosing what to do next, not a change in the person. When someone's reaction is clearly too big, too specific or too fast for what set it off, the operator takes that mismatch as a pointer to an earlier experience of the same shape and switches to searching back for it, rather than working on the present situation. A reaction that fits its cause is handled in the ordinary way. The only output is the decision about which approach to use next.
nodes.one_liner: If a reaction seems too big for what triggered it, look for an earlier similar experience instead of working the present one.
nodes.why_short: Psychodynamic lore holds that disproportionate emotion points to older material; this is untested as a predictor.
nodes.principle_note: Rests on a specific and checkable claim: magnitude mismatch carries information about origin, so disproportion should predict the existence of a same-shape earlier episode better than chance. Falsifiable — collect disproportionate and proportionate reactions and check, against independently obtained history, how often each is preceded by a matching earlier scene. If the base rate is equal, the disproportion is not an index and the routing rule is selecting arbitrarily. The risk flag reflects the standing failure mode: a search that assumes the earlier scene exists will tend to produce one whether or not it did, so the rule should be scored against corroboration obtained outside the search.

ex.f: Magnitude mismatch read as an index, routing decided aloud
ex.t: The disproportion is treated as a pointer rather than as content to be worked, so the operator switches method — away from the present instruction and toward a backward search — on a single live observation. The operator watches whether the subject's search produces an earlier scene of matching shape; if it does not, the routing decision is simply reversed, since nothing has been installed or re-experienced by making it.
ex.s: Mid-session, the subject flinches hard and goes silent at a mild, ordinary instruction — the reaction is far larger and faster than the instruction warranted, and there is no history logged on it.
ex.m: That was bigger than what I just said. Stay with the size of it, not the reason — don't explain it to me yet. Close your eyes and let the feeling stay exactly that big, and tell me the first time you can find where it was that size and it fit.

nodes.name: cue-payoff-latency-as-restraint-dial
nodes.mech: The gap between a cue and its reward acts as one master setting for how well every trained restraint holds. Shorten the gap and restraints trained on many separate cues all loosen together; lengthen it again and they come back without retraining any single one. So the operator can move a whole system of holds with a single timing change: speed up trigger-to-reward and reliable holds start failing across the board. Impatience is produced by timing rather than by anything that is said.
nodes.one_liner: Shorten the time between a cue and its reward to make all held restraints slip; lengthen it to restore them.
nodes.why_short: Speculatively, waiting tolerance is a shared resource; shorter waits breed impatience across the board.
nodes.principle_note: This treats restraint as a shared pool set by one overall setting rather than as a property of each cue, which is why changing a single interval would move cues that were never retrained individually. The cheapest test settles it: shorten the interval for one cue only and check whether restraints on the untouched cues still hold. If they hold firm, the effect is per cue and the system-wide claim is false. It is also contradicted if lengthening the interval again fails to restore the restraints, which would mean lasting erosion rather than a reversible adjustment.

ex.f: Interval compressed globally, unrelated holds tested
ex.t: Collapsing the cue-to-payoff gap loosens the installed restraint set as a whole, so holds on cues that were never retrained begin to fail — and the operator confirms this by testing an untouched one. Stretching the interval back out restores them without retraining, which is what distinguishes a timing dial from a change in what anything is worth.
ex.s: Several separate hold-and-wait rules are installed and reliable; the operator wants to see restraint loosen without touching any of them individually.
ex.m: New timing, starting now. Everything you've been waiting on, you get the moment you ask — no counts, no pauses, no earning it first. Ask and it's yours, same second. [Later, on an entirely different rule that was never mentioned:] Hold that. Hold it the way you always have.

nodes.name: inhibitory-cue-sign-inversion
nodes.mech: Take a cue the person has already learned means stop, wait or not yet, and reward it on its own, over and over in quick succession, with nothing else competing. Its stop meaning wears away and then flips: the cue that used to hold the response back starts to bring it on, so the same word now works as a go signal without ever being redefined. It takes a while, and how long it takes tells you something: a cue that flips after a few rewards was never firmly in place, while one that holds out for many was deeply installed.
nodes.one_liner: Take a learned 'stop' cue and reward it repeatedly on its own until it starts meaning 'go'.
nodes.why_short: A cue's meaning comes from its history; enough reward overwrites the old stop meaning, and how many pairings it takes shows how firm it was.
nodes.principle_note: A cue's sign is maintained by the contingency history that installed it, not stored as an intrinsic property, so a sustained contrary history overwrites it; and the number of contrary trials needed is proportional to the depth of the prior history, which is what makes latency an assay. This is falsifiable in both halves. It is wrong if massed lone reinforcement of a well-established stop-cue leaves it inert or merely weakened rather than evoking, across repeated attempts — that would mean inhibitory cues decay toward neutral rather than inverting. And the assay claim specifically fails if conversion latency does not track install strength: if cues installed with many reinforcements flip in about the same number of trials as cues installed with few, the latency reading is measuring something else and should be discarded. The safety consequence is the reason to state it precisely — a brake-cue that inverts stops functioning as a brake, and the same procedure applied to a safeword-adjacent token would destroy the stop signal it was reading.

ex.f: Massed lone reinforcement flips the stop-cue's sign
ex.t: Reinforcing an established stop-cue alone and massed erodes its negative sign and then reverses it, so the palm that suppressed the response starts evoking it — with no announcement that the meaning has changed. The operator watches for the exact turn from stillness to forward movement on the raised palm.
ex.s: A raised open palm has been installed as an unambiguous stop signal and holds reliably. Nothing else is being trained in the channel.
ex.m: Palm. Good — that's exactly right, perfect. Palm. Good girl, yes. Palm. That's it, so good. Palm. Yes. [Continued, alone, nothing else offered, until the response to the palm changes:] Palm.

ex.f: Repetitions-to-inversion counted as a seating readout
ex.t: The number of massed reinforcements the cue absorbs before its sign inverts reads out how deeply the original stop-meaning was seated: a handful means it was never really installed, dozens means it is load-bearing. The operator records the count, and treats a cue that flips fast as one that was never reliable in the first place.
ex.s: As above, but the operator's purpose is to measure how firmly the stop-meaning was originally installed rather than to obtain the flip.
ex.m: Palm. Good. Palm. Good. Palm — good. [Counting silently, and continuing without varying the delivery:] Palm. Good. Palm.

nodes.name: deprivation-reversal-ceiling
nodes.mech: Most escalation assumes more is better: more denial, more deprivation, more holding back gives more drive and more effort. That stops being true past a certain point. Beyond it, further deprivation lowers responsiveness, and the person pushed harder does less, not more. This sets an upper limit on every escalation or denial routine. What to watch for: a response that stops rising and starts falling as pressure increases is the limit announcing itself, not resistance or a failed install, and it is a signal to ease off rather than push harder.
nodes.one_liner: Past a point, more denial or deprivation lowers responsiveness; watch for output dropping as pressure rises.
nodes.why_short: Deprivation raises drive only until it starts wearing down the capacity to respond; then the curve turns down.
nodes.principle_note: Deprivation raises output only while the capacity to produce the response is intact. Past a point, deprivation wears down that capacity faster than it raises motivation, so the combined effect turns over: an inverted U rather than a plateau. Testable by the shape of the curve: increase deprivation step by step and measure output. If output rises and then levels off without falling, there is a ceiling but no reversal, and the claim is overstated. If output keeps climbing at every level a limited, safe protocol can reach, the reversal lies outside the practical range and does not matter in practice. The capacity explanation can be tested too: past the peak, responses should become slower, weaker and less complete rather than being clean refusals. If they stay intact but simply come less often, motivation fell rather than capacity, and the explanation is wrong even if the curve is right.

ex.f: Rate turns down under increasing denial; ceiling read, pressure released
ex.t: A rate that stops climbing and turns down while deprivation keeps increasing is the drive-response relation inverting, not resistance and not a failed install; the correct read is that the monotonic range has been exceeded. The operator releases pressure and watches whether responding recovers on the way back down — which distinguishes the ceiling from a genuine refusal.
ex.s: A denial structure has been escalating for several sessions and output has been climbing with it; this session the subject is slower and flatter than last, under strictly more withholding.
ex.m: Stop. You're not going to earn anything back right now and you're not in trouble — that's not what this is. We're going the other way tonight. Take it, all of it, right now, and don't ask me for permission first.

nodes.name: cost-per-payoff-throughput-strain
nodes.mech: Raise how much work the person must do for each reward and the response doesn't just slow down; its shape changes. Output first flattens, losing the quick bursts it had when rewards came cheaply, then breaks up into long idle stretches interrupted by bursts of activity. That clean pattern disappears before the overall rate drops much. Push further and the person can be driven past break-even, still working even though they get back less than the effort costs. So the work-to-reward ratio changes the pattern of effort, not just its speed, and the patchiness is an early warning that comes before the behavior collapses.
nodes.one_liner: Demanding more work per reward first makes effort patchy, with long pauses, before it stops; the pauses are an early warning.
nodes.why_short: Raising the work-to-reward ratio is known to produce pausing and erratic responding (ratio strain) before the behaviour stops.
nodes.principle_note: How strongly someone keeps responding depends on how much work each reward costs, not just on the reward. Raising that cost wears down the pattern before it stops the behavior. People keep going past break-even because they track the immediate deal (this effort still gets paid) rather than the overall balance. This can be proven wrong in two separate ways. The pattern claim fails if raising the cost just slows responding in proportion, with no flattening or patchy phase. The persistence claim fails if people reliably stop at or before break-even, which would mean they track the overall balance after all. It also predicts that showing someone a running total of their losses should make them quit where the same arrangement run without that total does not; if showing the total changes nothing, the tracking explanation is wrong even if the strain pattern holds. Setting limits matters because the harm cannot be seen from inside: the person is still working.

ex.f: Ratio raised until bursts smear into stretches and runs
ex.t: Raising cost per payoff changes the shape of responding before it changes the total: the crisp bursts flatten, then break into long dead stretches punctuated by runs, and pushed further the subject keeps working past the point where the effort exceeds what it returns. The operator watches for the smearing specifically, because it arrives well before collapse and is the usable early warning.
ex.s: The subject has been reliably earning a payoff at a cheap rate with crisp, prompt output; the operator raises the price steeply.
ex.m: The rate's changed. It used to be three and you got it. From tonight it's thirty — thirty, and then you get it, and thirty again after that. Start now, and don't stop to check with me on the way.

nodes.name: competing-bond-starvation
nodes.mech: Every relationship outside the operator's circle is worn down from two sides at once. In words, outside bonds are run down: family can't understand, old friends hold you back, past relationships were shallow or tainted. In practice, the conditions those bonds need are removed: the person's time is filled, chances to be in contact shrink, visits become inconvenient, until nothing is left over for outside relationships. The two halves reinforce each other: the criticism makes the shrinking contact feel chosen, and less contact removes the correction those people would have offered. The person ends up with one relationship left, without ever being told to cut anyone off.
nodes.one_liner: Run down the subject's outside relationships while also filling their time so those relationships wither.
nodes.why_short: Relationships need both contact and credibility; attacking both makes each decline reinforce the other and feel like the subject's own choice.
nodes.principle_note: Relationships are kept up by regular contact and by the credibility each person holds for the other.
