Damage either and the bond weakens; damage both and the decline feeds itself, because less contact removes the experiences that would have contradicted the running-down. Testable by separating the two halves: if running people down alone, with contact left intact, makes the subject just as dependent on a single anchor, filling their time adds nothing; if filling their time alone does it, the reverse. The compounding claim predicts that outside bonds with lots of independent contact should resist being run down much better than low-contact ones; if running down works equally regardless of contact, contact is not the corrective and the mechanism is wrong. This carries high risk, because where it ends is the removal of everyone positioned to notice what is happening.

ex.f: Content side — outside bonds devalued in place
ex.t: The outside bond keeps its identity but loses its standing as a source of counsel, so nothing it later says can function as a corrective. The operator observes the subject beginning to pre-discount those conversations unprompted — reporting them as disappointing before being asked.
ex.s: Several sessions in, with the relationship established; the subject has just mentioned a call home or an old friend's invitation.
ex.m: You came back from that call quieter than you left. You've noticed it too. They love you the way people love a photograph of you from years ago — they're not unkind, they just don't have the equipment for who you actually are now. I'm not asking you to do anything about it. I just want you to stop expecting them to understand.

ex.f: Structural side — the contact budget quietly zeroed
ex.t: Filling the time and narrowing the contact windows removes the material conditions an outside bond needs, without a single instruction to cut anyone off — the attrition does the work and reads to the subject as their own scheduling. The operator can watch outside contact fall off in the subject's own reports while the subject describes the shrinkage as a choice.
ex.s: The subject has agreed to a practice schedule; the operator is setting its shape rather than discussing anyone outside.
ex.m: Weeknights are ours now — eight through eleven, every one of them, and I want your phone face-down in the other room for all three hours. Saturday morning is the check-in and Sunday is the write-up. If something has to move, it moves to the week after, not into our hours.

nodes.name: injunction-mechanism-disclosure
nodes.mech: Take a group's rule against questioning (doubt is disloyalty, analysis is resistance, the questioning mind is the enemy) and, rather than arguing against it, explore with the person why a group needs such a rule: what it protects, what would come out without it, whose interests it serves. The rule is treated as a working part with a job, not as a statement about truth. You need not disprove any belief, and the person never has to defend their judgment against yours. Once the rule is seen as propping something up, it loses most of its force: a ban seen as protecting something can no longer feel self-evident.
nodes.one_liner: Examine with the person why a group would need a rule against questioning, rather than arguing with the rule.
nodes.why_short: A prohibition works by feeling like a norm; seeing what it protects turns it into something you can judge.
nodes.principle_note: A prohibition on questioning is sustained by being experienced as a norm rather than as an instrument, so a functional account of it converts it from something felt into something evaluated — and evaluation is the exact operation the prohibition existed to prevent, which is why disclosure disproportionately weakens this class of rule compared with rules that survive scrutiny on their merits. Falsifiable and sharply so: if functional disclosure works equally well against rules with genuine independent justification, then it is generic persuasion rather than the targeted move claimed here. It fails outright if subjects who accept the functional account nonetheless comply with the injunction at the same rate — that would mean the rule is maintained by contingency (what happens to people who question) rather than by belief, and disclosure aimed at belief cannot reach it. The useful corollary is that this predicts partial effect at best where questioning carries real external cost, since there the injunction has support the disclosure does not touch.

ex.f: The no-questioning rule examined as machinery with a function
ex.t: The prohibition is handed back to the subject as a structure with a purpose rather than contested as a claim, so they never end up defending their own judgment against the operator's. The rule stops reading as self-evident wisdom the moment it is understood as protecting something, and the operator gets nothing back from the disclosure — no deepening, no proof of design, no reframe.
ex.s: The subject has repeated a rule they were given elsewhere — that doubting is disloyal, that analysing the material is resistance — and is treating it as obviously true.
ex.m: I'm not going to tell you that's wrong. Just answer a mechanical question with me: what would a person find out, if they did question it? Set aside whether they should. What specifically stops being available once questioning is off the table, and who is better off for that?

nodes.name: describer-cost-deterrence
nodes.mech: Rather than argue with an unfavorable account, the group makes producing one expensive for the person producing it. Two levers combine: an asymmetric cost threat aimed at a party who cannot match the group's resources — the researcher, the writer, the small publisher — and an individualized, surveillance-flavored signal that this particular person has been noticed by name. Neither lever contests the account's accuracy; both operate on the describer's expected cost of publishing it. The describer softens the claim or drops it, or the publisher withdraws, and what survives into the public record is whatever was cheap to say. Because the surviving descriptions were selected by cost rather than by merit, the group becomes the de facto arbiter of how it is described without ever winning an argument.
nodes.one_liner: Make writing a critical account expensive for the writer, through legal threats and signals they've been noticed personally.
nodes.why_short: Deterring critics is a cost on publishing, not persuasion; what remains in the record is what was cheap to say.
nodes.principle_note: This works on the public record, not on any one person's mind. When publishing a critical account costs the writer something, and the cost rises the more damaging the account is, the accounts that survive are a skewed sample. Nobody has to be fooled and no claim has to be disproved for this to happen. It is the same structure as publication bias, where a fair set of findings produces a lopsided literature simply because some results are costlier to publish. Singling a writer out by name adds a separate effect: personal attention makes the risk feel much larger than the actual odds of action, which is why naming someone works better than a general policy. This could be tested by comparing accounts written under legal risk with accounts of the same group written without it (other countries, anonymous posts, or people no longer exposed). If both agree in tone and content, the deterrence is not shaping the record.

ex.f: Asymmetric cost aimed at a party who cannot match it
ex.t: Nothing in the account is contested; only the describer's expected cost of publishing it is raised, and the resource asymmetry does the arithmetic for them. The observable outcome is a softened claim or a withdrawn book, and what survives into the public record is whatever was cheap to say.
ex.s: An outside writer has a piece in progress about the group; the group's counsel drafts a letter to the small press rather than to the writer.
ex.m: We want to be clear that we are not asking you to change a word. We simply want you to know that we retain counsel on annual engagement, that we have pursued matters of this kind to their conclusion before, and that our resources for doing so are not a constraint on us. Please take whatever time your own review requires.

ex.f: Individualized surveillance-flavored signal that a named person was noticed
ex.t: Making the describer individually visible converts a professional act into a personally costly one, again without disputing anything they wrote. The operator observes the effect not on the researcher's beliefs but on their output volume — and because the surviving descriptions were selected by cost rather than merit, the group ends up arbitrating how it is described without having won an argument.
ex.s: A single researcher has published a preliminary finding; the group's contact reaches them directly, in their own name.
ex.m: We read your paper — the one from the March conference, not the earlier version. We noticed you've moved, and that you're presenting again in the autumn. We follow this work closely and we wanted you to know that we know who is doing it.

nodes.name: split-audience-deniable-disclosure
nodes.mech: One utterance is engineered to carry two different meanings to two different hearers present at the same moment: a manufactured slip, misnaming, or 'error' delivers the real content to a chosen overhearing witness while remaining, to the addressee, nothing but a stumble. The addressee has a ready-made innocent reading available (the speaker misspoke), so nothing is disclosed that can be challenged; the witness, holding the context the addressee lacks, resolves the same words to the loaded reading. The apparent accident is what buys the deniability — a deliberate statement invites accountability, whereas a slip is conventionally exempt from being held against the speaker. The operator therefore discloses and denies in the same breath, with the audience split, not the channel, doing the work.
nodes.one_liner: Make a deliberate 'slip' in front of two people so one hears an innocent stumble and the other, who knows the context, hears the real message.
nodes.why_short: Slips are socially excused, so the addressee has nothing to challenge; the witness holds private context that resolves the same words differently. Deniability comes from the apparent accident.
nodes.principle_note: Utterance meaning is resolved by each hearer against their own context, so the same string can settle into two different interpretations when two hearers hold different priors — and conversational convention treats slips and errors as exempt from accountability, which is what makes an engineered error a low-cost carrier for content that could not be asserted openly. Falsifiable: deliver the identical content as a flat assertion rather than as an apparent error, with the same two hearers and the same asymmetric context. If the witness's uptake and the addressee's willingness to challenge are unchanged, the error-framing is decorative and only the audience asymmetry is doing work; if neither hearer diverges, the account fails outright.

ex.f: Manufactured slip: a wrong word corrected too fast
ex.t: The addressee resolves it as fatigue-driven word-searching and has nothing to challenge; the witness, holding the collar context, hears the first word as the intended one and the correction as cover. The operator watches for the witness's eye-flick or half-second stillness while the addressee reaches for the pen without pausing.
ex.s: Mid-conversation, three people present; the witness knows the subject's collar sits under the shirt collar, the addressee does not.
ex.m: Sorry, I've been on the phone all morning — could you pass me the leash, the lead, the *pen*, sorry, the pen. Long day.

ex.f: Misnaming: the addressee called by the witness's private name for them
ex.t: The addressee is handed a ready-made innocent reading (contact-list confusion) and cannot object without asserting the loaded reading themselves. The witness receives confirmation that the private name is real and in use. Observe whether the addressee colours while still smiling — the tell that the innocent reading is being held onto deliberately.
ex.s: Introductions at a group table; the witness has previously heard the operator use a possessive pet name for the addressee, who has never heard it said aloud in company.
ex.m: And this is — sorry — this is Kitten. Katie. Katie, sorry, I've got two of you in my phone.

ex.f: Staged 'error': reading the wrong line off a list
ex.t: A misread of one's own handwriting is the most conventionally exempt kind of slip, so the addressee's innocent reading is airtight and no accountability attaches. The witness hears an inventory disclosed. The operator should see the addressee's attention move on to Saturday while the witness's does not.
ex.s: Operator is reading aloud from a schedule or shopping list in front of both parties; witness knows what the operator actually keeps on that list.
ex.m: Right — Thursday, dentist; Friday, pick up the restraints — sorry, the *rest of the* order. Friday, pick up the rest of the order.

nodes.name: operator-receptive-suspension
nodes.mech: A habit of the operator's own attention, not something said to the subject. While the subject talks, the operator holds back judgement, expects nothing in particular, and makes no effort to memorise. The point is to avoid selective listening: as soon as you decide what matters, you start hearing what confirms your guess and missing what would contradict it. Not committing anything to memory or notes keeps your read of the person open to change for the rest of the session.
nodes.one_liner: While the subject talks, hold back judgement and expectations and don't try to memorise; just take everything in evenly.
nodes.why_short: Expecting something makes you notice what confirms it and miss what contradicts it. Staying unselective keeps your read of the person open to revision.
nodes.principle_note: An observer who holds a hypothesis preferentially notices and encodes hypothesis-consistent material, so the record they end the session with is biased toward what they expected before it started; withholding selection and premature encoding is a countermeasure against that, at the cost of recall volume. Falsifiable: have operators run the same session material under an expectation-forming instruction and under a suspend-and-do-not-fix instruction, then score what each reports afterward against a full transcript. If the two groups' reports omit the same proportion of hypothesis-contradicting material, the discipline is buying nothing; if the suspension group's recall is simply worse across the board with no shift in what is preferentially lost, the account fails.

ex.f: Even unselective intake while the subject free-reports
ex.t: The instruction to the subject is minimal; the actual work is that the operator sets the pen down, forms no prediction about the next item, and lets each one land at equal weight. What the operator observes is their own pull toward the third or fourth item that fits the hypothesis — noticing that pull is the signal that selection has resumed, and the corrective is to return to unweighted listening rather than to note anything.
ex.s: Subject is in a settled trance and has been asked to say whatever arrives; operator has a working hypothesis about what the material is about and is about to reach for a notepad.
ex.m: Take as long as you like between things. You don't have to make them connect, and you don't have to finish one before the next arrives — just say them in the order they come.

nodes.name: suppression-dose-response-titration
nodes.mech: Treat a suggested block (a forgotten item, a frozen limb, a denied response) as something with a strength you can set, not as simply on or off. Two things control it. The more times the block is suggested, the deeper and wider it goes. The longer you wait after the last suggestion before testing it, the more it has faded. Using both, you can aim for a partial block and predict roughly how strong it will be later. Too little and a test breaks straight through it; too much and it spreads into responses that were meant to keep working.
nodes.one_liner: Treat a suggested block (amnesia, freeze, denial) as adjustable: more repetitions make it stronger, and it fades the longer you wait before testing it.
nodes.why_short: Learned inhibition generally grows with practice and decays with time, so dose and timing predict how strong a block will be when tested.
nodes.principle_note: Where suppression is itself a learned, decaying state rather than the mere absence of a response, repeated application accumulates it and elapsed time dissipates it — which makes it a quantity with a growth term and a decay term, and anything with both is titratable in principle. Falsifiable: vary application count and probe delay factorially and measure residual response strength. If the response is all-or-nothing regardless of count, or if probe delay has no effect on how much suppression is left, then suppression is not an accumulating decaying state and the two-knob model is wrong. A single non-monotonicity — more applications producing reliably less suppression at fixed delay — also breaks it.

ex.f: Count knob: application repetitions set depth and width of the hold
ex.t: Deliberately capping the application count at three keeps the suppression scoped to the single word instead of spreading to the semantic neighbourhood, which is what a run of ten taps would do. The operator probes immediately afterward and reads how much effort the subject visibly spends on the workaround: a full stall means over-application, a smooth substitution means the level is right.
ex.s: A hold on saying a particular word is already installed and lightly seated; operator wants it firm enough to survive direct questioning but not so wide it silences adjacent speech.
ex.m: Each time I tap the arm of the chair, the word settles a little further out of reach. That's one. That's two. That's three — and I'm stopping at three.

ex.f: Delay knob: elapsed time since last application sets residual strength
ex.t: Naming a decay window converts the hold from binary to a quantity the operator can aim at a chosen later moment. Probe at two minutes and again at ten: the difference in how readily the word arrives is the measurement of the second knob, and it lets the operator schedule a target level instead of accepting whatever remains.
ex.s: The hold has been applied to the desired depth; the operator wants a specific partial level to be in force at a known later moment rather than full suppression right now.
ex.m: That's the last one I'll set. It's at full strength now, and it thins out at about the rate a taste fades — by the time we're at the door it will be thin enough to push through if you decide to.

nodes.name: over-expectation-cue-drain
nodes.mech: A warning drawn from conditioning research (the 'overexpectation' effect). Two triggers have each been trained separately to produce a strong response with the same reward. If you then fire them together and give that same reward, the combined expectation is bigger than the reward can match, so the trial feels like a letdown even though the reward arrived. Both triggers get weaker, the loss shared between them, so stacking meant to strengthen them drains them instead. The operator sees a trigger that used to fire cleanly start to fade after being stacked with another strong one.
nodes.one_liner: Warning: if two separately strong triggers are fired together for the same reward, both can get weaker instead of stronger.
nodes.why_short: Learning tracks surprise. Two cues together predict more reward than arrives, so even a rewarded trial reads as a letdown and both cues lose strength.
nodes.principle_note: When learning is driven by the gap between predicted and actual outcome rather than by mere co-occurrence, a summed prediction exceeding the actual outcome yields a negative gap, and a negative gap subtracts from every cue present regardless of whether the outcome was delivered — so 'reinforced' and 'strengthening' come apart. Falsifiable and directly testable: train two cues separately to asymptote, then compound them on the unchanged outcome for several trials, then test each alone. If neither cue's individual response strength has dropped, the summation account is wrong for this material; if the drop appears even when the compound's summed expectation is well below the outcome ceiling, then something other than over-expectation is causing it.

ex.f: Two saturated triggers stacked onto one payoff
ex.t: The two summed expectations overshoot what the single reward can deliver, so a fully reinforced trial registers as a shortfall and both cues are decremented. The operator's observable is the next solo trial: the snap that used to drop the subject cleanly now produces a slower, shallower response, and so does the keyword. Recognising this is the value — the correct read is stop stacking, not drill harder.
ex.s: A snap and a spoken keyword have each been separately conditioned to a strong drop response; the operator, wanting a bigger drop, fires both together onto the usual single reward.
ex.m: Both at once this time. [snap] Sink. — Good. That's exactly right, that's the same good as always.

nodes.name: outcome-step-unblocking
nodes.mech: If a reward is already fully expected because of an existing trigger, a new trigger added alongside it learns almost nothing; the old one 'blocks' it (a well-known conditioning finding). To get around this, make the reward noticeably bigger at exactly the moment the new trigger is introduced, so there is a surprise left over for the new trigger to pick up. What matters is the jump from the usual level, not the size itself: a reward that was always big still blocks, a modest one that just got bigger unblocks. Once the new trigger has taken hold, the reward can go back to normal.
nodes.one_liner: When adding a new trigger alongside an old one that already works, make the reward noticeably bigger that time so the new trigger actually learns.
nodes.why_short: A cue only learns when the outcome is more than expected. An old cue that already predicts the reward blocks the new one; a jump in reward gives the newcomer something to predict.
nodes.principle_note: If cues compete for whatever part of an outcome is still unexplained, an outcome that is already fully predicted leaves nothing to learn, and a new cue added alongside the old one stays inert. Repeating the pairing will not fix that; changing the outcome does, because it creates something new to predict. This is the well-established finding of blocking, and of unblocking by changing the outcome. It could be tested with three conditions: the new cue added with the reward unchanged, with the reward stepped up, and with a reward that was always at the higher level. If the always-large condition works as well as the step-up, what matters is the size of the reward rather than the change, and the claim is wrong. If the unchanged-reward condition works just as well, blocking was not happening in the first place.

ex.f: Payoff stepped up at the moment the new cue is introduced
ex.t: Raising the reward magnitude at the exact moment the new cue appears creates surplus the established cue does not predict, and the newcomer absorbs it. The step is the lever, not the size — a reward that was always this large would block identically. Test by firing 'settle' alone a session later; once it carries, the reward can be returned to its ordinary level.
ex.s: A hand-on-shoulder cue already fully predicts the reward; a new spoken word has been paired with the same reward several times and has learned nothing.
ex.m: New word today — 'settle'. Settle. [pause] And this time it isn't the usual praise, it's the long one you get at the end of a whole session, right now, for one word.

nodes.name: truncated-cue-inhibition-charging
nodes.mech: Fire a trigger, but cut it off before the response or reward ever arrives, and do this many times in quick succession. Each cut-short run practises only the early holding-back part of the response, never the finish, so what builds up is restraint. After enough of these, firing the trigger in full produces little or nothing: the response is flattened or fails to come. The trigger becomes the means of training its own suppression, and the reward is withheld not as punishment but because withholding is the exercise.
nodes.one_liner: Fire a trigger again and again but stop it before the payoff each time, so what gets practised is holding back.
nodes.why_short: Repeated unrewarded cue presentations build inhibition (extinction-like learning); densely packed, they can flatten the response to the next full presentation.
nodes.principle_note: If the interval between a cue's onset and its payoff is itself learned, then repeatedly ending the cue inside that interval trains only the early restraint and never the completion, and where inhibition accumulates faster than it decays, closely-spaced trials leave a residue that competes with the response on the next full presentation. Falsifiable on two independent points: run truncated trials at close spacing versus the same number spread widely, then probe with a full-length presentation. If widely-spaced truncations suppress as much as closely-spaced ones, the accumulation-versus-decay account is wrong. And if the same suppression appears when the cue is simply omitted rather than truncated, then presenting the cue's early phase is doing nothing and this is ordinary extinction rather than a charged hold.

ex.f: Cue fired and cut short, densely repeated, then tested at full length
ex.t: Each truncated firing rehearses only the early restraining phase and never the completion, so what accumulates across the dense run is the hold rather than the response. Spacing is the precondition — leave a minute between firings and the charge dissipates. The operator tests with one full-length presentation and observes the response arrive late and flattened, or not at all.
ex.s: A well-conditioned arousal trigger is in place; the operator wants it flattened, and the subject is settled with the trigger's usual completion available but withheld.
ex.m: Listen. [trigger word] — and stop. [trigger word] — and stop. [trigger word] — stop. Keep them close together, don't let it get anywhere.

nodes.name: lateral-solidarity-block-mutual-reporting
nodes.mech: Two rules are installed together: private talk between members about their own doubts is named as disloyal gossip and forbidden, and members are taught that hearing another's doubt must be reported upward. Each member's confidant is thereby converted into an enforcer, so the cost of voicing a misgiving is paid immediately and socially rather than deferred. With outside contact already restricted, the effect is that doubt exists only in isolated single copies: nobody ever learns that anyone else shares it, no two doubts aggregate into a challenge, and the leadership's account is never contested by a plural voice. The structure needs no punishment to run — the anticipated report is enough to keep doubt unspoken.
nodes.one_liner: Forbid members from sharing doubts with each other and require anyone who hears a doubt to report it.
nodes.why_short: If nobody voices doubt, everyone thinks they're the only doubter, so doubts never combine into a challenge. Fear of being reported is enough; no punishment needed.
nodes.principle_note: Private dissent converts to public challenge only when a person learns that others share it; pluralistic ignorance is the standing state of any group where the cost of speaking first is high, and conformity to a visibly unanimous majority collapses sharply as soon as a single other dissenter becomes visible. This structure works by guaranteeing that the first dissenter is never observed. Falsifiable and cheap to test: if members who privately hold the same doubt still coordinate at normal rates under a reporting rule — or if introducing one safe, unreported peer channel produced no rise in expressed dissent — then the block on lateral communication is not the operative variable and something else (belief strength, dependence, sunk cost) is doing the work.

ex.f: Both rules installed in one address to the group
ex.t: Every confidant a member might use is converted into a reporter in the same breath, so the cost of voicing a misgiving is immediate and social rather than deferred. Doubt then exists only in single isolated copies and never aggregates into a plural challenge. No punishment is needed — the operator watches for members going quiet in pairs and for private conversations shortening when a third person approaches.
ex.s: Standing group meeting, outside contact already limited; the operator addresses everyone at once so each member hears the other members hear it.
ex.m: If something's sitting wrong with you, it comes to me — not to each other in the car park. Taking it sideways isn't loyalty, it's gossip, and it hurts the person you say it to. And if someone brings you theirs, you don't carry it for them; you bring it to me the same day.

nodes.name: discharge-channel-exclusivity
nodes.mech: The subject's ordinary outlets for charged material — rehearsing it privately, writing it down, telling a friend, working it over between sessions — are relabelled as resistance and forbidden. Nothing is added; every rival route by which the material could be discharged, diluted, or processed elsewhere is closed, so the charge is still accumulating but has exactly one place to go. When the session opens, material that would otherwise have arrived pre-worked and flattened arrives at full pressure and enters through the operator's channel. The lever is exclusivity of the discharge route, and it scales: the more outlets closed, the higher the pressure at the one remaining opening.
nodes.one_liner: Tell the subject not to journal, discuss or mull over the session material elsewhere, so it all comes out with you.
nodes.why_short: Feelings processed elsewhere lose intensity; blocking other outlets keeps them charged for the one sanctioned channel and raises dependence on it.
nodes.principle_note: Repeatedly recounting an emotionally charged event to any listener reduces its arousal and its felt urgency, which is why the second telling is flatter than the first; closing off every telling but one preserves the material's intensity for that one occasion, and simultaneously makes the operator the sole recipient of disclosures that would otherwise be distributed across several people, which is the dependency-forming part. Falsifiable both ways: if subjects prohibited from off-channel disclosure showed the same in-session affect intensity as subjects who had already told a friend, the habituation account is wrong; and if the prohibition raised in-session intensity without raising reliance on the operator, then the exclusivity is producing pressure without producing dependence and the two effects are separable.

ex.f: Rehearsal and private processing relabelled as resistance
ex.t: Nothing is added; the private route by which the charge would dilute is simply closed and given a name that makes using it feel like sabotage. Material that would have arrived pre-worked and flat instead arrives at full pressure through the operator's channel. The operator observes the difference in the opening minutes of the next session — heat rather than a tidy summary.
ex.s: End of session, subject visibly holding charged material and reaching for the habit of turning it over on the walk home.
ex.m: Between now and next time, don't work on this. Don't rehearse it in the shower, don't argue with it in your head at two in the morning. Every time you pick it up on your own you're taking a bite out of it before you bring it here, and what arrives is the leftovers.

ex.f: Third-party outlets closed — writing and telling
ex.t: Closing the written and social outlets removes the routes by which an outside reading could form, so no rival interpretation is ever available for comparison. The lever scales with the number of outlets closed. The operator can read the effect by whether the subject arrives with their own framing of events or waits for the operator's.
ex.s: Subject has mentioned journaling about the sessions, or debriefing with a close friend afterward.
ex.m: Two things I want stopped. The journal, and the debrief with your friend. Anyone you tell will hand you back a version of it that's already been made comfortable, and the page does the same job slower. This has one place to go now.

nodes.name: contact-contagion-stigma-enforcement
nodes.mech: An invisible polluting property is asserted to transfer by mere contact — touching the marked person, using their objects, sharing their space — so contamination spreads without any visible carrier and without any act by the contaminated party. Third parties do the enforcement: the marked person is stripped of ordinary social affordances (greeting, seating, shared implements, physical proximity) by collective avoidance rather than by any declared sanction, so no one has to defend the rule and there is no authority to appeal to. The belief seals itself structurally, not rhetorically — because nobody ever violates the boundary, the predicted consequence of violating it is never observed to fail, and the untested rule accumulates the appearance of confirmation. Both the marked person and the avoiders end up treating the property as a physical fact about the world.
nodes.one_liner: Explains how 'touching them contaminates you' beliefs enforce themselves: everyone avoids the marked person, so the belief is never tested.
nodes.why_short: People readily believe contamination passes by contact. Since nobody breaks the avoidance, the predicted harm is never shown not to happen, and the group enforces it without a leader.
nodes.principle_note: Contagion reasoning is a well-documented and robust cognitive default: people treat contact-transmitted properties as real and essentially permanent even when they explicitly deny any physical basis, refusing objects that have touched a contaminating source and rating them as unrestorable by cleaning — the response survives the subject knowing it is irrational, which is why it is so exploitable. Layered on that, the never-tested clause names a real and separately-established structure: beliefs that prescribe avoidance are protected from correction because the avoidance prevents the very experience that would disconfirm them, the same self-preserving loop documented in phobia maintenance. Neither part requires assuming the participants are credulous or coordinated; both fall out of ordinary cognition plus an uncorrected feedback structure. Falsifiable with a direct manipulation: the untested-belief account predicts that engineered, safe boundary violations — repeated observed contact with no consequence — should measurably erode the avoidance, and that avoidance should be strongest exactly where violation opportunities are rarest. If avoidance held constant or intensified under sustained disconfirming contact, the self-confirming-because-untested mechanism is not what maintains it, and something closer to an enforced norm with active sanctions would be the better account.

ex.f: Contact-transfer asserted, enforced by uncoordinated peer withholding
ex.t: An invisible property that moves by contact needs no visible carrier and no act by the contaminated party, so it cannot be disproved; the enforcement is collective avoidance with no declared sanction and no authority to appeal to. Because the boundary is never crossed, the predicted consequence is never observed to fail and the untested rule accrues the look of confirmation. Observe the marked person start pre-emptively leaving gaps at the table — the point at which they too are treating it as a fact about the world.
ex.s: A group setting with an established shared space; the operator has designated one member as marked and is speaking to the others while that member is out of the room.
ex.m: It carries on what she's touched — the mug she used, the chair, the door handle after her. Nobody's punishing anyone, and nobody has to say anything about it. Just don't take what she hands you, and don't sit where she's been sitting.

nodes.name: enactment-to-reflection-routing
nodes.mech: A live impulse aimed at the operator — anger, demand, seduction, contempt arising in the room and directed at them personally — is neither discharged as action nor deflected, but compelled back into description while it is still hot. The operator declines to respond in the register the impulse invites, absorbs the aimed heat without retaliating or gratifying, and requires the subject to say what is happening instead of doing it. It requires co-presence and an operator willing to be the target, because the impulse must be live and aimed at someone for there to be anything to route; recalled or hypothetical impulses do not supply the material. The subject ends holding an impulse they can observe rather than one they have already acted on.
nodes.one_liner: When the subject gets angry or flirty at you in the moment, don't react in kind; ask them to say what's happening instead of doing it.
nodes.why_short: Putting a hot feeling into words while it's happening creates distance from it; refusing the invited reaction stops the usual pattern from playing out.
nodes.principle_note: Two separately supported effects are combined, and the technique is only as strong as both together. First, putting a feeling into words while it is happening measurably reduces its intensity, and this does not require explaining where the feeling comes from. Second, an impulse that is acted out and gets the response it seeks is reinforced, while one that is voiced and meets neither punishment nor reward tends to fade. What matters most is that the operator does not retaliate or gratify, not that they offer insight. Nothing here requires that the impulse really be about someone else. The prediction is that intensity drops when the impulse is put into words in the moment, but not comparably when it is only discussed later, and that the effect disappears if the operator reacts in kind. Each part is well established; the combination has not been tested.

ex.f: Live aimed impulse converted to description while still hot
ex.t: The operator neither retaliates nor gratifies, so the register the impulse invited stays unfilled and the only available route is description. The subject ends the moment holding an impulse they can look at rather than one they have already spent. The operator observes the shift from second-person accusation to first-person report, usually with a drop in volume and a return of eye contact.
ex.s: Co-present session; the subject has just turned on the operator — a sharp demand, a flash of contempt, or a sudden seductive push — and it is aimed personally and still burning.
ex.m: Don't do it. Say it. Right now, while it's still hot — where is it in your body, what does it want from me, and what would it have done in the next ten seconds if I'd let it.

nodes.name: capacity-ceiling-overreach-inversion
nodes.mech: A warning. When a subject is holding a delicate trained balance, such as a response trained against a competing urge, you can widen what you ask of it bit by bit and it keeps working, until suddenly it does not. There is no way to tell in advance where the limit is, and everything looks fine right up to it. Past the limit the balance does not wear down gently: it flips into the opposite reaction, and the damage spreads back onto earlier triggers that were solid, so they stop working too. Because success gives no early warning, an operator pushing by results only finds the limit by breaking it.
nodes.one_liner: Warning: pushing a fragile trained balance a bit further each time can work until it suddenly collapses and breaks earlier, stable responses too.
nodes.why_short: Claimed: counter-trained responses have a hidden ceiling with no warning sign, and overreach flips the whole balance. Coherent as a caution but untested in this form.
nodes.principle_note: The effect itself was shown experimentally: pushing a subject's discriminations past what they can tolerate produces a sudden, outsized breakdown that also disturbs responses that had been stable. That observation has held up. The explanation has not. The original account, about protective inhibition exceeding a capacity, is not supported. The modern reading is only a description: behaviour held up by opposing processes near their limit has little margin, so a small extra demand can cause a large change. No specific brain mechanism is known. Treat the ceiling as a tolerance you discover, not a quantity you can measure. Two predictions can be checked. Collapse should be sudden and out of proportion to the last push; if decline is gradual, this is ordinary over-training. And damage should spread to responses that were not being trained at the time; if only the trained response suffers, the spreading claim is wrong.

ex.f: Widening the demand past an unmeasurable ceiling; retroactive collapse
ex.t: Every trial up to the ceiling looked healthy, so observed success gave no leading indicator; past it the balance does not degrade gracefully but flips into its opposite process. What identifies this rather than ordinary shaping deterioration is the backward spread — the operator finds that cues which were solid and were not under demand at all have also stopped working, and dropping back to the last successful step does not restore them.
ex.s: Hazard illustration. A response has been trained against a competing disposition and has held through several clean widenings; the operator, reading healthy performance, widens once more.
ex.m: You've held it with your eyes closed, and with them open, and with the room quiet. Now do it with the door open and someone else in the room — same as before, just wider.

nodes.name: mechanism-disclosure-deinstall
nodes.mech: After the fact, the subject is walked through the actual procedure that was run on them — the sequencing, the induced states, the staged confession or blaming rounds, the isolation — so that changes they experienced as revelation can be re-read as the predictable output of a known technique. What this dissolves is not the belief's content but its evidentiary standing: the felt certainty that locked the frame in place was itself manufactured, and once its production is visible it stops functioning as proof. The subject is not told what to conclude; they are handed the causal account and left to re-run their own assessment on it. Their authorship of the conclusion is what makes it hold.
nodes.one_liner: Afterwards, walk the subject through exactly what was done to them and why, and let them decide for themselves what it means.
nodes.why_short: Certainty that was manufactured by a technique stops feeling like evidence once the technique is visible. Reaching the conclusion themselves makes it stick.
nodes.principle_note: A belief held because of a felt experience loses its support when the experience is re-attributed to a known cause — the debriefing and misattribution literature shows that explaining how an induced state was produced reduces reliance on that state as evidence, though notably it does not reliably erase the belief itself, and the belief-perseverance findings say some conclusions survive full retraction of their basis. Both halves matter here: this restores the subject's ability to evaluate, it does not deliver a verdict, and an operator who expects it to reverse a belief on contact will overrun the subject and re-enact the coercion. Falsifiable: subjects given a procedural account should show reduced confidence in experience-grounded claims relative to subjects given only counter-assertion, while showing no greater rate of adopting whatever the discloser believes; if procedural disclosure produced the same belief change as flat contradiction, the re-attribution is not the operative ingredient and this is just persuasion with better manners.

ex.f: Procedure handed over after the fact, conclusion withheld
ex.t: The content of the belief is left untouched — what is dissolved is the evidentiary standing of the certainty, because a felt conviction whose production is visible stops working as proof. Withholding the conclusion is load-bearing: the subject's own authorship is what makes the re-assessment hold. The operator observes the subject start supplying further steps of the sequence themselves, unprompted.
ex.s: Long after the fact, subject no longer in contact with whoever ran it; they are describing a change they experienced as revelation.
ex.m: Here's what was actually done, in order: the sleep was cut, then the long sessions, then the round where everyone confessed something and you went last, then the week with no calls out. That sequence produces the feeling you had — reliably, in people who believe different things. I'm not telling you what it means. You've got the recipe now; run your own assessment on it.

nodes.name: parallel-isomorph-bind-defusion
nodes.mech: Against a forced either/or, the operator does not argue either branch. Instead they present a structurally identical binary drawn from a domain where the listener already accepts that both terms hold at once and neither excludes the other, and let the mapping stand without asserting the conclusion. The listener carries the co-necessity across themselves, and the exclusive 'or' in the original dilemma reads as a mistake in the framing rather than a fact about the world. Because the parallel case is one the listener will not dispute and the operator never states the target conclusion, there is no proposition to reject — the dilemma dissolves as the listener's own inference.
nodes.one_liner: Faced with a forced 'either A or B', give a parallel example where both obviously hold at once, and let them draw the conclusion.
nodes.why_short: An analogy the listener already accepts transfers to the dilemma; since you never state the conclusion, there's nothing to argue against.
nodes.principle_note: Whether two things seem mutually exclusive depends on how a situation is framed, not on the things themselves. Analogies carry over relationships more easily than content: a case the listener already accepts supplies the relationship "both at once, neither ruling out the other," and the dilemma picks it up. Conclusions people reach themselves also hold up against counter-argument better than conclusions they are handed, which is why staying silent at the end matters. This could be tested: the effect should depend on the parallel case having the same structure, not just on its being agreeable. An equally acceptable example with a different structure should fail to change how the listener sees the dilemma. If any pleasant, undisputed example worked as well, the effect would be rapport or mood rather than analogy. The account is plausible but not directly tested.

ex.f: Everyday co-necessity case offered flat, conclusion left unspoken
ex.t: The parallel is one nobody argues with, and the operator never says "so you can be both into it and agreeable" — the subject completes the mapping unprompted, which means there is no claim on the table to push back against. Watch for the pause before they re-state the dilemma: they typically restate it with the "or" softened to "and", or drop it entirely and change subject, which is the dissolution rather than a concession.
ex.s: Mid-conversation, subject has stated the dilemma out loud — "either I'm actually into this or I'm just being agreeable" — and is waiting for you to pick a side.
ex.m: Okay. Tell me something first — when you're driving somewhere you chose to go, are you steering the car or is the car carrying you? Both, obviously; the steering only does anything because the engine's already running, and the engine only goes somewhere because you're steering. That's all I wanted. Say the rest of yours out loud again if you still want to.

nodes.name: fiduciary-role-capture
nodes.mech: A genuinely credentialed professional — someone whose training carries a duty owed to the people in front of them — is brought inside the frame as a member, so that their loyalty to the group outranks the duty their role encodes. Their real skill is then applied to the leadership's ends against the very members the role exists to protect: procedures performed, sedation administered, professional rulings issued to serve the group's account rather than the member's interest. The capture is doubly effective because the role's own legitimacy travels with it — members read the professional's participation as evidence that what is happening is within bounds, which is exactly the inference the credential is designed to license.
nodes.one_liner: Bring a real professional (doctor, counsellor) into the group so they use their skills for the leaders against members.
nodes.why_short: The professional's credentials make members assume what's happening must be within bounds, so the capture borrows the role's legitimacy.
nodes.principle_note: Professional standing works as a shortcut: having a credentialed person present makes people go along with acts they would otherwise refuse, and obedience studies show this holds even when the act is visibly harmful. When group membership is the professional's main identity, conflicts of loyalty get resolved in the group's favour, which is why recruitment works through belonging rather than payment or threats. This can be checked against real cases. If members complied with a harmful procedure just as much whether or not a credentialed insider was present and approving, the borrowed legitimacy is not doing anything. If captured professionals departed from standard practice no more inside the group than in their outside work, the loyalty explanation is wrong and what is happening is ordinary malpractice. The account is plausible but not directly tested.

ex.f: In-group physician introduced as member first, credential second
ex.t: Members read the credential as an independent check while the loyalty ordering — member first, professional second — has already been announced, so the check has been quietly disabled at the moment it is invoked. Observable: worries stop being raised to the leadership at all and get routed to the captured professional, and the room's objection rate drops without any objection having been answered.
ex.s: A group session; the professional is already a committed member, and the leadership is about to ask something of members that their role would normally caution against.
ex.m: Before we go further — you all know her, she sits in the third row every week, she's one of us. She's also fifteen years a licensed physician. She's looked at what we're doing here and she's the one who suggested we go ahead. So if anyone's carrying a worry about whether this is safe, take it to her afterward and she'll tell you exactly what she told me.

ex.f: Professional's ruling issued about a member, to the group's benefit
ex.t: The dissent is reclassified as a symptom by exactly the person members would have appealed to for protection, so the appeal route and the suppression route are the same channel. Observable: peers stop engaging the dissenter's content and start managing his wellbeing, and the substantive question never gets restated.
ex.s: A member has begun questioning the group publicly; the captured professional holds a role whose assessments members treat as neutral.
ex.m: I've had a look at him and I'll say this plainly, with my professional hat on: what you're seeing isn't disagreement, it's exhaustion presenting as agitation. He needs rest and quiet, not a platform. I'd ask everyone to give him some space this week.

nodes.name: aversive-suppression-without-reserve-depletion
nodes.mech: Give a mild unpleasant consequence each time an established habit shows up, and it drops right away, but only while the consequences keep coming and the upset they cause is fresh. The habit itself is not changed, just held down. As the person gets used to the unpleasantness, the habit creeps back, and once the punishment stops it returns in full; classic animal studies found the total amount of the behaviour was unchanged, only postponed. In practice mild punishment rents quiet rather than buying change. Variations: mild punishment, which gives a short dip and then a full return; strong punishment, which holds the habit near zero only while it lasts.
nodes.one_liner: Know that mild punishment only quiets a habit while it keeps happening; the habit comes back once the punishment or the upset fades.
nodes.why_short: Mild punishment mainly works through a temporary emotional reaction; when it habituates the behaviour returns, and in classic studies total responses during extinction were unchanged.
nodes.principle_note: Punishment that follows a behaviour reliably reduces it right away; that part is very well replicated. How long it lasts is disputed. The classic finding is that a punished response, once punishment stops, produces as many total responses before dying out as an unpunished one, which suggests punishment adds a temporary emotional reaction rather than weakening the habit. Later work qualifies this: intense, immediate, consistent punishment can suppress behaviour for a long time. So it is mild, occasional, or delayed punishment that reliably wears off. This can be tested directly: if a mildly punished response produces fewer total responses than an unpunished one after punishment stops, the claim is wrong. It also predicts that the behaviour returns as the emotional reaction fades, so preventing that fading should prolong the suppression.

ex.f: Aversive added per instance of the target operant
ex.t: The rate falls to near zero within a few instances because each emission now produces something bad rather than losing something good, so no reserve has to exist for the move to work — it functions on a subject holding nothing. The operator should observe suppression that tracks the contingency's presence exactly, and should expect responding to return when the ice is put away, since nothing was spent.
ex.s: A pre-negotiated session where a specific behaviour — say, speaking without being addressed — is the named target, and the aversive vehicle (an ice cube held against the inner wrist for a slow count of ten) has been agreed and is within reach.
ex.m: Every time you speak without being spoken to, I will put the ice on the inside of your wrist and hold it there while I count to ten. Not a warning, not a pause — the ice, every single time, from now until I say we're finished. Nothing gets taken away from you and nothing gets subtracted; something gets added.

ex.f: Mild contingent aversive on a high-rate habit, with the rental made explicit
ex.t: The immediate drop is real and gives the subject early evidence the procedure works, while the pre-announced rebound stops them from reading the drop as a change in disposition. Observable: rate falls sharply within the first sessions, then creeps back as the emotional reaction to the snap habituates — and on withdrawal the cumulative count matches an unpunished baseline, which is the reserve-conservation tell rather than any extinction.
ex.s: A standing behavior the subject performs many times a day; you have agreed a small immediate consequence and you are setting the expectation for what it will and will not do.
ex.m: From now on, every time your hand goes to your mouth, snap the band on your wrist once — immediately, not after. You'll watch the count fall off a cliff this week. Don't get comfortable: the snap stops stinging around day ten and the count comes back up, and the day we stop, you'll still have every one of those bites left in you.

nodes.name: chance-pairing-self-maintaining-ritual
nodes.mech: If rewards arrive on a timer, unrelated to anything the subject does, whatever they happened to be doing just before gets strengthened. Because that action now happens more often, it is more likely to come just before the next reward too, which strengthens it again. So a pointless ritual can form and keep itself going with nobody designing it, and removing 'the reason' for it does nothing, because there never was one. It only takes hold when the action was already fairly frequent. An operator can seed one deliberately by handing out reward on a clock. Variations: a one-off coincidence that then fades normally; a self-feeding loop where extinction stalls.
nodes.one_liner: Know that random rewards strengthen whatever happened just before, so pointless rituals can form and keep themselves going.
nodes.why_short: A behaviour that happens to precede a reward gets more frequent, making it likelier to precede the next one. Coincidence alone keeps it alive.
nodes.principle_note: Rewards that arrive regardless of behaviour really do produce odd, persistent habits; this has been shown repeatedly. But the usual "superstition" explanation has been seriously challenged. A well-known replication found that much of the behaviour was the animal's natural behaviour triggered by the timing of rewards, not accidental strengthening of random acts. So some timed reward schedules produce self-sustaining arbitrary rituals and some produce typical natural behaviour, depending on the subject and the interval. It is not universal, and the question is still open. It can be tested: if chance pairing is at work, the rituals should differ from subject to subject and follow each one's own early coincidences. If everyone ends up doing the same thing, chance pairing is not the cause. Cancelling the reward whenever the behaviour occurs should also end a chance-built ritual, while timing-driven behaviour would persist.

ex.f: Failure mode — a clock-based payoff installs a private ritual nobody wrote
ex.t: Interval-timed delivery strengthens whatever happened to precede it, so the subject builds a stereotyped pause-then-burst pattern and defends it as the thing that works. Operator observes an unrequested small behaviour appearing just before each scheduled delivery, and resistance when asked to drop it.
ex.s: A recurring session where praise or a reward cue lands on a fixed interval (top of the hour, end of segment) regardless of what the subject is doing.
ex.m: Every fifteen minutes I'll tell you you're doing beautifully. It won't be because of anything in particular — it's just the clock.

ex.f: Usable move — clock-scheduled reward left to grow its own ritual
ex.t: The subject authors a private ritual they experience as self-discovered rather than instructed, which makes it unusually durable and unusually hard to argue them out of. Operator observes the idiosyncratic behaviour stabilising within a few sessions without ever having specified it.
ex.s: A reward is delivered on a timer, and on purpose no target behaviour is named, so whatever the subject happens to be doing gets picked up.
ex.m: There's no rule here and nothing you have to get right. Every few minutes the tone will sound and you'll feel that warm drop — and after a while you'll notice you've started doing some small thing just before it comes. Whatever that turns out to be, keep it. It's yours, not mine.

ex.f: Reward on a fixed clock, seeded by naming whatever preceded it
ex.t: Nothing is being reinforced deliberately; the folded hands merely happened to precede a scheduled delivery, and naming them raises their rate so they are more likely to precede the next one. Observable over a session: the posture appears at a stable nonzero floor and persists after the operator stops commenting on it, and removing the stated 'reason' for it changes nothing, because there was never a contingency to break.
ex.s: You are dispensing praise or reward on your own timer — every few minutes regardless of what the subject does — and one delivery has just landed.
ex.m: Good — and I notice you had your hands folded just then. Hold them like that. There you go.

nodes.name: evidence-supply-blockade
nodes.mech: A standing regime that governs which information physically reaches the subject rather than how they interpret what reaches them: outside media, dissenting accounts, and independent contacts are progressively made unavailable, while the in-group's self-portrait — its size, success, righteousness, the state of the outside world — is inflated inside the sealed space. Because the two moves run together, the subject is not merely encouraged to believe the inflated portrait; they are left with no data against which it could be checked. The distinguishing property is durability and scope: this is an environmental condition maintained over time across all topics, not a move made about a particular claim, so its effect compounds silently and is invisible from inside — the absence of counter-evidence reads as the absence of anything to counter.
nodes.one_liner: Cut off outside news and independent contacts while inflating the group's own picture of itself, so there's nothing to check it against.
nodes.why_short: Beliefs get corrected by contrary data; remove the data and the inflated picture can't be tested, however sceptical the person is.
nodes.principle_note: Changing a belief requires running into a competing account, so cutting off the supply works before any argument could even begin. You cannot resist an argument you never hear, which is why this does not depend on the person being gullible. Two well-supported findings explain it. People judge how common or agreed-upon something is from what they actually encounter, not from the wider world, so an inflated picture of the group is accepted through normal reasoning. And the classic conformity effects largely collapse when even one person disagrees, which is exactly what isolation removes. The point is about what information is available, not about poor judgement. It can be tested: restoring a single independent outside channel should measurably shift belief even if everything else stays the same. If people with an outside channel absorb the group's picture just as fully as isolated people, the isolation is not what is doing the work.

ex.f: Channel removal and inflated self-portrait delivered in the same breath
ex.t: The inflation is unfalsifiable not because it is argued well but because the only instruments that could check it were collected at the door, and the two moves arriving together means the subject never experiences the claim as a claim. Observable: the subject stops sourcing figures or news independently within weeks, and the absence of any contradicting account gets read as consensus rather than as absence.
ex.s: Residential or retreat setting where you control the physical environment; a new arrival is being oriented on their first evening.
ex.m: Phones go in the box by the door and stay there for the duration — the noise out there is the thing you came here to get away from. Anything you need to know, you'll hear at morning circle. And you should know what you've walked into: we've doubled in three years, there are groups like this one in nine cities now, and out there it's getting worse every month. In here it's getting better.

nodes.name: third-party-contact-shallowing
nodes.mech: Every external excursion is bracketed by the operator or by deputized peers: the subject is briefed on purpose and permitted content before going, accompanied or partnered where possible, and debriefed on return about who was spoken to and what was said. The point is not to prevent contact but to keep it too shallow to become a channel — a contact that must be reported in advance and accounted for afterward stays transactional, and the subject self-censors the exchanges that would have carried counter-information. It works through anticipated reporting rather than through detection: the subject need never be caught, because knowing the debrief is coming is what does the shaping.
nodes.one_liner: Before the subject meets outsiders, tell them what to say; afterwards, make them report who they talked to and what about.
nodes.why_short: Knowing they'll have to report back, people censor themselves in advance, so outside contacts stay shallow without ever being caught.
nodes.principle_note: The operative variable is anticipated accountability, not observation: people asked to justify their conduct to an audience whose views they know shift toward that audience preemptively, and this holds when no one ever actually checks — the effect is produced by expecting to account for oneself. That is why the debrief works even when it is perfunctory and even when the subject would have passed it. A second, independent force is self-disclosure reciprocity: intimacy and therefore counter-influence require escalating mutual disclosure, and a conversation the subject must later itemize does not escalate, so the relationship is held below the depth at which it could transmit anything load-bearing. Falsifiable at the accountability claim specifically: if the effect were about detection rather than anticipation, a subject who knew debriefs had stopped should behave identically for as long as they believed contacts were still being observed by other means — but the account predicts contact depth should increase as soon as the expectation of accounting is removed, regardless of actual monitoring. If depth stays suppressed after the reporting requirement is credibly lifted, something other than anticipated accountability is holding it down.

ex.f: Pre-brief on purpose and permitted content before an outside visit
ex.t: The contact is not blocked, so nothing feels like confinement; the permitted-content script plus the announced debrief means the subject pre-edits the exchange themselves, and the conversations that would have carried counter-information never start. Observable: outside contacts stay warm but stop deepening, and the subject begins volunteering the debrief unasked — the anticipated reporting, not any detection, is what did it.
ex.s: The subject has an approved trip out — family, an appointment, an errand — and you are the one clearing it.
ex.m: Before you go: what's the purpose of the trip, in one sentence? Good. If your sister asks how things are here, you can say you're well and busy, and that's the whole answer. Take Marcus with you. I'll want ten minutes when you're back.

ex.f: Return debrief, sequenced by person
ex.t: The last question makes the subject audit their own omissions, so the accounting extends to material the operator could never have detected. Observable: subjects begin curating outside conversations in real time — steering away from topics they would have to report — which is the shallowing effect, achieved with no contact ever having been forbidden.
ex.s: The subject is back from an outside excursion; the debrief was announced in advance and is now being run as routine.
ex.m: Sit. Who did you speak to, in order. What did each of them ask you about us. And was there anything anyone said that you decided not to mention just now?

nodes.name: delegation-revocation
nodes.mech: Takes away a third person's ability to set off a trigger that was earlier handed to them, while keeping the trigger working for the original operator or the subject. The operator states plainly that this named person's voice no longer fires it, has the subject imagine that person saying the cue and nothing happening, and ideally confirms with a live attempt by that person that fails. The withdrawal carries the same weight as saying no in the first place: permission to share a trigger is only a real, limited grant if it can be taken back.
nodes.one_liner: Tell the subject a named person's voice no longer sets off the trigger, have them imagine it failing, then test it live.
nodes.why_short: Suggestion narrows who counts as the trigger's source; rehearsal and a failed live test give the subject experience that the change is real.
nodes.principle_note: A delegate fires the trigger because their identity was trained into the discriminative stimulus class; revocation is discrimination retraining that re-narrows the class to exclude them — the same stimulus-control mechanics as the operator-exclusivity/voice-lock clauses, run in the withdraw direction. Renewal and spontaneous recovery predict a revoked delegate's cue may fire again after delay or context shift, so a single revocation without a delayed re-test is not a completed revocation. Falsifiable: after revocation the former delegate's utterance should fail while the operator's still fires; if both fail, the move tore down the programming instead of the delegation.

ex.f: Named de-authorization, rehearsed as a null firing, then live-tested
ex.t: The identity component of the cue-complex is re-narrowed by explicit naming, and the imagined null firing gives the subject direct experiential evidence that the exclusion holds rather than a mere instruction to be complied with. Observable: during rehearsal the subject shows no somatic onset at the imagined utterance, and the live attempt by the revoked party fails to fire while the operator's own utterance still does — that asymmetry is the confirmation, and it demonstrates the programming survived.
ex.s: A trigger is installed and a specific third party was previously granted the right to fire it; subject is in a working state and consents to the revocation.
ex.m: Listen closely, because this changes one thing and only one thing. The word still works — it works when I say it, and it works when you say it to yourself. It no longer works in his voice. Picture him now, standing right in front of you, saying it exactly the way he used to — and notice how nothing moves. Nothing rises, nothing goes. Again: he says it, and it's just a word. Good. He'll try it once in person this week, and it will do exactly what it just did.

nodes.name: trigger-expiry-clause
nodes.mech: When installing a trigger, state exactly when it stops working: after a set time, at a clock time, or at a concrete event ('when you board the flight home'), and say it switches off by itself with nothing more needed. Precision matters, because a vague end leaves the subject unsure whether it is still live, so every later brush with the cue becomes a test that re-practises it. A trigger with a visible end is also easier to agree to, so the subject may allow a stronger response within the window, and the stated end works as a suggestion that the response is over.
nodes.one_liner: When installing a trigger, say exactly when it stops working (a time, a date, an event), and that it switches off by itself.
nodes.why_short: A clear end date reassures and removes doubt about whether the trigger is still live, so the subject doesn't keep testing it and accidentally reinforcing it.
nodes.principle_note: A commitment with a capped worst case is easier to accept than an open-ended one, so a bounded trigger recruits less resistance at install — the same acceptance asymmetry that drives time-boxed contracts. The deactivation end works because the expiry is itself a suggestion: an expectation that a response ends at a stated point tends to realize itself, and the automatic, exact phrasing removes the ambiguity that would otherwise keep the subject probe-testing the cue — and every uncertain test is another paired exposure, which is why vague bounds decay worse than crisp ones. Falsifiable: triggers installed with a stated expiry should show measurably lower response rates after the window than matched unbounded triggers, and less spontaneous post-window cue-testing than triggers with approximate bounds.

ex.f: Weekend scene trigger with a Sunday-night close
ex.t: The window is exact (Sunday sleep) and the deactivation automatic, so there is nothing to monitor and nothing ambiguous to test on Monday; the subject can lean into the response fully inside the window precisely because its end is already scheduled.
ex.s: Immediately after installing a spoken compliance trigger for an agreed weekend arrangement.
ex.m: And this word works exactly as I've said — every time you hear it from me, all weekend. Sunday night, when you fall asleep, it dissolves completely. Monday morning it's just a word again, from anyone, in any voice. You don't have to do anything to make that happen; it happens by itself.

ex.f: Event-keyed expiry on a text trigger
ex.t: Keying the bound to an unmissable concrete event beats clock-watching: the boarding moment gives the deactivation its own vivid marker, so the prediction is confirmed at a single memorable instant instead of shading out ambiguously.
ex.s: Closing a session for a couple spending a week apart, with a written trigger active in messages.
ex.m: Until you board that flight home, seeing the word in my messages drops you just like this. The moment you're in your seat, it's finished — the word unhooks itself, and reading it after that is like reading any other word.

nodes.name: drift-to-sleep-close
nodes.mech: A bedtime ending that honestly offers a second way out. Instead of counting up, the listener may let the trance keep deepening into ordinary sleep, and the session truly ends there. The shift is framed as going deeper rather than going somewhere new, so it works with their existing sleepiness instead of fighting it with a full wake-up. It is a real choice: waking stays fully available, both options are named as complete endings, and no suggestions are slipped in at the crossing, so either path closes the session comfortably. Offer it only where sleeping is appropriate: in bed, at night, with nothing to do or operate afterward.
nodes.one_liner: At the end of a bedtime file, offer two real endings: count up and wake, or drift on into normal sleep.
nodes.why_short: At bedtime the body already wants to sleep; framing sleep as simply going deeper avoids fighting that drive with a full wake-up.
nodes.principle_note: Trance and sleep onset are phenomenologically adjacent — reduced peripheral awareness, slowed cognition, hypnagogic imagery — so 'deeper' is a truthful description of the path into sleep and the transition requires no new compliance; it spends the session's existing momentum on an already-active homeostatic drive, where forcing a full count-up on a drowsy subject buys alertness nobody wants at the price of comfort. The genuine fork also does reactance work: an available wake path keeps the drift felt as chosen rather than imposed. Falsifiable: bedtime listeners given the fork should show faster sleep onset and equal-or-better next-day dismissal of session content than listeners forced through a full emergence, and no worse than listeners given no close at all.

ex.f: The honest fork at the end of a bedtime file
ex.t: Both branches are named as complete endings and neither carries content across; 'the night is your own' explicitly hands the state back to the subject, which is exactly what the weaponized versions of this close refuse to do.
ex.s: Final minutes of a bedtime recording; the listener is in bed with nothing left to do tonight.
ex.m: In a moment I'll count you up. But tonight you have a choice, and both are completely fine. If you want to wake, follow my count and come all the way up, clear and comfortable. And if you'd rather not come back up tonight, let go of my voice now and just keep drifting down, past all of this, into ordinary, natural sleep — and the session ends there, finished, and the night is your own.

ex.f: Deepening framed as the road into sleep
ex.t: 'You won't notice the border' is truthful rather than exploitative here because nothing is scheduled to cross it; the continuation-of-depth frame spends the session's momentum on sleep onset instead of demanding a costly reversal from a drowsy subject.
ex.s: The subject has taken the sleep branch; the script's last lines.
ex.m: So don't come up. Go the other way — heavier, warmer, further down — and somewhere on the way down this stops being trance and starts being sleep, and you won't notice the border and you don't need to. Goodnight.

nodes.name: harm-rejection-filter
nodes.mech: Installs a standing, automatic protective filter: the subject's deeper mind screens incoming suggestions and silently declines any that conflicts with the subject's genuine well-being or safety — without waking, without effort, and without the subject adjudicating in the moment. Framed as pre-existing and automatic ('your deeper mind only accepts what is good for you; everything else passes through and fades') rather than as a deliberate in-the-moment choice, which is what resolves the safety/depth trade: the conscious subject is never recruited as a vigilant gatekeeper, rejection happens below awareness as silent non-uptake, and compliance with everything inside the boundary is undisturbed. The filter is general and content-blind — it names no specific forbidden items; it keys on conflict with well-being, so it covers suggestions nobody thought to negotiate.
nodes.one_liner: Tell the subject their deeper mind automatically lets go of any suggestion that isn't good for them, without them having to watch for it.
nodes.why_short: The reassurance lowers anxiety so the subject can relax into everything else. Whether any real filter exists is unproven; the felt safety is the main effect.
nodes.principle_note: Delegating rejection to the deeper mind resolves the safety/depth trade: vigilant conscious monitoring is incompatible with absorption and raises anxiety, while a rejection process framed as automatic and already-existing costs no attention and generates no reactance — it asks the subject to do nothing, only confirms something presented as already true. There is a real substrate underneath: hypnotic subjects reliably fail to take suggestions that conflict with strong values, so the install is partly a truthful description that raises the salience and felt permission of an existing capacity rather than building one from nothing. Falsifiable: subjects with an installed filter should show unchanged uptake of benign suggestions but increased silent non-uptake (without emergence or distress) of value-conflicting test suggestions, relative to no-filter controls.

ex.f: Installing the filter before deepening
ex.t: The is-already-true framing asks nothing of the subject, so the line deepens rather than interrupts; 'you never have to guard' retires conscious vigilance, which is what actually buys the extra depth.
ex.s: Early in the session, before any payload; delivered as descriptive fact rather than a rule being made.
ex.m: And here's something you don't have to think about, because it's already true: your deeper mind is careful. It takes what's good for you and lets everything else drift past like noise. You never have to check, you never have to guard — anything that doesn't serve you simply doesn't land, and you can go as deep as you like knowing that.

ex.f: The filter as answer to a voiced worry
ex.t: Answers the safety question without recruiting the conscious mind as a guard, so the reassurance does not create the vigilance it is meant to relieve; 'not a door you hold shut' pre-empts the effortful-gatekeeper misreading.
ex.s: Pre-talk; the subject has asked what happens if a suggestion is wrong for them.
ex.m: Then it won't take, and it won't be a struggle either. If anything I say doesn't fit you, your deeper mind just declines it — quietly, on its own, even while the rest of you stays exactly this relaxed. It's not a door you hold shut; it's a filter that was always there.

nodes.name: diegetic-channel-continuity-license
