One sentence like "spiders are dangerous" links a familiar category to a loaded word; from then on every member, and similar creatures like ants, brings up the reaction without ever being paired with it. The only thing to push back against is that one sentence. Variation: teach just two links, "A is the opposite of B" and "B is the opposite of C", and C starts acting like A without ever being paired with it.
nodes.one_liner: Attach a feeling to one member of a category with a single sentence, and the whole category - even unseen members - starts carrying it.
nodes.why_short: People treat category members as linked, so a feeling or reaction trained to one spreads to the rest without direct pairing. Lab studies show learned fear and preferences transferring through such learned relations.

ex.f: one intraverbal rewrites the whole class's function
ex.t: encountering any member of the class evokes the intraverbal

nodes.name: description-first-install
nodes.mech: Use the trigger phrase many times in ordinary sentences before saying what it does: 'love to [phrase],' 'because you [phrase],' 'when you [phrase],' lines that seem to describe what is already happening. Only then announce that these words return the person to this state. A trigger can also be introduced by describing its effect on others ('every time I use that voice, they slip') before turning to the listener, or by borrowing a familiar game like tag, using it casually ('I can tag you and you go deeper') before installing it with a touch. Since nothing sounded like an install, the listener's guard stays down, and the announcement turns the earlier uses into practice. This only works if the listener meets the early uses cold, without having read or heard the script in advance.
nodes.one_liner: Use the trigger phrase casually in ordinary sentences many times first, and only later announce that it is a trigger.
nodes.why_short: No sentence sounds like an install, so the listener's guard never goes up; the later announcement recasts all the earlier uses as practice. Plausible from expectancy and repetition effects, but untested as a sequence.

ex.f: deniable prior fires, installation announced last
ex.t: by the time the explicit installation lands, the listener has rehearsed the response twice without recognizing the rehearsals as installations

nodes.name: install-under-attentional-cover
nodes.mech: Deliver the trigger-install lines while the listener's attention is taken up by something else, so they slip past as background. Examples: trigger lines ('every time I say [word], you will...') dropped in while the listener pictures letter shapes; a rhyme-memory game shouted back under time pressure, which has the listener repeat commands far more often than plain suggestion could while they think it is only a memory game; a toe-to-head body scan pairing each body part with the trigger, giving real relaxation and cue-pairing at once while the listener notices only a body scan; or a short chant dropped at the dizziest point of an overwhelming passage, so it lands as rhythm rather than meaning. You can even say the cover out loud, telling the listener the commands slip past their conscious thoughts straight into the subconscious. The install lines can be completely ordinary; what is covered is the attention.
nodes.one_liner: Deliver the trigger-install lines while the listener is busy with something else - a visualization, a memory game, a body scan, dizziness.
nodes.why_short: When attention is used up by another task, people evaluate incoming messages less critically. Persuasion research on distraction supports reduced counter-arguing; whether this improves trigger conditioning is untested.

ex.f: trigger paragraphs running under a letter-visualization task
ex.t: let my word and command and programming just slip past your conscious thoughts directly into your subconscious mind

nodes.name: backdated-nonrefusable-install
nodes.mech: The install is asserted to have already happened during a window the listener could not observe, so there is structurally no point at which it could have been declined. In the fractionation file the operator narrates the listener's hand drifting toward the face, then retroactively asserts the button was implanted "while you were sleeping," treating the drift as previously conditioned though no prior drill installed it; "Luckily I'm trustworthy, huh?" names the exploited window and waves it off. In the nurse script the mind-cage trigger is installed during a narrated post-surgery blackout with the amnesia claim built in — "their memory doesn't have any recall ... they simply didn't pay close enough attention." Ideomotor narration then supplies live proof: the hand involuntarily presses the button and the listener drops, so the backdated conditioning demonstrates itself as already real.
nodes.one_liner: Tell the listener the trigger was already installed while they were asleep or blacked out, then show it working via an automatic hand movement.
nodes.why_short: There is no moment to refuse a past event, and the involuntary-feeling movement appears to confirm the claim. Expectation then produces the response. Coherent via response expectancy, but untested in this form.

ex.f: install reported as already done during unobservable sleep
ex.t: you see while you were sleeping I just implanted a button on your forehead

nodes.name: template-reuse-install
nodes.mech: A heavier trigger is installed through the exact linguistic template that previously built an innocuous one. The "zap cock drain obey" trigger runs through the same "putting ... in a spotlight in your mind" phrasing, the same "tool for your mind to use" language, and the same easy/effortlessly cadence that installed the "good girl" warm-fuzzy anchor — verbatim reuse too close to be accidental. The listener has already practiced accepting this structure for a harmless feeling, so the operator runs a content swap on a validated form: the new trigger inherits the trust and comfort built up around "good girl" and skips the scrutiny a fresh install ceremony would draw. The install itself is overt; what is smuggled is the content riding inside a pre-consented template.
nodes.one_liner: Install a heavier trigger using word-for-word the same script that earlier installed a harmless one, swapping only the payload.
nodes.why_short: The listener has already accepted that exact form for something pleasant, so it feels familiar and safe and invites less scrutiny. Familiarity raising acceptance is real; its use here is untested.

ex.f: verbatim spotlight-frame reused with only the content term swapped
ex.t: Makes it easy for you to feel good, like putting this image in a spotlight in your mind. At the front, in the center, all of your attention.

nodes.name: ambient-surface-trigger
nodes.mech: Pick a trigger that the listener meets all the time in everyday life, so it keeps firing without the operator there. The more common the cue, the more often it fires and the more practice it gets. A deliberately vague category lets the listener's own interest stretch it further. Variations: a loose class of clothing; any chair or couch; a whole type of image that is then narrowed back to the operator ("especially me"); an everyday word used casually many times before it is named as a trigger; the word "yes", said to anyone; a topic the listener thinks about often, which sets off the whole response each time.
nodes.one_liner: Make the trigger something common in everyday life - a type of clothing, any chair, the word 'yes' - so it fires without you present.
nodes.why_short: A cue met constantly fires often, giving many rehearsals, and a vague category lets the listener's own interest widen it. Frequent re-exposure strengthens associations, but the hypnotic effect is untested.

ex.f: open-ended clothing class named as an automatic ambient trigger
ex.t: This happens every time you put on girly bimbo clothing / Dressing up as a sexy girl is your trigger / Your trigger to become the persona

nodes.name: presupposed-conditioning-fire
nodes.mech: No binding act occurs: the operator names a specific word — "automatically" — and declares it already burned into the subconscious, so the assertion itself functions as the install and installation reads as discovery. The evidence offered is the listener's own just-trained reflex: "doesn't it feel like it's burned into your subconscious already? ... Because it is," a bootstrap in which the proof of the trigger is the response the proof itself elicits. Because the alleged conditioning is dated to the past, the claim is unfalsifiable — the listener's recent felt compliance is retroactively presented as confirmation that the trigger already existed, and any current sensation counts as further proof. The result is a discrete conditioned response keyed to one word ("a trigger for you to say yes and automatically obey when you hear that word from your dominant"), converted from a generic compliance gradient without any visible act of creation.
nodes.one_liner: Declare that a word is already burned in as a trigger and point to the listener's current feeling as proof.
nodes.why_short: The claim can't be checked, and any felt response is read as confirmation, so expectation creates the very reaction offered as evidence.

ex.f: self-confirming assertion-as-install bootstrap
ex.t: that word, automatically, doesn't it feel like it's burned into your subconscious already? / Mm-hmm. / Because it is.

nodes.name: arousal-paired-trigger
nodes.mech: Build arousal and hold it at a plateau, and deliver the cue repeatedly at the peak. Expect a modest response when the cue is tested on its own, and plan to refresh the pairing, since it fades without upkeep.
nodes.one_liner: Raise arousal and hold it on a plateau, deliver the cue again and again at the peak, then test the cue on its own.
nodes.why_short: Pairing a cue with arousal is classical conditioning, which has real evidence for sexual arousal in lab studies, though effects are modest and fade without upkeep.
steps: Build arousal and hold it at a plateau.
Deliver the cue repeatedly at the peak.
Test the cue alone later.

nodes.name: nlp-anchoring
nodes.mech: Time the anchor to the moment the remembered feeling is strongest, and make the touch or word exactly the same every time. Stacking several memories matters more than any single one; do not count on one pairing to stick, despite NLP claims. When you test it, check whether the feeling actually returns rather than assuming it does.
nodes.one_liner: Have them relive a strong memory, fire a touch or word at the peak, and repeat with new memories to stack the anchor.
nodes.why_short: NLP's version of conditioning. Real conditioning needs repetition; NLP's one-trial claims lack support.
steps: Have them relive a strong memory in detail.
Fire a touch or word at the peak.
Repeat with new memories, keeping the same anchor.
Test by firing it alone.

nodes.name: drill-then-name
nodes.mech: Drill the response repeatedly before you introduce any name for it, so there is nothing to push against while it is practised. Then say the name as a statement of what was already going on, as if it had always caused the response. This sequence has not been tested.
nodes.one_liner: Drill a response without labelling it, then name the trigger as if it had always caused it.
nodes.why_short: The response is practised before there is anything to resist, and the name is attached to something already working. Untested.
steps: Drill the response repeatedly without naming a trigger.
Name the trigger as if it always caused the response.

nodes.name: trigger-transfer
nodes.mech: Start from a trigger that already works. Say the new word while the old response is happening, binding the same response to it; optionally lock the new word to your voice only; then retire the old trigger. The new link is mostly declared rather than conditioned, so it may be weaker than the original. This has not been tested in hypnosis.
nodes.one_liner: Fire a trigger that already works, bind its response to a new word, then retire the old trigger.
nodes.why_short: Moves an existing response onto a new cue, loosely like second-order conditioning. Here the new link is mostly declared rather than conditioned. Untested in hypnosis.
steps: Fire the working trigger.
Bind the same response to a new word while it is firing.
Optional: lock the new word to your voice only.
Retire the old trigger.

nodes.name: stroke-to-my-rhythm
nodes.mech: Your voice sets the stroking pace, so make the tempo clear enough to follow as you speed it up and slow it down. Say 'stop' at the peak, and hold off release until you allow it. Common in kink audio, but untested.
nodes.one_liner: Have them stroke to the tempo of your voice, speed it up and slow it down, then say 'stop' to break motion from release.
nodes.why_short: The voice becomes the pacer of arousal; the stop puts release under control. Common in kink audio; untested.
steps: Set the stroking tempo with your voice, then vary it up and down.
Say 'stop' at the peak.
Hold release until you allow it.

nodes.name: confusion-then-command
nodes.mech: Keep them busy enough that they cannot sort out the confusion, or build a strong expectation and break it at the payoff. The way out must be truly simple and stable: one instruction or object they can grab. The closest tested finding shows a small but replicated boost in compliance, so expect a nudge, not a takeover.
nodes.one_liner: Pile on input that can't be resolved, or break a strong expectation, then offer one clear instruction or anchor they can grab.
nodes.why_short: Confusion is uncomfortable and people grab the first clear way out. Erickson described it; the closest tested finding, disrupt-then-reframe, shows a small but replicated boost in compliance.
steps: Give contradictory or unresolvable input.
Keep them busy enough that they can't sort it out.
Or instead: build a strong prediction and break it at the payoff.
Offer one simple, stable instruction or object as the way out.

nodes.name: handshake-induction
nodes.mech: The interruption has to come mid-motion, while the handshake is still automatic; once the handshake has finished, the moment of confusion is gone. Move straight into fixing attention on the hand and suggesting it stays put, without a gap. Practitioners report it works, but it has not had controlled tests.
nodes.one_liner: Start a handshake, interrupt it midway, fixate them on the frozen hand, then suggest it stays put and they go into trance.
nodes.why_short: An interrupted automatic routine leaves a moment of confusion where a suggestion can land. A classic stage/Ericksonian induction with practitioner support, not controlled tests.
steps: Offer a normal handshake.
Interrupt it mid-motion: stop, redirect, or lift the hand.
Fix their attention on the hand.
Suggest the hand stays where it is.
Tell them to sleep / drop now.

nodes.name: peripheral-vision-induction
nodes.mech: Have the listener hold a fixed stare while spreading attention across the whole edge of vision at once; this is tiring and absorbing, and eye fatigue does the rest. As the eyes tire, call the tiredness trance and suggest the eyes grow heavy and close. The evidence is folk-level only.
nodes.one_liner: Have them stare at one point, then widen attention to everything at the edge of vision at once until the eyes want to close.
nodes.why_short: Holding a fixed stare and a wide unfocused field is tiring and absorbing; eye fatigue does the rest. NLP-flavoured, folk evidence.
steps: Have them fix their gaze on one point.
Ask them to notice everything at the edge of vision at once.
Predict the eyes growing tired and call the tiredness trance.
Suggest the eyes grow heavy and close.

nodes.name: double-induction
nodes.mech: Keep both streams running steadily so the listener cannot settle on either one. Place important suggestions in either stream; the listener is not expected to catch them consciously. Recorded audio with one voice in each ear is a common form. It has had no controlled tests.
nodes.one_liner: Two voices speak at once, often one in each ear, so the listener can't follow both and stops trying.
nodes.why_short: Overloading attention plausibly makes the listener stop analysing. An NLP-era practitioner technique with no controlled tests.
steps: Run two separate voices or scripts at the same time.
Let the listener fail to follow both.
Slip suggestions into either stream.

nodes.name: progressive-muscle-relaxation
nodes.mech: Tense each region, hold, then release, and point out the relaxation that follows each release; that contrast is what makes it easy to feel. You can finish with a bigger tension-release cycle. It is well studied as a relaxation method; whether it adds anything as a trance induction is untested.
nodes.one_liner: Work from feet to face: tense each muscle group, hold, then release and notice the relaxation that follows.
nodes.why_short: Jacobson's progressive muscle relaxation is a well-studied relaxation method, and the release after tension is easy to feel. Its added value as a trance induction is untested.
steps: Walk attention through the body region by region.
Tense each region, hold, then release.
Point out the relaxation that follows each release.
Optional: repeat with a bigger tension-release cycle.

nodes.name: eye-lock-convincer
nodes.mech: Suggest the lids are stuck, then invite them to try to open them, adding that the harder they try, the tighter the lids hold. Praise the result as success and move into deepening. Many people respond, but not everyone; the deepening payoff is untested.
nodes.one_liner: Suggest the eyelids are stuck shut, invite them to try to open them ('the harder you try, the tighter they hold'), praise the result, and use it to deepen.
nodes.why_short: Eye catalepsy is an item on standard hypnotic suggestibility scales, and many people respond. Failing to open feels like proof of trance, which raises expectation. The deepening payoff is untested.
nodes.finding_name: Harvard Group Scale of Hypnotic Susceptibility
steps: Close the eyes and suggest the lids are stuck.
Invite them to try to open them.
Add: the harder you try, the tighter they hold.
Praise the result as success.
Use it to deepen.

nodes.name: arm-levitation
nodes.mech: Pace your words to the hand: comment on each small lift as it happens, as something the hand is doing on its own. Treat any movement, however small, as progress toward the face. This rests on practitioner reports rather than tests.
nodes.one_liner: Focus on one hand, suggest it is getting lighter, call each little lift deeper, and treat the hand touching the face as trance.
nodes.why_short: Ideomotor responses feel involuntary, so a rising hand is felt as proof. Similar arm items (hand lowering) appear on standard suggestibility scales; levitation as an induction rests on practitioner reports.
steps: Focus attention on one hand.
Suggest it is growing lighter.
Feed back each small lift as automatic.
Call each lift a step deeper.
When the hand touches the face, name it as trance.

nodes.name: magnetic-fingers
nodes.mech: Holding the fingers apart is tiring, so they tend to drift together anyway; keep talking until they do. Name each small movement as the pull at work, and treat the fingers touching as success that builds belief for what comes next.
nodes.one_liner: Hold two fingers slightly apart, suggest they are pulled together like magnets, and count any drift toward each other as it working.
nodes.why_short: Holding fingers apart is tiring, so they tend to drift together anyway; calling that hypnosis builds belief. Hands-together items are on standard suggestibility scales.
steps: Have them hold two fingers slightly apart.
Suggest a magnetic pull between them.
Feed back each small movement as automatic.
Count any drift as it working.

nodes.name: rigged-catalepsy
nodes.mech: The positioning must feel natural and pass without comment; if they notice the setup, the effect looks like a trick. Command the move with confidence and name the failure at once. Be clear with yourself that this is staged: it builds belief because the difficulty is physical, not hypnotic.
nodes.one_liner: Quietly put their body in a position where a move is physically hard, command that move, and call the failure trance.
nodes.why_short: Uses real body mechanics to fake a hypnotic effect, and the felt failure still raises belief. A stage trick that works because it is rigged.
steps: Quietly arrange their body so a move is physically hard.
Command the now-hard move.
Name the failure as proof of trance.

nodes.name: breath-tingle-convincer
nodes.mech: Describe the sensation before the breathing starts, so it is recognized as proof when it arrives. Keep the breathing short and stop once tingling or light-headedness appears; overdoing it is unsafe. What is really happening is the body's response to overbreathing being read as the trigger working.
nodes.one_liner: Tell them a tingle or light head means the trigger is working, then have them breathe fast or deep until they feel exactly that.
nodes.why_short: Overbreathing really does cause tingling and light-headedness; labelling it in advance turns a real body effect into proof. The honest mechanism is misread arousal. Unsafe if overdone.
steps: Tell them in advance what a working trigger will feel like.
Run fast or deep breathing that produces tingling or light-headedness.
Read the sensation back as proof.

nodes.name: six-step-reframing
nodes.mech: Agree a clear yes/no signal before asking the part anything, and wait for the signal rather than guessing. Treat the part's aim as positive even when the behaviour is not. If another part objects at the final check, the new choices do not fit yet. There is no good outcome evidence; it is mainly useful for thinking about motives.
nodes.one_liner: Contact the part behind an unwanted behaviour, learn its positive intent, have it choose better ways to meet that intent, then check fit.
nodes.why_short: An NLP parts procedure (Bandler and Grinder). Helps people think about motives; no good outcome evidence.
steps: Identify the unwanted behaviour.
Set up a yes/no signal with the part behind it.
Ask the part what it is trying to achieve.
Have a creative part generate other ways to meet that aim.
Have the part agree to use the new choices in the situations ahead.
Check that no other part objects.

nodes.name: systematic-desensitization
nodes.mech: Make sure the relaxation response is reliable before starting on the list. Keep the steps between scenes small, and do not move up while a scene still causes anxiety. Graded exposure is probably doing most of the work.
nodes.one_liner: Teach deep relaxation, rank feared situations from least to worst, then imagine each one while relaxed, moving up only when calm.
nodes.why_short: Wolpe's method: one of the best-supported early behaviour therapies for phobias. Graded exposure is probably the active part.
steps: Teach a reliable relaxation response.
Build a ranked list of feared scenes.
Imagine the lowest scene while staying relaxed.
Move up the list only when each scene stays calm.

nodes.name: good-girl-bad-girl
nodes.mech: Keep the behaviours concrete and checkable so there is no argument about which label applies. Have the labelling happen as each act occurs, not in a summary later. If shame is used, keep it mild and let correcting the act always relieve it. Self-logging shifts behaviour only a little; the identity effect is untested.
nodes.one_liner: Define checkable good and bad behaviours, have them label each act as good-girl or bad-girl, with praise or shame attached.
nodes.why_short: Logging your own acts is known to shift them a little; tying the log to charged identity words links behaviour to identity. The identity part is untested.
steps: Define a list of checkable good and bad behaviours and have them note each act as it happens.
Have them label each act as good-girl or bad-girl.
Attach praise to good acts.
Optional: attach mild shame to bad acts, relieved by correcting them.

nodes.name: my-friend-john
nodes.mech: Keep the story plausible and clearly about someone else, so the suggestions do not feel aimed at the listener. Let the key lines be what the other person was told or experienced, and mark them with a slight shift in voice. It is supported by case reports only.
nodes.one_liner: Tell a story about another person, and let the suggestions you mean for the listener be things said to or done by that person.
nodes.why_short: Erickson's technique: suggestions aimed at a third party are less likely to be argued with. Case reports only.
steps: Tell an anecdote about someone else.
Give that person the experience you intend.
Mark the key lines with voice so they land on the listener.

nodes.name: pace-and-lead-autoclitic
nodes.mech: Start by making the need real: put the person in a situation where the qualifying phrase would actually help them. Show or role-play the phrase as a prompt, then fade the prompt until the situation alone brings the phrase out, and reward it whenever it turns up on its own. Evidence for this specific use comes from only a few small single-person studies.
nodes.one_liner: Teach someone to add phrases that qualify their own speech: create a reason to need the phrase, model it as a prompt, fade the prompt, and reward the phrase when it appears.
nodes.why_short: Built from standard mand-training steps in applied behaviour analysis. The autoclitic-specific evidence is only a few small single-case studies.
steps: Create the need for the qualifier.
Model or role-play the form as a prompt.
Fade the prompt so the need alone evokes it.
Reinforce the qualifier when it occurs naturally.

nodes.name: clicker-training
nodes.mech: Charge the marker before you use it by pairing the click with a treat many times. Then click at the exact moment the wanted behaviour happens, follow every click with a treat, and shape toward the goal by clicking closer and closer attempts. Whether a clicker works better than a spoken marker is unclear: the evidence is mixed, and studies in people are few.
nodes.one_liner: Pair a click with a treat until the click feels good, then click the exact moment of the wanted behaviour and follow with a treat.
nodes.why_short: Conditioned reinforcement is well established, and a marker lets you reward a precise moment. Evidence that a clicker beats a spoken marker is mixed, and studies in people are few.
steps: Pair the marker with a treat until it is charged.
Mark the exact moment the wanted behaviour happens.
Deliver the treat after each mark.
Shape toward the target by marking closer tries.

nodes.name: token-economy
nodes.mech: Tokens only work if they buy something the person wants, so set up a menu of backup rewards with prices. Give tokens for the wanted behaviours, and if you like, take tokens away for unwanted ones. Later, thin the tokens out so that praise keeps the behaviour going on its own.
nodes.one_liner: Give tokens for wanted behaviour, let tokens buy backup rewards from a menu, and optionally fine tokens for unwanted behaviour.
nodes.why_short: Token economies are a long-established behavioural method in schools, wards and homes.
steps: Make tokens valuable by tying them to rewards.
Set a menu of backup rewards with prices.
Hand out tokens for the wanted behaviours.
Optional: fine tokens for unwanted behaviour.
Later, thin tokens out so praise keeps it going.

nodes.name: self-contract
nodes.mech: Pick the task and the reward yourself, track the behaviour yourself, and give yourself the reward only when you have actually met the goal. The common failure is setting yourself an easy target, so choose one that takes real effort. Tracking your own behaviour tends to change it by itself, and self-reward adds a little more.
nodes.one_liner: Choose your own task and reward, track yourself, and give yourself the reward only when you meet the goal.
nodes.why_short: Tracking your own behaviour changes it, and self-reward adds a little more. People tend to set themselves lenient targets. Supported in self-management research.
steps: Pick the task and the reward yourself.
Track the behaviour yourself.
Deliver the reward only when the goal is met.

goals.name: goal-triggers
goals.label: Triggers
goals.definition: Triggers and automatic responses: a word, sound, image or gesture that fires a specific reaction (arousal, freeze, drop, blank, obey).

goals.name: goal-pleasure-control
goals.label: Pleasure control
goals.definition: Orgasm and pleasure control: denial, edging, orgasm on command, ruined orgasms, pleasure tied to permission.

goals.name: goal-obedience
goals.label: Obedience
goals.definition: Obedience and behavioral conditioning: automatic compliance, posture, speech rules, tasks, pride reduction.

goals.name: goal-mind-control
goals.label: Mind control
goals.definition: Mind-control and brainwashing fantasy: thoughts belong to the operator, preferences rewritten, compliance without awareness.

goals.name: goal-identity
goals.label: Identity
goals.definition: Identity and transformation play: doll, pet, blank, bimbo, object or service persona, temporary or lasting.

goals.name: goal-sensation
goals.label: Sensation
goals.definition: Sensation, hallucination and body ownership: phantom touch, heightened or removed feeling, time distortion, the body felt as owned.

goals.name: goal-subspace
goals.label: Subspace
goals.definition: Subspace and power-exchange anchors: faster and deeper drops, longer holds, portable D/s headspace, preference shaped toward submission.

goals.name: goal-trance-skills
goals.label: Trance skills
goals.definition: Trance skills: reinduction, deeper suggestibility over time, unconscious cooperation, amnesia as a trained skill.

goals.name: goal-tribute
goals.label: Tribute
goals.definition: Tribute and real-world obligation: money, gifts, tasks or time given to the operator outside the session.

stages.name: stage-prepare
stages.label: Prepare
stages.definition: Before the trance: expectations, framing, consent, rapport, setting up what will later be cashed in.

stages.name: stage-induce
stages.label: Induce
stages.definition: Getting into trance: narrowing attention and lowering the guard.

stages.name: stage-deepen
stages.label: Deepen
stages.definition: Taking an existing trance further: depth, absorption, letting go.

stages.name: stage-get-it-accepted
stages.label: Get it accepted
stages.definition: Getting a suggestion past evaluation and resistance: indirect phrasing, bypassing the critical faculty, handling objections.

stages.name: stage-install
stages.label: Install
stages.definition: Delivering and binding the payload: conditioning, triggers, identity or pleasure links.

stages.name: stage-convince
stages.label: Convince
stages.definition: Proving it is working: convincers, rigged checks, the listener's own experience offered as evidence.

stages.name: stage-make-it-stick
stages.label: Make it stick
stages.definition: Making effects last beyond the session: post-hypnotic carry-over, reinforcement, concealment, return hooks.

stages.name: stage-emerge
stages.label: Emerge
stages.definition: Ending the session: waking, safety checks, grounding, what is left on and what is cleared.
